The clothing problem remains visible while you work. The single fox shoulder panel and small waist pad do not become broader because the bed is better organised. A coarse wearable plant covering is the next related experiment, with flexibility and movement to test before relying on it.
Return to the same short line
At the practice ground you check the flight space and earth bank, retrieve the ground markers’ positions by the reference staff, and inspect the dart’s rear seat. It shows slight compression from use but no opening split. That condition permits only another short cautious session, with reinspection.
Six thrower attempts give six observations. Three reach the broad bank patch; the others fall short or to a side. The result is encouraging only in the narrow sense that you can sometimes maintain engagement through release. The group is too scattered for a useful hunting claim, and the changing green shaft prevents a clean equipment comparison.
You record all six, keep the effort modest and stop at the allotted interval. You have not attached the feathers or a point, prepared the second shaft as ammunition, or compared yourself with the neighbours. The remembered lever still needs a practised body and a stable projectile.
Take stock before the next week
The nettle bundle has not passed its separation check. The clay pieces are drying at the surface but are not accepted as dry throughout. Both remain processes awaiting observations, not capabilities completed by elapsed days.
The model ends the week with 1.71 kg of kernels and 19 kg of dry fuel: roughly three and a half days of kernels at the recent ration, less than you had on Day 28. Twenty-four grams of prepared nettle fibre, 2.6 m of loose nettle cord and 16 m of single yarn remain. Loose bark cord is gone.
Estimated active work is nine hours, with eight hours for sleep. Survival Ledger records every allocation. The alternative bench remains unsupplied, and the neighbours remain independent people who can choose to watch or warn.
Next decision
Day 36 should begin with supply and repair priorities, then examine the dart’s changing fit before another trial. Improve the fish cage only after inspecting a specific weakness. Do not make the next encounter depend on a technology already being impressive.

01_survival/moon-2-day-7---a-better-clos.title: Moon 2 Day 7 - A Better Closure
01_survival/moon-2-day-7---a-better-clos.content:
Moon 2 Day 7 - A Better Closure
Fix a fault you can actually see
The fish cage is empty. When you lift it from the sheltered western river margin, the rear cap shifts against one side of the body. A worn tie lets the cap lift farther than you intend. That is an observable escape opening; it is not proof that fish have been entering and leaving overnight.
You want to make retrieval dependable before changing the entrance or moving the cage. A smaller funnel might exclude the fish you hope to catch. A larger cage would need more material and another installation trial. Repairing the closure offers a limited question you can answer today.
From the known downstream willow stand you select flexible withes, rejecting ends that split when bent. At the bank you take out the damaged tie and fit a light collar around the rear opening. You leave the inward funnel and the main woven cylinder alone. A short new portion of nettle line holds the removable cap against its seat; the old worn tie is discarded, not returned to the loose stock.
You work the closure open and shut, then lower the cage into the shallow margin and retrieve it again from stable footing. The cap stays in place in that handling trial. You check the existing anchor and reset at the same location below the tributary confluence. An empty check after repair will still be possible. Better retention cannot create fish.
Collect tomorrow’s covering today
On the western gathering circuit you look for long, clean dry grass rather than another armful of mixed leaf litter. The bedding pad showed that a retained plant layer is possible. A wearable version must bend with the shoulders and should not put hard willow foundations against the back.
You sort a small grass lot, shaking out grit and removing sharp stalks. A few handfuls survive bending and light pulling without immediately breaking apart. Those portions go under ventilated cover, away from sparks, for a possible hanging back panel. They remain loose stock. The bed is not stripped to furnish a garment, and no mantle has been made.
The longer gathering round provides about the same edible nut portion as you eat. This holds the reserve rather than rebuilding it. Food work still occupies more of the day than either repair.
Check the fit before asking for another flight
At the clean craft spot you inspect the compressed rear seat of the trial dart. There is no spreading split, but a raised rough edge catches during slow disengagement. You remove only the loose projection and repeat the fit check against the actual thrower’s hook. You do not deepen the hollow or reshape the hook at the same time.
The movement is freer in your hands. A launch will impose a different load, so you leave that question for a short session tomorrow. The second shaft still bows noticeably and remains a blank. The feathers stay dry and unused.
Before settling, you gather usable dead wood and protect the ignition kit from ground damp. You check the shelter’s southeast exit before putting small equipment away. You can make a closure harder for a fish to open; you have no comparable way to keep determined people out of camp.
End of day and next choice
The author account ends with 1.71 kg of edible kernels and 21 kg of dry fuel. The cage consumes 0.8 m of loose nettle cord and four cumulative metres of newly gathered willow withes; 1.8 m of nettle cord remains. The separately collected dry grass lot is 0.8 kg. These are model estimates, not readings from a balance.
Eight estimated active hours include gathering, water treatment, fuel, the cage repair, grass selection and a brief fit inspection; eight hours remain for sleep. The clay comparison pieces and nettle bundle have produced no new usable output. Survival Ledger records the allocations.
Tomorrow you can test the small fit correction at the same modest effort. If the dart still disengages badly, the next step is diagnosis, not a point, stronger throw or another visit to the neighbours.

01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.title: Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm
01_survival/moon-2-day-8---a-lever-and-a.content:
Moon 2 Day 8 - A Lever and a Practised Arm
The audience you did not invite
You finish the morning’s water and supply work before taking the thrower west/southwest to the Projectile Practice Ground. The ordinary wooden-pointed spear rests within reach behind the start position, clear of your movement. You inspect the bank, footing and both approaches. The little rear-seat correction is today’s equipment change; you intend to keep the effort and short line familiar.
Two modest casts release without the loose edge catching. One reaches the broad bank patch and one lands short to its left. While retrieving the dart you notice movement on the open ground north of the line. Two people have stopped there. Their position is off the flight path, but you lower the equipment and stay on your side of the open ground.
The broader adult carries a well-kept stone-pointed spear. Low brow, projecting face and compact, heavily built limbs distinguish him from you even at this distance. The other watches your hand and then the short wooden lever. You cannot tell whether either was among the people who rebuffed you. Their attention does not tell you their intentions.
You leave a clear way back towards camp. When they remain still and the flight space is empty, you make two more modest casts. The observer’s head follows the movement from lever to dart. That looks like curiosity about what the device does. One flight reaches the patch; the other veers wide. There is little in the landings to recommend you as an instructor.
The spear does not need your lever
The spear carrier points towards a bare part of the same bank and moves onto open ground, keeping away from your equipment. You step back with the dart lowered. He waits until the space ahead is clear, then throws his own spear by hand.
The movement is economical: a planted step, a coordinated turn and a release without your last-moment correction. The spear crosses the open space with a decisiveness your casts lack and strikes near the ground he indicated. He retrieves it himself, checks its stone head and binding, and makes another controlled cast from a position farther from the bank. Again it reaches the chosen area. His companion remains behind him during each throw.
There is no fair numerical experiment here. His spear has a different mass and point, and penetration cannot be compared with your blunt wooden front. You have no speed measurement. What you can see is that his chosen casts cover more ground, land much closer together and arrive with useful force, while your lighter projectile wanders. His strong, practised body and well-made weapon are part of the system. The lever’s mechanical promise has not compensated for your unstable release.
He looks towards the thrower once more, then holds his own spear upright. You do not read a precise message into the gesture. Neither person offers equipment or comes to examine yours. They leave along the northern side of the opening. You wait until they are out of sight before collecting your things and leaving in the other direction.
Choose what the comparison is for
At camp the disappointment arrives after the relief. You had hoped an obvious useful result might make another approach less dangerous. Instead, they have seen an odd device and a poor thrower. You still do not know whether that will encourage watching, ridicule or another warning.
The result gives you a better work question. Preserve the repaired fit and practise a repeatable movement before adding another variable. A stone head cannot fix a release that sends the dart to the wrong side. A second dart will eventually help distinguish specimen behaviour from technique, but the bowed candidate has not earned that role.
You record your four attempts, including the two before the observers arrived: two reach the broad patch, two miss it. The neighbours’ two casts occupy a separate hand-spear comparison entry. Their equipment leaves with them; nothing is borrowed, traded, recovered or taught.
End of day and next choice
Shortened gathering leaves 1.56 kg of kernels; dry fuel reaches 22 kg. The dart survives with no new opening split, but remains green, blunt and unfletched. Eight estimated active hours include the cautious session and waiting, ordinary supplies, inspections and dry-stock care, with eight hours for sleep.
The cage and three deadfalls are checked without a retained catch. Tomorrow’s priority is the supply circuit and cold-weather material. The observed difference justifies continued practice, not spending the remaining buffer on an immediate second demonstration. Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing separate that decision from a claim of technological superiority.

01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings.md
01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.title: Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings
01_survival/moon-2-day-9---a-rabbit-and-.content:
Moon 2 Day 9 - A Rabbit and the Work It Brings
A catch changes the order of work
At the western trap circuit one deadfall has fallen. A rabbit lies beneath it, with no obvious scavenger damage. You approach with the spear ready, inspect the surrounding ground and collect the animal rather than remaining bent over an occupied feeding place. The other two trials are empty.
Back at the southern processing flank you assess the catch before counting it as food. The protected meat has no obvious deterioration, although appearance alone cannot establish safety. You retain a small dressed lot and discard damaged tissue. Small Game Butchery takes place apart from the clean craft and food-storage areas. Hands, edge and handling surface need cleaning before you return to those jobs.
You divide the retained meat for prompt cooking at the ordinary outside hearth. There is no preserved rabbit ration at the end of the day. The useful catch lets you eat slightly fewer kernels; it does not let you skip gathering or claim several days of meals.
A pelt is an urgent job, not a finished jacket
You wanted broader core protection before the colder nights. The rabbit supplies some new skin, but the usable area is still small, and thin edges tear more easily than the remembered garment drawings suggest. You flesh it promptly and support it on the existing dirty-material drying frame under moderate tension. No new large tanning frame appears.
The pelt is intended for a later small clothing addition, if it remains usable. You have not chosen its final coverage. It cannot become both a carrying bag and a chest panel, and today’s damp skin is neither sewn clothing nor durable leather.
On one small edge you compare careful flexing with a neighbouring area left undisturbed as moisture begins to leave. The worked area bends more readily for now. That is an observation about handling this skin at this stage, not a tanning result. You stop when the thin edge starts to stretch. Neither the catch nor the old fox panel provides an unrecorded supply of dressing fat, brains or preservative.
You retain no separate bone, tendon or fat stock from this catch. The meat and the one pelt are its recorded outputs. Further extraction would add work, and you choose prompt food and skin care over accumulating every possible material.
Reset one mechanism before trusting it again
The catch-bearing deadfall’s bearing notch has polished and shifted. Before returning it to service, you brace the weight, keep out of the fall path and recheck the wooden members. You clean the seating surface without making the lock tighter merely to make it look secure.
A modest non-animal test, released remotely with a long locally selected branch while you stay clear, confirms that the assembled weight drops when the trigger is displaced. You then reset the existing trial. A successful catch and a successful release check answer different questions. Neither makes this a dependable food system.
Let warmth take the spare interval
During gathering you collect another small portion of clean dry plant material. This lot refreshes a compacted section of the bed and is allocated there immediately. The longer grass reserved for clothing stays separate under cover. The small bedding pad is lifted, aired and returned, rather than counted as a second object.
The wet pelt requires repeated brief attention through the day. You do not fit an atlatl session into those pauses. Looking up from scraping also reminds you how little warning the dirty flank offers: the spear stays on the accessible side of the frame and the route to the shelter remains open. Today’s benefit has created exposed work and attractive waste as well as food.
End of day and next choice
The model records 0.32 kg of cooked-and-eaten rabbit meat, one freshly cleaned pelt in process, 1.59 kg of remaining kernels and 21 kg of dry fuel. The new 0.3 kg bedding refresh is fully allocated; the 0.8 kg garment grass lot is untouched. Work is estimated at 9.5 active hours, including capture inspection, butchery, cooking, skin care, resetting and supplies; sleep retains an eight-hour allowance.
Tomorrow, inspect the pelt rather than assuming it is dry or supple because a night has passed. The plant covering remains the route you can expand without requiring another catch.

01_survival/moon-3-day-1---a-material-be.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 1 - A Material Before a Vessel.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-1---a-material-be.title: Moon 3 Day 1 - A Material Before a Vessel
01_survival/moon-3-day-1---a-material-be.content:
Moon 3 Day 1 - A Material Before a Vessel
Inspect cold results
After the overnight wait, you approach the old firing place. The remaining ash and support have lost their heat. Only when the pieces are cold do you move them to a separate non-food test stone at the craft spot.
Both main pieces remain recognisable. The thinner one has no new visible split. The thicker one has a fine line extending beyond the chipped corner marked before firing. You distinguish that new line from the damage you deliberately made; neither specimen is thrown away merely because the result is imperfect.
Ask what water changes
You pour a small fresh water charge onto the test pieces and the unfired comparison chips, keeping them out of the clean bark containers. The vessel pours; it does not become a basin for unknown clay. You give the wetted pieces the same pause before probing them gently.
The raw chips soften and smear. The fired thin piece remains coherent, with no paste lifting under the light check. Water also darkens the thicker piece, which stays together, but its hairline keeps it a less attractive candidate for a vessel wall. The softened raw controls are discarded after the comparison; the fired pieces are retained as non-food specimens.
This is a useful material result. It is a short wetting comparison, not an immersion-life test, proof of waterproofing or acceptance for cooking. Absorbing water and losing the body’s structure are different observations. A small flat piece that stays firm has no corners to leak and no vessel wall to survive repeated heating.
Give the next vessel a smaller claim
The next candidate should use the same prepared-body approach, an approximately even modest section, protected drying and a recorded firing arrangement. Then it must hold cold water and earn separate operating tests. You do not shape it today simply to have a finished object at the turn of the moon.
Pottery is becoming a programme of preparation, heat and acceptance checks. It has not become repeatable cooking-pot production. The existing bark route gives you room to learn without gambling every drinking vessel on the next firing.
After ordinary supplies and care, you mark what the specimens actually showed and turn to the wider account. Your footwear fastening has improved; a few material tests have become clearer; neighbours have watched a better example of the lever. None yet supplies a workforce or a dependable reserve.
Read Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1 at this completed day’s end. The new cycle begins with a choice of useful projects, rather than a requirement to invent something for every supply round.

01_survival/moon-3-day-10---the-spear-at.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 10 - The Spear at the Water Margin.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-10---the-spear-at.title: Moon 3 Day 10 - The Spear at the Water Margin
01_survival/moon-3-day-10---the-spear-at.content:
Moon 3 Day 10 - The Spear at the Water Margin
Choose an opportunity, not a fishing shift
A dry interval brings clearer water at the familiar shallow margin. You can see the pale bottom from a firm bank shelf, with a near-side pocket beside the main flow. This is worth a short return to Basic Spear Fishing. Cold deep wading would make it a very different bargain.
You bring the original single-point wooden spear, the same ordinary tool made earlier and tried at the water margin. Its point is part of the shaft. After inspecting a small rough place, you scrape it smooth and keep the gradual taper. Repeated charring would not make damaged wood sound again. The separate Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear remains an unmade handbook design.
The fish cage remains at its established anchor and continues its separate role. You are adding an active method for a visible opportunity, rather than replacing a trap with a promise of daily fish.
Shorten the uncertain part of the thrust
You wait with both bast soles planted on the dry bank, well back from the crumbling edge. The wrap’s overlap stays held at the hip, and the new cap leaves your face and sight line clear. There is no reason to discard warm clothing for a task you can do from land.
Looking obliquely through the surface displaces the apparent fish. You use your remembered optics to expect that error, then attend to this water and this angle. The first approach ends when glare hides the fish; you lift the point and wait instead of striking blind.
When a fish pauses within the near pocket, you lower the wooden point close to the surface before making a short controlled thrust. You aim below the apparent body. The point catches and holds long enough to bring one small fish onto the bank. You move it onto a separate handling surface and dispatch it promptly, clear of the working edge.
Learn what the point did
The catch is useful, but lifting exposes the weakness of a smooth taper: without a barb or extra prongs, retention depends on the actual engagement and the fish’s movement. You inspect the wood for a split and find only a little surface bruising. A small repair is enough to keep the ordinary spear in service.
You stop rather than treating the catch as a target that must be repeated before you may leave. The short session has produced one meal contribution and an observation about retention. The Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear is a useful later project to compare retention and point durability, not an automatic improvement or an object already beside you. The next workshop task remains a separate stone-pointed hunting spear; the split-tip fishing design can follow when you return to this water work. A brittle stone hunting point would have its own risks against a stony bottom.
Put the catch to its actual use
At the separate animal-processing area you dress the fish, keeping raw handling away from the food rack and treated water. It is cooked thoroughly at the outside hearth and eaten today. No fish is hung as winter stores, and no unearned pile appears beside the basket.
The small catch broadens food access without making the season secure. The important equipment distinction is now clearer: the old wooden spear can remain a simple fishing tool while a new shaft and stone point serve a different hunting project. You do not need to dismantle every working object to make the next one.
At the overhang, yesterday’s cap and waist adjustment have survived a useful outing. The small wall bay has not sagged. You can let its drying continue while selecting material for the hunting spear’s joint.

01_survival/moon-3-day-11---make-the-poi.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 11 - Make the Point for the Joint.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-11---make-the-poi.title: Moon 3 Day 11 - Make the Point for the Joint
01_survival/moon-3-day-11---make-the-poi.content:
Moon 3 Day 11 - Make the Point for the Joint
Keep the working spear intact
The original single-point wooden spear, used for yesterday’s fishing, stays beside the entrance. The Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear is still unmade. For the next hunting tool you want a separate shaft and a replaceable stone point. A sharper tip may be useful, but its edge cannot compensate for a weak seat or a splitting shaft. Today you will prepare compatible parts; assembly and a controlled load test can follow when the fit is ready.
On the accessible woodland edge you inspect fallen oak growth. One straight section has remained off wet ground, with sound wood beneath the weathered surface. You reject an attractive piece whose split follows a knot into the intended head. The selected length is about your height, with enough diameter at its thicker end to leave wood on both sides of a future seat.
You remove the remaining bark and small branch projections. The shaft is reasonably straight as selected; there is no instant fire-straightening or claim that a dry surface proves the centre seasoned. It rests under cover while you make the insert.
Choose stone for the mounting as well as the edge
A fresh visit to the known gravel source supplies a sound small blank, separate from the useful cutting edges you already carry. At a cleared knapping place outside the living floor, you use the familiar Hammerstone and Bifacial Knapping. Sharp waste stays away from the entrance, food and open toes.
The intended Stone Spear Point is a short stout leaf form, roughly a finger-length long and two finger-widths across. You retain thickness along the middle. Controlled alternate removals shape a working tip and leave a broad base that can sit in wood. This is not an attempt to reproduce a long thin ceremonial blade or a point copied exactly from a distant excavation.
You stop thinning when the blank already suits the job. The base’s sharp projections are reduced on a coarse expendable stone so they will not cut the binding. The forward working edges remain sharp. Minor asymmetry matters less than a sound body and a base that can be supported.
Compare the two parts before committing
With the shaft lying on the craft stone, you hold the point alongside its end and compare width, thickness and remaining wood. The stone lies separately on bark when you put it down; it is not lodged into an unbound split for display. There is enough shaft to make the intended shallow seat, but its exact fit is tomorrow’s work.
You wrap the point for storage away from food and feet. New line will be made for the binding rather than silently borrowed from the cap, trap or screen. Pitch may eventually help a joint, but glue is not being used to hide an unsupported gap.
The local people already use composite spears. Your contribution to this handbook is to explain the load path and its dependencies clearly, not to claim you have invented their weapon. A completed point, an assembled spear and a successful hunting system are three different states.
What has been drying meanwhile
The wall trial has now had several mild drying intervals. One witness patch breaks with a firm centre rather than smearing. Fine shrinkage lines show near an exposed edge; the installed small bay remains keyed to its rods under a light hand check, without a falling flake or shifted support. You leave its surface visible for inspection and retain the bark rain protection. This justifies keeping the trial, not coating the entire front or promising freeze resistance.
You finish with a usable new point and a selected shaft, still separate. Next comes the joint: shape the seat around the actual stone, restrain the wood, bind it, and test small loads before trusting a thrust. The warmer working home is beginning to make that sustained technical sequence possible.

01_survival/moon-3-day-12---a-seat-befor.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 12 - A Seat Before a Binding.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-12---a-seat-befor.title: Moon 3 Day 12 - A Seat Before a Binding
01_survival/moon-3-day-12---a-seat-befor.content:
Moon 3 Day 12 - A Seat Before a Binding
Give the point somewhere to bear
The stone point and oak shaft are now compatible parts on the craft stone. They will become a Stone-Pointed Spear only when the point is seated and retained. Wrapping cord around a loose stone would hide the problem rather than solve it.
You inspect the shaft end for the split that a careless wedge could start. A short retaining binding goes below the intended seat first. With a cutting flake you open a controlled shallow cleft at the end, removing small amounts and comparing the actual stone rather than forcing it down into the wood.
The broad base comes to rest against a supported stop. Its faces bear on wood, with useful forward edges clear. You ease one high contact rather than widening the whole slot. Viewed from two directions, point and shaft follow the same intended thrust line.
Restrain movement without sawing the line
You sort and clean another modest portion of the protected retted nettle remainder, accepting fibres which separate soundly and drying them before twisting new line. Coarse rejected material goes aside. This new preparation supplies the binding rather than a tie taken from the shelter. You work the line around the socket and mounting zone, keeping it behind the sharp working edges. The reduced projections at the stone’s base now matter: line pressed against a fresh razor edge would be damaged before the spear reached a target.
You tension the turns and secure the end where it can be inspected. There is no adhesive in this joint. Pitch might help an appropriate fit later, but today the wood must support the load and the binding must hold the parts together on its own.
With the point directed away from your body, you make small axial and sideways hand checks. The stone does not visibly slide or turn. You inspect the slot and the binding after each change of direction. Nothing has yet experienced a hard impact. That test belongs on expendable material with a clear line, not against your palm or the limestone wall.
Keep the old tool working
The original integral wooden-point spear remains separate. It can still serve at the water margin; the multi-pronged fishing design is still unmade. The new composite is intended for hunting work, not for striking stones beneath shallow water.
For transport and storage, a folded bark guard covers the new point without becoming part of the joint. You choose a protected place where lifting it will not sweep the cutting edges across bedding, food or the entrance.
A skin that starts another job
One of the existing deadfalls supplies a rabbit during the ordinary trap round. You assess the fresh catch and complete any needed dispatch before handling. At the separate animal-processing place, its meat is prepared, cooked and eaten today. The pelt is recovered with its body area intact and fleshed promptly.
You arrange a small removable pelt support from sound light sticks and short new ties over the dirty-material work area, separate from the food rack. The skin can receive protected moving air there and be lifted for brief working as it dries. The old large frame has not travelled from the abandoned camp.
A single new rabbit skin does not become two shoes this evening. It is an input with work attached. For now the practical result is the assembled joint, with a clear distinction between its light fit checks and the impact it still needs to survive.

01_survival/moon-3-day-13---keep-the-coa.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 13 - Keep the Coarse Meal in the Work.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-13---keep-the-coa.title: Moon 3 Day 13 - Keep the Coarse Meal in the Work
01_survival/moon-3-day-13---keep-the-coa.content:
Moon 3 Day 13 - Keep the Coarse Meal in the Work
Find the step that consumes the day
Stored acorns are useful only if you can turn them into meals. The familiar hot-water route is workable in small charges, but shelling and crushing scatter fragments and leave an uneven mixture. Large pieces need more work; very fine material is harder to retain when changing water. You want control of that preparation before asking a larger pot to solve every part of the problem.
From the known gravel area you select a broad sound stone with a shallow natural hollow and a separate rounded handstone. You reject a friable piece that sheds grit under rubbing. The selected pair is cleaned and reserved for food, away from the hammerstones and flake waste. These Pounding and Grinding Stones need useful surfaces, not a carved mortar acquired by naming one.
Make the batch uniform enough to handle
On clean bark beside the slab you shell a modest part of the untreated acorn stock. Damaged kernels are excluded. Controlled vertical strokes crack sound pieces within the hollow; short rubbing strokes reduce the larger fragments. You lift and turn the material rather than pounding the same fine patch until the whole batch is dust.
A spread on clean bark makes the remaining large pieces easy to pick out and return to the hollow. The pieces which already suit the familiar small-charge route stay separate. No fine cloth, new sieve or lossless milling system has appeared.
The difference is visible without a stopwatch: less meal lies beyond the working surface, and the next charge does not begin with a few nearly whole kernels mixed into powder. The handstone has not removed tannin. It has made the next operation more manageable.
Work within the containers you have
You use one bark vessel for the established small hot-water charges while the other remains available for treated drinking water. The fresh-water changes, heat and separation of food from dirty implements still matter. The batch stays small enough to move and retain using the existing route; finer crushing is no reason to promise that the same water treatment suits every oak or particle size.
Acorn Leaching produces a limited wet meal, which is cooked and used today. The untouched dry acorns remain storage input on the rack. You do not wet the whole reserve merely because its first stage now goes better.
The next ceramic vessel has a clearer purpose: a manageable water-and-food charge with less fragile handling. It will still need forming, drying, firing and operating checks. Today’s stone pair supplies a useful improvement before that vessel exists.
Let skin preparation continue alongside it
A second rabbit is recovered from a different existing deadfall. Its meat is cooked and eaten today; its pelt is a second separate skin, promptly fleshed and put beside the first on the protected dirty-work support. The first has begun losing its loose wet feel and receives gentle stretching and flexing, with the thin margins supported.
Two modest catches do not establish a daily return, but they give a real material reason to attempt enclosing foot coverings. The work can proceed in short sessions while the meal route continues. Neither new skin is assigned to the cap: the old fox panel already has that job.

01_survival/moon-3-day-14---form-the-pot.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 14 - Form the Pot for the Meal.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-14---form-the-pot.title: Moon 3 Day 14 - Form the Pot for the Meal
01_survival/moon-3-day-14---form-the-pot.content:
Moon 3 Day 14 - Form the Pot for the Meal
Choose a vessel you can handle
The food work has given the next pot a particular job. You want a small open vessel which can eventually hold and heat a useful charge, not the largest bowl you can make stand up while wet. A broad enough mouth will make stirring and inspection easier; an even body will avoid repeating the old thick-base problem.
You take fresh material from the known clay exposure and work it on a separate non-food surface. Roots and coarse debris are removed. A little of the same local body which supplied the comparison pieces informs the choice, but the two fired remnants stay whole as references. They are not crushed for temper, and the grass-rich wall mixture is not borrowed as pot clay.
You knead the modest charge until no obvious dry lumps remain, then compare short pinched and rolled samples. The material works at this moisture without an extra sand addition. That is reason to proceed with this batch, not proof that untempered clay is always preferable.
Carry the wall through the base
The pot grows from a compact pinch form. You turn it repeatedly, feeling thickness between fingers rather than leaving a heavy lump beneath a thin rim. The base curves into the wall. Its resting patch is small but stable; the mouth remains wider than the belly so there is no tight neck to obstruct the intended work.
You aim for roughly the modest even section used in the earlier comparison, easing the lower wall instead of forcing a sharply squared corner. There is no added foot ring, handle, spout or decorative work. A small pot that survives useful handling would be a larger advance than an impressive shape that cannot finish drying.
While the clay is still workable, you check the inside for folds and open joins. A soft bark edge smooths the rim without polishing it into a claim of watertightness. You leave enough space around the form to inspect it without gripping its wet lip.
Give greenware its own place
On a clean removable bark-lined board at the dry front-right craft side, you set the new vessel where neither a foot nor the food basket needs to pass. It is separated from the rear-right food rack and the damp fissured corner. A loose cover moderates the first surface drying without sealing moisture into a closed bundle.
This is Clay Vessel Making: one newly formed greenware vessel and a small witness piece of comparable section. Neither is fired. You do not pour water into the pot, put it over the hearth or call it a second working container. The bark vessels continue their ordinary jobs.
Use the waiting time
The two rabbit skins receive another short supported working session as their condition allows. You lift folded margins so they do not remain wet in a pocket; where the skin is leathery rather than soft-wet, flexing over smooth rounded wood makes a tangible difference. A thinning or tearing margin stops the pull. The work does not require a chemical recipe to have an effect, and that effect does not make the skin durable tanned leather.
You finish with three processes proceeding under protection: one pot drying, two skins drying and being worked, and the little wall bay still exposed for inspection. A more useful home lets waiting become part of production rather than a reason to manufacture another unnecessary experiment.

01_survival/moon-3-day-15---close-the-ga.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 15 - Close the Gap Above the Soles.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-15---close-the-ga.title: Moon 3 Day 15 - Close the Gap Above the Soles
01_survival/moon-3-day-15---close-the-ga.content:
Moon 3 Day 15 - Close the Gap Above the Soles
Keep the parts that already work
The bast soles hold better than their first fastening did, but wind can still reach toes and the top of each foot. The two rabbit pelts have enough sound body area for a low wrap apiece. They have had different lengths of drying, so you inspect them separately rather than treating a pair of catches as a pair of finished materials.
Their margins bend under supported working, with firmer areas through the centre. A fresh look at the thicker folds finds no wet smear. That is enough to attempt removable dry-use coverings, not to declare durable shoe leather. You keep the thin skins out of ground contact as far as the existing soles allow.
Learn where working changes the skin
You draw a leathery section over smooth rounded wood, easing it in more than one direction while supporting the surrounding area. It becomes more pliable than a nearby patch left untouched. Pulling harder where a margin is already thin would simply trade stiffness for a tear.
The useful judgement is when and where to work, not how long a clock says a skin has hung. The second pelt needs a little more attention at its heel fold. You leave it open to the air between sessions, then return when it bends without being soft-wet. Drying and softening are related work; neither operation alone supplies a permanent answer to rain.
Give each foot one actual skin
One whole pelt goes to each foot. Hair faces inward, surrounding a modest renewable layer of clean dry grass; dull pale tan skin faces outward. You bring sound margins around the toes and heel, using a few widely supported stitches to retain the folds. The upper edge ends just above the ankle. No spare panels remain for gloves or leggings.
The old bast soles and their retention remain outside and beneath the wraps as the wearing layer. You lead the existing ties around the combined package and add short new plant-cord extensions only where the greater girth needs them. Knots stay out from under the foot. A loose top can be opened readily; a tight ring at the ankle is not insulation.
This layered footwear keeps sole, insulation, cover and fastening as separate functions. Thin rabbit skin does not become deer hide by being called a shoe. Its immediate job is to close the exposed top and retain dry lining during camp work.
Test the fit before the route
You stand on the level dry strip and take slow steps, turn, then crouch. A crowded toe fold needs less stuffing, not a tighter tie. After that adjustment the same short movements leave both heels over the footbeds and the toes enclosed. You remove each wrap and look for rubbing and dampness before putting it back.
The new coverings are useful, modest work. You do not test them by walking into the river or following a deer all afternoon. Lower legs are still exposed; stronger hide, a better weather strategy and further coverage remain worthwhile. For tonight, two skins from your own traps have closed a real gap above the soles without taking material away from the cap or body wrap.

01_survival/moon-3-day-16---let-the-join.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 16 - Let the Joint Carry the Thrust.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-16---let-the-join.title: Moon 3 Day 16 - Let the Joint Carry the Thrust
01_survival/moon-3-day-16---let-the-join.content:
Moon 3 Day 16 - Let the Joint Carry the Thrust
Give the spear a limited real load
The new spear has passed light hand checks, not a strike. Before it accompanies a hunt, you want to see whether a controlled axial load drives the point back, opens the slot or cuts the binding. That is a question you can ask without an animal.
Outside the overhang’s working area you choose clear level ground, away from the food, entrance and firing place. A thick loose bundle of coarse spent plant cover is tied against a low sound stump, with no stone behind the intended point path. You inspect the line, sides and the space beyond before taking position. No one is invited to stand where a miss or slipping bundle could reach them.
The cap and wrap remain on. Both new foot coverings are fitted over their dry lining within the original bast soles; this short trial stays on the same dry camp-side ground. You keep the shoulders loose enough to work without drawing the garment’s chest tie into your throat.
Change the load, then inspect
The first contact is a slow push into the bundle. You withdraw along the same line and inspect the stone, wood and turns. The joint still follows its original alignment. You then make a short two-handed thrust with restrained effort, keeping the target close enough to control the point and avoiding a sideways levering motion on withdrawal.
The stone enters the loose plant mass. You stop after a few such contacts, looking between them instead of driving until something breaks. There is no visible point shift, new split or cut turn. A slightly settled outer cord turn can be taken up without remaking the seat. The repeated inspection makes that small change visible while it is still repairable.
This is a useful Stone-Pointed Spear result: the mechanical joint survives this limited loading and can be reinspected. It is not a measurement of penetration into an animal, proof of superiority over wood or a hunting-range certificate. Flight remains a different test, and the atlatl still has its own blunt unfletched dart.
Keep the warmth removable
Back at the dry entrance, you lift the foot coverings and replace grass which has compressed. Opening them makes both feet and the skin surfaces inspectable; covering a rubbing spot more tightly would not solve it. The low wraps stay useful for this kind of dry work. Wet woodland travel and longer use still need a separate decision.
The greenware pot remains on its craft-side board. Its rim is firmer, but the thicker witness centre is still cooler and more yielding. You do not move the firing forward because the moon is full. The small wattle-and-daub bay remains attached; the surrounding bark and brush still supply most of the screen.
Pause after the work
Ordinary food preparation uses the established small-charge route. The dry reserve is being used and replenished when worthwhile gathering allows; two rabbits and one recent fish have not become a meat store. Your home is better able to support the next project, with ongoing supply still part of it.
As the light leaves the valley, the full moon appears between clouds. The point is guarded and put away, not held as an answer to everything outside. Read Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16 after this day’s work: the useful question is now which of these arrangements can support the next sustained step.

01_survival/moon-3-day-17---let-the-sole.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 17 - Let the Sole Hold the Wrap.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-17---let-the-sole.title: Moon 3 Day 17 - Let the Sole Hold the Wrap
01_survival/moon-3-day-17---let-the-sole.content:
Moon 3 Day 17 - Let the Sole Hold the Wrap
The skin coverings have made your feet warmer, but they still work loose when you walk. As your heel rises, the cord pulls against a fold of rabbit skin while the woven sole lags behind. You could tighten everything around the ankle, but the skin is already creasing where the line catches it. Sooner or later it will tear.
You sit beside the overhang entrance and take the layers apart. The grass inside has flattened, and grit has worked between the skin and the bast sole. Underneath it all, the sole’s edge bindings are still sound. Those bindings are a better place to take the strain than the thin pelt.
Using flexible inner-bark strips, you make a short length of bark cord and pull firmly on a spare piece to check it. You thread a loop through the bindings on either side of the heel, lead it behind the covered foot and secure it to the side ties. When you lift your heel now, the loop brings the woven sole with it. The skin is held in place by a broad band instead of being tugged at a few stitch holes.
You replace the flattened grass, taking care not to crowd the toes, and make the same adjustment to the other foot. A few steps and turns on the dry ground outside show that the layers are moving together. The ankle ties can stay comfortably loose.
The real test comes while you gather a few light, dry branches near camp. On the rise and among the loose leaves, you can feel the sole following your foot instead of slipping away from it. You keep to the dry edge of a damp patch; the rabbit skins are thin, and soaking them would make the rest of the walk much colder. Back at the entrance, you open the coverings to brush out grit and let the lining air. Both heel loops have stayed in place.
This small change to your footwear is worth the morning’s work. Winter will ask more of it, but you can now walk and carry without continually stopping to pull the layers back into position.
Inside, the pot is still drying on its board beside the little test piece made from the same clay. You leave them undisturbed. The next job can be done while they dry: the atlatl’s blunt dart has had several weeks under cover, and the feathers you saved are still waiting to be used.

01_survival/moon-3-day-18---give-the-dar.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 18 - Give the Dart a Working End.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-18---give-the-dar.title: Moon 3 Day 18 - Give the Dart a Working End
01_survival/moon-3-day-18---give-the-dar.content:
Moon 3 Day 18 - Give the Dart a Working End
Today you take out the original hazel dart and lay it beside the thrower. You have practised with its blunt end often enough to know how awkwardly it can fly. Before taking it hunting, you want a point that can do useful work and feathers to help keep that point facing forward.
First you check the shaft. It is straighter than the bowed second blank, which you leave unfinished, and it springs back when gently flexed. The repaired hollow at the rear, where the thrower’s hook rests, has not split further. After several weeks under ventilated cover, this piece looks sound enough to keep working on.
From the feathers you saved, you select enough undamaged material for two small vanes. You trim them to similar shapes and lay their quill bases along opposite sides of the shaft. They belong near the back, where their drag should help steady the dart, but the very end must stay clear so it can sit on the hook and come away freely.
For the bindings, you clean and dry a little more of the retted nettle fibre, then twist it into fine line. You bind the feather sections in place and run a finger along them. One end lifts under the light pressure, so you secure it again before going any further. The feathers need to stay attached when the shaft bends and accelerates, not merely look tidy on the ground.
At the front, you scrape the old blunt end into a gradual wooden point. You keep enough thickness behind it to support the tip. The whole dart is still the same piece of hazel, now with a pointed front and two feather vanes at the rear.
You fit it to the thrower and slowly rehearse the movement, watching the clearance around your hand and the hook. Then, after checking the ground around the near-camp earth backstop, you make a few gentle trial casts. The dart releases without catching, and the bindings stay where you put them.
That is enough work for today. At the larger practice ground you will have room to judge how the modified dart behaves beside the stone-pointed hand spear. You have changed the point, added feathers and allowed the shaft more drying time since those first trials; tomorrow you need to find out how the finished combination feels in use. You cover the point and put the dart away with its thrower.

01_survival/moon-3-day-19---choose-the-t.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 19 - Choose the Tool for the Ground.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-19---choose-the-t.title: Moon 3 Day 19 - Choose the Tool for the Ground
01_survival/moon-3-day-19---choose-the-t.content:
Moon 3 Day 19 - Choose the Tool for the Ground
You carry the modified dart, the atlatl and your stone-pointed hand spear to the Projectile Practice Ground. The broad earth bank gives you somewhere to try them without losing every miss in the woods. Before starting, you walk the ground again, checking above and beside the bank and making sure the landing area is clear. You choose a patch free of exposed stones and cover it with coarse plant material.
The fletched dart flies more steadily than it did in the early trials, when the green shaft swung visibly sideways. Even so, one cast drops below the patch you aimed at. Between throws you examine the wooden point, the repaired rear seat and the feather bindings. Everything remains secure.
Next you try a few restrained, short throws with the stone-pointed spear. Until now you have only tested this joint by thrusting. The point stays aligned after the throws, and the binding has not shifted. You keep the trial short rather than risk damaging a useful tool simply to see how hard you can cast it.
Using the two weapons in turn makes their differences easier to understand. The lighter dart suits an open space where you can set up the throw and follow through. The hand spear feels heavier, but you can bring it into position with less movement in front of you. In close woodland, where branches interrupt a long casting motion, that may matter more than the distance you can achieve here.
You set both projectiles aside and turn the short thrower in your hands. Its hook is intact, with no fresh crack in the wood beside it. After clearing away the grit, you pack the kit for the return.
Near the meeting ground, you find the familiar man with two other hunters at the edge of the clearing. You approach with the points covered and lowered, then stop where they can see you. The man looks at the dart’s feathers and gestures towards them. You hold the rear within reach while keeping the point turned away. He examines the bindings briefly before returning his attention to the others.
They gather their spears and carrying materials. The familiar man points towards the western ground, looks back at you and beckons. You follow for a short way, encouraged when he pauses to let you catch up. The company soon breaks up as they turn to other work, leaving you unsure how much of an invitation was intended. Tomorrow you will come back when they are preparing to leave and see whether he beckons again.
On the walk home, you think less about making an impressive throw than about being useful to the hunters. You could carry a load or help with an animal once it was down. Those are things you can offer even while their speech remains beyond you.

01_survival/moon-3-day-2---let-the-rock-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 2 - Let the Rock Carry the Roof.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-2---let-the-rock-.title: Moon 3 Day 2 - Let the Rock Carry the Roof
01_survival/moon-3-day-2---let-the-rock-.content:
Moon 3 Day 2 - Let the Rock Carry the Roof
Choose a winter home
The morning cold makes the decision simpler. You have improved the lean-to, but every new layer still depends on its wooden bearings and weather-facing cover. Before adding more, you want to find ground where the landscape supplies part of the enclosure.
You follow the western gathering route uphill, staying on this side of the main river. Near the southern foot of the rocky spur, a short limestone ledge projects over a shallow recess. You have passed below this ground before; today you leave the path and examine it as a possible home.
The Western Overhang faces broadly southeast. The valley remains open below it, while the rock takes the weather from the back. It is a shallow shelter, not a tunnel into darkness.
Read what the weather has left
From outside the projecting edge, you inspect the face, loose fragments and the ledge’s ends. One corner has a damp streak. You trace it towards a fissure and keep that side out of the proposed sleeping space. Beneath the central roof, old fallen leaves lie dry over a firmer surface.
You look for fresh dung, bedding, ashes, tools and recent disturbance before entering. None appears in the part you examine. That does not tell you who has used it before or whether someone claims it. It gives you a reason to continue looking, rather than treating an empty patch as permission.
At the mouth, rain has marked a line beyond the dry central strip. Ground falls away towards the southeast instead of into the recess. You crouch where a bed could fit, then turn and stand nearer the opening. There is room to sleep and get out without building a tall room.
These observations belong to Shelter Construction. A promising roof is not a rock-stability certificate. You avoid the loose corner and do not lever or strike the overhead stone.
Put the work around the roof
The known seep remains reachable by a contour route to the southeast. You retrace it before committing to the site. A home that saves roof work but makes water inaccessible would exchange one daily difficulty for another.
You choose the dry back-left part for sleep, leaving space between bedding and the rock face. The front-right stone will serve as the clean craft surface. Beyond the drip edge lies open mineral ground for an ordinary hearth; skin work and waste can stay farther downslope and southwest. Nothing needs to put combustion behind a sleeping screen.
Rock-Shelter Enclosure starts with this separation of roles. The rock carries the roof. Light timber and plant covering will reduce wind at the exposed mouth, while clean dry material deals with ground contact.
Commit to the move
You return to the old camp for the night and select what will travel first. The new site is close enough for staged carrying, but you will not keep improving two homes. Tomorrow’s work is the bed and a modest weather screen; the old lean-to will cease to be the occupied camp.
There is a useful lesson here for the handbook. A better site can remove more labour than a cleverer roof joint. Your remembered buildings begin with manufactured structure. This one begins by deciding which structure you do not have to manufacture.

01_survival/moon-3-day-20---the-work-aft.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 20 - The Work After the Hunt.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-20---the-work-aft.title: Moon 3 Day 20 - The Work After the Hunt
01_survival/moon-3-day-20---the-work-aft.content:
Moon 3 Day 20 - The Work After the Hunt
Early in the morning, you return to the clearing’s outer approach with your equipment. The familiar man sees you waiting, beckons and pauses while you join the three hunters. This time you stay with them as they head into the woods.
Their pace changes with the ground. They slow where you would have walked on, stop to look through gaps in the brush, then move again with scarcely a sound. You follow the man ahead of you and stop when he raises his hand. Although you brought the atlatl, the branches leave little room for a clear throw. You keep the dart secured and watch.
The hunters separate beyond a fold in the ground. There is a sudden movement in the brush, followed by several close sounds you cannot quite place. By the time the familiar man calls you forward, a red deer lies dead. You have missed most of the action. What you can see now is the work that follows it.
He takes your hands and places them against a leg, showing you how he wants the body held. You brace it while he cuts, then release when he shifts position. Working this way, with each task made clear by a touch or gesture, you can help without understanding the words passing between the hunters.
The rabbits you have cleaned gave you some experience of separating skin, meat and gut. Here the scale changes everything. A thick body holds heat, the portions are heavy, and several people need room to work. The hunters open and divide the animal promptly, keeping the meat apart from the ground where they handle the gut. You help as directed while they make the cuts that need more experience. The cold air helps the opened portions cool, but there is still good reason to get on with the job.
Once the first loads are ready, the hunters fold them into their bark carrying sheets. You lift a parcel, settle its weight in your arms and follow the familiar man back. There is more to bring, so you make another short carrying trip while the others finish. By then, you have a much better sense of what recovering a deer involves. The successful strike was only the beginning.
At the clearing’s work edge, the man gives you a small portion of meat with some fat. Nearby lies a narrow damaged strip trimmed from the hide. You point to it; he cuts away a dirty edge and hands you the rest. Before leaving, you hold up both pieces towards him. He lets you take them. Most of the animal remains with the group, but your share makes the walk home feel different from the journey out.
You deal with the fresh skin first, at the place outside the overhang where you do the dirty hide work. Adhering tissue comes away under the scraper, and you spread the cleaned strip on the small support so air can reach it. It will need more work before you can decide how best to use it.
Then you cook the meat and fat thoroughly and eat the whole portion. As you sit beside the fire, you remember how little your atlatl mattered today. What mattered was recognising when to wait, following the hunters’ lead and taking a share of the work. You would like to go with them again.

01_survival/moon-3-day-21---four-points-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 21 - Four Points at the Water Margin.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-21---four-points-.title: Moon 3 Day 21 - Four Points at the Water Margin
01_survival/moon-3-day-21---four-points-.content:
Moon 3 Day 21 - Four Points at the Water Margin
Yesterday’s hunt has given you a good meal and a little fresh hide to work, but you still need ways to find food close to home. At the shallow river margin, your old wooden spear caught a fish; keeping it on a single point was another matter. You have been thinking about a forked head which might hold a fish between its prongs. Today you make the fishing spear to try it.
You choose a straight, sound piece of willow from the wood you have available. One end is thick enough to divide into four short prongs. After checking for knots and awkward grain, you bind the shaft below the place you intend to split, then open the end carefully. Small wooden spacers keep the prongs a little apart while you shape their tips and secure the head with fresh cord.
The spread is modest. It gives you several possible points of contact without making the thin prongs too long and fragile. You smooth the wood where it touches the binding, then take the finished spear to the water.
From a broad, dry place on the bank, you press the head against a small piece of plant material in the shallows. After a few controlled contacts, you lift it to examine the split and bindings. The spacers are still seated, and no crack has opened below the band around the shaft.
You move to a nearby pocket where the bottom is visible and wait. Glare keeps crossing the water, so you let the surface clear before trying. When a small fish comes within reach, you lower the head and make a short thrust. It catches between two prongs and stays there long enough for you to lift it onto the bank, where you dispatch it promptly.
One tip has roughened and needs a little scraping, but the head has held together. You take the fish home rather than follow another into deeper water. The trap can continue its usual work; this new spear gives you another way to use a clear, shallow margin when an opportunity appears.
At the overhang, you put the fork beside the other spears and clean the fish away from the food rack. You cook and eat it that day. While the fire is going, you check yesterday’s strip of deer hide. Its exposed surfaces are drying, but a folded edge is still damp. You open the fold and spread it out again.
The pot on its separate board is also firmer and drier. You turn your attention to the small clay test piece beside it. Soon you will need to judge whether they are ready for firing. A usable pot could turn the coarse meal you have been preparing into something much easier to cook.

01_survival/moon-3-day-22---a-cover-for-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 22 - A Cover for the Cutting Edge.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-22---a-cover-for-.title: Moon 3 Day 22 - A Cover for the Cutting Edge
01_survival/moon-3-day-22---a-cover-for-.content:
Moon 3 Day 22 - A Cover for the Cutting Edge
The strip of deer skin has stiffened as it dries. When you lift it from the support, the edges hold their shape instead of falling back into folds. The last damp crease is now open to the air. You work away a little tissue left near that edge, supporting the skin so the scraper cannot drive through it.
It is a small, irregular piece. Held against your leg, it plainly cannot make the warm wrapping you would like. Beside the tools, however, its size suggests another use. A loose flint cutting edge is awkward to carry: the sharp part catches whatever surrounds it, and a knock can chip the edge before you need it.
You set the flake beside the skin and fold the margin loosely around a smooth wooden sliver of similar size. Where the dried skin resists the bend, you dampen just the fold and wait until it yields. Then you work it gradually over the wood. Forcing it while stiff would leave a split exactly where the cover needs to be strongest.
Two loose turns of bark cord hold the shape. The wooden sliver keeps a space inside while the skin dries again, and the open end lets air reach that space. You turn the piece so it cannot sit on a damp underside. It can stay on the small support outside the dirty-work area; the actual flake remains in its old protected place for now.
This is the useful side of drying untanned skin. The stiffness that makes an undressed pelt uncomfortable as clothing can help a small cover keep its form. Rawhide will still soften if it gets wet, so the guard must be easy to open and dry rather than becoming a tightly sealed packet.
You brush the support clear and move its little rain cover so that the new fold stays sheltered without cutting off the air. There is room to reach the piece and turn it, and it remains well apart from the food rack. By evening it is beginning to hold the bend around the wooden former. Tomorrow you can remove the wood and see whether the flake fits.
Before going inside, you look at the pot on its separate board. Its sides have grown lighter as they dry. The hide cover and the clay vessel are both waiting on the same thing now: moisture has to leave the material before it will do the job you have chosen for it.

01_survival/moon-3-day-23---getting-the-.title: Moon 3 Day 23 - Getting the Pot Ready
01_survival/moon-3-day-23---getting-the-.content:
Moon 3 Day 23 - Getting the Pot Ready
The rawhide cover is firm enough to lift from its support this morning. You loosen the cord and draw out the wooden former. The fold keeps its shape. After brushing the inside clean, you ease the flint flake into it, keeping the sharp edge away from your fingers. The tie closes around the cover without squeezing the blade against it, and the flake comes out again readily when you open it.
You now have a small guard for the cutting edge. It belongs with the light tools in your carrying kit, where nothing heavy can drive the flake through it. You put the kit away and turn to the larger job waiting under the overhang.
The pot has been drying for more than a week, but the underside is the part you most want to inspect. You lift it with both hands and turn it in the light. The base is now as pale and firm as the sides. No new line has opened where the thicker bottom joins the wall, and the rim has kept its shape.
The little piece you made from the same clay gives you a closer look. You break it across its thickness. The fresh section is evenly dry-looking, without the darker, yielding centre you found earlier. You keep one half as an unfired comparison and set the other beside the pot to go through the fire with it. Together with the pot’s condition, this makes you willing to begin a cautious preheating tomorrow. Judging the drying has meant looking at the awkward parts, not simply counting the days.
Outside, the separate firing patch lies northeast of the ordinary hearth. You clear loose leaves and check that the ground itself is dry. There is room to work from the sides, and the rising heat will be well clear of the rock roof, bark screen and stored materials. You sort the dry fuel nearby, keeping the smaller pieces accessible so that you can build heat gradually without dropping heavy wood onto the vessel.
For once, the weather is helping. The air is dry and there is no strong wind. You leave the pot under cover overnight rather than loading it early onto ground that may grow damp. Everything else is ready. The next time you lift this vessel from its board, you intend to take it out to the firing place.

01_survival/moon-3-day-24---the-pot-goes.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 24 - The Pot Goes into the Fire.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-24---the-pot-goes.title: Moon 3 Day 24 - The Pot Goes into the Fire
01_survival/moon-3-day-24---the-pot-goes.content:
Moon 3 Day 24 - The Pot Goes into the Fire
The dry weather holds. After the usual morning work, you carry the pot and the selected half of its clay test piece to the prepared firing patch. They are light enough in your hands, yet you find yourself moving more carefully than their weight requires. There has been a long wait between shaping this bowl and finding out whether it will survive.
You settle both pieces on the dry firing bed before lighting anything. The pot is upright, with space around it for the fire to grow. You arrange light, dry fuel so that it can burn without a heavy stack collapsing across the rim, and keep the next supply within reach outside the cleared patch.
The first flame is small and off to one side. You let warmth reach the vessel gradually, then feed the fire around it. The bowl is soon too hot to handle, so it stays where it is. You work from outside the fire, using a long piece of wood to ease fuel into place rather than reaching through the flames.
As the heat builds, smoke darkens part of the surface. Other areas take on a warmer colour. You watch the fuel and the movement of the flames, remembering that a bright patch on one side tells you little about the heat on the other. When the lighter fuel burns away, you replenish it without striking the pot. The open firing demands steady attention, but no elaborate chamber.
Eventually you stop adding wood and let the fire burn down around the load. The rim is still visible among the embers. You resist the urge to uncover it for a better look. A pot can survive the hottest part and still crack when one side cools too quickly; lifting it now would gain you nothing useful.
As the light fades, you check the cleared ground and remaining fuel for spreading sparks. The vessel and its test piece stay in place to cool. The untouched raw comparison is back at the craft spot, ready for tomorrow.
You cook the evening meal by the familiar bark-vessel route. There is still no new pot to use tonight, only a shape somewhere in the cooling fire. From the overhang entrance you can see the dark patch where you left it. In the morning you will find out what the clay has become.

01_survival/moon-3-day-25---a-pot-that-h.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 25 - A Pot That Holds Water.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-25---a-pot-that-h.title: Moon 3 Day 25 - A Pot That Holds Water
01_survival/moon-3-day-25---a-pot-that-h.content:
Moon 3 Day 25 - A Pot That Holds Water
You wait until the firing bed and everything in it are cold before clearing the ash. The bowl comes out in one piece. Smoke has left darker patches across its grey-brown surface, but the rim is intact. When you turn it in the daylight, you cannot find the crack that spoiled your first pot.
The small fired test piece comes out beside it. Back at the separate testing spot, you wet this piece and the raw half you kept yesterday on different parts of a spare stone. The raw clay softens under rubbing; the fired piece stays firm. You discard the softened raw material there and keep the fired piece with the other non-food samples. The heat has changed the clay, although the mottled colour alone could not have told you that.
The whole bowl needs its own test. You brush away loose ash, rinse it, then set it on a clean, dry piece of bark with a small charge of water. You watch the base and the join between wall and bottom. A faint damp patch develops underneath as the clay takes up moisture, but no line of escaping water appears.
After checking it again, you add a little more. The water remains in the bowl while you get on with the nearby work. When you return, there is still a useful charge inside and no steady drip beneath it. This fired clay is porous, but the vessel can hold water long enough to be useful. It is a better result than the cracked first attempt.
You pour away the test water and look over the wet body once more. Nothing has softened or begun to flake away. Then you leave the bowl to air under cover, where its rounded base cannot roll into the passage.
For the first time, the clay pot has a practical task within reach. It has survived forming, drying and firing, and now it can hold a working amount of water. Bringing it through a cooking fire will be the next step. You will need to support it securely and warm it gradually, rather than treating it like a metal saucepan.
As you clear the testing spot, you find yourself planning the first meal. The acorn meal has been awkward to stir around hot stones in the bark vessels. If the new pot can take heat through its walls, that same food could be much easier to cook.

01_survival/moon-3-day-26---the-first-me.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 26 - The First Meal in the Pot.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-26---the-first-me.title: Moon 3 Day 26 - The First Meal in the Pot
01_survival/moon-3-day-26---the-first-me.content:
Moon 3 Day 26 - The First Meal in the Pot
A rounded pot needs more than a convenient gap between burning sticks. Before lighting the ordinary hearth, you arrange three low, sound stones on its bare ground and try the cold bowl on them. You have chosen dry stones from the ground away from the water, leaving aside anything split, layered or damp. You bed them firmly and adjust the gaps until the pot stays level when gently pressed at the rim. There is room underneath for a small fire and an opening through which to feed it.
This simple pot support remains outside the overhang, at the ordinary hearth. The separate pottery-firing patch can stay cold. You fill the bowl with a modest amount of water before starting the fire, then build the heat slowly underneath it. The cold pot and its contents warm together.
You stay beside it as the first bubbles appear. They gather and rise until the water is plainly boiling. You keep the fire modest and watch for a new wet line or a crack running from the base. Neither appears. When you let the fuel burn down, the bowl remains on its supports while the water cools with it.
During that wait, you prepare a small fresh batch of acorn meal by the usual crushing and water changes in the bark vessels. Leaching is still needed before cooking; the new container does not remove the bitterness by itself. Once the pot is cold, you empty and inspect it, rinse it and begin again with the meal and room-temperature water.
The second fire is easier to manage because you know where to place the fuel. You stir with a clean, smooth wooden stick as the mixture thickens, keeping it loose enough to move across the base. There are no hot stones to lift out of the food or work around. Heat comes through the vessel instead. You reduce the fire as the meal swells, and keep stirring until it cooks into a soft porridge.
You let the heat fall away before serving the food into the bark vessel. The whole little batch is eaten today. Afterwards, when the pot has cooled, you wash it and check the base again. It is sooted, but still sound after both heating and cooling cycles.
Cooking this way will not replace every use of bark or heated stones. It does make a thick meal much simpler to tend. You leave the washed bowl where air can dry it, then put the wood-working tools together for the next job. Tomorrow you want to look for a suitable bow stave.

01_survival/moon-3-day-27---choose-the-w.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 27 - Choose the Wood Before the Bow.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-27---choose-the-w.title: Moon 3 Day 27 - Choose the Wood Before the Bow
01_survival/moon-3-day-27---choose-the-w.content:
Moon 3 Day 27 - Choose the Wood Before the Bow
The bow in your memory is a simple object: a length of wood, a string and an arrow. The piece you need for its body is less simple. A straight-looking stick can hide twisted grain, a knot in the wrong place or damage that only appears when it begins to bend.
At the hazel patch on your familiar gathering circuit, you take time over the stems. You leave the dead wood for other uses and pass over a promising-looking length with a sharp bend above its base. Eventually you choose one sound, fairly straight stem with a useful clear run. Cutting it with the stone chopper takes patient work from more than one side. You bring back that one length rather than a bundle of uncertain candidates.
At home, the wooden wedge and mallet open it along the grain. The split wanders slightly before settling, showing you something you could not see through the bark. One half gives you the continuous strip of wood you want. You set the other half aside as ordinary working stock; it has not become a second bow stave.
You remove the loose bark carefully, watching the outer wood beneath it. That continuous face will become the bow’s back, which must stretch as the bow bends. The split face will become the belly, where the wood is compressed. Knowing which is which now prevents an attractive shape from costing you the fibres it depends on.
The new stave is still green. You can begin preparing it, but loading it heavily now would tell you little about the bow you hope to make after it dries. You leave generous wood at the ends and around the future working body.
Beside the clean craft area you set up two low forked rests, steadying them with light ties. Their rounded bearing pieces hold the stave off the ground with air beneath it. This separate drying support keeps the long stock clear of the passage, the food rack and the dirty pelt frame. It also keeps it away from the hearth’s uneven heat.
By evening, the bow project has a real beginning: one chosen piece, its grain understood a little better, and somewhere suitable to leave it. The work is now tied to this particular hazel stem. You will have to learn what it can bear, rather than carve a remembered bow out of whatever wood happens to be in your hands.

01_survival/moon-3-day-28---the-line-and.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 28 - The Line and the Shafts.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-28---the-line-and.title: Moon 3 Day 28 - The Line and the Shafts
01_survival/moon-3-day-28---the-line-and.content:
Moon 3 Day 28 - The Line and the Shafts
While the stave begins to dry, you can work on the parts that will eventually go with it. The string is the first question. A line that holds a cap or a light bundle has an easier life than one that must repeatedly take up the force of bending wood.
You prepare a small portion of the retained retted nettle material, picking out woody scraps and weak fibres. Once the cleaned fibres are dry, you twist a short trial line with particular care at the overlaps. You also make a small bark-cord sample for comparison. Neither needs to be long enough for the bow yet; today you want to see how the material and its end attachment settle under repeated gentle pulling.
Around a smooth wooden peg, both first loops take up slack. On the nettle sample, one overlap begins to open as the fibres slide. You untwist that section and remake it with the fibres spread more evenly through the join. The loop then keeps its shape through the next light pulls, though the line still beds down a little.
It is worth finding that movement here, in a short sample held well away from your face. The eventual bowstring will need more than a stout appearance: its length, attachments and response to repeated use must suit the bow. You put the trial line aside without fitting it to the green stave.
Later, on the familiar near-camp ground, you select three slender hazel shoots for arrow-shaft stock. Each has enough straight length to be worth keeping once the crooked tips are trimmed. You work away small side growths without cutting a deep notch into the stem, then turn each piece in your hands to inspect its line.
The three shoots go loosely onto the clean support where you can lift and examine them separately. As with the dart shafts, drying may change what looked straight when it was green. They have no points, feather vanes or rear slots yet. For now, keeping their identity and watching how they change is more useful than making them look like finished arrows.
At the end of the day the bow still rests untouched beside them. The short nettle sample lies with the fibre work, its remade join easy to find. You have found two jobs that can proceed while the main piece waits, without asking that piece to dry any faster.

01_survival/moon-3-day-29---rough-out-th.title: Moon 3 Day 29 - Rough Out the Stave
01_survival/moon-3-day-29---rough-out-th.content:
Moon 3 Day 29 - Rough Out the Stave
You take the stave from its rests and sight along the split face. The wood is still fresh enough to cut readily. Today you want to remove the obvious excess and leave a rough body that can dry, with enough spare wood for the more exact work later.
