The curved outer face remains the back. You keep your cutting away from it as you begin on the split side, supporting the work on a low piece of wood so it cannot rock beneath the edge. Short controlled cuts establish the middle and the broad lengths on either side. You turn the piece often, following the grain rather than forcing a straight line through a place where the fibres turn.
The aim is not to make both sides look perfectly alike. When the bow is eventually loaded, the wood will have to share the bend along its limbs. A thin weak place could move too much while a thick neighbouring section scarcely moves at all. Removing wood simply to tidy the outline could create that weak place before you have even tested the body.
That later process of watching and adjusting the bend is tillering. It needs wood in a suitable condition and careful changes based on what the particular limbs do. The stave in front of you is still green, so today you leave a substantial margin for it. You do not need to force it into a curve to understand the next decision.
The flint edge slows as it loses its keenest bite. You stop to restore it, then use lighter scraping cuts to soften the roughest tool marks. The small rawhide guard keeps the edge protected when you put it down between tasks. By the time you finish, the split half-stem has become a recognisable rough body, still thick and straight, with plain ends and plenty of wood left to work.
You return it to the clean rests. Its underside is open to the air, and nothing pulls it into a forced curve. The arrow blanks stay separate beside it; the little string sample remains with the cordage.
There is satisfaction in seeing the shape begin to emerge. There is also a useful stopping point. The existing spear and atlatl can keep serving while this new piece changes slowly under cover. Tomorrow, the home that makes such waiting possible deserves some attention of its own.

01_survival/moon-3-day-3---make-a-dry-pl.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 3 - Make a Dry Place to Sleep.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-3---make-a-dry-pl.title: Moon 3 Day 3 - Make a Dry Place to Sleep
01_survival/moon-3-day-3---make-a-dry-pl.content:
Moon 3 Day 3 - Make a Dry Place to Sleep
Begin with the bed
At the overhang, you clear loose material from the chosen resting strip without cutting a hollow into the ground. The damp corner stays beyond it. You lay clean small boughs across firm bearing points, then add a generous layer of separately gathered dry grass and leaves. The old small bedding pad comes with the first load.
When you lie down, the first arrangement compresses enough for one hip to feel a hard point. You redistribute the foundation and replenish the fill there. The purpose is a dry, comfortable layer beneath the whole body, not a neatly woven object to admire.
Dry Plant Insulation works through its condition and arrangement. Wet fill or a flattened hollow would change the result; the rock roof cannot compensate for either.
Screen the exposed side
Sound light forks and a cross-rail give you a low support near the northwestern edge of the mouth. The rail carries brush and overlapping bark pieces, not the limestone above it. You seat it against rolling, using natural bearings and a few short retaining ties.
The first screen blocks the direct breeze at the bed. You leave an offset opening towards the southeast and room above for air movement. There is no fitted door or mud wall yet. A broad push from outside shows where one foot shifts; you reseat that bearing before loading the screen again.
This is the first local use of Rock-Shelter Enclosure. A short rest behind the screen feels different from sitting at the open mouth. More front closure and weather inspection will follow, but there is a usable sleeping place tonight.
Move the working camp
The carrying takes several trips. You bring the ignition sets, bark vessels, edges and small woodworking tools, food and protected materials. The clay comparison pieces travel wrapped against knocks; the rejected pot remains an unwanted specimen at the old site. The dart and thrower move as existing equipment, not as a newly improved hunting system.
You leave the old large drying frame rather than dragging a dirty structure uphill. Its future work will need an appropriately separated support here. The riverside fish cage remains at its established anchor and can still be checked on ordinary rounds.
At the new site, you set the hearth on open ground beyond the rock’s drip line and the weather screen. The first fire there uses a carried dry kit. Water still comes from the known seep; there is no invented spring at the overhang. The clean craft stone and the downslope processing area give the same activities new positions.
Sanitation and Camp Hygiene travels as a working principle, not as the old camp’s compass labels copied blindly onto new ground.
Occupy one home
You sleep at the overhang. The grass clothing and small crown piece remain your dry outfit, with the bast soles removed beside the bed for the night. Dry bedding and the screen give immediate sheltering value, while the poor coverage of your body makes the next priority plain.
The old lean-to is now an abandoned camp. You have moved rather than supplied a second refuge. Tomorrow you can offer useful labour to people who already know how to make skins serve through a colder season.

01_survival/moon-3-day-30---close-the-dr.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 30 - Close the Draught at Its Source.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-30---close-the-dr.title: Moon 3 Day 30 - Close the Draught at Its Source
01_survival/moon-3-day-30---close-the-dr.content:
Moon 3 Day 30 - Close the Draught at Its Source
A change in the wind makes the sleeping place feel colder along one edge. The entrance screen is still breaking the main gust, but near the small earth-filled bay you can feel a thin stream of air where the dry infill has drawn away from its backing. A little extra bedding would hide the symptom while leaving the gap open.
You clear space to look at the join. Most of the bay is firm and remains keyed into the woven rods. The supporting wood is steady, and there is no new drip above the gap. The movement appears to be at the drying edge itself, so you can repair that place without loading the whole screen with more wet earth.
Using a small fresh mixture of clay-rich building earth and short grass, you work a narrow repair into the edge and around the sound backing. The material needs something to grip. A thick smear on the outside would add weight without necessarily closing the air path behind it. You keep the little patch sheltered by the existing bark overlap and leave it exposed to air on the dry side.
The improvement is apparent when the wind returns. Air still moves through the deliberate opening above the screen, but the low stream beside the bed is much reduced. You settle the bedding back into place and renew the compressed part where your hips have been lying. The small wall repair and the sleeping layer now help each other instead of asking one to compensate for the other.
At the craft side, the green stave and arrow stock are clear of the repaired area. You make sure the supports have not worked loose and put the tools within reach for the next session. There is no reason to bring the wood close to the fire merely because the air has turned cold.
As the last daylight goes, you sit behind the screen in the body wrap. Your covered feet are better than they were at the start of the moon, yet the exposed lower legs still remind you how much of winter clothing remains to be solved. The narrow deer margin has already become a tool guard; a larger useful skin will have to come from actual hunting or accepted shared work.
That can be the next substantial commitment while the stave dries. You leave the bow project on its rests and turn your attention back to the people and food routes that will have to carry you through the colder weeks.

01_survival/moon-3-day-4---work-worth-a-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 4 - Work Worth a Warm Skin.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-4---work-worth-a-.title: Moon 3 Day 4 - Work Worth a Warm Skin
01_survival/moon-3-day-4---work-worth-a-.content:
Moon 3 Day 4 - Work Worth a Warm Skin
Return with a useful offer
You take the familiar route towards the meeting ground, carrying your small splitting tools rather than arranging another projectile display. The adult who examined the lever is near the outer edge of the neighbouring clearing. You stop where he can see you. He looks at the mallet and wedges, then indicates a heap of fallen branchwood a little beyond him.
You point between the sound pieces and the nearer working pile. He takes up a branch and sets it there himself. When you begin moving another, he stays and clears a place for it. You have enough shared meaning for this small task. You do not need to turn every word into a promise.
Communication and Exchange begins to support useful work instead of another hopeful presentation.
Fit your work to theirs
You carry the selected dry wood and help break down awkward branch ends. A straight-grained short billet is worth splitting. The first wedge starts the opening; the second holds it while you advance the split. You leave the knotty piece when the opening runs away from the intended grain.
The adult examines the resulting light stock, chooses two pieces and sets them beside his own material. He returns one rough end to the fuel pile. His selection is a better sign of usefulness than applause would be.
You spend the available work interval on his chosen pile. You are not teaching this group that wood can be split, nor claiming that your tools are superior. The wedges simply let you contribute something they can use.
Observe an actual transfer
Later he brings out a folded, worn skin from under the edge of his cover. When he opens it, the brown coat and surviving outline suggest red deer. It has plainly been worked before: the centre bends, the edges show old stitch holes, and one shoulder margin has a small tear. The piece is large enough for a body wrap, though some margins are ragged.
You touch your chest and spread the fold against yourself, then put it back within his reach. He examines the wood pile, folds the skin again and pushes it towards you. When you pick it up, he releases it and resumes sorting the split pieces. You show it once more before leaving; he makes no move to take it back.
There is no agreed price you can translate. There is an observed day of accepted work and an observed transfer. The skin is yours to use.
Bring home material that can become clothing
At the overhang, you unfold it away from food work. You inspect the old damaged margin and compare how the centre and edges bend. You do not know its full treatment history, and a supple used skin is not proof of waterproofing. It is nevertheless a very different starting material from a little untreated pelt.
You keep it protected and dry. Tomorrow you can place the sound parts around shoulders and core, using Fur-On Pelt Clothing and your existing stitching tools to mend the limited damage. You have acquired one substantial skin, not a second blanket, hood, boot supply and spare coat hidden in the same fold.
For the first time, familiar contact has produced a practical exchange. Neither of you needed the other to be astonished.

01_survival/moon-3-day-5---a-wrap-that-c.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 5 - A Wrap That Covers the Body.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-5---a-wrap-that-c.title: Moon 3 Day 5 - A Wrap That Covers the Body
01_survival/moon-3-day-5---a-wrap-that-c.content:
Moon 3 Day 5 - A Wrap That Covers the Body
Use the sound area
The skin wants to lie around you in a particular way. Its broad centre covers the back; the longer sound margins can meet across the chest and abdomen. You place it over the shoulders before making any cut. The ragged ends fall around the thighs, stopping above the knees.
You turn the hair towards the body and leave the dull tan skin surface outside. A shallow fold at the upper edge keeps a rough margin away from the neck. This is an overlapping wrap without sleeves, not a tunic pattern forced onto unsuitable material.
The small tear falls near the left shoulder fold. You mark that place, remove the wrap and put the grass screens back on for the repair work.
Let the seam support the fold
A small turned edge brings sound skin together beside the tear. You test the awl on the damaged margin first and move the holes inward where they hold a gentle pull. The needle carries a short portion of the reserved sinew through the fold. A few loose stitches support it without dragging the weak edge into a tight puckered line.
You flex the repaired area over a smooth piece of wood. Its movement matters more than a tidy seam. The old preparation has left useful flexibility in the centre; you ease a stiff margin by working it gently rather than soaking the whole skin and starting another drying problem.
Stitching and Fur-On Pelt Clothing meet in the distribution of load. A seam cannot strengthen material that tears beside every hole.
Close it where the body can move
You fit the wrap again. A short tie from loose bark line closes the overlap below the throat, across the upper chest. The existing waist fastening gathers the lower overlap lightly. The neckline remains open enough for turning and the tie is readily released; there is no constricting cord around the neck.
You reach, crouch and take a short dry walk beside the shelter. Pulling one forearm out through the side lets you use a tool. Bringing the arm back inside closes that gap while you stand still. You ease the waist fastening after the first crouch pulls the repaired shoulder.
The wrap covers both shoulders, back and core much more continuously than the hanging grass screens. It also reaches farther down the thighs. Wind at the entrance now meets an overlap rather than an open flank.
Make the wardrobe change explicit
Both grass screens come off and are stored dry at the back of the sleeping area. The bark waist layers and small pelvic pad remain underneath. The old narrow fox strip lies under the wrap at your anatomical left shoulder; it has not become a new collar. The plain rabbit crown piece and both bast soles remain in use.
The new dated clothing reference fixes this appearance for subsequent pictures. The cap still leaves ears and nape exposed, and the soles still leave toes and ankles open. Head, lower-leg and foot coverage are worthwhile next work; one skin has not silently supplied it all.
For now you have a substantial working wrap and a warmer covering to draw around yourself at rest. The next useful construction is a place where the autumn harvest can remain protected while you spend time on clothing and tools.

01_survival/moon-3-day-6---give-the-harv.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 6 - Give the Harvest a Dry Place.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-6---give-the-harv.title: Moon 3 Day 6 - Give the Harvest a Dry Place
01_survival/moon-3-day-6---give-the-harv.content:
Moon 3 Day 6 - Give the Harvest a Dry Place
Separate stored food from the bed
A better roof makes it tempting to put every precious thing beside the sleeping place. Food needs its own clean, inspectable arrangement. Damp ground, tightly packed wet nuts and concealed damage would undo the value of a larger harvest.
At the rear-right of the usable dry recess, away from the drip-stained corner, you fit a small Raised Storage Rack. Two low fork-supported end assemblies carry rails and light crosspieces. Trimmed bearing faces and short retaining bindings keep the pieces from rolling. The rack carries food and containers, not the roof above.
Before loading it, you press each end and then the centre. One support settles on a loose surface fragment; you clear and reseat it on firmer ground. The shelf stays low enough to inspect without climbing and high enough to separate the load from ordinary ground damp.
Keep a harvest open to inspection
Clean bark sheets make shallow working surfaces on the slats. The existing basket rests beside them rather than burying everything in one deep pile. A little overlapping bark at the exposed edge interrupts wind-driven wetting while leaving the sides open. The rock supplies the main overhead cover.
Dry Nut Storage concerns the condition of the input as well as its container. You spread newly gathered nuts in a modest layer and keep visibly damp pieces separate for further drying. Damaged or visibly spoiled material does not join the reserve. A dry-looking shell alone cannot certify everything inside it.
A loosely woven cover made for the basket excludes some falling debris and makes the contents easier to keep in order. It is not a seal against every rodent or a substitute for looking through the stored food.
Use the remaining season
The known western patches now receive a purposeful gathering session. Hazel returns are thinner than at arrival. You collect worthwhile sound remnants and a useful acorn batch rather than pretending that every bare twig still supplies the old harvest.
You bring the acorns back as untreated processing stock. Some of the established acorn route supplies the day’s meal; the rest can be kept in an inspectable state and prepared as needed. Wet cooked meal does not go onto the rack as winter rations.
There are no new edible species in the basket. The work improves the use of resources already identified, and the storage arrangement can now grow with an actual harvest rather than with a number written beside it.
Make stored food serve the workshop
You compare what needs immediate handling with what can remain protected. Ordinary water and fuel work continue, without another account of each trip. Tomorrow’s enclosure work can proceed with food preparation already organised around the new home.
The existing fish cage still has a role. A renewed shallow-water spear session can add a different opportunity later, when conditions justify it. Neither an empty trap nor this rack obliges an animal to appear.
For the handbook, the new structure and process belong together: the rack separates material from ground damp, the spread makes condition visible, and the processing plan turns collected inputs into meals. That is the beginning of seasonal provision, not a declaration that winter is funded.

01_survival/moon-3-day-7---an-entrance-t.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 7 - An Entrance That Breaks the Wind.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-7---an-entrance-t.title: Moon 3 Day 7 - An Entrance That Breaks the Wind
01_survival/moon-3-day-7---an-entrance-t.content:
Moon 3 Day 7 - An Entrance That Breaks the Wind
Close the exposed line
The rock has relieved you of building a roof. The opening still lets a gust travel straight across the bed. You want a screen that interrupts that path while leaving an entrance you can use with an armful of wood. More covering is useful only if the light frame holds it.
You begin outside the sleeping strip, pressing the existing forks and checking their feet. A loose retaining turn is replaced. Sound light poles from the accessible slope provide a short return at the screen’s open end. New nettle line, twisted from protected prepared fibre, secures the junctions; you do not strip the food rack or fire kits for ties. The frame supports its covering independently of the rock overhead.
The extension gives the southeast entrance a dog-leg. You can still see daylight around it, but the bed is no longer directly behind an open slot. There is room to turn and carry the water vessel without striking a projecting stick.
Make weather fall away
Brush fills the larger gaps. Bark pieces overlap with upper edges outside lower ones, so water meeting the outer face has a path down rather than into each seam. Light crosspieces retain them. A small separate bark-and-brush baffle stands beside the entrance, not across the walking line. You can lift it aside from inside without undoing the main frame.
You leave a high gap beneath the natural roof and the offset entrance open. This is a sheltered sleeping place, not a sealed box. The ordinary hearth stays outside beyond the drip edge. Bringing it under the new covering would create a different problem, not complete this one.
Rock-Shelter Enclosure now has a more useful front. You push the screen from both sides and watch the feet rather than trusting a tight-looking knot. One bark edge catches your wrap as you pass; turning it outward removes the snag.
Give the bed its depth back
Lying down reveals where the first bedding has flattened. You lift the upper layer, remove a damp handful at the outer margin and add dry grass beneath hips and shoulders. The clean bough foundation stays clear of the rear rock and does not block the open floor beside the entrance. Bedding which looks deep from above can still leave a hip pressed against a hard cold point.
A brief shower supplies an ordinary use check. Drops remain outside the sleeping strip; the front screen moves a little without a support lifting. From the bed you feel less direct wind at shoulder height. You have not measured a temperature gain or proved the shelter through a winter storm, but the change answers the particular draught you set out to stop.
Reserve a small place for earth
At the lower left panel, under the roof’s protection, fine gaps remain between woven twigs. A supported earth coating might close them without adding another whole layer of brush. You leave one small bay accessible for tomorrow’s trial. The rest of the screen already works without waiting for mud to dry.
Food preparation and ordinary gathering fit around the construction. The covered nut batch lets you choose a building day without pretending that it will feed you indefinitely. A dry bed, a usable entrance and manageable stores are beginning to support work beyond the next night.

01_survival/moon-3-day-8---earth-held-by.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 8 - Earth Held by a Frame.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-8---earth-held-by.title: Moon 3 Day 8 - Earth Held by a Frame
01_survival/moon-3-day-8---earth-held-by.content:
Moon 3 Day 8 - Earth Held by a Frame
Ask the wall to stop a draught
The gap at the lower screen is small enough to treat as a material trial. You want to close air paths, not hang a mass of wet earth over your head. A patch that stays attached after drying would justify extending the method later.
You take a modest charge of clay-rich subsoil from the known stable exposure. Roots and dark loose surface litter are removed. This is a fresh building charge, kept apart from the protected pottery material and the two fired comparison pieces. Those pieces have not suddenly become ingredients.
Beside the outside craft area, you work the earth on a spare bark scrap. A little water makes it kneadable. Short dry grass is mixed through until the fibres are distributed, rather than laid as a slippery mat between coats. The damp handful keeps its shape when pressed; if it slumps, adding more of it to the wall will not fix the mixture.
Let the twigs retain the earth
You strengthen the selected low bay with slender interwoven rods, supported by the screen frame at their ends. The opening is only about a forearm across. Pressing it first shows whether the backing itself shifts.
The earth goes through the spaces and is worked against the opposite face, making connected keys around the rods. A thin supported layer is enough for this trial. Fibres help hold the small mass together; they do not turn wet earth into a beam. The lower edge stays off the ground on its wooden bearer, with bark outside to interrupt splash. The whole bay lies inside the natural drip line.
The new wattle-and-daub infill is one small lower panel. The woven twigs are the wattle; the earth-and-grass mixture worked through them is the daub. Bark and brush still cover the surrounding screen. You leave the entrance and high gap untouched, and keep all wet mixing away from the food rack and dry bed.
Give drying somewhere to happen
Two small witness patches from the same mixture rest on loose woven twig scraps beside the bay. They offer something you can inspect without breaking the installed panel. You do not call a dry-looking face a dry wall.
By late afternoon the exposed surface has lost some wet shine, but a witness patch remains cool and yielding within. Nothing is ready for a hard push or another heavy coat. You leave air access to both faces and retain the rain cover. An outside fire does not become a drying stove inside the sleeping enclosure.
Earth construction makes water management more important. You clear leaf debris from the natural runoff line outside the entrance without cutting a trench beneath a support or diverting water towards the seep route. The frame and bed stay on their existing dry bearings.
Keep the comparison useful
From the sleeping side, the freshly filled gap no longer passes a direct thread of wind. That is a limited immediate result. Attachment, shrinkage and repeated weathering remain to be observed over the next days. No hard frost is forecast by a calendar in your head; an approaching freeze while the patch is still wet would be a reason to defer further work.
For the handbook, this is a composite: wood provides support, the woven backing retains the coating, and the earth closes openings. You can obtain a useful wall function without firing a brick or inventing a roof made of mud.

01_survival/moon-3-day-9---warmth-withou.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 3 Day 9 - Warmth Without Losing Your Hands.md
01_survival/moon-3-day-9---warmth-withou.title: Moon 3 Day 9 - Warmth Without Losing Your Hands
01_survival/moon-3-day-9---warmth-withou.content:
Moon 3 Day 9 - Warmth Without Losing Your Hands
Follow the pull through the garment
The body wrap is warmer while you stand still than while you reach. Lifting both arms pulls its front overlap apart and brings tension back to the old shoulder repair. Cutting large armholes would throw away useful coverage. You first try changing where the existing skin is held.
With the waist fastening loose, you lift a water vessel and crouch beside the craft stone. The wrap slides better. You retain a little fullness over each shoulder, then catch the overlapping front margin beneath the waist line at one hip. A short reused cord keeper stops that margin creeping free. The chest tie stays below the throat and the hem remains above the knees.
You repeat the movements with the fastening secured. The repaired fold does not have to take the whole pull, and one forearm can work outside while the other side stays covered. The garment has not gained sleeves or a second skin. At rest you can still bring both arms inside.
Move warmth to the exposed place
Ears and nape are the next exposed parts. Beneath the new body wrap, the old narrow fox panel adds a second layer at one shoulder while leaving those parts bare. You take it out and lay it beside the plain rabbit crown.
This is the skin recovered from your own snare catch in Moon 1 Day 23 - A Difficult Catch and a Repair, then made into a limited shoulder panel the next day. It has already had weeks of protected drying and intermittent working. It is still a moisture-sensitive skin, not newly acquired durable leather, but the sound narrow pieces can do more useful work here.
You release the old shoulder ties and ease the joined panel around the rear of your head before cutting anything. Its ends reach over the ears and its lower edge reaches the upper nape. The body wrap now covers the shoulder it leaves behind. You are reallocating one small skin, not adding another garment’s worth of material.
Extend the cap you actually have
The existing panel is already pieced together around damaged areas. You retain those sound joins, fold the least even edges and place the hair inward. Dull tan-brown skin faces out. Only the rough margin needs trimming; you do not sacrifice the useful length to make both ends perfectly alike.
Stitching joins folded sound margins to the side and back of the rabbit crown with inspected plant thread made from protected fibre stock. The existing forehead-and-back band retains the cap. Nothing ties tightly beneath the chin or circles the throat. You turn your head, bend down and take the whole cap off with one hand before accepting the fit. The side pieces can fold up for close work.
This is Fur-On Pelt Clothing improved through fit and allocation. The fox panel is now entirely part of the cap extension; none remains hidden at the left shoulder. The stored grass screens stay stored, the bark waist layers and pelvic pad remain beneath the wrap, and both bast soles remain the same open footwear. Head and core are better covered, while lower legs and toes still need work.
The traps remain a way to obtain food and future pelts when they actually catch something. A new catch would still need prompt fleshing, preparation and working before it could supply another garment. Today’s improvement uses material you already possess and leaves the day available for fitting rather than another journey to ask for a skin.
Leave a useful pattern
You note where the new seam joins the old crown and how much fullness the wrap needs at the shoulder. Those relationships matter more than a neat outline: another piece must fit the person and the work, rather than merely resemble this one on the ground.
You do not spend the evening rebuilding yesterday’s wall. The small panel still feels firmer at the face than the centre of a witness patch. Letting one process continue while another useful object is fitted is already changing what a working day can accomplish.

01_survival/moon-4-day-1---a-warm-meal-a.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-1---a-warm-meal-a.title: Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain
01_survival/moon-4-day-1---a-warm-meal-a.content:
Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain
Rain passes through during the night. In the morning, drops still fall beyond the overhang’s lip, while the bed and the long wood on its separate rests remain inside the dry strip. You look at yesterday’s little wall repair. It is still drying under the bark cover, so you leave it alone rather than prodding it into a result before it is ready.
Once the weather clears, you prepare a small fresh acorn charge by the usual route and check the ordinary hearth’s supports. The cold pot and its wet contents warm together over a modest outside fire. You stir as the meal thickens, tending the fuel from the open side of the supports.
The familiar work gives you time to notice the difference this home has made. At the old camp, a wet night often decided the morning’s entire task. Here you can cook, leave the wood to dry and keep the delicate work protected while rain crosses the valley. The pot is still sound after this use; when it has cooled, you wash it and put it where air can reach the inside.
You take out the short nettle sample and examine its remade join, then put it away again. The next job is not to pull harder on a string just because you have begun a bow. Better skin material and a more regular share in food work deserve the useful weather while the wood waits.
By evening the new moon has brought the next boundary in your reckoning. You sit at the sheltered mouth, looking out over the darkening valley, with a warm meal eaten and tomorrow’s priorities clearer. It is time to look back over the whole change of home and purpose in Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1.

01_survival/moon-4-day-10---make-the-hol.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 10 - Make the Holes Do the Work.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-10---make-the-hol.title: Moon 4 Day 10 - Make the Holes Do the Work
01_survival/moon-4-day-10---make-the-hol.content:
Illustration note: the small wooden gauge is schematic; its pictured perforations are not part of the tool or method described.
Moon 4 Day 10 - Make the Holes Do the Work
At the river margin you retrieve the woven trap and open its rear cap over firm ground. It is empty. While clearing leaves from the body, you notice how awkwardly the cylinder rests against your knee when one hand holds the closure and the other tries to reach inside. A small net beneath the opening would give a catch somewhere to fall while you kept control of the trap.
Back at the overhang, you choose the short-handled version first. It needs only a small bag of mesh and a light frame, and it will work beside the existing trap without changing the river. You put aside a flexible willow rod for the frame, then take prepared fibre from the dry bundle and twist a new length of fairly fine nettle cord. The trial bow line and the separate snare candidate stay with their own projects.
Netting begins with a cord stretched between two low supports. You smooth a little wooden mesh gauge, a flat slip with rounded edges, and use it to keep the first row of hanging loops alike. On the next row, each new loop joins one above it. The knot is a small sheet bend: the working end passes through the older loop, goes around both its sides, then tucks under its own crossing part. You draw the knot up before sliding the new loop off the gauge.
The first strip takes concentration. Loose loops gather where you have allowed the gauge to tilt, and you undo those few knots while they are still easy to reach. Soon your hands find a steadier sequence. Each completed row supports the next, and a regular open mesh grows below the starting cord.
This is a different use of fibre from the solid baskets you have made. Water will pass through the spaces while the joined cords retain something larger. Those spaces must remain small enough for the fish you intend to handle, including when the mesh is pulled sideways. You stretch the little panel in both directions and correct an opening that is larger than its neighbours.
By late afternoon you have enough for a shallow bag. You fold the rectangle and join its sides, leaving one open mouth. A gentle wet pull reveals one slipping join, which you remake before hanging the bag to drain. Tomorrow it can be fitted to the willow frame.
You have spent most of the day sitting at the craft stone. The new sleeves let you keep your hands on the cord in the cold air; only when you stand do you realise how long it has been since you last needed to huddle beside the hearth.

01_survival/moon-4-day-11---keep-the-cat.title: Moon 4 Day 11 - Keep the Catch Inside
01_survival/moon-4-day-11---keep-the-cat.content:
Moon 4 Day 11 - Keep the Catch Inside
The mesh bag has dried without its repaired join opening again. You take it down and pass your fingers along the edges, checking for a loose end before fitting it to the frame. Yesterday’s knots are now numerous enough that one careless attachment could waste a great deal of work.
The willow bends into a small oval. You overlap its ends beside a short wooden handle and bind the joint so that both ends bear along the wood. A pull at the far side of the oval shows a little rotation. You reseat the ends and tighten the binding until the frame holds its direction against a modest load.
Next you lace the bag mouth around the oval, spreading the mesh evenly and leaving enough slack for a shallow pocket beneath it. If you pull the edge straight and tight, some of the openings narrow while others stretch wide. With the cord eased, the bag settles into a more useful shape. You inspect the joined sides and the bottom before trying it in water.
At the familiar river margin you lower the hand net into a quiet shallow patch. Water passes through readily, though a few leaves collect against the mesh. You lift a wet bark-wrapped pebble from the edge, empty it, and inspect the lacing. The simple trial shows where the load sits: in the bag, with its weight carried around the rim and back through the binding to your hand.
The woven trap contains one small fish today. You keep the cylinder controlled on the firm bank and hold the net close beneath its retrieval opening before releasing the rear cap. A slight tilt brings the fish into the shallow bag. It cannot fall straight back through the opening, and you can set down the closed trap before dealing with it. You dispatch it promptly, carry it back, and cook it with the day’s meal.
Afterwards you rinse the net, check the joins and hang it where it can drain. The rim has kept its shape. One lacing loop has moved towards the handle, so you redistribute it before putting the tool away. The bag can be removed for repair without rebuilding the wooden frame.
From your seat beneath the rock, you can see the new mesh hanging beside the older woven work. A bundle of fibres has become a line, a line has become a surface, and that surface can now be fitted to an object with a useful shape. Your hands turn the little gauge once more before you lay it with the cord. There are other things you could make with the same method.

01_survival/moon-4-day-12---a-straight-p.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 12 - A Straight Piece for Fishing.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-12---a-straight-p.title: Moon 4 Day 12 - A Straight Piece for Fishing
01_survival/moon-4-day-12---a-straight-p.content:
Moon 4 Day 12 - A Straight Piece for Fishing
The hand net hangs dry beside the woven work. It makes retrieving a fish easier, but it still depends on a fish entering the trap. Looking down towards the river, you think about reaching the quieter water beside a deeper bank, where the spear would be awkward to use.
A line would let you put bait there while staying on firm ground. The catch need not depend on a curved hook. A short pointed piece tied at its middle can lie lengthways inside bait and turn across the pull once a fish has swallowed it. You remember the name: a fishing gorge.
You select a sound sliver of hard wood and work it into a small tapered bar. Its centre remains thicker than the ends. A shallow seat gives the binding somewhere to settle, but you stop before cutting deeply into the wood. The point will be of little use if the line breaks the piece in half.
The line takes longer. You clean another small portion of the retained nettle material, separate sound fibres and lay them aside to dry fully. Prepared dry fibre already in the bundle supplies today’s twisting. The slender line needs even overlaps, especially near its end, where it will bend around the gorge. You make it long enough for a modest near-bank trial and wind the spare length onto a smooth short stick.
With the gorge tied at its middle, you draw it through a loose fold of wet bark. It goes through lengthways; when you change the pull, the little bar turns across the fold. You repeat the movement while watching the attachment. The seat keeps the tie near the centre without burying it in a sharp notch. This gives you a useful shape to try in water tomorrow.
There is time before evening to settle another unfinished job. At the old practice ground, you inspect the landing bank and make a few restrained casts with the repaired dart A. Its shortened wooden point enters the soft plant-covered target, and the shaft, rear seat and two feather bindings come back sound. You can take it out again when a hunting opportunity is worth following.
Back beneath the overhang, you put the gorge and its line together, with the points covered by a small folded piece of bark for carrying. The new clothes have stayed clear of your hands and the cast. As you loosen the sleeves for airing, the unfamiliar little fishing piece rests beside the much larger equipment it may sometimes replace.

01_survival/moon-4-day-13---feel-the-riv.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 13 - Feel the River Through the Line.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-13---feel-the-riv.title: Moon 4 Day 13 - Feel the River Through the Line
01_survival/moon-4-day-13---feel-the-riv.content:
Moon 4 Day 13 - Feel the River Through the Line
The morning is overcast, with damp leaves lying loose on the lower ground. Beneath a fallen branch near the familiar river margin, the sheltered leaf mould is soft enough to move with your fingers. You find a few earthworms there and take a small amount for bait, replacing the cover over the disturbed patch.
You choose a firm low place beside a quiet pocket of water. From here the bank gives you access without putting the thin foot coverings into the river. The hand net lies within reach, its short handle pointing towards you. You unwind only the line you need, leaving the rest on its smooth stick.
The bait covers the small gorge lengthways. Lowering it slowly gives you time to see how the current moves the cord. At first the bait drifts back against the bank, so you shift a little along the firm edge and try where the water moves past the pocket. A small smooth stone, tied separately above the gorge, helps it settle lower.
The new work is mostly in your fingers. A touch against the line could be a fish, a leaf or the stone brushing the bottom. You lift and lower it slightly, learning the difference between a steady drag and an interruption that moves on its own. When a definite pull comes, you give the fish time to take the bait before gradually drawing the cord taut.
Something holds and moves away. You keep a steady pull as the fish comes nearer, taking in the line by hand. Near the edge it turns sharply. You lower your hand enough to follow the movement, then guide it over the submerged net rather than trying to lift its whole weight on the little wooden piece. The shallow bag brings one modest fish onto the bank.
You dispatch it promptly and free the tackle during cleaning. The gorge has turned across the pull as intended; the attachment is still near its middle. You inspect the wetted line and put it into a loose coil for the walk home. This way of fishing has reached water you could not work comfortably with the spear, though it has taken patience and a supply of suitable bait.
Light rain begins as you return. You cook the fresh fish with the day’s meal, then spread the line to dry. The outside of one sleeve is damp, and its cuff firms as the moisture leaves. You gently work the edge before hanging it with air around it. The better outfit lets you spend useful time at the river; keeping it fit for that work will take some attention too.

01_survival/moon-4-day-14---make-two-thr.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 14 - Make Two Threads Work Together.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-14---make-two-thr.title: Moon 4 Day 14 - Make Two Threads Work Together
01_survival/moon-4-day-14---make-two-thr.content:
Moon 4 Day 14 - Make Two Threads Work Together
The wet line is hanging loose, where you can inspect it in daylight. A few sections are thicker than their neighbours, and the knots have made handling them more noticeable. The small net took another kind of patience: every loop meant drawing a loose length through by hand. Better fibre work could make both jobs less cumbersome.
You bring out the wooden spindle made as a replacement in the first month. It has already spun light retaining yarn. Today you want to use it for another stage: joining two spun threads into a line that handles more steadily.
The extra nettle material cleaned yesterday is now dry. You pick away the remaining woody fragments and align a modest portion. One hand draws out the fibres while the spindle puts twist into them. When the thread begins to thin, you overlap another small supply before the old one ends. You wind the first single thread onto a smooth temporary stick, then make another in the same spinning direction and wind it separately.
With both threads feeding freely, you attach their ends to the spindle and turn it the opposite way. The individual threads begin to wrap around each other. You control their feed together, keeping one from running ahead while the other hangs slack. The movement is familiar from hand cordage, but now the spindle carries the turning while your fingers attend to the two incoming threads.
At first you put in more twist than you need. A short released section curls back on itself, so you let some of the turning out and compare it again. Further along, a loose section needs a little more. The aim is a manageable line with sound joins, not the greatest number of turns you can force into it.
By afternoon a small useful length of plied yarn is wound onto the spindle shaft. You run it through your fingers, looking for thin places and opening overlaps. A separate short sample gets a wet comparison; the rest stays dry for the next piece of netting. It is firmer and easier to manage than the loose singles, though you will learn more when knots and repeated handling work on it.
Your shoulders feel the long session, and you put the spindle down. The coarse retained fibre is a diminishing bundle rather than a field that replenishes itself. There is enough prepared work here for modest projects, but a large net or a woven garment would demand another scale of supply. For tomorrow, a small tool that carries this yarn through the mesh will do.

01_survival/moon-4-day-15---carry-the-co.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 15 - Carry the Cord Through the Mesh.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-15---carry-the-co.title: Moon 4 Day 15 - Carry the Cord Through the Mesh
01_survival/moon-4-day-15---carry-the-co.content:
Moon 4 Day 15 - Carry the Cord Through the Mesh
A loop of netting is simple enough. Passing the entire loose working length through it, again and again, is what makes the work awkward. Yesterday’s plied yarn gives you a better line to handle; a small carrier should let you keep more of it under control.
You choose a narrow sound strip of wood from the retained split stock. It needs to pass through the intended mesh when it is carrying yarn, so you keep its body slim. You round the sides and work an open notch into each end, leaving short stout arms rather than thin points that would snap or catch the cord.
The first winding shows where the wood needs more attention. A rough inner corner catches a few fibres as you draw the yarn off. You smooth it with a fine abrasive patch, then run the line around it again. Now you can wind lengthways between the two notched ends, adding a compact layer over the flat faces. The loaded piece still passes through a loose sample loop.
This netting shuttle carries the working yarn. The separate plain wooden gauge still determines the size of each new loop. With the starting cord fixed low in front of you, you hold the gauge at the unfinished row, pass the loaded shuttle through the older loop, and draw up the familiar mesh knot. A short length pays out from the tool as you need it.
Soon a small rectangle hangs from the support. You turn the row and continue, watching that each new loop joins the one intended above it. The shuttle cannot correct a missed loop, but it keeps the spare yarn from lying in a loose tangle across your knees. The work has become easier to stop and resume without losing your place.
You finish the little panel’s edge before the light goes. It is a separate repair-sized piece, made from the new yarn, and you put it with the hand net for a future damaged patch. The hand net itself is still intact. Enlarging it now would use more line without answering a problem you have actually met.
Later, the rising moon brightens the open ground beyond the overhang. The small pieces of fishing tackle are dry under cover, and your sleeves are hanging where you can reach them. You sit with your usual evening meal and look over the work of this half-moon. There is more here than a collection of promising objects now, though the food each method brings is still uneven. It is time for the full-moon review in Reflection 08 - Full Moon - Moon 4 Day 15.

01_survival/moon-4-day-16---a-string-the.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 16 - A String the Length of a Bow.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-16---a-string-the.title: Moon 4 Day 16 - A String the Length of a Bow
01_survival/moon-4-day-16---a-string-the.content:
Moon 4 Day 16 - A String the Length of a Bow
A light dusting of snow lies beyond the overhang’s dry edge this morning. You set the short old bowstring sample beside the new fibre work. Its remade eye has survived the small pulls you gave it, but the whole piece is much too short for the bow. The next useful step is to make a candidate at the scale the actual wooden body will need.
The stave comes off its clean rests for inspection. You sight along it and turn the surface into the light. The back is still continuous, and you find no new split that would end the project today. Its condition under a bending load is another question. You lay it down unstrung and use its length to guide the new line, leaving allowance for later attachments and adjustment.
This string gets its own selected portion of prepared nettle fibre. The fine yarn used in the shuttle stays with the netting work. You sort long sound fibres and begin with fuller bundles than those you made for the little fishing line. The joins are spread along the length so that both sides do not thin at the same place.
For the eye, you turn the working bundles back and incorporate their returning fibres gradually into the line. A smooth peg holds the loop while you settle the transition into its neck. The free end remains long enough for a later adjustable attachment. You do not need to fix the final working length before the wooden body’s bending and attachments have been established.
Most of the day goes into keeping the construction even. When a rough splice forms a bulky step, you open that part and spread the fibres more gradually. When the whole candidate is laid out, you compare its straight sections with the worked-back eye and mark where a join needs watching.
Away from your face, you give the line a few gentle repeated pulls around smooth supports. The first pulls take out some settling. Afterwards you inspect the eye, the transition and the marked overlap. They remain together under that modest handling. You coil the full-length candidate loosely and put it with the original sample, keeping the two recognisable.
The stave goes back on its separate rests without a string fitted. You have made the next component, and can examine its own weaknesses while the wood continues to change. There is no need to force both questions into one risky pull tonight. Beneath the rock, the shuttle and the fishing line can already earn their place while the larger project takes the time its materials require.

01_survival/moon-4-day-17---a-small-skin.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 17 - A Small Skin for Cold Hands.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-17---a-small-skin.title: Moon 4 Day 17 - A Small Skin for Cold Hands
01_survival/moon-4-day-17---a-small-skin.content:
Moon 4 Day 17 - A Small Skin for Cold Hands
The thin snow has gone from much of the lower ground, leaving damp leaves and pale patches in the shade. On the short western circuit, the deadfall moved onto firmer ground has taken an adult rabbit. You collect it during the morning check, then inspect and reset the existing device before returning to the overhang.
It is a useful meal, but you find yourself looking most carefully at the skin. Your arms and legs are covered now. Your fingers still stiffen when you stand at the river or stop to inspect a trap. A small pelt cannot improve the whole outfit, but it may be enough to give your hands somewhere warm to rest.
At the separate processing side you remove the skin carefully and clean away the clinging tissue. The rounded support lets you work a small area at a time without pulling against an unsupported edge. There is a sound broad part through the body. You open it on the existing little pelt support with light ties, leaving air behind it and space to examine the margins.
The food goes through fresh cooking in the single pot during the day. Once the dirty work is cleared away and your hands are washed, you sit at the clean stone and consider the garment. Individual fingers would take narrow pieces, many seams and more skill than this little skin deserves. Even a separate thumb would complicate the first pattern.
You bring one hand loosely closed and turn it as though it were inside a small bag. A simple closed pocket could keep the thumb beside the fingers. It would be useful while walking or sitting, and easy to take off for a knot or a cutting edge. Two compact pockets are a more plausible use of the actual skin than two large gloves with long cuffs.
You leave the cutting decision until the pelt is worked and can be laid around both hands. For now it needs the same attention that made the larger skin usable: clean surfaces, protected air and repeated work where it begins to firm. The process is familiar enough to fit around another project.
Before evening you bring the rough bow body off its rests. The pale wood and the coil of new string have been waiting together since yesterday. You sight along the limbs, turning each face into the light. There is room left for careful shaping. Tomorrow you can begin asking the wood to move, while the new little skin continues drying beside its own work area.

01_survival/moon-4-day-18---let-the-limb.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 18 - Let the Limbs Share the Bend.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-18---let-the-limb.title: Moon 4 Day 18 - Let the Limbs Share the Bend
01_survival/moon-4-day-18---let-the-limb.content:
Moon 4 Day 18 - Let the Limbs Share the Bend
The bow body looks even when it lies on the supports. Its movement soon tells a different story. With one tip against a protected patch of firm ground, you give it a small controlled bend, then turn it and compare the other limb. One begins to move while a thicker section on the other barely answers.
The wood has been losing moisture since you roughed it out last moon. It now scrapes more cleanly and the worked surface feels drier, but you keep this first examination gentle. What matters today is seeing where the movement occurs before a deeper bend gives a thin patch too much work.
You lay the body down and mark the stubborn section lightly. A sharp stone edge lifts fine shavings from the belly, the face that will be compressed as the bow bends. The continuous outer back stays untouched. You take away little wood, smooth the worked patch and compare the movement again.
This is tillering: adjusting the distribution of bending through the actual limbs. Carving both sides until they look identical would miss the differences in the grain. So would scraping the most flexible patch simply because it feels easiest under the tool. You follow the section that is still resisting, keeping the change gradual where it meets its neighbours.
The repeated lifts and short checks slow the work, but they begin to give you a useful picture. Both limbs now contribute to the small movement. You stop to examine the wood along the bend, looking for a lifted fibre or a fresh split, then leave it resting without load while you attend to the pelt.
Its thin margins are ready to work. You use a smooth blunt edge and gentle hand flexing, turning each part as it responds. The thicker centre gets more air before you return to it. A worked edge folds around your fingers, which helps you judge how much of the skin will be useful for the proposed hand covers.
Later you make another brief comparison of the bow limbs. Their movement is still modest, and the handle remains substantially thicker than the working lengths. You put the body back on its clean rests, leaving the string beside its own sample. Tomorrow the end attachments can give you another way to examine the two limbs together. For tonight, the small pelt is open under cover and the wood is free to rest.

01_survival/moon-4-day-19---fit-the-stri.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 19 - Fit the String and the Arrow.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-19---fit-the-stri.title: Moon 4 Day 19 - Fit the String and the Arrow
01_survival/moon-4-day-19---fit-the-stri.content:
Moon 4 Day 19 - Fit the String and the Arrow
The first end attachment needs less carving than you expect. You work a shallow seat at the side of the bow’s tip and smooth the surfaces where the string will bear. A sharp corner there would undo much of the care spent on the line. The other tip receives its own seat, with the long back fibres left continuous.
The worked-back eye settles over one end. At the other, you use the free length for an adjustable hitch, giving yourself room to change the fit. The first arrangement leaves the string almost against the wooden body. You draw it a little by hand, watching the two limbs together, then let it return without releasing the line.
A short bend reveals more than the separate floor checks. The thicker limb is still reluctant near its middle. With the string taken off, you shave that area cautiously and try the comparison again. As the movement becomes more evenly shared, you shorten the working string enough to leave a modest resting gap at the handle. The little bow is finally holding its string, though you keep the pulls short and controlled.
Now the arrow has to fit this particular line. You choose the straightest of the three hazel blanks, turning it in the light and passing your fingers along it for a split or damaged place. The shaft stays long enough for the short pull you intend to use, with its front remaining beyond the bow hand.
You smooth a rounded wooden nose at the front and cut a small open groove at the rear. This groove, the nock, receives the string. A short fine plant-thread binding just behind it helps support the end. The first fit pinches the line, so you ease and smooth the groove until it seats and comes away cleanly by hand.
This first practice arrow has no feathers or separate head. It gives you one plain specimen for a short trial, with the other two blanks still on their support. Before any shot, the fit, shaft and bow must all work together; a good-looking groove alone would tell you little about the whole movement.
You take the string off when you stop. The eye and hitch have stayed in place through the restrained pulls, and you examine the contact areas before coiling it. Beside the wood lies a small projectile quite different from the long dart. You leave both ready for a clear working spell, while the pelt still needs its last drying and fitting work.

01_survival/moon-4-day-2---put-the-traps.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 2 - Put the Traps Where the Animals Go.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-2---put-the-traps.title: Moon 4 Day 2 - Put the Traps Where the Animals Go
01_survival/moon-4-day-2---put-the-traps.content:
Moon 4 Day 2 - Put the Traps Where the Animals Go
The rain has left enough soft ground to read what has passed in the night. Along the familiar western circuit, you find a small worn passage beneath the brush, but the ground beside one of your deadfalls has been washed by a trickle. The bait is gone and the weight is down. You cannot tell whether an animal reached it or water and loose debris disturbed the trigger.
You brace the weight before touching the sticks. Grit has worked into a bearing surface, and the ground beneath the upright yields when you press it. Recutting a finer trigger would leave that loose foundation unchanged. You move this existing set a short distance onto firmer ground beside the passage, keeping it clear of the little runoff channel.
Before setting it again, you test the empty mechanism and then make a remote release with a long branch, standing clear of the fall. The fitted pieces release more consistently on their stable base. A small overlap of bark above the trigger turns direct drips away without blocking the animal’s approach. You leave the other working trials where their own signs justify them.
The useful change is in how you arrange the whole circuit. You can approach the sets without repeatedly walking through the narrow passages you want animals to use, and visit them while travelling between familiar work areas. Trapping is beginning to look less like a collection of clever wooden locks and more like a way of working with this particular ground.
Beyond the brush, deer tracks cross a softer patch. You follow them only far enough to see that the animals have moved between the more open feeding ground and cover. A sheltered place lets you watch without standing in the passage. When two red deer appear farther off, you stay still and study where the scrub would interrupt a cast.
On the way home you pass the hazels. Their bare branches carry no new harvest. Food already gathered will give you some time, but the next substantial skin has to come from an animal you can actually take. At the fork towards the neighbours’ approach, you turn back towards your own overhang. For now, you want to know whether you can make this winter work here.
You eat behind the screen with your forearms tucked inside the wrap. The bow wood rests at the craft side. Tomorrow you will deal with the line for a new trap, and then with a problem that follows any larger catch: carrying it home.

01_survival/moon-4-day-20---a-pocket-of-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 20 - A Pocket of Warmth for Each Hand.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-20---a-pocket-of-.title: Moon 4 Day 20 - A Pocket of Warmth for Each Hand
01_survival/moon-4-day-20---a-pocket-of-.content:
Moon 4 Day 20 - A Pocket of Warmth for Each Hand
You lay the small worked skin on the clean surface and rest both hands above it, loosely closed. The useful area is narrower than the fur had made it look. You turn one hand’s outline beside the other, allowing a fold, a sewn edge and enough room to slip each hand out again.
Two simple pockets will fit. Separate thumbs and long cuffs would use the sound margins you need for the seams, so you keep the first design plain. Each thumb will rest beside the fingers inside one rounded compartment. These are covers for warming your hands between tasks; delicate work will still mean taking them off.
You cut the two main pieces and keep their small edge scraps together. On one actual scrap you try the folded seam with newly prepared fine nettle thread. The awl makes holes in the supported margin, and the old bone needle draws the thread through. When the seam bends without pulling the holes into slits, you begin the first pocket.
The hair faces inward. A folded edge and a short line of stitching close the side and rounded end, leaving the wrist open. You put your hand inside before completing the other piece. A corner presses against the thumb, so you ease the fold and resew that short part. The second cover goes more readily because you can compare its shape with the first.
At the wrists, loose retaining ties keep the short openings from slipping away. They sit beneath the ends of the sleeves and loosen easily. There is no need to pull them tight enough to hold the skin against the pulse. You try removing each hand cover with the other hand still inside its own pocket, then put both back on for a walk across the dry ground.
The warmth is most noticeable when you stop. Your fingers lie together inside the fur instead of cooling separately in the wind. You can turn your head towards the valley and remain still long enough to listen. For a little while, the cold does not choose the length of the pause.
Back at the craft stone, you remove the covers before handling the arrow’s nock. They rest as a pair beside you while your fingers check the groove and binding. You have given the new skin one clear job. There is no material left in it for stronger shoes, but your hands now have a useful shelter of their own when they are not working.

01_survival/moon-4-day-21---the-bow-send.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 21 - The Bow Sends Its First Arrow.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-21---the-bow-send.title: Moon 4 Day 21 - The Bow Sends Its First Arrow
01_survival/moon-4-day-21---the-bow-send.content:
Moon 4 Day 21 - The Bow Sends Its First Arrow
The practice ground is clearer now that the lower snow has melted. You walk the short line and the earth bank before bringing the equipment forward, picking out exposed stone and checking the ground beyond the target patch. A thick layer of loose plant material covers the soft landing area.
You take off the new hand covers and put them together on a clean dry piece of bark beside your gear. The loose sleeve near your bow arm is drawn back with a light removable tie so that it will clear the string. Your fingers need to feel the nock and the line directly.
With the bow strung, you inspect its resting shape and make a short slow pull, returning the string under control. Then you seat the single practice arrow. The rounded front stays ahead of your bow hand at the short pull you are using. You settle your grip, turn towards the broad target patch and draw only as far as the recent checks have allowed.
The first release feels abrupt after all the slow woodwork. The arrow goes forward with a visible wobble and reaches the lower part of the plant-covered bank. You lower the bow and walk to it. The wooden nose is marked, but the shaft and nock are intact. You run your fingers along the binding before returning to the same place.
The next few attempts teach you different things. A clumsy release moves the arrow sideways. A steadier hand sends it more directly into the broad patch, though its unfletched flight is still untidy. You keep the distance short and recover the same arrow after every attempt, inspecting both projectile and string rather than filling the air with hurried shots.
When you stop, the string’s eye and hitch are still seated and you find no fresh split along the limbs. You unstring the bow and sight along it beside its earlier resting profile. These brief trials have given you a working beginning. More drying, careful observation and a better-prepared arrow can now be judged against something you have actually used.
You put the hand covers back on for the return. The atlatl and spear remain the equipment you would choose for an immediate serious hunting opportunity. The little bow has another task for now: letting you learn the linked behaviour of wood, string, arrow and release without trying to make a meal depend on the first few shots. At the overhang, you leave it unstrung on the clean rests and set the recovered arrow apart from the two unfinished blanks.

01_survival/moon-4-day-22---give-the-arr.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 22 - Give the Arrow a Tail.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-22---give-the-arr.title: Moon 4 Day 22 - Give the Arrow a Tail
01_survival/moon-4-day-22---give-the-arr.content:
Moon 4 Day 22 - Give the Arrow a Tail
Two long grey-brown feathers are caught beneath a low bush beside the path. Several smaller scraps lie around them, but these have sound shafts and much of their vane still joined. You turn them in the light, comparing their curve before carrying them back separately from the food basket. The bird remains unidentified.
At the clean stone, you take off the hand covers and lay them together on bark. The arrow from yesterday’s trial rolls beneath your fingers. Its rounded nose is marked and the rear binding is still tight. You have seen enough of its wavering flight to give the tail some work to do.
The dart already carries two modest vanes. You leave those where they are and prepare the newly found material for this smaller shaft. A stone edge opens each quill lengthways. You reduce the thick underside until a useful strip will lie against the wood, then trim the two chosen vane sections to a similar outline. Their curves run the same way when you place them side by side.
You try their position before tying anything. The string notch needs room around it, and your release fingers must be able to reach it. Farther forward, the feather edges must pass the bow hand without a hard quill corner catching against skin. You smooth those ends carefully and leave a clear length behind the vanes.
Fresh fine plant thread holds the two strips on opposing sides of the shaft. You secure the ends, then carry light turns between the barbs to keep the quills seated. There is no need to turn the tail into a thick wrapping of cord. When a turn gathers a tuft of feather, you loosen it and separate the barbs before continuing.
This is fletching, the deliberate fitting of a projectile’s tail surfaces. Air pushing against those rear surfaces can help a wandering shaft settle towards its line of travel. The same surfaces add drag, and their attachment must survive the launch. That makes alignment and clearance as useful as an attractive feather shape.
You rotate the finished arrow slowly and inspect each attachment. It is still the same single practice specimen, now with a pair of small vanes. The other two shaft blanks remain on their rests. The afternoon wind has begun to gust across the opening, so you leave the bow unstrung. A calmer spell will let you see what this alteration actually changes.

01_survival/moon-4-day-23---the-fishing-.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 23 - The Fishing Fork Earns Its Place.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-23---the-fishing-.title: Moon 4 Day 23 - The Fishing Fork Earns Its Place
01_survival/moon-4-day-23---the-fishing-.content:
Moon 4 Day 23 - The Fishing Fork Earns Its Place
The river has fallen enough for the shallow margin to clear. From dry ground you can see a quieter pocket beside the current, with pale gravel beneath it. The fish trap remains farther along its usual reach. Today the visible water gives the fishing fork a more immediate job.
You inspect the four-pronged head before going closer. A rough place near one tip needs a light scrape, but the binding below the split is seated and the small spacers have not shifted. The thin points flex a little under your fingers. You leave their spread modest rather than forcing them wider.
On the bank you set the hand covers together on clean bark and keep both feet on the firm dry shelf. The spear is long enough to reach the pocket without a step into the river. You settle there until the disturbance of your arrival has passed. A small fish moves into the quieter water and holds briefly beside the gravel.
You lower the wooden tips close to the surface. The fish’s apparent place shifts as you alter your view, so you bring your body into a steadier position before committing. One short thrust reaches below the image you have been watching. The fish is held between the spread points long enough for you to lift it onto the bank, where you dispatch it promptly.
The return is modest, but it comes from reading a particular stretch of water and choosing an existing tool to suit it. You inspect the fork again before leaving. One tip has a fresh rough mark; the split has not travelled below the binding. Back at camp, a little scraping restores the damaged surface.
You dress the fish at the separate processing side, clean your hands and cook the retained food in the pot that day. While it heats, the vessel cannot also be the clean-water pot you would like beside the fire. The old bark-and-hot-stone route is still available, but it brings another round of heating, transferring and watching seams.
You work around the delay and eat the fish fresh. Once the pot has cooled and been cleaned, you turn it in your hands. Its successful use has made a second vessel worth the labour. One could hold the meal while the other heats water, with their turns at the hearth planned around the same fire. The next pot has a clear task now, and the first can remain in service while you make it.

01_survival/moon-4-day-24---a-second-pot.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 24 - A Second Pot for a Second Job.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-24---a-second-pot.title: Moon 4 Day 24 - A Second Pot for a Second Job
01_survival/moon-4-day-24---a-second-pot.content:
The vessel and witness are shown schematically, not as a scaled drying comparison. Readiness depends on the actual body and fresh-section observations described in the text.
Moon 4 Day 24 - A Second Pot for a Second Job
You take a modest fresh clay charge from the familiar bank exposure, choosing material away from the coarse roots and loose surface debris. At the overhang, you pick through it on a separate clean board. A hard lump that will not soften comes out with the larger grit. The finer natural inclusions stay within the body you are testing.
A small rolled piece bends around your finger without opening into a ragged split. You knead the charge until the wetter and firmer parts feel more alike, then set aside a small witness from the same body. It will dry beside the vessel at a comparable thickness, where a later fresh section can tell you something the pot’s outside cannot.
The first pot is useful for a small charge. This one will be an open cooking bowl with a little more room across the mouth, so that food can be stirred and lifted without crowding the rim. You keep the increase modest. A broad heavy basin would take more clay, be awkward on the hearth and leave a thicker base to dry.
Your thumbs open the centre while the fingers support the outside. You turn the growing wall a little at a time, feeling for the heavy places rather than judging only by its outline. At the bottom, you smooth the change from base to side into a gradual curve. You remember how easily an attractive rim can distract from a thick, poorly joined floor.
As the mouth widens, you keep it level enough to hold a meal without a low pouring edge. There are no added handles or foot ring. Each extra join would need its own careful drying and firing, while the plain body already has a useful job. A damp fingertip finishes the rim and removes the sharp irregularities left by pinching.
You place the bowl and witness on the protected craft-side board, clear of the dirty skin area and the food rack. The natural rock roof keeps rain from falling on them. The screen softens the draught without closing off the air. You leave room to reach the underside later, once the body is firm enough to move without distorting it.
The old pot cooks tonight’s meal. The new one is still soft clay, carrying the promise of a second task rather than doing it. Before leaving the board, you look from its open mouth to the stick you use for stirring. A broad shallow spoon would make this new shape more useful, and it can be worked while the clay slowly firms.

01_survival/moon-4-day-25---a-spoon-from.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 25 - A Spoon from a Piece of Willow.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-25---a-spoon-from.title: Moon 4 Day 25 - A Spoon from a Piece of Willow
01_survival/moon-4-day-25---a-spoon-from.content:
Moon 4 Day 25 - A Spoon from a Piece of Willow
The new bowl’s rim has begun to hold its shape, though the underside is still yielding. You leave it on its board and bring a short piece of freshly cut willow to the craft stone. Its grain runs cleanly along a section broad enough for a shallow spoon. There is no knot where the bowl and handle will meet.
You remove the bark and work down the outside first. The broad end stays thick while the handle narrows behind it. With the wood supported on a small rest, a stone edge takes short shavings in the direction that the grain allows. When a cut begins to lift a long splinter, you turn the piece and approach that place more gently.
The hollow is slower. You choose an edge that can scrape across a small area and begin near the centre of the broad end, keeping the supporting hand clear. Repeated shallow cuts leave a rough depression. You widen it gradually, stopping often to feel how much wood remains beneath it.
A deep ladle would demand a thicker blank and much more hollowing. This spoon only needs enough curve to carry a small mouthful and a smooth edge to move soft food around the pot. You keep the neck substantial, then round the outside of the bowl so that there is no abrupt thin corner beside the handle.
The last work is easier to feel than to see. You scrape the raised fibres from the rim and thumb the handle for splinters. After a rinse, a few rough places rise again. You let the surface settle, then smooth those spots with the edge. The pale wood is left plain, without an oil finish taken from food you do not have to spare.
At the outside hearth, the old pot holds a small meal made from the already stored and properly processed autumn food. The spoon reaches its base without bringing your fingers against the hot rim. Its broad end moves the thickening food more deliberately than the old stirring stick, and the shallow hollow lifts a small portion to cool before you taste it.
You clean it after the meal and leave it where air can reach both faces. Fresh wood will continue to change as it dries, so the neck and rim will need another look. On the craft board beside it, the unfired bowl is still waiting. You have used the drying interval to make an object that helps the working pot now and can serve the second one later.

01_survival/moon-4-day-26---a-straighter.title: Moon 4 Day 26 - A Straighter Flight
01_survival/moon-4-day-26---a-straighter.content:
Moon 4 Day 26 - A Straighter Flight
A quieter morning gives you the comparison the gusts had prevented. You carry the bow and its single fletched arrow to the practice ground, then walk the bank and the short line before setting them down. Loose plant cover still softens the landing patch. A stone exposed near its edge is moved out of the working area.
The hand covers come off together onto clean bark. You secure the loose bow-arm sleeve with the same kind of light temporary tie used before, then inspect the string, its attachments and the wooden limbs. The bow has been resting unstrung. A slow restrained pull lets you compare its movement with the recent trial before seating the arrow.
You turn the shaft to check how the new vanes will pass the bow hand. The quill ends are smooth beneath their bindings, and the rear notch is clear of the feather work. The first draw stays within the short movement you have already used. You let it forward under control, examine the clearance once more and prepare for a release.
The arrow reaches the plant-covered bank with a shorter visible wavering motion than you remember from the bare shaft. You retrieve it and look first at the feather bindings. One small tuft has folded beneath a turn of thread, but the quill strips remain seated. You tease the barbs free before the next attempt.
Over a few short shots, the tail settles more readily when your release is clean. A clumsy pull still sends the shaft to one side. The change is useful to watch, but your hands are also learning, and the morning air differs from the first session. You keep those possibilities together while deciding what deserves the next adjustment.
You stop while the small practice set is still easy to inspect. The same arrow has been recovered each time. Its rounded wooden nose shows the day’s contacts, while the shaft, notch and two vanes remain serviceable. The string comes off, and the bow returns to its rests without carrying a held load.
At the overhang, the new clay bowl is firmer at the rim than below. You wait until it can be supported without sagging, then gently lift it to inspect the base and change the board’s contact position. The witness still yields within its thicker part. Both stay protected from rain and direct heat. Tonight the old pot and new spoon do the cooking work, while the bow and unfinished vessel wait for their next useful step.

01_survival/moon-4-day-3---the-line-must.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 3 - The Line Must Hold in the Wet.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-3---the-line-must.title: Moon 4 Day 3 - The Line Must Hold in the Wet
01_survival/moon-4-day-3---the-line-must.content:
Moon 4 Day 3 - The Line Must Hold in the Wet
At the craft stone, you twist a short new length of nettle line from the retained prepared fibre. The remade bowstring sample stays with its own work. This line has a different job: it must run freely at a trap and keep holding after a night outside.
