You put a separate short offcut in water while you finish the new line’s end. A smooth peg gives the fixed eye something to bear against. Under a gentle pull, the line beds down and its twist tightens. You work the adjustable loop back and forth, feeling where it catches against the eye.
The damp sample behaves differently. Its surface fibres have risen, and the loop moves less freely. You notice that one rough place on the peg is catching them. After smoothing it, you compare the dry and wet samples again. Some of the resistance belonged to the support; some remains in the wet line itself. The distinction matters because a stronger-looking cord would not have removed the roughness.
Next you test attachment and trigger movement separately. With a modest wrapped stone held close to the ground, you can see whether a join creeps without standing beneath a suspended load. You also check the line where it bends around its support. A sharp change of direction is beginning to polish and flatten the fibres, so you give that contact a broader, smoother surface.
This cordage check gives you useful changes to make before putting the new arrangement into service. You set the line and trigger aside for a later field trial. The old broken fox snare has been gone for weeks; its one catch is a poor reason to hurry another uncertain set into the brush.
Outside, the air is clearing and the wet ground is losing its shine. You take the atlatl, dart and stone-pointed spear out long enough to inspect them. The dart’s rear seat and feather bindings remain sound. The spear point is firm. You rehearse how you would lay the heavier weapon within reach before using the thrower, instead of trying to manage both in the casting hand.
The exposed forearms cool quickly when you stop moving. You draw the wrap around them and go back under cover. A skin large enough to change that will also be heavier than the little skins you have carried before. You lay two suitable light poles beside the working stone for tomorrow.

01_survival/moon-4-day-4---build-for-the.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 4 - Build for the Load You Hope to Bring Back.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-4---build-for-the.title: Moon 4 Day 4 - Build for the Load You Hope to Bring Back
01_survival/moon-4-day-4---build-for-the.content:
Moon 4 Day 4 - Build for the Load You Hope to Bring Back
Your small hide sling was made for a small load. The foraging basket is more useful, but a heavy awkward parcel can pull against its weave and leave you trying to hold everything in place with one hand. Before going after a larger animal, you want something that will carry a secured load close to your back.
You cut the two light wooden rails to a manageable length and smooth the places that will touch you or a binding. Two shorter crosspieces keep the rails apart. You bind the joints firmly and add a diagonal cord brace, then twist the empty frame gently to see where it racks sideways. One joint turns until you reseat and tighten it.
For the shoulder bands, you plait selected retained bast strips into broader lengths. At the lower bearing points you fold bark around a little dry grass to spread the pressure. These pads belong to the carrier, not a new garment. The load ties are separate, so you can open them without loosening a shoulder band.
You begin with a few wrapped stones secured low against the frame. Around the nearby ground, the first arrangement hangs too far away and shifts when you step across a fallen branch. You bring the parcel closer and redistribute the ties. The frame then moves more quietly with your body. You stop before the trial becomes a contest in how much you can lift; tomorrow’s ground will be less convenient than this short circuit.
Later, carrying only the hunting equipment, you return to the place from which you watched the deer. You see them emerge farther along the edge of cover. Their movement gives you time to examine a shallow opening where a cast would have room to leave your hand. The nearer brush would interfere with the atlatl’s long dart. You can wait beyond that brush instead of trying to throw through it.
You leave without approaching them. Back at home, the empty frame stands beside the protected cutting tools. You make sure its ties are ready to open and close, then turn the fire towards the meal. There is no one to take the other end of a load or stay with an animal while you fetch help. Preparing for that is part of the hunt.

01_survival/moon-4-day-5---a-deer-of-you.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 5 - A Deer of Your Own.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-5---a-deer-of-you.title: Moon 4 Day 5 - A Deer of Your Own
01_survival/moon-4-day-5---a-deer-of-you.content:
Moon 4 Day 5 - A Deer of Your Own
Frost lies in the shaded hollows when you set out. You take the cutting tools and empty carrying frame, the stone-pointed spear, and the thrower with its pointed dart. The ground where you watched yesterday is within a manageable return on your own side of the river. If an opportunity comes, you will have daylight to deal with it.
You settle beyond the brush that would foul the long cast. While waiting, you keep your arms inside the wrap. The spear rests where you can recover it without crossing the opening. You listen to the valley and make small changes in your position as the air moves across the slope.
When the deer emerge, the larger animal remains partly screened. A smaller antlerless one comes into the opening and pauses. You have room to lift the dart and follow through. The cast reaches it; the animal bounds away, falters in the lower brush and falls.
You stay where you are until its movement has ceased, then approach cautiously with the spear. It is dead. For a while you simply stand beside it. The hunt with the neighbours had ended in work among other hands. Here the weight of the animal, the food and the skin are all yours to deal with.
The dart has come through with a damaged wooden tip but an intact shaft, rear seat and feather bindings. You recover it before beginning the work. A fresh flake opens the necessary cuts, and you release heat from the body while keeping the skin and dirty material clear of the food you intend to retain. Working alone, you keep turning and supporting the parts instead of reaching through a place where your cutting hand is going.
You preserve the main skin as you remove it. There is a small opening from the dart and some uneven edge, but a much larger continuous panel than any loose material you have owned. You remove clinging tissue while it is still easy to lift. Then you divide what you can use promptly into manageable carrying parcels.
The frame earns its place on the return. One trip carries the protected skin and a limited food parcel; a second brings further selected food and the recovered equipment. Clean bark keeps food away from the frame’s dirty contacts. You leave the remaining carcass material at the working place rather than promise yourself another supply that you cannot protect.
At the overhang, you open the skin immediately at the dirty-work side and continue cleaning it before spreading it over temporary supports. The retained cuts go onto a separate airy bark-covered rest, clear of the sleeping and skin work. The cold weather buys a short interval for cooling and prompt use. You cook a fresh meal at the outside hearth. The remaining food will need attention tomorrow.
As the light goes, the whole skin lies open where you can see its shape. There is warmth in it, but a great deal of work still stands between this evening and a garment.

01_survival/moon-4-day-6---support-the-s.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 6 - Support the Skin Before You Scrape.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-6---support-the-s.title: Moon 4 Day 6 - Support the Skin Before You Scrape
01_survival/moon-4-day-6---support-the-s.content:
Moon 4 Day 6 - Support the Skin Before You Scrape
The shaded puddles still hold ice in the morning. You inspect the food left on its separate rest and put the remaining selected cuts through fresh cooking during the day. The deer has given you useful meals, but bringing home a larger share next time will require a better way of keeping it. For now, the skin is the work you cannot put off.
You have been cleaning it across low supports, moving around a broad slippery surface. A thin part pulls away from the edge just as you begin to work a thicker one. You stop and fetch a sound round pole for a more controlled support.
After removing projecting knots and roughness, you smooth a broad rounded face. Its lower end bears securely against a ground stop, and its upper part settles into a low forked support. When you lean against it, the pole stays still. This fleshing beam puts a small part of the skin at a useful working height while the rest hangs clear.
You drape the skin hair-side down over the rounded wood. On the uppermost patch, the pale inner surface stays supported as you lift the last clinging tissue with the scraper. Short pushes work better than trying to clear a wide strip in one forceful stroke. Where the thickness changes, you ease the pressure and turn the skin so that you can see what the edge is doing.
The result is easier to judge. A patch that looked clean while it sagged now shows a film you can lift; a thin edge needs gentler handling than the thicker centre. You work around the small opening left by the dart rather than pulling the whole skin against it. The supported action lets you clean more evenly without chasing a moving fold across the ground.
Once the main cleaning is done, you arrange a larger open support at the existing dirty-work side. Light ties hold the margins apart without drawing them hard enough to tear. Air can reach the surface, and you can lift and turn the skin to find places that remain damp. The little rabbit support stays separate; this larger panel has a different span and weight.
Before leaving it, you lay two short guide lengths across the skin, then hold them against an arm and lower leg. The main panel has useful room, though the damaged edges will affect the cutting layout. You will work out the shoulder and arm coverage alongside the leg pieces while the material develops, keeping enough overlap for movement.
After washing, you sit at the clean craft side and scrape the damaged wooden tip of the recovered dart back into a serviceable shape. Its next field use will wait for another check. The bow remains on its rests. Today has been occupied by a less graceful piece of wood, and by learning how to put a whole skin under control.

01_survival/moon-4-day-7---work-the-skin.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 7 - Work the Skin Until It Bends.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-7---work-the-skin.title: Moon 4 Day 7 - Work the Skin Until It Bends
01_survival/moon-4-day-7---work-the-skin.content:
Moon 4 Day 7 - Work the Skin Until It Bends
The skin has changed overnight. Yesterday it sagged between its supports; this morning its thinner margins hold a shallow curve when you loosen them. The centre still feels cool and heavier. You turn it into the moving air and begin at an edge that is ready to work.
There is no useful supply of dressing fat put aside, and you do not want to leave your winter clothing waiting on another kill. You remember a different route: a carefully cleaned skin can be dried, scraped and repeatedly worked until it becomes flexible. Such clothing needs care, especially in wet weather, but the materials for this attempt are already in front of you.
The rounded beam gives you a firm surface again. This time you are attending to the skin itself rather than lifting clinging flesh. With a smooth, blunt working edge you ease a small area, turn it, and compare the bend with the neighbouring patch. Where the scraper begins to bite, you change its angle and lighten your hand. The sound skin must survive the work.
After scraping, you draw the patch back and forth over the smooth wood, then gather it in your hands and flex it in several directions. At first it wants to return to its old shape. Gradually it folds more easily. You move on, overlapping the worked areas so that stiff bands do not remain between them. The thicker centre needs another spell in the air before it responds in the same way.
The labour takes much of the useful daylight. There are pauses for the ordinary work of the camp and a meal from the autumn stores, but you keep returning to the skin. By afternoon the changed surface is easy to feel. A worked margin settles over your wrist; the neglected section beside it stands away like thin board. You bring that section onto the beam and continue.
By evening the useful body of the skin will bend around an arm or a calf without forcing a hard crease. Some of the thick, uneven margins will be better left out of the garments. You open it under the dry part of the overhang, away from food and bedding, with air able to reach both sides. There is still cutting and sewing to do, but the material has become something you can shape.
As you put the scraper away, you rub your aching palms together. Preparing the skin has taken more effort than its pale inner surface suggests. Tomorrow you can decide how much warmth its actual shape will give you.

01_survival/moon-4-day-8---find-four-cov.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 8 - Find Four Coverings in One Skin.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-8---find-four-cov.title: Moon 4 Day 8 - Find Four Coverings in One Skin
01_survival/moon-4-day-8---find-four-cov.content:
Moon 4 Day 8 - Find Four Coverings in One Skin
You spread the worked skin hair-side down and lay four lengths of cord across it. Two carry the length from shoulder to wrist; the others reach from beneath the hem of your wrap to the tops of your foot coverings. They are simple body guides, taken while bending an elbow and a knee so that the finished pieces will have room to move.
At first the four shapes seem to fit easily. Then you allow for the width around each limb, the edges that must overlap, and the material that stitching will use. The skin becomes a much smaller resource. You move the guides again, reserving the broader sound areas for your legs and turning the arm pieces to avoid the dart opening.
The result is a modest set: two loose sleeves and two overlapping lower-leg wraps. Their upper ends will meet the existing body wrap, and the lower ends will reach the low foot covers. The old clothes can do their present jobs while the new pieces cover the gaps. There is no sound area left for the stronger footwear you had also hoped to make.
Before cutting the main panels, you take a narrow piece from an uneven margin. You fold its edge, make holes with the awl, and try a seam with fine thread newly twisted from the retained nettle fibre. The old bone needle passes through the prepared holes without being forced. Pulled flat, the join looks neat; bent over your wrist, it is too tight. You ease the stitches and try again until the fold can open without dragging the holes into slits.
Now you cut, supporting the skin while guiding a sharp flake through it. Each piece is returned to its place in the layout before you move to the next. The four panels, a few small reinforcement tabs and the seam scraps account for the useful area. You keep the pieces together on the clean craft side once the cutting debris has been cleared away.
The late afternoon goes into the long sleeve seams. You bring each panel round into a loose tapered tube, leaving enough ease at the elbow. At the upper edge you fold a small tab that will tie to the body wrap near the shoulder. This takes the weight off a tight band around the arm. The calf pieces remain open along their overlapping edges so that you will be able to loosen or remove them easily.
When the light fails, the pieces are recognisable as clothing. The last attachments and a proper fit must wait for daylight. You put them under cover and draw your familiar wrap close for another night.

01_survival/moon-4-day-9---warmth-that-m.filePath: 01_Survival/Moon 4 Day 9 - Warmth That Moves With You.md
01_survival/moon-4-day-9---warmth-that-m.title: Moon 4 Day 9 - Warmth That Moves With You
01_survival/moon-4-day-9---warmth-that-m.content:
Moon 4 Day 9 - Warmth That Moves With You
The first sleeve goes on easily until you raise your arm. Its upper edge pulls against the old wrap, and the seam turns towards your elbow. You loosen the temporary attachment and let the sleeve settle where your arm wants it to lie. A little more freedom at the top makes a large difference.
You finish the folded tabs and tie each one beneath the corresponding shoulder edge of the body wrap, using sound material clear of the old repair. The sleeves hang from those attachments instead of gripping your upper arms. Their seams hold the shape loosely around the elbows, and their ends stop at your wrists so that your hands remain free for work. The hair faces inward; the dull brown skin faces the weather.
The leg coverings take longer to fit alone. You bring each panel round the leg with a generous side overlap, then add loose retaining ties. A separate narrow keeper rises to the existing waist fastening and supports the top beneath the wrap’s hem. When you crouch, the overlap opens a little and settles back as you stand. At the ankles the panels lie over the tops of the pale foot covers without replacing them.
You walk across the dry ground, climb the short uneven approach and kneel beside the craft stone. The first keeper is too short: it draws on the leg panel when you step up. You lengthen it, retie it, and repeat the movement. Once the ties stay in place without cutting into your legs, you trim the few projecting threads and put away the needle.
Outside the sheltered mouth, the wind is much more noticeable on your face than on your shins. For the first time you can stand still with your arms down without the cold finding the whole length of them. You spend the afternoon on the nearby trap circuit, carrying out the usual checks while paying attention to the new seams. The improved deadfall ground is still firm. There is no catch to bring home today, but you return with your clothes sitting where you put them.
The tan body wrap, full fur cap and low foot covers are familiar; the darker sleeves and leg panels make the outfit feel complete enough to work in. Stronger soles and hand protection will still be useful, but you can give the next project sustained attention without repeatedly stopping to warm bare limbs.
At dusk you loosen the new pieces and hang them separately where air can reach the skin. You sit with the ordinary evening meal and flex a slightly firm sleeve margin between your fingers. Keeping the clothing serviceable is part of owning it now.

02_reflections/reflection-01---arrival--.title: Reflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-01---arrival--.content:
Reflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1
End of Moon 1 Day 1 · Arrival near new moon · Continuous Day 1 · Read after Moon 1 Day 1 - Immediate Priorities.
Everything remembered, almost nothing held
You lie inside the low debris frame and listen to the valley disappear into darkness. The work of the afternoon still aches in your hands. There is no fire to watch and no food left for tomorrow. Bark covers a little skin; dry litter separates you from some of the ground. Every sound beyond the entrance reaches you without a visible source.
The departure is already beyond recovery. People who could explain this valley with instruments are somewhere behind you in time, facing an approaching catastrophe. You cannot send a question back or return for one forgotten object. Their knowledge is present in your memory, but their workshops, shelter and company are absent.
You expected the difference. You are only beginning to feel it. A useful stone edge has cost failed strikes. A bed has taken hours of carrying. The future you came to change has narrowed tonight to whether this covering stays in place and whether the ground takes too much heat from your body.
What is real tonight
You have a chosen terrace, a provisional shelter, a useful flake and a sound hammer cobble. A short bark line can hold the rough waist panels. You have found a seep and positively identified a little food. Those observations give tomorrow a starting point; they do not establish the valley’s yearly supply, ownership or safety.
The nuts you collected have been eaten. The dry fuel is merely a pile: without a prepared ignition kit it supplies no warmth. The seep has relieved thirst, but the water is untreated. There is no vessel, no spear, no animal skin and no dependable protection for your feet.
Your altered lifespan does not make a fall, a wound or cold harmless. The gaps between what you can describe and what your hands can do matter immediately. They will matter again at every larger scale.
A home has not been granted
You have seen enough ground to choose a stopping place, not enough to understand its occupants. The absence of people on your short circuit proves little. Other humans might know the nearby resources far better than you; predators might use routes you have not noticed. Darkness removes the small advantage of seeing an approach.
You keep the cutting edge where it will not injure you when you reach for it, and leave the shelter entrance usable. These are small precautions, not a defence. Tomorrow’s observation must include tracks, unstable branches and a way to move away from trouble, alongside useful plants and stones.
Loneliness is part of the exposure. There is nobody to keep watch while you sleep, hold a branch while you bind it, or fetch water while your hands are occupied. The work plan must allow for one body.
The first intentions
Tomorrow begins with food, inspection of the bed and covering, and care of the edges already made. A complete ignition kit is the first major preparation. You need its parts to work together before an ember can become an ordinary service. An attempt at fire cannot spend the light required to keep the shelter usable or find another meal.
A container and water treatment will follow only when the materials and tools support them. Protection for skin and feet remains urgent. You cannot name those needs into completed equipment, and the same bark tie cannot hold two different things at once.
The long purpose remains rebuilding enough capability to change humanity’s eventual fate. The immediate test is smaller and exacting: make tomorrow possible without spending the conditions which made tonight possible. If the first shelter fails, repair outranks the ignition experiment. If food collection fails, the experiment shortens. Your memory must serve those decisions rather than distract you from them.

02_reflections/reflection-02---full-moon.title: Reflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15
02_reflections/reflection-02---full-moon.content:
Reflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15
End of Day 15 · First full moon · Read after Day 15 - Fire Holds Shape.
A place to return to
The brightening sky gives the valley a shape beyond the little circle of fire. You have spent half a moon here. A remembered civilisation still fills your mind, but what keeps you alive is smaller: one dry resting place, a maintained ignition set, a vessel which can sometimes tolerate repeated water treatment, useful cutting edges and the food you can carry back.
Those are real gains. Their maintenance is also real work. A bark seam has already interrupted the water routine. Clothing is still scraps of plant covering and small animal panels. The fact that you expect to live for centuries does not make tonight’s exposed skin less vulnerable.
The camp has begun to acquire an arrangement: clean work above the ordinary hearth, animal processing on another flank, firing on separate bare ground. That organisation matters as much as another small object. The bed and water source cannot follow the dirty work wherever convenience suggests.
A fired shape is still a question
The clay vessel remains in the firing bed, cooling. You want tomorrow to reveal something useful. That desire cannot decide the result.
You have formed, dried and heated a specimen. You have not inspected it cold, established that it holds water or shown that it survives repeated cooking. A useful outcome would ease part of the water problem. Failure would cost clay work and fuel, but it should also identify a more specific question for the next trial.
The nettle bundle has been waiting downstream for a different reason. It might supply fibre, but the stems must separate without becoming weak. Pottery and retting both expose the same mistaken temptation: treating elapsed time as completion because you know the name of the process.
What supplies the time to think
Nuts still carry most meals. Small-game returns add useful food and small material lots, but three mechanisms are not a dependable supply of animals. A needle and an awl help use what has already been caught; they do not enlarge the animals or bring the next catch.
The firing has drawn down the dry-fuel reserve. Your food buffer is short enough that another long experiment immediately competes with gathering. The cold will increase those costs, while the nearby patches can be exhausted.
You have no identified neighbours or agreement about this ground. That does not mean the valley is empty. The spear’s wooden point and your inexperience would offer little reassurance against several skilled people, and an animal can approach while your attention is on a seam. Work should keep an exit available rather than turn the shelter into a place where you are cornered.
Intentions before the next moon
First replenish usable fuel and inspect the cold clay load. Keep the bark treatment route working whether the vessel succeeds or fails. Check the nettle bundle by its material condition, then allocate any actual fibre between immediate repairs and future work.
Improve dry resting coverage and body protection with the modest materials you can obtain. Do not make clothing depend on finding a large hide. Maintain the small trap circuit, but keep gathering time until returns justify changing that balance.
Observation can extend the known ground in short affordable outings. You need routes, material sources and warning signs; you do not need an ambitious excursion that consumes the last food margin. A smaller experiment with a clear result is worth more than several unfinished objects competing for the same fuel and cord.
At the next review, ask whether the camp is less easily interrupted: another failed seam, a wet night or an empty trap circuit should not immediately consume tomorrow’s choices.

02_reflections/reflection-03---new-moon-.title: Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-03---new-moon-.content:
Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1
End of Day 30 · New moon · Read after Moon 2 Day 1 - Six Attempts and No Advantage.
The valley is inhabited
The night has no bright moon to broaden the view beyond camp. Since the last reflection, you have seen a maintained fire beyond the ridge, watched skilled people at their work, approached them and been made to leave.
The first pitch was based on a true possibility and a false expectation. New knowledge might be useful to them; possessing it did not make your awkward demonstration better than their familiar cordage and practised handling. They had no reason to give you the time or space you wanted.
Their warning belongs to that encounter. It neither proves that they mean to hunt you down nor assures you that another visit will be welcome. Your smoke makes concealment uncertain. You should plan for the possibility that this terrace is already known, without inventing an intention you have not observed.
A lever has not made a hunter
Today’s six attempts answer a modest question: the wooden thrower can launch the prepared trial dart on some attempts. It has not supplied stable release, accuracy or a demonstrated advantage.
Three hand casts and three thrower casts are not a fair contest between two perfected technologies. You are inexperienced with one and uncomfortable with this particular projectile in both. The shaft is green and changing. The rear engagement, your timing and the flight need work before you can isolate a useful improvement.
The second shaft is still a bowed blank. The feather lot is unused. No pointed or fletched hunting dart exists. The ordinary spear remains the immediate defensive object; the atlatl is an experiment which can occupy your hands while leaving you exposed.
Even a much better cast would not supply a companion to watch another exit, help recover a wounded animal or stand guard during processing. Hunting alone is an organisational limit as well as a technical one.
Improvements which still need supply
The first pot failed its operating test. A better-looking new shape would not remove the need to compare clay, drying, firing and leakage separately. The small bark vessel remains the water-treatment route, with repairs and handling costs.
The cage has supplied a fish, and the damaged snare still supplied useful fox meat and a narrow skin panel. Those gains were worth keeping; neither establishes a regular food source or a winter garment. The fox covers one shoulder, not the entire core.
Prepared fibre and usable line are small, finite lots. Spun yarn is not a substitute for every binding. Another trap, a dart fitting, a broader covering and an escape provision could all demand the same material. A new fibre batch must start with your own harvesting and pass its own checks before you can spend the output.
The measuring staff and scratches are useful because they make comparisons repeatable. They are not a balance, a calibrated metre or an agreement with the neighbours. Their value will be shown when a disappointing record changes tomorrow’s allocation.
Priorities before the next full moon
Keep supply ahead of pride. Gather, shell, treat water and collect genuinely usable dry wood. Protect and inspect the existing reserve; a long demonstration or reconnaissance draws on food even when it produces nothing.
Begin the additional fibre batch. Work towards better bedding and a coarse body covering using available plant material, adding independently acquired pelts where they help. Do not wait for a deer to provide an entire wardrobe.
Inspect an alternative route and resting site. A possibility on the landscape is not a supplied refuge: any cached food, fuel or spare kit must be made or transferred from the actual stock. Decide what you would carry and what you would leave before a hurried departure forces that decision.
Retain short, inspected casting sessions and change only a manageable part of the experiment. If curious neighbours watch, do not interpret attention as admiration, access or an alliance. Their own practised spear use deserves to be taken seriously.
Before the next review, look for a camp that is harder to interrupt and a projectile system whose limitations you can describe more precisely. There is no need to win a contest in order to learn something useful.

02_reflections/reflection-04---full-moon.title: Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15
02_reflections/reflection-04---full-moon.content:
Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15
End of Day 44 · Full moon · Read after Moon 2 Day 15 - A Frame Before a Promise.
The gap between a design and a life
Through breaks in cloud, moonlight reaches the open valley. You can see more of the ground beyond camp than on the last new moon, but seeing ground is not knowing who moves through it. The people beyond the ridge remain independent of your plans.
Since the last reflection, they have watched your camp, watched your odd lever and shown you what a practised spear arm can do. The device interested an observer; your landings offered little advantage. Another adult warned you from an occupied nut patch. Curiosity did not grant access, and a quiet departure did not grant protection.
You are less certain that the first useful thing you show must be a weapon. A repeatable method could still matter later. For now, proving yourself to an audience has to compete with the need to get through a colder night. Their experience is not an obstacle invented for you to overcome. It is part of the world you have entered, and you have learned how much of it you cannot yet match.
Several improvements, very little margin
The repaired fish closure has remained usable, with a few small catches. The deadfalls have supplied a rabbit; its meat was useful immediately, while its skin created urgent work and is still unfinished. Neither route gives a dependable meal each day.
The bed has gained a small retaining pad and renewed loose material. Your grass back panel is wearable in a short dry trial, yet your front, head and feet remain poorly protected. You have used real fibre, yarn, cord and gathering time to reach those modest results. Remembering a coat is easier than obtaining a coat’s worth of material and making it survive use.
The second retting batch has left the pool. Only a selected 18 g portion has become accepted dry fibre; the coarse remainder is not stock simply because it lies under cover. The vessel samples remain unfired. They can wait. The one repaired bark container has supported water treatment and small acorn charges, at a pace that exposes its limited capacity.
The acorns have been another meal route, not a store. All the new input is now processed and eaten. You have about two recent kernel portions remaining, with no reserve of dried meat and no large hide waiting to rescue the clothing problem. The next gathering round matters more than the number of methods you can name.
A frame is an intention made visible
Today you have set a light rail and the first return ribs beside the old roof. One brace foot moved during the trial; you unloaded it and corrected the seat. That small failure changed the work before it was hidden beneath covering.
The open frame gives your decision a physical shape: a compact sleeping chamber, still in the same footprint, with the exit kept clear and the fire outside. It does not yet shelter the new side. Four ribs and the protected cover lot still need fitting. A claim about winter would be premature even after they are installed.
You can feel the attraction of finishing everything tomorrow. The food account prevents that wish becoming a plan. Construction consumes the daylight which produces meals and usable fuel. You need to build in stages without making an exhausted, hungry body the hidden price of a better-looking roof.
What must happen before the next review
Finish and inspect the return covering and its junction, protect and renew the whole resting layer, and work towards practical front, head and foot protection. Keep fuel and tinder dry. A second tested water vessel and a spare ignition provision remain worthwhile, but neither has been made. The fallback bench is still a route to an unsupplied place.
Continue short private projectile practice only when it fits the survival work. A second suitable dart and better release may eventually narrow the gap. A scouting outing can teach approach and retrieval limits without forcing a dangerous cast or requiring a deer kill. Contact can remain limited; there is no reason to assume that the next observer offers an alliance.
A wet spell, a poor harvest or a shifting support should change the allocation immediately. You are beginning to choose work by what it makes reliable, rather than by how far ahead its idea belongs. Before any distant industry can exist, you need a place where you can rest, wake and do useful work again.
Author continuity snapshot

02_reflections/reflection-05---new-moon-.title: Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-05---new-moon-.content:
Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1
End of Day 59 · New moon · Read after Moon 3 Day 1 - A Material Before a Vessel.
The work is serving the wrong shelter
The valley darkens beyond the terrace. On the separate test stone, two cold fired pieces keep their small, unheroic shapes. Behind you, the repaired lean-to carries more covering than it did at the last full moon. Neither comparison piece is a pot, and the shelter which has carried you this far is still a poor commitment for the colder season approaching.
You have been asking how to improve the camp you happened to make. The more useful question is where a winter home ought to be. Each extra armful on this roof leaves you responsible for that roof, its wet edges and the same exposed ground beneath it. The work already spent is a reason to understand the design, not a reason to remain under it.
There is rocky ground within the known landscape. A shallow sound overhang, if one can be found with dry floor, manageable runoff and access to water, could supply the hardest part of a roof. A screen and an insulated bed beneath it would still take work. You would need to inspect overhead stone, drips, old occupation and the route rather than deciding that any dark recess is a home. Tomorrow’s first useful enquiry is whether such a place exists, not another addition to the present lean-to.
Make warmth cover a person
The grass screens, plain rabbit crown and narrow fox shoulder strip have earned particular small results. The bast soles stay on better through a short dry test. Together they still leave sides, limbs, ears and much nape exposed. It is becoming harder to defend this arrangement as the beginning of a winter outfit simply because you can describe each component.
A larger sound skin could cover shoulders and core with an overlap. A real piece would have to come from an actual catch, an earned processing share or an exchange somebody willingly accepts; knowing the shape does not supply the skin. Your own small-game pelts can cover smaller gaps after preparation, and layers already made may be better reassigned than accumulated on the body.
Head, enclosed feet and lower limbs will then need attention. Dry plant lining and bedding can contribute warmth without pretending to be waterproof. The useful order is substantial coverage, workable fit and repeated care, rather than another ingenious fastening on an inadequate amount of material.
Give food a seasonal purpose
The remaining food margin is short. Small catches and the acorn route have supplied meals, not a reserve to finance an industry. Hazel returns will not remain those of arrival as the season advances. Winter provision needs a combination: sound nuts collected while available, protected storage, a manageable processing route and continuing animal-food opportunities.
Keeping untreated acorns dry is different from keeping a bowl of wet meal. A raised, inspectable store and cleaner crushing work could make a gathering session useful beyond the next meal. The fish cage can continue; the ordinary wooden spear can be tried again when shallow clear margins justify it. Better tools should widen actual opportunities, not create animals or a daily yield on paper.
You can compress the uneventful rounds in your account. They remain necessary work, but the handbook should explain what changes capacity: shelter that stays dry, a useful garment, a better processing arrangement, a joint which survives use. A recital of every journey would obscure the dependencies you came to reveal.
Put vigilance in proportion
The canid visit and the warning at the occupied patch are reasons to watch, keep distance and respect access. They do not require the next cycle to become a sequence of escape preparations. The fallback bench is still unbuilt and unsupplied. Its existence as a candidate does not make another home ready or oblige you to spend the coming weeks furnishing one.
Maintain the wooden spear and choose a better hunting configuration when materials allow. The local makers’ stone-pointed weapons offer a real comparison; a supported point and a sound binding would be worthwhile work. Continue improving the atlatl where the dart and actual hunting opportunity justify it. Neither weapon removes danger, and neither needs to be a performance aimed at winning an audience.
Relations can develop through ordinary useful contact and respect for what these people already know. The observers’ interest is an opening, without a lesson, skin transfer, food share or promise yet. Contributing and learning can matter before you have a device that somebody independently copies.
Make the next pot earn its place
Two ignition kits and two tested bark vessels reduce particular interruptions. Both pairs still share your camp’s protection and your care. A better dry home would protect that productive capacity as well as your body; preparing to carry essentials if necessary belongs to ordinary judgement, not the main building programme.
Today’s thin fired piece remains coherent under a short wetting check; the thicker one has a new hairline. Neither holds a charge as a vessel. Their differing heat histories are unknown, and the old cracked pot remains rejected for food and drinking-water use.
One modest new vessel is worth pursuing for the meals and water work it could simplify. Form it deliberately and allow its drying to run beside clothing and food preparation, then fire and test it when its condition permits. Keep the bark route functioning. There is no need to defer warmth until a specimen has become a pot, or to invent a larger firing industry before there is a useful container.
Build the conditions for the mission
You came to give humanity more time and capability before the impact which your departure civilisation could not avert. Remembering a furnace or spacecraft does not shorten the material work between this valley and those systems. Cold, poorly supplied people cannot maintain that work just because its distant purpose is immense.
The next cycle therefore begins with the foundations: seek a better roof, make real coverage, organise seasonal food and develop useful hunting and cooking equipment. The older camp has kept you alive; you can leave it when a better site is actually ready. You do not yet know the place, the source of a larger skin or the next catch. You know enough to put those questions ahead of another catalogue of trials.

02_reflections/reflection-06---full-moon.title: Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16
02_reflections/reflection-06---full-moon.content:
Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16
End of Day 74 · Full moon · Read after Moon 3 Day 16 - Let the Joint Carry the Thrust.
A better place for the work
Moonlight reaches the ground beyond the overhang. You sit inside the dry strip, where rock rather than another layer of gathered branches carries most of the roof. The entrance turns the wind before it meets the bed. The small earth-filled bay is still only a small bay; the bark and brush around it remain useful.
At the new moon you decided that maintaining the camp you happened to find was consuming too much of the coming winter. You have now inspected another site, made it occupiable and moved the working essentials. The old lean-to is abandoned as the home. Nothing about that move has made the rock permanently safe or the weather harmless, but the daily building question has changed. You can improve a dry working place instead of continually earning the same poor roof again.
There is also a real arrangement beneath it: bed apart from stores, food off damp ground, dirty skin work outside, and ordinary combustion beyond the drip edge. These relationships are not spectacular inventions. They make the useful objects less likely to interrupt one another.
Coverage is beginning to look like clothing
The large worked skin obtained in the earlier exchange now wraps shoulders and core. Easing its fit lets you work without making the old repair carry every reach. The narrow fox piece from your own earlier catch has moved entirely from beneath that wrap to the ears and nape of the rabbit cap. You did not need to acquire the same small improvement twice.
The two recent rabbit pelts now cover a foot apiece, with grass inside and the old bast soles beneath. They close the exposed tops and hold removable lining during brief dry camp work. The first useful result is modest but tangible: toes need no longer be left open every time you stand to work.
They are thin, mechanically worked skins rather than durable tanned footwear. Damp, rubbing and sustained travel remain hard questions. Lower legs and much of the working arms are still exposed; no pair of leggings or sleeves is hidden in the material already used. The next wardrobe work needs real material and a suitable process, not a declaration that you are winter-ready.
Food has a route beyond the next handful
Protected nuts and a separate clean stone pair make the acorn work more deliberate. You can leave most of the input dry and process a limited meal charge, rather than wetting the reserve to make the store look productive. Keeping coarse particles in the work improves preparation without changing the water treatment into a universal recipe.
The two rabbit catches and the recent spear-caught fish have all been eaten. They gave food and, in the rabbits’ case, real skin material. They are not hanging somewhere as preserved meat. The trap checks remain variable, the hazel season is declining and the new home does not replenish a basket merely by keeping it dry.
This is enough organisation to choose useful workshop sessions, with continued gathering and processing around them. It is not food security through the winter. Better animal-food access, actual fat when available and protected usable reserves remain more urgent than a sequence of ever more refined demonstration targets.
A weapon is becoming a system of parts
The stone point has a compatible seat, restrained wood and an inspectable binding. Today’s controlled plant-target thrusts leave the insert aligned, with an outer turn taken up after settling. That result explains the joint better than merely holding an assembled spear in a picture of your mind.
It does not tell you how a moving animal will be approached, struck or recovered. The old wooden spear remains useful and the multi-pronged fishing design is still ahead. The atlatl has not gained a new hunting dart merely because another weapon now has a stone tip. Select the limiting part of that system next, then seek the opportunity to use it rather than repeating broad target practice indefinitely.
You need workable relations as well as tools. The earlier accepted wood work and skin transfer remain the actual exchange; this fortnight has not produced a standing arrangement for food, unrestricted access or a pupil. The local people’s expertise remains something to approach respectfully and learn from, without turning every encounter into a test of technological status.
Let drying remain part of production
The new pot rests at the separate craft side. It is still greenware: an unfired open form with a more deliberate wall-to-base transition and a witness piece beside it. The witness centre is still yielding. You can wait for its condition to change while other work continues; the calendar does not require another premature firing.
The bark vessels still provide the working route. Even a successful firing will need cooling, containment and suitable operating tests before the clay object replaces anything. A bowl in the drying place is useful progress, with its remaining dependencies still visible.
The next useful commitments
Continue improving lower-limb coverage and the durability of the footwear material. Develop the atlatl through an appropriate dart and a real field opportunity. Keep the nut route useful while exploring food and material work alongside willing neighbours. Return to the split-tip fishing design when conditions give it a fair comparison. Prepare and fire the pot when ready, then establish what job it can actually carry.
Bow development can follow from suitable wood, string and arrow stock as those foundations permit. It need not steal the next warm day from feet, food or a pot ready for firing. Remembered alternatives give you choices; the conditions here determine which choice can now become useful.
The mission has not become smaller. Its first workshop has become more credible. A warm enough body, an adequate meal route and a protected place for work are productive capacities in their own right. The next advance should make that arrangement more capable, and eventually useful to people who can carry it beyond you.

02_reflections/reflection-07---new-moon-.title: Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1
02_reflections/reflection-07---new-moon-.content:
Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1
End of Day 89 · New moon · Closing review of Moon 3, read after Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain.
The valley darkens beyond the shelter mouth. There is no bright moon above it tonight. You sit with the wrap drawn around your body and your feet inside the low skin coverings, listening to the last drops fall outside the dry strip. At the previous new moon, you were still trying to make the old camp answer every new demand. This month you finally chose a better place to work.
Rock now carries most of the roof. The screen turns the wind before it reaches the bed, and the little supported earth bay closes part of the low draught. Yesterday’s edge repair is still drying under its bark cover; there is no need to pretend that every part is finished. What matters tonight is that a wet night has left the sleeping place and the delicate work protected. You can plan beyond the next roof repair.
The improvement in clothing is just as tangible. The worn larger skin covers shoulders and core; the small cap now protects the ears and upper nape; the rabbit skins close the tops of your feet above the old bast soles. The heel ties are doing their work through the stronger woven edges. You can feel these changes when you sit still as well as when you move. You can also feel the remaining exposed lower legs. The foot skins are thin, and prolonged wet use could take away much of the comfort they now provide. Better coverage and more durable skin work belong near the top of the next month’s work.
That will require real material. The narrow deer margin was useful, but it has all become the small guard for a cutting edge. Remembering a garment pattern cannot enlarge it. Hunting, recovery and an accepted share of skilled work are the routes towards another useful skin, and each asks something of you beyond knowing how to cut one.
The day with the hunters has stayed in your mind. You carried the atlatl and never found a proper opening to use it. The people who knew the ground took the deer; you held where you were shown, helped with the processing and carried a load home. You ate the share you were given. That experience has made the relationship more real than another display at a target could have done. You would like to return and help again, with more attention to what their work needs. A familiar face and one shared outing give you somewhere to begin, without telling you everything about the group or its intentions.
Food now has several workable routes. The stored nuts remain worth protecting and preparing in small charges; the trap and the fishing opportunities add useful variety when they produce. The split-tip fishing spear has had an actual catch. None of those routes fills an entire winter by itself, and the shrinking gathering season makes more regular access to animal food and fat increasingly important. A productive day can support workshop work. A string of poor days could quickly change its order.
Beside you, the washed pot is a quieter success. You remember lifting the cracked first attempt and watching the water escape. This one has come through drying, firing, cooling and its own water test. It has now cooked wet meals and cooled again without opening a visible crack. Stirring food without moving hot stones through it makes the task easier to manage. A small container has changed an ordinary piece of work, which is exactly the kind of advance this handbook is meant to make possible.
The new wood on its clean rests is at an earlier stage. You have one green rough stave, three shaft blanks and a short nettle-line sample. The back of the stave is still continuous, and there is wood left for later decisions. Nothing is strung. The early tests of a fibre join have not settled what a complete bowstring will do. You can let those questions develop while the stave seasons, rather than spend your best effort trying to hurry the material into the shape in your memory.
This is also a useful change in how you think about the mission. You arrived with knowledge of an industrial world, including the scale of the danger waiting in its future. It is easy to let the distance between a flint edge and a spacecraft make every small task seem inadequate. Yet the missing capacity is not only a more advanced object. It is the ability to keep people warm and fed, to make useful things again, and to pass the work between willing hands.
You have begun a workshop that can wait for a pot to dry and a piece of wood to season. The next step is to make its food and clothing foundations stronger, and to find a more regular useful place alongside people whose local knowledge you still need. When a process is ready to share, it should solve a problem they recognise. Their participation will have to be earned through the work itself.
For the next stretch, you will give the useful weather to food access and skin material, keep the home dry, and continue the bow only as the wood and line justify it. Another vessel or a more reliable way to preserve food may become worthwhile when the actual need and materials are there. Tonight, there is a meal eaten, a protected bed and unfinished work waiting under cover. You can begin again from those things in the morning.

02_reflections/reflection-08---full-moon.title: Reflection 08 - Full Moon - Moon 4 Day 15
02_reflections/reflection-08---full-moon.content:
Reflection 08 - Full Moon - Moon 4 Day 15
End of Day 103 · Full moon · Read after Moon 4 Day 15 - Carry the Cord Through the Mesh.
Moonlight reaches the open ground beyond the rock. You have loosened the sleeves for the evening and hung them within reach, where the skin can air. The body wrap and leg coverings stay around you while you sit. A few weeks ago, sitting still in this air would have driven you back towards the fire much sooner.
The greatest change is the one you can feel. You took a deer yourself, brought back the whole main skin and enough selected food for useful fresh meals, then worked that one skin into sleeves and overlapping leg panels. You remember its weight on the pack frame and the effort of scraping and flexing it. Those things belong together now: a hunting result became warmth because you could recover, carry, prepare, cut and join the material.
The new clothes have already had a little wet use. A damp cuff firms as it dries and asks for more work. The thin foot covers still depend on their lining, the old woven soles and sensible choices about where to stand. Your hands remain exposed. There is better protection here, but another useful skin would still have real work to do. You will need to earn it rather than cut the same hide into one more garment in your imagination.
Food is less settled. The deer meals are long eaten. The stored autumn food remains worth protecting, and fishing has supplied fresh meals through the existing trap and the new attended line. The hand net makes retrieval easier; the little wooden gorge lets you work a quiet pocket from the bank. Each method opens a different opportunity, and each has days when it may give you nothing.
That still leaves the problem of a larger return. The deer offered more food than you could use and carry promptly, and the rest stayed where it fell. The pack frame helps with a manageable load; it does not preserve what reaches home. Before another large result, a useful next investigation is a controlled way of keeping a small surplus, with a real food input and enough attention to heat, drying and protection. Calling it smoked or leaving it in cold air would not settle those questions.
Trapping has improved in less dramatic ways. One deadfall stands on firmer ground with better protection from drips. The new snare line has only had its non-animal comparisons and remains set aside; it has not quietly become another producing trap. The woven fish trap still needs visits and an intact closure. You have chosen a small mesh project rather than building a new cage merely to add another design to the collection.
The spindle and shuttle make that choice more interesting. You had already spun single yarn; now you have deliberately plied new threads and carried the result through regular loops. The repair-sized panel beside the intact hand net is small, but the method can be repeated. Its next limit is the supply of clean fibre and the time your hands can give it. A larger net would need those things before it needed a more ambitious drawing.
The older hunting equipment also has a clearer place. Dart A has taken its first large animal, survived recovery and passed a short target trial after its point was reshaped. The hand spear remains a different choice for closer ground, and the fishing spear still has work that neither can do conveniently. The bow body is on its clean rests with the three shaft blanks. There is only the short original string sample so far. A full-length candidate can be made separately; bending and fitting the wooden body will still depend on its condition.
No one has shared these recent days with you. There are moments when you turn a finished object in your hand and feel the absence of another person to show it to. For this winter, making a workable life alone is the task you have chosen. In spring, useful cooperation may grow from having something reliable to bring to it, along with a better understanding of what you cannot do efficiently by yourself.
The mission remains far beyond this shelter, but the connections are becoming easier to recognise. Warmth gives your hands time to work. Fibre becomes line; line joins clothing, carries a load and makes a net. The pot turns small food charges into manageable meals. These are the beginnings of productive capacity. Tonight they are enough to let you leave the next piece of work under cover and expect to take it up again tomorrow.

02_reflections/reflection-artwork-propos.title: Reflection Artwork Proposals
02_reflections/reflection-artwork-propos.content:
Reflection Artwork Proposals
The user approved these compositions and the recommended watercolour/gouache treatment. Five frontispieces are now generated and embedded; view the selected series. The proposals below retain the artistic intent. Each picture follows its own end-of-day knowledge cutoff, with the original Day 1 protagonist as the identity reference.
Recommended visual language
Give Reflections the feeling of a painted chapter frontispiece: translucent watercolour and matte gouache on lightly toned paper, with sparse graphite or fine brown ink. Keep the recognised traveller, valley and material scale, but use a more deliberate composition, deeper tonal range and stronger negative space than the daily action illustrations. Light should carry the emotional argument. Objects can work as a quiet still life rather than an inventory spread.
Use one shared wide format, paper tone and palette across the series. Let colour evolve from cold darkness at arrival, to an uncertain warm centre at the first full moon, to the divided warm/cold light of the second new moon. Avoid labelled diagrams, decorative collage, heroic portraits and literal magical visions of the future. A lunar phase may be suggested by light and composition; new-moon scenes have no bright disk.
Two alternatives worth considering: tonal charcoal with restrained watercolour, for a more austere psychological series; or matte egg-tempera/gouache landscape frontispieces, with simplified masses and meticulous small material details, for a timeless illustrated-book quality. The watercolour/gouache approach is the strongest bridge to the existing Survival art while giving this section its own weight.
Reflection 01 — Arrival: knowledge without sheltering power
At the end of Moon 1 Day 1, look from outside towards the mouth of the very low debris shelter. The traveller sits or curls just within its leaf-lined opening, keeping his eyes on the dark valley. He occupies a small part of a broad composition. A single flake and hammer cobble catch the last cool light; a few dry fuel sticks lie unused, while empty hazelnut shells mark the meal already eaten. Rough bark waist panels provide the only clothing. No fire, vessel, spear or animal products.
The shelter opening becomes a fragile oval of enclosure within a much larger dark landscape. The unfinished roof is held together visually by the fallen limb, echoing how precarious his new starting point is. Pale indigo and slate washes, a narrow remnant of dusk and warm leaf tones convey exhaustion, loneliness and irreversible departure. No moon is visible. The contrast between remembered civilisation and present vulnerability is conveyed by his expression and the emptiness around him, without showing imaginary cities or machines.
Reflection 02 — First full moon: a small island of working capability
At the end of Moon 1 Day 15, use an elevated, intimate view across the correctly arranged camp. The traveller sits at the uphill clean craft spot, watching the separate firing patch as its last heat subsides. The small open pinch cup remains untouched on its non-combustible support, cooling and untested. The ordinary hearth is separate and farther downhill. Within the foreground still life, select only the bark water vessel, tiny awl/needle and a modest nut portion; leave other earned equipment outside frame.
The low shelter and organised working patches suggest genuine gains without making an established homestead. His hands rest rather than work: hope for tomorrow’s vessel test competes with fatigue and the smallness of the reserve. The unprocessed nettle batch stays downstream and off-screen; no fibre, whorl, basket or known neighbours appear. Retain the modest rabbit pelvic pad and bark coverage, with no fox panel yet.
Use silver-blue moonlight if clouds allow, small amber accents from the distinct outside heat sources, and quiet breathing space around the untouched cup. An airy, broad sky and small warm camp communicate both possibility and exposure. The image must not pre-empt the next day’s crack or represent a completed pottery success.
Reflection 03 — Second new moon: being seen, learning limits
At the end of Moon 2 Day 1 (continuous Day 30), seat the traveller at the uphill craft spot with the day’s six attempt marks on the bark register. A single blunt unfletched green dart and the wooden-hook thrower lie apart, imperfect tools rather than triumphant weapons. A modest food portion, the old rejected cracked pot and unused feathers form a sparse secondary still life. The narrow fox shoulder panel provides a small new comfort and makes the continuing exposure of his body visible.
His gaze leaves the objects and follows the remembered western approach beyond the spur. A far, faint wisp from the neighbours’ known clearing may be seen only if the mapped view permits it; otherwise let the obscured ridge and the direction of his attention carry their presence. No visiting observers appear, since those belong to Day 31. No new retting batch, mat, clay comparison pair or inspected fallback refuge appears either.
The visual centre is a triangle between the six recorded attempts, the dwindling provisions and his outward gaze: technical ambition, subsistence and unease about the people who may locate him. Warm low hearth light gives way to deep blue-grey beyond the terrace, with no lunar disk. His mood is chastened and watchful, yet intentional. It should feel like a person revising a plan after costly lessons, not a conquered valley or despairing defeat.
Reflection 04 — Second full moon: ambition gives way to enclosure
At the end of continuous Day 44 (Moon 2 Day 15), the traveller appraises the bare first return frame beside the retained old roof. The new side has only three ribs and no covering. A small kernel basket and the set-aside blunt unfletched dart and wooden thrower carry the competing demands of food and ambition. A full moon appears through breaks in cloud; the valley remains large, cold and uncertain. The standing profile keeps the anatomy simple. The section’s watercolour, gouache and spare graphite language gives the moment quiet weight.
The selected artwork is embedded in Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15. It depicts no Day 45 covering, new cord or fish catch; the accompanying snapshot remains fixed at Day 44. The complete prompt and fresh replacement record are in the Days 41–45 commission.
Reflection 05 — Third new moon: choose the winter foundations
At the end of continuous Day 59 (Moon 3 Day 1), the traveller sits at the protected camp edge in the complete dry-use outfit established by Character Sheet - Moon 2 Day 23. The plain folded fur crown, narrow anatomical-left fox strip, distinct front and back grass screens, bark waist layers and both bast soles are retained. Ordinary seated anatomy and resting hands keep the image contemplative.
Two small cold roughly rectangular fired comparison remnants on a separate test stone stand for a limited material result, without a new pot or a completed firing programme. Raw controls have already been discarded. The existing covered shelter remains modest in a broad darkening valley, with warm spill from the outside hearth beyond frame and no bright lunar disk. Watercolour, matte gouache and sparse graphite follow the established Reflection language; no imagined industry or spacecraft appears.
The frontispiece and review refer only to completed Day 59. The original Day 1 image supplies identity, the dated sheet supplies clothing, and Reflection 04 supplies painted palette/style only. The first output was rejected for changing the specimen form to round discs; the fresh replacement uses the original inputs. Exact prompts and provenance.
Reflection 06 — Third full moon: a useful home with unfinished work
Completed Day 74 uses the natural overhang, correct new low foot coverings and unchanged cap/body wrap in a broad silver-blue full-moon valley. A small grey-brown pot on its separate board remains greenware, without water or heat. Resting hands and simple seated anatomy support appraisal rather than another daily workshop scene. The original identity and dated wardrobe stay distinct from Reflection 04’s palette/mood reference. Selected image and full records.
The previous Reflection 05 prose now makes the winter course correction intentional before its discoveries occur. Its original moonless frontispiece is retained: the modest old shelter and two cold comparison remnants still fit that completed-Day-59 assessment.
Reflection 07 — Fourth new moon: a useful workshop, with winter work ahead
The closing Moon 3 review follows completed Day 89, the new-moon boundary at Moon 4 Day 1. A seated traveller beneath natural rock looks across a moonless late-autumn valley. His full fur cap, tan wrap and two low closed foot covers retain the Day 73 clothing. One empty cool pot on its board represents the useful ceramic achievement. The composition adds no equipment, skin, full wall or indoor hearth. The original cap-deficient output was rejected; the fresh replacement uses the original identity and dated clothing, with the pot reference supplying object form only. Gallery and full generation records.
Reflection 08 — Fourth full moon: warmth and productive capacity
The completed Day 103 appraisal sits beneath the natural overhang with a bright round moon beyond. The current cap, tan body wrap, leg panels and both low closed foot layers remain; two sleeves are deliberately hung within reach for airing, explaining the bare arms. One cooled pot accompanies the pause. Original Day 1 supplies identity/style and the Moon 4 Day 9 sheet supplies retained clothing; no future full-length string or other person appears. The selected frontispiece belongs to Reflection 08 - Full Moon - Moon 4 Day 15. Full prompt and review records.

02_reflections/reflections.title: Reflections
02_reflections/reflections.content:
Reflections
The moon offers a recurring pause to review what actually sustains you. At arrival, then at each new-moon or full-moon milestone, a reflection gathers the state of play: reliable capabilities, unfinished work, resources, dangers, intentions and choices worth postponing.
Read a reflection after its associated Survival day. It knows only events through that day’s end. It does not introduce a catch, acquisition, agreement or success which the daily entries have not earned.
Completed reflections









































MilestoneState-of-play entryMoon 1 Day 1 · arrival near new moonReflection 01 - Arrival - Moon 1 Day 1Moon 1 Day 15 · first full moonReflection 02 - Full Moon - Moon 1 Day 15Moon 2 Day 1 · next new moon (continuous Day 30)Reflection 03 - New Moon - Moon 2 Day 1Moon 2 Day 15 · full moon (continuous Day 44)Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15Moon 3 Day 1 · new moon (continuous Day 59)Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1Moon 3 Day 16 · full moon (continuous Day 74)Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16Moon 4 Day 1 · new moon (continuous Day 89)Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1Moon 4 Day 15 · full moon (continuous Day 103)Reflection 08 - Full Moon - Moon 4 Day 15
Rhythm and future milestones
Lunar Calendar anchors a fictional new moon around arrival, with reviews roughly fifteen days apart. The latest completed review is Day 103, full moon, Moon 4 Day 15. The next review is Day 118, new moon, Moon 5 Day 1, closing Moon 4. These are scheduled milestones, not unwritten narrative outcomes. The real phase cycle is about 29.5 days, so exact repeating fifteen-day halves would slowly drift.
The existing “Month Two” outline names a four-week planning block, Days 29–56; it is not silently renamed a lunar month. Moon cycles are the story’s reflective rhythm, alongside continuous day numbering. Survival page titles use Moon/Day labels from the same model; continuous day metadata still governs stocks and chronology.
Shape of an entry
A reflection should identify what can actually be relied upon, what is only a specimen or trial, the current bottleneck, threats and uncertainties, the priorities before the next review, and what outcome would change the plan. It should also admit a mistaken expectation when observations justify it.
Write reflective second-person present-tense prose rather than reciting every daily task. Use the hero’s rough practical judgement in the narrative. Historical reflections through Day 59 retain their checked author-continuity tables. From the next milestone, reviews use qualitative prose without numerical stock tables; the associated completed day’s knowledge cutoff remains mandatory.
Reflection time sits within ordinary pauses/planning; the entry creates no additional workday or resource events. The reflection series uses painted frontispieces in the approved watercolour/gouache style. Browse the series; Reflection Artwork Proposals records the approved compositions and style choices.
