The large body skin, underlying waist layers and two open bast soles remain. The fox panel is wholly allocated to the cap and is no longer a concealed shoulder layer. No new pelt or material exchange is recorded; future trap pelts require their own preparation. The reused panel supplies neither footwear nor a second cloak. R39 supports attention to body coverage, not this invented pattern or its thermal performance.
From pelt stock to foot coverage — Days 70–74
Two distinct fresh rabbit skins are fleshed promptly and worked as they dry under protection, not worn on the catch day. Thin margins are supported; mechanical flexing changes bendability but is not durable tanning. Day 73 gives one whole skin to each low foot covering, hair inward, plant lining inside and the existing bast sole outside/beneath. Plant-Fibre Footwear holds the combined design and maintenance guidance. A dry short-fit result and Day 74 repeat use leave wet/durable service unresolved. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15 supersedes the Day 67 appearance after fitting; body wrap and cap remain unchanged.
Independent arm and leg coverage — Days 95–99
The Day 93 whole deer skin follows Dry Pelt Working on Day 95 and a body-based four-panel layout on Day 96. Day 97 fits Skin Limb Coverings: two loose sleeves and two overlapping leg panels, hair inward, supported from the existing wrap/waist line. Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 9 records the completed outfit. This is the sole new skin allocation; existing cap, wrap and low foot covers persist. No extra coat, boots, mittens, blanket or uncut hide remains. Dry-use work on Days 97–99 requires airing and renewed flexing; rain durability remains unresolved.
Removable hand pockets — completed Day 108
The sole new Day 105 adult-rabbit pelt becomes a pair of small thumb-less Mittens after cleaning, staged working and actual layout. All head/body/arm/leg/foot layers persist. Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 20 fixes their optional worn state and the explicit bare-hand work variants. This new skin supplies no sole patches, separate thumbs or large garment. Drying, flexing and moisture care remain necessary.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/mittens.title: Mittens
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/mittens.content:
Two compact thumb-less warming pockets, smooth skin outside and hair inside. This conceptual study is not a measured cutting pattern or a warmth rating.
Mittens
Design family
Removable hand coverings that group fingers in a common insulating compartment. Separate-thumb patterns allow some grasping; very simple thumb-less pockets serve warming pauses and must be removed for precise manipulation. Material area, fit, moisture and fastening determine their usefulness. This family is distinct from sleeves and enclosing footwear.
Current simple route
Start with a sound, flexible hair-bearing skin; the narrative uses the established mechanical route in Dry Pelt Working. Lay out both hands and all seam/fold allowances on the actual useful area before cutting. If the pair will not fit, reduce the intended coverage or obtain material rather than spending the same skin twice.
Day 108’s base variant places the thumb alongside the fingers in a loosely closed hand, inside one rounded pocket per hand. Fold and close the end/side through supported sound margins using Stitching. Use an actual allocated scrap for seam comparison. The Bone Awl prepares holes; the retained Bone Needle assists the plant-thread route. Hair faces inward. Short open wrists overlap beneath the existing sleeves and have loose, easily released keepers.
Fit and operation
Check pressure at thumb, fingertips and seam corners; confirm each hand can come out without trapping the other. Keep circulation unrestricted. These are warming covers, not gloves suitable for fine tools, a bow release, fire handling or climbing. Take them off for those duties and put the pair somewhere clean and recoverable. Do not use an unsecured long connecting cord around the neck.
Air after wear, dry gently away from direct heat and rework firm skin. Dampness and abrasion can quickly reduce useful service. No temperature rating, waterproofing or durable tanning is established.
Narrative and evidence
One adult rabbit taken on Day 105 supplies the sole new pelt. It is promptly cleaned, worked across the next days and allocated on Day 108 to two small thumb-less hand pockets and minor test scraps. No separate thumbs, gauntlets, sole patches or spare skin remain. Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 20 records the fitted state and deliberate removal for work.
R65 supports grouping fingers and skilled skin clothing; R66 supports working and continued care. R75 is a much later mixed-material museum comparison, not evidence for this particular rabbit-only pattern or its adequacy in winter. The skin area, fit and dry-use result are authored, requiring replication.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.title: Plant-Fibre Clothing
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.content:
Plant-Fibre Clothing
Object, function and scope
Wearable plant coverings form an equipment family: hanging grass panels, broader mantles and later wrapped or plaited variants. Their material and fastening requirements differ. Fine spun cloth, footwear and waterproof clothing are not acquired by making the first coarse screen.
The present base route is a flexible twined grass back panel. Its purpose is to reduce direct airflow over part of the back while leaving the arms free. Plant-Fibre Mats covers bedding and other retained sheets; its stiff willow-foundation pad should not simply be worn as a garment.
Materials and construction route
Select long, clean, flexible dry grass from Dry Plant Insulation. Reject fouled, moulding, sharp or rapidly crumbling material. Keep a separate garment lot; do not count the same bundles in bedding, loose stores and worn equipment. Local grass suitability remains a field trial, not a botanical guarantee.
Arrange small overlapping hanging bundles to the chosen coverage. Practise a short top-edge section before committing to the panel. Twining crosses two working elements between neighbouring bundles. Inspect migration, bundle retention and row spacing as the width develops.
In the first instance, paired lengths of the existing single nettle yarn form light retaining rows. Pairing them in twining does not ply them into certified cord. Inspect and rework weak joins; use separately tested Nettle Cordage for the supported top edge and shoulder attachment. Rounded margins and accessible loose fastenings matter more than neat decoration. Avoid a tight loop around the neck or ties that hinder breathing, arm movement or removal.
Account for grass, working yarn, header and fastenings before construction. Stiff splints, wool, imported fibres and unrecorded pelt panels do not belong to this base route. Bark and pelt clothing are alternatives with their own preparation and coverage limits; a mixed covering must allocate each part explicitly.
Construction and performance checks
Lift and bend the panel before wearing it. Inspect creeping rows, slipping bundles, harsh stalks and loose ends. Check walking, crouching and arm raising in a short dry trial. Rework a pressure point and repeat the movement rather than treating first assembly as acceptance.
Observe covered area and actual handling separately from warmth. A reduction in felt airflow is not a measured insulation rating. Wind penetration through gaps, loft, fit and the remaining exposed body all affect the result. Rain can wet and collapse the material; a dry fit check does not establish weather resistance.
Projectile use needs a separate snag and movement check. Do not assume that a panel harmless during walking will clear the thrower’s sweep. Remove it for wet processing or close fire work if it would be exposed to water, heat or sparks; secure it away from the working area.
First narrative specimen and allocation
Day 39 makes a small separate top-edge sample using 0.05 kg grass and 2 m single yarn. Day 40 makes grass-back-panel-a, about 0.5 by 0.6 m, from another 0.55 kg grass, 12 m single yarn in paired rows and 1.2 m tested nettle cord. These are authored consumption estimates, not an experimentally validated bill of materials or a universal yield.
The panel survives short dry walking, crouching and arm-raise checks after one rubbing end is trimmed. It covers part of the back with an open front. The bark waist covering, rabbit pelvic pad and separate fox shoulder panel remain. The new Day 38 rabbit pelt is not yet incorporated. No head covering, footwear, waterproof cape or whole-core winter outfit is established.
Labour, maintenance and further variants
Day 36 gathers and sorts the grass. Day 39 tests the structure at small scale. Day 40 spends three active hours on construction and fitting, in addition to supplies and other inspections. Harvesting and sorting are not removed by the apparent simplicity of twining.
Air under cover and inspect after use. Repair creeping rows; replace crumbling or wet bundles with newly acquired material. Worn ties consume stock. Keep garments away from sparks and the separate firing area. Damp or compressed material cannot be restored to the usable dry inventory merely by renaming it.
A broader core mantle needs additional grass, fastening stock, construction time and front/side fit checks. Added insulation must be retained without blocking movement or encouraging chafing. A second panel cannot be counted until those materials and work exist. Fine textiles depend on a different supply and construction chain.
Evidence and limits
R23 supports the structure of twining. R26 records later museum examples and the disputed cape interpretation of Ötzi’s grass mat. Neither demonstrates this garment at 40,000 BP in Iberia, specifies the local grass or validates thermal performance. The present back-panel design and short-term result are authored physical trials. Replication must test wear, damp recovery, fastening safety and useful coverage before presenting a dependable field design.
Use through Day 45
The back panel is worn briefly on dry gathering/walking portions. Day 41’s brush snag is freed without a counted tear or new allocation. It is taken off for wet bank work, casting and frame construction so the fringe cannot catch. There is still no wet-weather, prolonged-wear or casting-clearance result, no front panel, head covering or footwear. The rabbit pelt D38 remains unassigned.
Separate front panel and use, Days 46–50
Days 46 and 48 each allocate 9 g ready fibre to about 7 m uneven single yarn after rejection within the portion. Day 49 uses 12 m single yarn, 0.5 kg newly gathered long grass and 1.2 m inspected light cord for a roughly 0.45 by 0.6 m front panel. The supported header sits below the collarbones, with loose accessible shoulder/side adjustment and no tight neck loop. The existing back panel remains a separate object. These are author allocation estimates, not experimentally validated yields.
Lift/bend checks and a short dry walk, crouch and reach expose a rubbing stem and migrating row; adjustment precedes repeat fitting. Together the two pieces screen most of the front/back core, leaving side gaps, upper chest and limbs exposed. Day 50’s dry gathering walk reveals header creep which is corrected with the existing tie. There is still no damp-weather, insulation-rating or casting-clearance result. Remove both pieces for water, fire and projectile work and keep them protected when off. The stiff willow bed pad remains bedding. The later pelt crown piece is separately allocated in Fur-On Pelt Clothing.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.title: Plant-Fibre Footwear
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/plant-fi.content:
Plant-Fibre Footwear
Design family and intended use
Coarse plant footwear can separate the sole from some dry ground contact and hold a replaceable insulating layer. The first design is a small flexible bast sole with simple forefoot and heel retention, open toes and no tall upper. It is a short dry-ground trial, without waterproofing, a durable tread or established winter protection.
Boots, closed basket-like uppers and plant soles combined with hide are possible later variants. They need separate material allocations and fit tests. Existing pelt clothing is not a supply of unallocated shoe leather.
Inputs and assembly
Select sound flexible Bast Fibre, tested Bark Cordage and clean Dry Plant Insulation. Use simple over-and-under work from Simple Coiling and Weaving to make a small close flat sole. Fold or return the margins so stiff ends face away from the foot; compare it with the wearer’s foot before closing the edge. The material must bend without opening into large unstable gaps.
Bind the edge and use broad enough, adjustable retention at the forefoot and heel. Keep knots out from under the sole. Avoid a tight ankle ring or a tie that becomes constricting as the foot moves. Thin dry grass is a removable liner, distinct from the load-bearing sole. Excess stuffing can worsen fit and slip.
Fit, ground tests and maintenance
Start beside a support on level dry ground. Check walking, turning, crouching, removal and the position of the heel. Inspect feet for rubbing and bindings for creep. Revise one obvious fit issue before extending the trial.
An inclined, wet or loose surface is a new test. Remove the footwear if it rolls under the foot, loses ground grip or obstructs balance. Inspect the underside for thinning and embedded grit; replace damp liner and dry the sole before reuse. A dry-fit success does not justify hunting, river work or a long escape in it.
First narrative instance
Day 52 allocates a new willow-bast lot to two soles and their bindings, plus a separate dry grass lining. After a heel-retention adjustment, the pair stays in place on a brief level dry walk. One sole creeps during a short incline check, so the trial ends. The pair is kept as experimental dry camp footwear. Day 55’s projectile session remains barefoot.
Evidence and alternatives
R37 records much later shoes combining bast mesh, grass padding and leather. The grass’s replaceable role informs a comparison; the traveller does not possess the source specimen’s hide layers, and its reported performance cannot be transferred to these plant soles. Plant suitability, wear, traction and insulation here remain authored trials needing replication. A future independently supplied hide may support another route after its own preparation and tests.
Rear-quarter retention revision — Day 56
The existing pair keeps its footbeds and thin liners. Reused retention line and 0.5 m newly allocated coarse bark line form low heel slings led diagonally to sound rear-side edge bindings. Tension is eased where an edge curls. Short level turns, crouching and a few slow steps on the same small dry rise hold the soles aligned. This authored improvement concerns retention; it changes neither underside grip nor weather resistance. No tight ankle ring, closed upper, long-walk result or reliable emergency footwear is established. The dated character sheet retains the same overall silhouette; later scene briefs describe the revised heel route.
Layered pelt-cover variant — Days 73–74
The design family can retain its plant sole/lining/retention while adding an independently sourced cover. The two rabbit skins obtained on Days 70 and 71 are promptly fleshed, air-dried under protection and worked in brief supported sessions across the intervening days. On Day 73 each whole skin becomes one removable low foot covering, hair inward, with sound margins folded and lightly stitched. Pale skin faces out; toes and heels are enclosed to just above the ankle.
Dry grass remains a renewable liner. The original bast soles go beneath/outside as the wearing layer; retained ties and short new plant-cord extensions hold the combined arrangement. No tight ankle ring or underfoot knot is introduced. Fit is checked on level dry ground, with toe crowding corrected by reducing lining. Day 74 repeats short dry camp use and inspection. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15 fixes the visible state.
This adds an optional cover route through Animal Pelt, Fur-On Pelt Clothing and Stitching; those are requirements of this variant rather than the original open plant sole. Thin untanned rabbit skin does not supply a durable outsole or waterproof boot. Open and inspect frequently, renew compressed/wet lining and dry the separate layers. Stop for rubbing, tearing, unstable soles or constricting fastenings. The two catches leave no skin stock for leggings. R37 informs layer separation; R43 informs caution with thin skins and work during drying, not this pattern, preparation duration or weather performance.
Heel load through the wearing layer — Day 75
A short new bark-cord keeper passes through the original rear-side sole bindings and around the covered heel, rather than drawing directly on thin rabbit-skin stitch holes. Retention remains adjustable and the top does not become a tight ankle ring. Renew only compressed lining where crowding changes fit. A short dry near-camp outing retains heel/sole alignment after this adjustment. The existing Day 73 character sheet remains valid in silhouette; no new skin, boots, leggings or wet-weather result is introduced.

05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/skin-lim.title: Skin Limb Coverings
05_tools-and-equipment/clothing/skin-lim.content:
Object-family study of the four pieces, not a measured cutting pattern, spare garment stock or proof of winter performance.
Skin Limb Coverings
Design family and role
Removable skin sleeves and overlapping leg panels cover exposed limbs while an existing body garment remains in service. These are modular clothing pieces, distinct from a complete new coat, trousers or boots. Their usefulness depends on prepared skin, fit, attachments and continued care. Fur-On Pelt Clothing gives the broader pelt-clothing context.
Actual base route
Use a sound, flexible worked skin with retained hair, the awl/plant-thread stitching route and existing body clothing with sound places for attachments. The chosen narrative route uses Dry Pelt Working. Previously dressed material is another route; this design does not require the traveller to perform one particular preparation process on every input. The base stitching route can guide plant thread through pre-made holes; an eyed Bone Needle is a convenience, not an unavoidable dependency.
Layout and construction
Take length and circumference from the wearer with joints bent. Allow for seams, overlaps and changes of shape at elbows and calves before making irreversible cuts. Lay out all proposed panels on the actual skin. Avoid holes, damaged margins and weak joins. Use a real offcut for seam trials; it must come from the same allocation.
Two loose tapered sleeve tubes can retain their shape with supported longitudinal seams. Small folded upper tabs attach beneath sound shoulder edges of the old wrap; avoid its earlier repair and avoid transferring sleeve weight to a tight arm band. Two leg panels overlap at the sides. Loose retainers preserve the overlap, while individual keepers up to the existing waist line support their upper ends. The tops meet beneath the wrap’s hem; the lower ends overlap the existing low foot covers. Leave hands and feet available for their own designs.
Fitting and maintenance
Reach, bend elbows, crouch, kneel, walk and step up. Adjust length and attachment positions before tightening anything. Restriction, numbness, slipping and dragging are reasons to stop and refit. Reinforcing folds distribute load only if the underlying skin is sound. Do not solve a poor hanging arrangement with tighter bands around a limb.
Loosen or remove pieces for airing. Dry away from direct heat and rework firm areas. Hair inward is the selected insulating arrangement, not a waterproof finish. The leg panels are removable clothing over the legs, not newly fabricated tall boots.
Narrative specimen
Day 96 cuts one independently acquired red-deer skin into four principal panels plus small tabs/test scraps. Day 97 completes and wears two sleeves and two leg panels. This allocation leaves no new whole skin, spare sole, mitten, sleeping cover or large offcut stock. New fine nettle thread is made; no new sinew is recovered. Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 9 fixes the completed appearance. Fit and one dry working walk are authored observations, not validated winter performance. R65–R66 inform material care and fitting questions, not this invented pattern.

05_tools-and-equipment/components/bowstr.title: Bowstring
05_tools-and-equipment/components/bowstr.content:
One full-length fibre-string candidate. The eye and gentle handling are not acceptance for repeated dynamic bow use; the stave remains unstrung at that Day 104 cutoff.
Bowstring
Component and route
A bowstring connects the ends of a bow body and must retain useful length, attachment and integrity under repeated loading and release. The candidate route here uses carefully prepared Nettle Cordage. Other fibres need their own preparation and testing; this is not a claim that one material is always best.
Material questions
Fibre condition, overlaps, twist, abrasion, loop geometry and moisture all affect service. A thin single yarn, a snare line and a bowstring are different uses. Local nettle fibres have already supported light tasks, but those results do not supply a dynamic bowstring rating.
Use short identified samples to observe obvious splice movement and settling before committing scarce fibre to full-length work. Load away from the face and inspect joins. Compare samples cautiously: different construction and section confound a simple material ranking. Successful gentle static pulls still leave repeated dynamic behaviour unresolved.
Day 86 sample
A short new nettle sample receives a remade overlap and sample eye, then gentle repeated pulls beside a bark sample. It is stored with the fibre work, not installed on the green stave. No full-length accepted component exists through Day 89. The plate shows this trial-line state rather than a completed string; the full component was still planned at that cutoff.
R52 supports nettle cordage in a very different ethnographic setting, not this candidate’s strength, bowstring acceptance or presence in the fictional valley.
First full-length candidate — Day 104
One new heavier nettle line has a worked-back eye and a long free end reserved for a later adjustable attachment. Its length is guided by the actual unstrung stave with allowance; final working length is not fixed. Gentle static pulls and inspection are the only current handling. The first demonstration date records manufacture of this full-length candidate, not dynamic acceptance or a working bow. The Day 86 short sample remains recognisable and separate. No string is fitted to the stave and no bow is drawn or shot. The existing short-sample illustration is retained below as historical comparison when the new full-length study is installed.
Earlier short sample — Day 86

One short trial line and sample eye. This is not a complete accepted bowstring or a rated load test.
Fitting and first short releases — Days 107–109
The SAME full-length candidate is fitted to the smooth side seats on Day 107, using its one eye and adjustable free end. Contact, creep and the arrow self-nock’s fit are inspected through short controlled pulls. Day 109 adds a few short releases with an actual arrow, followed by unstringing/inspection. This is bounded service evidence, not a certified dynamic rating. The older short sample stays separate; no new string lot or accepted lifetime is inferred.
Further limited service — Day 114
The same body and full-length nettle string candidate receive a few short practice releases with the existing arrow after its two-vane alteration. Attachments remain inspectable, no new damage is authored, and the body is stored unstrung afterwards. This is not a full-seasoning measurement, increased draw specification, endurance test or hunting acceptance.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Bark Container
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Bark Container
Purpose
A modest folded bark vessel carries dry material or, after testing, water. This is an equipment specification with its construction method; capacity and leakage are properties of a particular object.
Procedure
Find a sound pliable sheet of suitable bark. Test a small piece before stripping a large one. Fold a shallow vessel with overlapping corners, make supported fastening holes and bind without splitting the material.
Keep sharp stored flakes separate from the vessel. Any lining or sealant for drinking water needs its own suitability assessment; resin is not a default food-safe coating.
Test
Fill with a small volume and observe leakage on dry ground. Mark the successful level. The first-month vessel is tested around 0.6 L, not assumed to hold six to ten litres.
Heat treatment requires Hot-Rock Boiling and repeated inspection. Loss of the vessel ends that route until repaired or replaced.
Limits
Seams can leak and repeated heating can fatigue bark. A basket improves dry carrying; a sound ceramic pot may later improve some cooking operations. Neither is required to make a first bark vessel.
Historical first dates and guaranteed water independence are omitted.
Deliberate second specimen — Day 54
The old vessel supplies a comparison for worn folds and fastenings. A separately collected birch sheet and fresh coarse line make vessel B; a small marked scrap records a rough fold pattern, adjusted for the sheet’s weak areas. One corner is eased and re-bound after a damp trace in the cold test. B then holds two supported boiling charges at an authored working level around 0.5 L. A remains the original 0.6 L specimen. Both stay at the main camp; two short heat tests do not establish B’s lifetime, a ceramic success or a supplied refuge.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Clay Vessel
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Clay Vessel
A ceramic vessel is a product of Pottery. A shaped unfired pot is greenware, and a cracked fired specimen is not automatically a cooking vessel.
Inspect after complete cooling. Check cracks, water stability and leakage before any intended heat cycling. Food suitability and operating strength require additional verification.
The first-month vessel is formed on Day 11, fired on Day 15 and tested on Day 16. It leaks through a crack and is rejected for cooking and storage of drinking water. Its surviving body remains a non-food experimental specimen. Water treatment continues using the tested bark vessel.
A future sound vessel may reduce handling and offer direct heating, but it remains one route among alternatives. It does not become a compulsory predecessor for wooden spindles or every food-processing method.
New greenware is not a second working vessel — Days 72–74
The new open pot formed on Day 72 remains protected greenware through the Day 74 review. It has no containment, firing or cooking result yet; both bark vessels remain the working route. Clay Vessel Making records the new charge and witness. This page’s cracked historical illustration remains the earlier rejected specimen, not a depiction of the new sound-looking but unfired form.
One new vessel reaches service — Days 82–84
The Day 72 bowl is gradually fired on Day 82 and left until cold. Day 83 finds no visible crack and tests small increasing water charges. Initial absorption dampens the support, but no steady drip, softening or new crack appears. It therefore becomes the first useful vessel of this family. It is porous unglazed Fired Earthenware, not waterproof glazed ware.
Day 84 rests that same pot on an Open Cooking Hearth: a water-only gradual heating/cooling cycle precedes a second cycle cooking a freshly leached acorn meal. Both are followed by cold inspection. No lid, handles, new second pot or universal cooking reliability is added. The current illustration depicts the later useful bowl; the earlier rejected specimen is preserved in the historical section below.
Historical rejected first-month specimen

This earlier specimen cracked and leaked. Its image is retained as the record of that failed trial; the current working bowl is the separate Day 72 vessel shown at the top.
A second object is still greenware — completed Day 114
Day 112 forms a modest wider open cooking bowl and one drying witness. The purpose is to separate food and water tasks across planned turns at the existing hearth and provide eventual vessel redundancy. It has no handles, spout or foot ring and is not yet a working Clay Vessel. Through Day 114 only the older fired pot is used; no second firing, acceptance trial or concurrent supported heating is credited.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Pack Frame
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
An object-family portrait of the new lightweight carrier. The illustration supplies no dimensions or rated carrying load.
Pack Frame
Object and duty
A light wooden frame carries a separately secured load close to the back through broad plant-fibre shoulder bands. It is distinct from the small Rawhide Carrying Sling and the Woven Foraging Basket. Neither old carrier acquires this frame’s construction or implied capacity.
Form and assembly
The Day 92 instance has two rails, two crosspieces, bound joints and a diagonal line brace against sideways racking. Smooth edges and bearing surfaces before tying. Plait selected prepared bast into broader shoulder bands; small bark folds with dry grass spread pressure at bearing points. Keep load ties independent from the wearing bands.
This is an authored wooden/plant-fibre design, not an archaeologically reconstructed local backpack or a measured engineering specification. It needs no new animal skin, metal fastener or complicated joinery.
Trial and operation
Start with modest wrapped inert loads and short walking checks. Attend to joint rotation, rubbing, shifting, balance and the ability to put the frame down. Bring the load close without obstructing movement or breathing. Cordage Testing informs contact and moisture checks; no stated rating follows from one trial.
Keep dirty skin surfaces separate from clean food, using appropriate removable barriers and cleaning. Split awkward loads into feasible trips. A frame does not solve cooling, daylight or protection of what remains in the field.
Narrative instance
Day 92 builds and trials one frame. Day 93 uses it over two manageable return trips for the single new skin, limited selected food and recovered equipment. It adds neither an entire transported deer nor a food reserve. Large-Game Processing records the recovery context.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.filePath: 05_Tools and Equipment/Containers and Carriers/Rawhide Carrying Sling.md
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Rawhide Carrying Sling
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Rawhide Carrying Sling
Purpose and size
A modest carrying cradle consists of one tested hide panel and a separate strap. One juvenile rabbit pelt provides limited area; it does not also supply long shoulder straps and a garment.
Method
Use Rawhide or a cleaned prepared panel, retaining as much sound area as possible. Fold or gather it into a shallow pocket, pierce supported edge holes with Bone Awl, and lace with Simple Cordage. Add a separate cord strap and distribute tension across several attachment points.
Allow the panel to dry in shape away from scorching heat.
Test
Begin with a small load. Increase gradually while inspecting tearing, creep and strap pressure. In the narrative the initial trial stays below a kilogram; later loads remain conservative. Bulk nut harvests use repeated trips and a bark carrier until a basket is made.
Limits
Keep away from hot stones and embers. Damp hide is not a safe high-temperature carrier. It can stretch or weaken when wet and become rigid again when dry.
Repair has a material cost. A bigger hide, woven strap or basket offers an alternative when the carrying requirement grows.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Rawhide Pouch
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Rawhide Pouch
Product and purpose
A small dry-storage case made from available Rawhide protects light implements. The first squirrel pelt yields a tool case, not a food sack.
Procedure
Inspect usable area and choose a fold that preserves it. Damp only what must bend. Use Bone Awl to open holes sufficiently far from edges, then guide a fine tested line by hand or through an eyed needle.
Fold and lace the sides, leaving a simple closure. Do not overtighten so that shrinking skin or thread cuts the holes. Dry around a modest temporary form that can be removed.
Test and maintenance
Load with a light blunt sample before delicate implements. Inspect holes and closure. Wrap sharp flakes separately so their edges do not slice the case.
Keep dry and check damp folds. The first-month case is a small asset made on Day 8, not a permanently unlocked possession.
Alternatives
A tied bark packet or other folded container can protect small objects without sewing. An eyed Bone Needle improves some operations but is not a necessary first route.
No universal lifespan or water-tightness is promised.

05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.filePath: 05_Tools and Equipment/Containers and Carriers/Woven Foraging Basket.md
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.title: Woven Foraging Basket
05_tools-and-equipment/containers-and-ca.content:
Woven Foraging Basket
Object
A small basket made with tested flexible uprights and woven strands. A stitched coiled basket is another route, not the required same construction.
Manufacture
Use Simple Coiling and Weaving to form a supported crossed base, introduce uprights, weave the walls and secure the rim. Splice material before it becomes too short; avoid sharp ends in the carrying surface.
Test
Load the base lightly, then inspect joining, rim and carrying points. Increase only while it holds shape and strands remain seated. The first-month object receives a conservative load trial rather than an assumed multi-kilogram capacity.
Maintenance and limits
Dry after wet use, repair worn material and protect it from crushing. Ventilation can reduce some moisture accumulation but does not prevent mould in wet food.
Historical first dates, universal recognition and fixed productivity multipliers are omitted pending evidence. Capacity helps collection only when resources, processing and carrying time remain available.
Loose storage cover — Day 64
The existing basket gains a loosely woven cover sized to the rim, made from separately selected flexible strands. Keep the weave secured against unravelling and leave it readily removable for inspection. It excludes some debris while preserving air movement; it is not a sealed pest-proof lid or a new basket. At Western Overhang the basket and clean spreading surfaces belong on the food-only Raised Storage Rack. Dry Nut Storage governs the condition of the input, not the attractive appearance of its container.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/ach.title: Acheulean Hand Axe
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/ach.content:
Acheulean Hand Axe
Object and role
A bifacially worked stone with a usable edge and a graspable area. The name is historical; the first month’s rough biface does not make the traveller enter a new era.
Manufacture
Use Bifacial Knapping with suitable stone and controlled removals from both faces. A hard hammer can make a rough example. A Soft Hammer Billet is an option for selected thinning work, not an absolute gate.
Preserve sound platform geometry and useful thickness. Do not pursue perfect symmetry at the cost of a broken tool when an adequate edge serves the task.
Test and limits
Test on a modest cutting job and inspect the handhold, edge and fracture. A finished-looking shape does not prove it outperforms a flake. It is not automatically a powerful wood axe, needle drill or precision antler saw.
No game damage statistic or universal butchery improvement is assigned.
Evidence
R04 supports hard-hammer manufacture. Local specialists may already produce more suitable tools; compare their use rather than assuming a design’s modern remembered name establishes superiority.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/haf.title: Hafted Knife
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/haf.content:
Hafted Knife
Object
A cutting flake held in a handle that leaves a useful edge exposed. The handle improves grip in some jobs, but transfers new stresses into the stone and joint.
Assembly
Use Simple Hafting. Choose a blade with a suitable base and a handle seat that supports it without concentrating stress on a thin edge. Bind mechanically; a tested adhesive is optional.
Leave binding away from the cutting path. Allow any adhesive to cool and any wet binding to settle before applying load.
Test
Begin with light controlled cuts in expendable material. Inspect blade movement, binding creep and cracks. Increase the task gradually; do not use shoulder force to pry a delicate flake through seasoned oak.
Maintenance
Clean after use, inspect the joint and renew damaged bindings. Replace the blade if needed. Modularity reduces replacement cost only when replacement parts fit and their performance is tested.
The first-month knife passes modest fibre and thin-wood work, not every imagined high-load task.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Knife Flake
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Knife Flake
Object
An unhafted stone flake with a useful cutting edge. The historical name describes a simple form; the traveller is not living through the Oldowan period.
Manufacture and selection
Use Flint Knapping Basics. Select a flake with a sound continuous edge and a surface that can be held securely. Remove or protect an uncomfortable projection only if doing so does not destroy the useful edge.
Use and test
Test on plant material, then use controlled slices for fibre, thin bark or butchery. Support the work so a slip cannot drive the edge into the body. Do not test on a thumb.
Maintenance and limits
Edges chip and dull. Replace or carefully retouch when required. A hand-held flake remains useful alongside Hafted Knife; hafting does not make every cutting task easier.
The ledger treats the working flake cache as replenished consumable tools rather than an exact count of all flakes struck.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Scraper
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Scraper
Object
A selected flake with an edge suited to controlled scraping. An edge for thin hide may differ from an edge for wood. Retouch is an option, not proof of a dedicated historical type.
Manufacture and use
Choose a sound blank from Flint Knapping Basics. If needed, make controlled small removals to produce a robust working edge. Support the work and keep the hand clear of a slip.
For hides, begin on a scrap or low-value edge with modest pressure. A sharp cutting edge can damage thin skin; a supported blunt scraping edge may be preferable for fleshing.
Test and maintenance
Inspect the removed material and substrate. Stop if the tool gouges, tears or only polishes the surface. Remove sharp waste and keep food-processing uses separate from dirty hide work.
Limits
One scraper is not ideal for every material. Continuous edge maintenance and user practice matter more than a nominal technological age.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.title: Oldowan Simple Chopper
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/old.content:
Oldowan Simple Chopper
Object
A core or cobble with a robust worked edge for limited chopping and rough shaping. It is heavier than a flake and can be less efficient for fine cuts.
Manufacture
Use Flint Knapping Basics to remove flakes from selected edges, leaving enough mass and a safe grip. Compare the intended task with a simple unmodified stone or sharp flake before investing more work.
Use and test
Support thin wood on a stable surface, make controlled strikes and inspect the edge. Do not use a brittle chopper as a universal axe for felling large trees or as a fine percussor on another core.
Maintenance and limits
Rework or replace a damaged edge. The tool can provide coarse shaping but does not supply the reach, load path or productivity of a later tested hafted woodworking tool.

05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/sto.title: Stone-Edge Guard
05_tools-and-equipment/cutting-tools/sto.content:
Stone-Edge Guard
Design and purpose
A removable cover protects a small flaked-stone cutting edge from incidental contact and light knocks during storage and carrying. This version is a folded untanned skin margin held by a releasable plant-cord tie. It is not a knife handle or a puncture-proof wearable sheath.
Inputs and assembly
Use a cleaned sound piece of Rawhide, large enough to turn around the particular edge with room at the fold. The Day 78 deer margin supplies one entire small cover; it supplies no garment or second panel. Keep dirty skin work separate from food surfaces.
Locally dampen a stiff fold until it yields, rather than cracking dry skin. Shape it over a smooth wooden former slightly more generous than the flake’s section. Tie lightly, leave an air path, and dry under protection while turning it to expose damp undersides. Do not trap an actual sharp blade inside a contracting wet fold.
Fit, use and failure
Remove the former once the shape is dry and firm. Brush out grit, inspect the fold, then check gentle insertion and withdrawal of the flake. The tie should retain the cover without driving the edge through it. A split fold, loose fit or edge pressing against a thin spot needs a changed shape or replacement.
Carry with the light tools where heavy loads and the body cannot press against an exposed sharp corner. Open and dry it after damp use. Rawhide changes shape when wet; this cover does not justify carrying a sharp flake against bare skin.
Narrative instance
Day 80 shapes the whole retained deer margin around a former; Day 81 completes the dry fit. The little cover reduces awkward loose-edge handling. Its exact pattern and performance are authored trials, not an excavated Neanderthal sheath or tested load rating.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.title: Bone Awl
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.content:
Bone Awl
Object and manufacture
A pointed bone implement for opening supported holes. Choose a suitable blank from Bone, score or split conservatively, and scrape and abrade a tapered point with Oldowan Knife Flake and a suitable abrasive surface.
An awl does not require an eye. A failed needle blank can become an awl if the shaft remains sound.
Test and use
Try a scrap panel supported on a safe surface. Rotate or press with control, stopping before the blank bends or splits. Keep the off-hand outside the point’s exit path. Use a thicker point for tougher material and a finer one only where it survives.
Limits
An awl hole still needs suitable spacing and thread. It does not make every rawhide panel strong. The Day 7 awl enables small hand-laced work while the eyed needle remains unfinished.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.title: Bone Needle
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/b.content:
Bone Needle
Object
A slender worked bone implement with a usable eye. It is a more demanding object than a pointed awl and is not necessary for every early sewn container.
Manufacture
Select a cortical blank with adequate width and thickness for an eye. Score and split carefully where appropriate, then scrape and abrade the shaft. Keep the point suited to the intended material rather than making a fragile needle-thin spike.
Work the eye gradually from opposite sides with a suitable fine stone point and abrasive. Leave enough tissue around it to resist cracking. Polish surfaces that contact thread.
Test and failure
Pass a fine test thread through the eye, inspect abrasion, and sew a scrap with pre-made awl holes. A cracked eye is a failed needle even if the shaft can become an awl.
The first attempt on Day 7 fails at the eye; a usable needle is made on Day 12. No guaranteed first-needle time or rare-breakage claim is retained.
Limits and evidence
A small animal’s bone may not supply a suitable blank. A Bone Awl and threaded hand seam remain an alternative. Exact manufacturing times and durability require replication.
R28 in Research Register compares early eyed needles in Siberia with later preserved European examples and explains sewing with awls. Day 12 is the traveller’s authored experiment, not evidence for an eyed needle in this local group’s kit. See Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/n.title: Netting Shuttle
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/n.content:
Two views of the same simple carrier design, not two owned shuttles. The separate plain gauge controls mesh size.
Netting Shuttle
Object and role
A compact carrier for the working length of cord or yarn during Knotted Netting. It passes through the loop with its wound supply and pays out the next length. The separate mesh gauge controls loop size. Carrying yarn and setting mesh are different jobs.
Simple base form
The selected field form is a slim flat wooden strip with one open rounded notch at each end. The remaining end arms are stout and smooth. Cord winds lengthways between the notches and across the two broad faces. Keep the loaded width and thickness small enough to pass through the intended mesh without force. This simple two-ended form does not need a drilled eye, a cut-out central tongue, a bobbin or metal.
Select sound stock, shape the body, smooth faces and contact corners, then test with a small winding. A catching inner corner can abrade fibre even when the outer face feels smooth. Stop for splits, sharp projections or thin end arms. Keep the free working length controlled rather than filling the tool so heavily that it no longer passes.
Use, variants and limits
Pay out only what the next loop needs and keep the working knot visible. A shuttle assists handling; it does not correct a missed parent loop or a wrong knot. Replace worn carriers and inspect snagged yarn. Needle-like forms with a central tongue are alternatives requiring their own more complex shaping, not extra owned tools in the current story.
Narrative and evidence
Day 103 makes one double-notched wooden specimen and uses the Day 102 plied yarn for one small repair-sized rectangle. No larger hand net or set net is assembled. R73 supports the separate carrier/gauge roles and comparative forked/notched forms. Medieval, historical and experimental analogies do not attest a 40 ka local shuttle; the particular field tool’s construction and benefit remain authored and unmeasured.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/p.title: Plant-Fibre Mats
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/p.content:
Plant-Fibre Mats
Design family and uses
Coarse sheets made from suitable plant foundations and working elements can organise bedding, cover ground or form an outer screen. Twined, plaited and other structures have different controls. The first narrative route is a small twined bedding pad; larger mats and wearable forms are prospective variants.
A mat’s form makes it equipment. Twining supplies one practised technique; Dry Plant Insulation supplies retained loft. A sheet which keeps leaves together is not automatically warm, comfortable, waterproof or suitable clothing.
Base route: small twined bedding pad
Inspect Split Wood Strips for sharp ends and splits. Arrange sound foundations across the chosen size and use paired portions of tested light nettle cord to retain them in spaced rows. Work gradually, checking earlier crossings and the edges against the small sample.
Spread dry grass and leaves into the open structure while keeping a loose layer between the body and stiff foundations. Preserve access for replacing filling. Record strip, line and insulation allocations; the same stock cannot also furnish a cloak or escape bed.
Variants and separate tests
A larger bedding mat requires more material and construction time, along with ground fit and drying checks. A loose covering mat may need different gaps and edges. A wearable panel needs softer materials, mobility, chafing, snagging, wind and damp-weather tests; it is not made by simply calling the bedding pad a mantle.
Plaiting is an alternative with its own material flexibility and edge controls. Fine spun cloth and netting are different constructions, not automatically acquired by twining a sample.
Operation and maintenance
Lay bedding variants on the existing dry resting layer, away from sparks. Try a brief rest before relying on a whole night. Inspect pressure points, sharp protrusions, migrating filling and margins which unravel.
Lift, air and replace wet or flattened material. Remove failed foundations rather than concealing their edges. Loose refreshed bedding is the fallback if the frame becomes uncomfortable.
Current narrative instance
Day 32 makes a small twining sample. Day 35 completes only a roughly 0.4 by 0.5 m pad covering part of the upper-body contact area, with a brief rest and lift trial. Its strip and insulation lots are allocated; it is not a full mattress or a worn garment. The asset bedding-pad-a remains the specific object identifier.
Evidence and limits
R23 supports the twining structure and R24 earlier plant bedding elsewhere. The local willow-strip/nettle-line combination is an authored trial, not an excavated Iberian mat design or an insulation rating. A mat cannot by itself solve a leaking roof, wet ground or incomplete body coverage.
Clothing remains a separate design family
Days 39–40 develop Plant-Fibre Clothing from soft hanging grass foundations, light paired yarn rows and a separately supported upper edge. The bedding pad stays on the bed with its stiff willow foundations and allocated filling. Sharing twining does not make the first pad a ready-made mantle; garment fit and movement require different checks.

05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/s.title: Spindle Whorl
05_tools-and-equipment/fibre-equipment/s.content:
Spindle Whorl
Object
A weight fitted securely to a spindle shaft. It helps maintain rotation while prepared fibre is drafted into yarn. The whorl is a component; a shaft alone can also be used with different handling.
First-month wooden route
Cut or select a balanced small wooden disc. Make a central hole by controlled piercing, scraping and abrasion with appropriate stone or bone tools. Fit the shaft without splitting the disc and without an off-centre wobble. Test rotation before attaching fibre.
Wood avoids a ceramic-firing requirement. The traveller makes a working wooden version on Day 21, loses it during the rebuffed approach on Day 25, and makes a replacement on Day 27.
Fibre and testing
Start with clean aligned fibre, attach a leader and draft a small section while controlling twist. Wind the finished yarn. For a strong line, ply appropriate singles rather than treating fine single yarn as finished cordage.
Alternative and limits
A clay disc can be formed, dried and fired through Pottery, then checked for fit and balance. It is not intrinsically the fastest or most reliable first route.
Total output still depends on harvesting, fibre preparation, drafting skill, winding and plying. No tenfold productivity claim or lithic-mode label is assigned.
Replacement spindle and light retaining yarn — Days 46 and 48
The Day 27 wooden replacement is used for two short sessions of turning, drafting, inspecting joins and winding. Each session credits about 7 m uneven single yarn from a separately allocated 9 g prepared-fibre portion, with rejects included. The output retains light grass bundles in twining; it is not certified cord or a measured productivity improvement. The three-dimensional whorl remains securely on its shaft; yarn is wound onto the shaft rather than made by twisting the disc in a flat horizontal circle.
A separate plying operation — Day 102
The same Day 27 wooden replacement produces two new modest singles from newly cleaned/dried retained nettle stock. Each is transferred onto a separate smooth temporary holder, freeing the spindle. Spindle Plying then combines them with rotation opposite their original twist. No new spindle, first invention of spinning, wool supply or recovery of old retaining yarn is implied. The small output supplies the next day’s mesh work.

05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/fi.title: Fireboard
05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/fi.content:
Fireboard
Object
A hearth board for friction ignition with a stable spindle socket and dust-collecting notch. Choose dry identified material compatible with the spindle, not merely any wood called softwood.
Manufacture
Use Oldowan Knife Flake to flatten a suitable natural piece and form a shallow initial socket. Establish the socket with controlled rotation. Cut a notch that admits air and allows hot dust to collect on a dry catcher while preserving socket support.
Test and maintenance
Use Bow Drill Fire or a separately tested Hand Drill Fire kit. Inspect socket depth, glazed surfaces, loose dust and scorching. Relocate a worn socket only where enough sound board remains.
Limits
A damp board or unsuitable pairing can fail despite correct posture. A dry-looking exterior is not proof of a dry interior. Keep a reserve kit protected from rain.
Making the board on Day 2 prepares ignition; a sustained ember and usable fire are later demonstrations.
Second board — Day 53
Day 51’s Wooden Splitting Wedge and Wooden Mallet produce a rough willow blank. Day 53 flattens it and adds a sound socket and dust notch; a full new kit then passes one dry ignition trial. Fireboard B belongs to kit B and is not counted as another independent kit. The splitting route is a useful alternative stock preparation method, not a new universal prerequisite for hearth boards.

05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/he.title: Heating Stones
05_tools-and-equipment/fire-equipment/he.content:
Heating Stones
Selected reusable heating stones are heat-transfer equipment. They transfer energy from an outside fire to water in a suitable vessel. Select sound, dry, dense specimens through Stone Selection. Wet river pebbles, porous material and cracked pieces are poor default choices. Even screened stones can fracture on heating or immersion.
Heat away from faces and bystanders. Handle with tested green-wood tongs or another suitable implement, and place rather than drop into the vessel. Replace a cracking specimen and keep fragments out of food.
Camp Fire and fuel supply determine the available heat; stone size, temperature and water quantity determine transfer. Two stones or twenty minutes cannot be a universal boiling recipe.
Use Hot-Rock Boiling for the complete process. Heated material is a temporary state, not an indefinitely stored resource.

05_tools-and-equipment/fishing/fishing-g.title: Fishing Gorge
05_tools-and-equipment/fishing/fishing-g.content:
A component-family study, not a complete line-fishing method, measured pattern or proof of an ancient local specimen.
Fishing Gorge
Design and action
A short tapered bar attached near its centre, intended to lie lengthways with bait and turn across the pull after being swallowed. It differs from a curved hook: retention depends on the bar’s position and orientation, not a J-shaped point catching the lip. Wood, bone and other recorded materials are variants; the field base route here uses wood.
Base construction and interface
Choose a small sound piece with useful grain. Keep the centre substantial while tapering the ends. A shallow centre seat may help locate an attachment, but a deep notch can weaken the most heavily loaded part or abrade the line. Inspect the actual wetted attachment before use. No universal length, wood species, knot or breaking strength is specified by the current trial.
Use a line appropriate to the intended small fish and actual bank conditions. Keep spare line under control. A smooth stick winder is a handling aid; a rod or reel is not required. A separately tied smooth stone may help a bait settle, but changes the load and snagging risk.
Trials, use and limits
An inert loose fold can show lengthways passage and a change to crosswise bearing. It cannot reproduce a living fish or establish catch retention. Actual Hand-Line Fishing also needs accessible water, suitable bait, judgement of the take and a way to land the animal without overloading the small component.
This is food-catching equipment capable of serious internal injury, not catch-and-release tackle. The narrative takes one modest fish for prompt dispatch and fresh cooking. Inspect line, attachment and wood after recovery; shelter and dry them. A single result supplies no dependable yield or permission to leave lines unattended.
Evidence and specimen
R69 documents historical gorge designs and plant-fibre fishing line in specific Indigenous contexts, with a separate NPS comparison. Neither attests this design in the fictional valley. Day 100 makes one wooden specimen and a separate new hand line; Day 101 supplies its first actual catch. Existing spear, woven trap and hand net remain different equipment.

05_tools-and-equipment/fishing/hand-net.title: Hand Net
05_tools-and-equipment/fishing/hand-net.content:
Object-family study of a modest active hand tool. It supplies no dimensions, load rating, extra trap or guaranteed catch.
Hand Net
Object and job
A small shallow mesh bag attached around an open frame and controlled by a handle. The narrative specimen assists retrieval from an existing Woven Fishing Trap. It is an actively held tool, not a passive set net, enclosing cage, gillnet, seine or river barrier.
Base field construction
Prepare a modest netting bag through Knotted Netting and test its joins. Select a sound flexible rod that will bend into a small oval without splitting. Overlap both ends along a short wooden handle and bind them to prevent frame rotation or opening. Smooth all contact points. Other frame shapes/materials are variants; modern metal hoops are not inputs in the field route.
Lace the open bag mouth around the oval, sharing slack evenly so there is a shallow pocket and the openings do not become long escape slots. Ensure the bag bottom and side joins are closed. Its mouth must suit the actual retrieval opening and handled animal; no universal dimensions or mesh are prescribed. The selected image is an object-family study, not a measured build drawing.
Tests and use
Inspect dry, wet and under modest inert loading before a live use. Check the frame joint, lacing movement, individual mesh knots and joined bag edges. Work from firm accessible ground with a load that can be controlled easily. Keep the net immediately beneath the trap opening during transfer and support the retained catch promptly; do not drag animals through coarse mesh or leave them entangled. The story’s one small fish is dispatched promptly for fresh cooking.
Drain, rinse and inspect after use, then dry with air access. Renew damaged lacing independently of the frame. Wet fibre and repeated grit contact may alter performance. A small retained fish supplies no breaking-load rating or proof of suitability for larger species, a rapid current or unsupported riverbank reach.
Evidence and narrative
R68 separates bag, frame and handle and explains why mounting affects mesh shape. Its modern aquaculture materials, dimensions, fish densities and metal-frame recipe are not adopted. The willow/plant-cord field assembly, inert test and Day 99 transfer are authored outcomes. One existing woven-trap catch provides one fresh meal; neither net nor trap becomes a dependable winter ration.
Landing a line-caught fish — Day 101
The existing small net lies within reach on the firm bank before attended line use. It lands one modest fish retained by the new wooden gorge, reducing the need to lift the animal on the unproved line. The fish is promptly dispatched and cooked/used that day. Day 103 adds a separate small repair panel, not a second bag or enlarged rim.

05_tools-and-equipment/food-equipment/wo.title: Wooden Spoon
05_tools-and-equipment/food-equipment/wo.content:
Conceptual one-piece shallow-spoon study; no dimensions, production rate, wood-species certification or oil finish are implied.
Wooden Spoon
Object and function
A one-piece wooden food utensil with a shallow bowl, substantial neck and handle. It can move thick food and lift a small portion. It is distinct from a straight stirring stick, a deep ladle, hot-stone handling sticks and a ceramic vessel.
Material and shaping
Select identified suitable sound wood with grain running through the neck and handle. Do not infer food suitability from softness alone; avoid unidentified, treated, resin-contaminated or decaying material. The authored field specimen uses one new fresh willow section, not the hazel bow/arrow stock or a food-rack member.
Support the blank, shape the outside conservatively and keep the neck substantial. Hollow a shallow bowl through small controlled scraping cuts with a suitable Oldowan Knife Flake, supporting hand outside the cutting path. Work with the grain where possible; change approach when long splinters begin lifting. Remove only enough material for the intended scoop, keeping sound wood beneath it.
Round the rim, scrape raised fibres and inspect the handle by touch. A first rinse may raise more roughness that needs reworking. The present route introduces no metal gouge, adze, controlled burning or oil finish. Those would be different methods with their own equipment and limits.
Use, maintenance and failure signs
Trial on a small meal in the existing sound pot after cleaning. Keep hands clear of hot rim and steam; the spoon is not a pot-lifting device. Avoid levering or leaving its handle in flame. A shallow scoop carries little liquid and does not replace a ladle.
Clean promptly, allow air to both faces and inspect while green wood dries. Splits, a weakening neck, loose fibres or inaccessible dirty cracks can end food service. A sound first use does not establish dishwasher-like sanitation, permanent dimensional stability or a universally suitable wood species.
Narrative and evidence
Day 113 shapes and first uses one plain shallow spoon; Day 114 keeps it with the single working pot while the second vessel is still unfired. R77 supplies later archaeological wooden-utensil comparisons and a stone-tool woodcarving study. Those do not attest this object in the fictional valley, certify this willow or provide a measured production rate. Its useful first trial is authored physical reasoning.

05_tools-and-equipment/food-preparation/.filePath: 05_Tools and Equipment/Food Preparation/Pounding and Grinding Stones.md
05_tools-and-equipment/food-preparation/.title: Pounding and Grinding Stones
05_tools-and-equipment/food-preparation/.content:
Pounding and Grinding Stones
Design family
A clean lower stone and a suitable handstone provide controlled cracking, pounding and rubbing of food. The contact surfaces, grip, material soundness and ability to retain the batch matter more than a carved mortar’s appearance. These food tools remain separate from dirty knapping and heated stones.
Selection and preparation
Use Stone Selection for a stable broad lower piece, preferably with a useful natural shallow hollow, and a comfortable sound handstone. Reject surfaces which shed grit, carry visible suspect deposits, open cracks or sharp corners into the work. Clean the selected pair and inspect after a modest expendable trial. Do not convert an already scarred knapping percussor to clean food work without addressing its condition.
The Day 71 pair is selected natural stone. No freshly carved deep mortar, polished quern or new mineral deposit appears. A bark catch surface beside the lower stone recovers scattered fragments without adding a manufactured sieve.
Operations and feedback
Crack sound shelled inputs with controlled short blows, keeping fingers out of the contact path. Turn and spread the material. Short rubbing strokes can reduce remaining large pieces. Separate coarse pieces for reworking rather than pounding the whole batch to the finest possible powder. Inspect tools and output for new gritty fragments or damage.
Match the particle size to the following process and its containment. Finer material may expose more surface while becoming harder to retain during water changes. An apparently uniform batch is not evidence of tannin removal, a safe new species or measured throughput.
Food sequence, maintenance and alternatives
Acorn Leaching retains its own water, vessel and completion questions. The stones can improve preparation without a new cooking pot. Keep dry unprocessed reserves separate from the limited wet meal intended for current use. Clean/dry the pair between tasks, protect them from dirty animal work and replace a spalling surface.
A flat slab can work with greater scattering; a naturally deeper hollow changes stroke and cleaning access. Carving a mortar or making a rotary mill are later routes with different tools and effort, not required for this selected pair.
Narrative and evidence
Day 71 selects a separate food-only pair, then compares coarse/finished particles visually on clean bark. A modest charge enters the established small hot-water route and is cooked/used that day. R33’s NPS account records pounding and repeated handling in much later Californian acorn processing. It is an analogy, not local species identification, a validated particle size or this valley’s operating rate.

05_tools-and-equipment/measuring-equipme.title: Marked Reference Staff
05_tools-and-equipment/measuring-equipme.content:
Marked Reference Staff
Object and scope
A straight, marked stick provides a repeatable local length. It does not realise a metre, measure mass or establish a community standard. Day 29’s staff is an author-chosen first reference for comparing range positions, shafts and small samples.
Making and checking the reference
Select sound dry Wood with a straight edge. Trim protrusions with Oldowan Knife Flake, round the ends and distinguish one end with a notch. Choose the usable length before adding subdivisions. Transfer equal subdivisions by repeated comparison or temporarily folding an existing line; do not assume equal-looking marks are equal. Keep the chosen master when the subdivisions are imperfect.
A companion bark slip can hold simple grouped scratches. Distinguish the reference length from the number of times it is laid along the ground. Label an experiment by a mark the traveller can recognise, rather than treating scratches as a shared writing system.
Check for warping and damaged ends against the original marks. Make a second reference only by comparison with the first. Replacing a staff with an unrelated arm-length stick quietly changes the unit.
Operation, maintenance and limits
Lay the staff end to end along an accessible line, count placements and note gaps or slope. This measures the chosen route or ground line, not an exact horizontal distance. For a target comparison, retain the same start position and procedure.
Store the master dry at the camp’s craft spot. The staff is not the traveller’s spear or a fuel billet. A carried copy would need its own construction and check; none exists on Day 29.
Measurement and Records combines the object, counting procedure and experiment register. Precise equal subdivisions, surveying, weights and independent reproduction remain further work. The author’s kilograms, metres and hours remain modelling estimates rather than quantities this staff suddenly lets the traveller measure.

05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/arrow.title: Arrow
05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/arrow.content:
Day 107 inspection of the one plain unfletched practice arrow. Its rounded wooden nose, rear notch and short binding belong to the actual authored specimen; no separate point or feather is added.
Arrow
Design family and interfaces
A bow-launched projectile with a shaft, rear string engagement and a forward end suited to its purpose. Points and fletching are variants with distinct materials and tests, not universal inputs to every first specimen. This family differs from Atlatl Dart: its nock engages a bowstring rather than a thrower’s rear seat.
Plain practice base route
Select one sound shaft from Arrow Shafts. Inspect grain, straightness, surface damage and splits before shaping. Retain adequate length for the actual intended short draw; a front end drawn behind the bow hand is a serious failure. The current specimen has an integral rounded wooden nose, no separate head and no vanes.
Shape an open self-nock with sound material around it. A short new fine plant-thread wrap behind the nock supports the end without occupying the groove. Test on the actual Bowstring by hand before loading: neither a pinching groove nor a loose, uncertain engagement is accepted. A decorative resemblance to an arrow is not compatibility.
Trial and maintenance
Use a modest matched Self Bow only after its own limited checks, with inspected short flight space and a forgiving backstop. Stop for damaged nock, opening wrap, shaft cracks or uncontrolled engagement. Recover and examine the same initial specimen between shots. Unfletched flight may be poor; it is not a hunting configuration merely because it reaches the bank.
Fletching, a separate point, a nock reinforcement insert and more consistent shafts are independently supplied improvements. Existing Flight Feathers do not become new stock through this page. A modern spine chart or assumed draw weight cannot rate this fictional shaft.
Narrative and evidence
Day 107 converts one of the three Day 86 hazel blanks into one plain practice arrow. Two blanks remain unfinished. Day 109 makes its first limited short flights, with the same projectile recovered each time. R74 supports nock/string fit, compatible systems and wood inspection in modern coaching; modern materials, ranges and performance specifications are not adopted. The stone-tool self-nock, rounded nose and field response remain authored and unvalidated.
Two-vane alteration and limited flights — Days 110–114
The same single Day 107 specimen receives two modest opposing feather vane strips on Day 110, using a separately found feather lot and new fine plant thread. Nose, shaft and original nock remain; no new point or second arrow appears. Fletching has its own preparation and clearance checks. Day 114 short flights give an authored impression of reduced wavering with intact recovered fittings, confounded by release and air. Two original blanks remain unfinished; no hunting or rated range is established.

05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/atlat.title: Atlatl Dart
05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/atlat.content:
Atlatl Dart
Design family and scope
An atlatl dart is a projectile matched to a spear thrower through its shaft, rear engagement, mass distribution and flight behaviour. Blunt practice, fletched and pointed forms are variants on this page. The former Practice Dart and Dart Making pages are incorporated here.
Construction is distinct from Atlatl Throwing and Projectile Testing. A blunt dart can still injure. A hunting point does not compensate for unreliable release.
Base route: blunt unfletched trial
Select a candidate from Dart Shafts and use Oldowan Knife Flake or an appropriate existing edge. Examine grain defects, knots, straightness and changing moisture condition. Compare gentle flex and recovery without inventing a certified strength.
Support and ventilate the blank while monitoring distortion. No number of drying days guarantees suitability. Day 30’s local green hazel candidate is accepted only as an expendable, cautiously tested specimen; it has not become seasoned.
Round the front and shape a conservative rear seat for the real Atlatl hook. Preserve sound end grain, avoid a deep wedging hollow, and remove projecting fragments. Try slow seating and disengagement before a modest launch. Convert the blank into one dart in the asset record; do not retain the consumed shaft as a second object.
Variants and added dependencies






























VariantPurposeAdditional work and acceptanceBlunt unfletchedDiagnose engagement and basic flightRepeated controlled trials; absence of a point does not establish safetyFletchedInvestigate stabilisationSuitable Flight Feathers, alignment, fastening, mass and flight checksIntegral wooden pointA possible field-use routeSound shaping, point durability and whole-system testsSeparate hunting pointDifferent cutting/penetrating formActual point material/component, supported joint via Simple Hafting, binding allocation and dynamic tests
Feathers and an added point are not universal prerequisites. Their presence can change the same dart’s state; fitting them does not automatically manufacture another projectile. A foreshaft or composite shaft is a further variant with its own joints, not an acquired feature of the opening design.
Inspection, performance and labour
Use a cleared and rechecked site; Projectile Practice Ground records the local example. Inspect shaft, rear seat and fittings after early casts, damp weather and storage. Stop for spreading splits, unstable seating or unreliable release. Record failed attempts alongside successful ones.
Compare whole sequences and change one significant factor at a time where possible. A green specimen is changing as it dries, so improvement cannot all be attributed to technique. Gathering, shaping, conditioning, fastening, inspection and retrieval count as work.
Current narrative instance
Day 30 completes one green, blunt, unfletched dart from shaft A and makes three hand casts and three erratic thrower attempts. Day 35 retains it after another short session, noting rear-seat compression and inconsistent landings. Shaft B is still a separate bowed blank. The feather lot is unused; no hunting point or adhesive has been allocated.
The asset key practice-dart-a is retained to identify that specimen. It is not the canonical page title or a promise of a separate hunting-dart article.
Maintenance, alternatives and evidence
Keep the dart supported under ventilated cover. Reinspect before reuse; a second blank needs its own preparation. Loss or damage must reduce inventory. Pointed/fletched variants require new work and relevant stock.
R22 supports examining release and engagement, not a universal recipe for green hazel, a learning rate or reliable hunting range. Tracking, approach, useful field accuracy and recovery remain separate capabilities. The existing plate shows candidate stock and a blunt trial-end detail; it makes no claim that later variants have been built.
Days 36–40: retain one experimental specimen
Day 36 removes only a raised loose projection at the compressed rear seat; slow disengagement improves. It does not deepen the seat, change the hook or fit a point. Day 37’s four modest casts include two broad-bank landings and two misses. The seat survives inspection without a new opening split. A local adult’s own hand-thrown stone-pointed spear visibly outperforms the traveller’s system, but different users, heads and masses prevent a controlled energy comparison.
Through Day 40, practice-dart-a remains blunt, unfletched and changing as it dries. Candidate B is still a bowed blank. Feathers, pitch and sinew are unallocated to projectiles. The new grass back panel has no casting-clearance trial; it must not appear as proven throwing clothing.
Day 42 private trial
Four modest casts include two broad-patch landings and two misses. The rear seat survives inspection without a spreading split. The traveller stops as timing deteriorates with fatigue. There is no new dart, point, fletching, measured range or reliable improvement; specimen A remains green, blunt and unfletched through Day 45.
No hunting configuration is inferred — Days 48–50
Day 48 leaves the green blunt unfletched practice dart at camp and attempts an approach with the existing wooden-pointed hand spear. Day 50 gives that same practice dart four short private casts: three reach the broad bank patch and one misses. The rear seat is intact on inspection. This small unsupervised result is not a local comparison, reliable hunting projectile, second dart or demonstrated accuracy improvement.
Repeat series and observer interest — Day 55
The same blunt unfletched dart survives inspection and eight modest casts from a familiar starting place. The first is low; seven reach the broad chosen bank patch, with closer grouping than the scattered opening trials. These two short series supply a useful own-baseline observation, not a calibrated range, energy, hunting or local-expert comparison. Wood is changing as it dries. Two adults watch and one gestures towards the engagement; no handover, instruction or independent use occurs. Bowed B and the feather lot remain separate unfinished inputs.
Same specimen, field-use variant — Days 76–78
Day 76 inspects the changing shaft, repaired rear seat and return after gentle flex before continuing. The same original dart A receives two modest bound vane sections from the retained Day 27 feather lot and a gradual integral wooden point. Fine new nettle line is prepared from another selected portion of protected retted stock; no adhesive, stone insert, separate foreshaft or second completed dart is added. The former green/blunt/unfletched descriptions remain dated historical states.
Fletching is set clear of hook, hand and rear release space. Slow fit and modest initial checks precede Day 77’s inspected practice-ground casts. More settled arrivals in that short series coexist with a low miss; changed point, changing shaft and technique prevent attributing the result solely to feathers. Bowed candidate B remains unfinished.
Day 78 carries this configuration on a permitted outing but makes no cast through obstructing brush. Local hunters, not this dart, take the deer. R44 records a modern tied-on route, not this exact two-vane configuration or local prehistoric attestation.
Completed Day 76 variant

Object study of the existing dart after its two small vanes and integral wooden point are fitted. The earlier practice-stage illustration remains above. Neither view is a dimensioned construction drawing.
Days 93–94 — dart A’s first large-game use
The same two-vane dart with integral wooden point takes one smaller red deer on Day 93. Recovery finds tip damage, without shaft failure, new vanes or stone head. Day 94 reshapes the damaged tip; another trial is needed before reuse. Bowed dart B and the three green arrow blanks remain separate and unfinished. The singular successful field outcome supplies no rated performance.
Post-repair check — Day 100
A brief restrained plant-covered-target trial at the existing practice ground checks the Day 94 reshaped tip before renewed field use. The same integral wooden point, shaft, two vanes and rear seat remain sound after recovery. This restores dart A to available field equipment; it adds no new head, spare dart, hunting success or measured performance.

05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/index.title: Projectiles
05_tools-and-equipment/projectiles/index.content:
Projectiles
Equipment pages are organised by design family. Variants with the same basic mechanism live within the family page.

Atlatl Dart — blunt practice, fletched and pointed configurations, with the current green trial specimen clearly distinguished.
Atlatl — the launcher, including its own construction routes.
Fire-Hardened Spear — a separate spear family that may be thrust or thrown; it remains under Weapons.
