06_structures-and-places/places/fallback.title: Fallback Bench
06_structures-and-places/places/fallback.content:
Fallback Bench
A higher bench southwest of the pine patch, inspected on Day 33 as a possible retreat destination. Natural rock screening offers limited wind cover and a resting surface appears reasonably drained. It is still a candidate, not a supplied refuge.
Route and water
The inspected route follows western ground upstream of the seep’s head, then turns south along higher contour ground. It avoids the larger river and does not require a new bridge. Allow roughly 35–50 minutes one way in ordinary daylight plus inspection and return; load, rain, darkness and vigilance can lengthen it.
There is no established drinking source on the bench. Access towards the known seep remains part of its practical cost. The traveller retraces a difficult portion in daylight, not the whole route under pursuit.
Current state and limits
Through Day 35 there is no constructed shelter, insulated bed, treated-water provision, stored fuel, food cache or second ignition kit here. An empty inspection does not certify absence of animals, other occupants or future danger.
Retreat Planning supplies the judgement. Building and supplying this place later must consume actual work and stock. The map’s dated written addition records it after the Day 28 illustrated state; it must not appear as an already built feature in that picture.

06_structures-and-places/places/meeting-.title: Meeting Ground
06_structures-and-places/places/meeting-.content:
Meeting Ground
Open approach ground south of Neanderthal Clearing, beyond the western flank of the spur. It is outside the neighbours’ hearth/work area and within sight of it. Valley Map fixes the route; no main-river crossing is required.
Dated use
Day 24 plans a cautious approach with room to withdraw. Day 25 attempts a cordage/spindle pitch and retreats after the warning. The original spindle and samples are abandoned, not accepted as gifts. Their loss remains in the daily ledger.
The traveller’s plain wooden spear is concealed at a stopping-place short of and south of this ground, then recovered while retreating. The local man’s weapon is stone-pointed. No equipment ownership transfers merely because objects are present in the same encounter.
Access and uncertainty
The name does not establish neutral ground, consent, agreed diplomacy or permission to return. The neighbours can observe and control the approach. The remembered route is a foot route, not an engineered road or protected corridor.
This location record holds setting relationships. Communication and Exchange describes relevant skills, while the narrative must still earn a shared language and willing interaction. Through Day 35 there is no alliance or community supply.

06_structures-and-places/places/neandert.title: Neanderthal Clearing
06_structures-and-places/places/neandert.content:
Neanderthal Clearing
The neighbouring living/working area lies northwest beyond the rocky spur, on the same western side of the larger river as Traveller’s Camp. Eleven people are observed on Day 21; that is a visit count, not the group’s total population.
What is known
Smoke and distant firelight appear on Day 19 before the occupants are identified. Day 21’s observation from cover shows maintained fire, hides, cordage and practised working. Day 25’s close warning shows a local hafted stone-pointed spear. The group’s broader arrangements, language and resource rights remain unknown.
Do not add permanent houses, pottery, a communal atlatl or a stereotyped technologically helpless population. Their practical skills exceed the traveller’s in several visible tasks.
Approach and limits
The known contact route skirts the spur’s west flank and stops at Meeting Ground south of this living area. It needs no main-river crossing. The traveller has not been admitted to the clearing; observation does not grant entry or ownership.
One rebuffed approach establishes a particular warning, not an intention to kill or a promise of future peace. Different individuals may respond differently. Nothing here supplies gifts, trading resources, instruction or shared provisions.
Use Valley Map for bearings and Setting Specification for the group’s authored technological/anatomical constraints. This is an atlas entry, not a generic model of every Neanderthal camp.
Bounded outer-edge work and exchange — Day 62
A familiar adult permits an immediate branchwood task near the outer working edge, accepts useful selected output and visibly releases one worn worked skin to the traveller. This is limited access for an observed encounter, not permission to enter the whole living area, use resource patches or claim group provisions. No food, weapon or permanent hosting agreement is gained.
Outing and recovery access — Days 77–78
The outer edge remains the contact/working limit. A familiar adult permits immediate accompanying movement on Day 77 and actual departure with three hunters on Day 78. The traveller returns carrying divided loads to the outer work edge, helps with the recovered animal and receives a small meat/fat share and trimmed fresh hide margin. No general entry, permanent supply arrangement or local use of the traveller’s atlatl is established.

06_structures-and-places/places/projecti.title: Projectile Practice Ground
06_structures-and-places/places/projecti.content:
Projectile Practice Ground
Particular site and status
The traveller’s short-cast site lies west/southwest of camp, above the tributary and short of the western trap circuit. Casts face west into a local earth bank, away from the river and established contact route. See Valley Map and its dated additions.
Day 29 selects and inspects the ground. Day 30 clears modest obstructions and places ground markers; short comparisons begin. Day 35 revisits the same short line. No engineered barrier, target hide, full-force containment or permanent ownership is established.
Access and changing conditions
The approach is a short local detour from the camp terrace. Do not move it to the ridge meeting ground or import the shelter and hearth here. Footing, bank condition, sight lines, possible entrants and retrieval space require inspection on each visit. Clear ground on one day is not a lasting safety guarantee.
The ordinary spear stays reachable outside the casting swing. Markers are small locally collected pieces, not cord stretched across a route or a defensive installation.
What is recorded here
This is an atlas entry, not an invention or generic manufacturing recipe. Projectile Testing contains reusable selection, inspection and comparison guidance. Atlatl Throwing develops movement; Atlatl Dart describes projectile variants.
The earlier site-unit annotation is recorded as dated place preparation rather than a manufactured stock item. Its physical description and the day’s labour remain unchanged. The prepared ground grants no permission over the valley and no ability to stop a visitor.
Day 37 observed use
Two local people stop on open ground north of the short west-directed flight line. After the traveller’s modest casts, one uses a clear part of the same bank for two hand-spear casts, recovering his own equipment. Start positions differ; no expanded full-force range or common ownership is established. The local adult’s presence is temporary, not a new camp landmark. Reinspect the space before later sessions.
Rechecked pointed configurations — Day 77
The existing west-directed short line is reinspected for its actual pointed equipment. A plant-covered patch avoids exposed stone, with crest, sides, entrants and retrieval checked. Modified dart A and the separate stone-pointed hand spear receive limited casts; no new range, surveyed distance or stronger barrier is acquired. Observer contact later occurs at the meeting approach, not inside the flight line.

06_structures-and-places/places/travelle.title: Traveller's Camp
06_structures-and-places/places/travelle.content:
Traveller’s Camp
The first camp occupies the drained terrace north of the tributary and west of the larger river. It is above the flood level selected for the opening; that judgement is not a promise against every future flood. Ground falls southeast and the fallen-limb shelter entrance faces broadly southeast. Valley Map and its camp inset fix the relationships.
Fixed arrangement
Basic Lean-to is northwest/upslope. The craft spot is south of it and west/upslope of the ordinary outside hearth. Drying and animal processing occupy the southern/southwestern dirty flank; waste lies farther beyond it. Experimental firing uses separate bare ground northeast of the hearth. Drinking collection remains at the upstream seep, away from retting and processing.
The low shelter stays a bark/leaf/branch structure under a thick mossy fallen limb. Repairs do not replace it with a tent or move the fires next to dry bedding. The map’s icons are enlarged, not metre clearances.
Dated state
Day 14 introduces the separate firing place, used on Day 15. Day 34 repairs the northwestern windward covering. Day 35 adds a small bedding-pad variant to the existing resting layer, not a whole mattress or new garment.
Tools and stocks are governed by Survival Ledger. A camp page does not duplicate them into an extra inventory. The practice ground and fallback bench are elsewhere.
Access and exposure
Known gathering and water routes radiate from the terrace. Smoke and visible movement can reveal the area; a shelter is not protection against several determined people. Keep clean/dirty handling separate and the exit usable. Retreat Planning describes the judgement; Fallback Bench remains unsupplied through Day 35.
Days 36–40
Dry grass for clothing is kept under the existing ventilated cover, separately from the bed. Day 38 puts one rabbit pelt into preparation on the existing southern/southwestern dirty frame. Day 39 checks the southeast exit and carrying order without building a barrier or moving supplies. Day 40 makes a removable back panel at the uphill craft spot. No fixed installation, hearth, firing patch or water route moves.
Days 41–45: same site, staged sleeping enclosure
Day 41 inspects the original northwest shelter and runoff. Day 43 brings ten selected light members and a separate cover lot. Day 44 installs two fork braces, a light rail beside the retained limb and three return ribs along the north/east side, keeping the occupied old roof and southeast exit. Day 45 seats four further ribs and partly covers that slope. The upper junction and southeast front remain incomplete. Hearth, craft, dirty frame, waste, firing patch and water routes do not move. This is Framed Debris Shelter work on the existing shelter asset, not a second dwelling. The fallback bench remains unsupplied.
Occupied weather and clothing work — Days 46–50
The northwest sleeping shelter receives upper overlap work, a shower-leak repair and a light movable offset brush bundle beside the southeast mouth. Its footprint, exit direction, retained fallen limb, outside hearth, clean craft spot and dirty flank do not move. Day 47’s large canid investigates the southwest dirty area and leaves; the drying frame remains intact. A narrow sight gap is cleared in loose approach brush, without building a fence or blocking retreat. No neighbour visits or works at camp in this span. The dry garment panels and later small crown pad remain removable items, not camp structures.
Closing second-moon work — Days 56–59
Sole fitting and clay inspection use the existing clean craft spot. The small Day 58 firing uses the established separate outside firing place and cools there overnight. Day 59 wetting checks take place on a separate non-food test stone; specimens stay out of clean bark vessels. Shelter footprint, southeast exit, ordinary hearth and dirty-material flank do not move. No kiln, new dwelling or supplied fallback site is introduced.
Abandoned home — Day 61
Movable working equipment and usable supplies transfer to Western Overhang. The old lean-to ceases to be occupied and is not maintained as a second home or defensive refuge. The large dirty drying frame and rejected non-food pot remain at this old site. Its earlier atlas relationships and dated artwork remain historical. The fish cage remains at its riverside anchor rather than moving with the bed.

06_structures-and-places/places/western-.title: Western Overhang
06_structures-and-places/places/western-.content:
Western Overhang
Position and discovery
A shallow southeast-facing limestone recess on the western slope near the southern foot of the rocky spur. It lies west/northwest and uphill of the original Traveller’s Camp, on the western side of the main river. Day 60 inspects it; Day 61 begins occupation. It is a newly observed site, not the previously inspected Fallback Bench.
The centre has a dry resting strip behind the drip line. A fissured corner near the eastern end shows wetting and is excluded from occupation. No recent occupant signs are seen during the first inspection; that observation grants no universal right of access or promise of rock stability.
Routes and orientation
Provisional ordinary daylight allowances are 15–20 minutes to the old camp, 10–15 minutes southeast along contour ground to the known seep, and roughly 30–45 minutes towards the meeting ground using the established west-of-spur route. Load, weather and the task add time. These are author geography, not measured distances.
The old riverside trap remains at its anchor. Water is carried from the established seep; no new drinking source, river crossing or deep cave appears. Existing resource patches remain finite and their access is not enlarged by moving.
Working arrangement through Day 64

Dry back-left: sleeping layer and protected personal materials, with space beside the rock face.
Mouth, northwest/left edge: low fork/rail-supported brush and overlapping bark wind screen. The offset southeast opening and ventilation remain; there is no daub or full front enclosure yet.
Front-right under the usable roof: clean craft stone.
Rear-right dry strip: low food-only storage rack, separate from the wet corner.
Outside and southeast beyond the drip edge: ordinary hearth on open mineral ground.
Farther southwest/downhill: animal-processing support area; waste farther beyond, away from the seep route.
Outside northeast of the hearth: separate future firing ground, still unused through Day 64.

Movable tools and supplies transfer on Day 61. The old dirty frame and rejected pot remain at the abandoned camp. Two comparison pieces, both ignition kits and both bark vessels are moved, not duplicated. There is no new drying frame, kiln, supplied fallback site or stored meat.
Use and limits
Rock-Shelter Enclosure describes the construction family. This atlas page fixes its actual local position and stage, not a generic engineering guarantee. Inspect weather, drips, supports, rock changes and water access as ordinary use warrants. The first screen and bed are functional early work; cold-season clothing and further closure remain projects.
The inset is not to scale. Written relationships govern where its oblique symbols are ambiguous. Area icons, including the processing symbol, do not record an extra catch or stock. Keep actual stored food on the raised surfaces described in the narrative rather than inferring load placement from the atlas icon.
Dated changes through Day 69
The inset above remains a Day 64 record. Day 65 adds a short return and a separate movable baffle alongside the southeast entrance, breaking the direct wind path without blocking passage or the high gap. The bed’s compressed outer/hip/shoulder fill is renewed. A small lower left woven bay receives earth/fibre infill on Day 66 and stays under bark/rock rain protection; by Day 69 its limited attachment/drying check is useful. No full mud front or indoor hearth appears.
Clean craft, food rack, excluded wet corner, outside animal processing and unused future firing ground retain their relationships. Day 68’s single spear-caught fish is processed outside and eaten the same day. Day 69’s new point is wrapped separately from its unhafted shaft. These are actual current changes; pictorial symbols in the older inset do not update themselves.
Working additions through Day 74
A small removable pelt support is installed at the separate dirty-material area on Day 70 and receives the Day 70/71 rabbit skins; the old large frame is not moved. Day 71 adds a selected food-only pounding slab and handstone. Day 72 places one greenware pot and witness on a protected front-right craft-side board, separate from food and traffic. No new firing occurs.
The finished composite hand spear is guarded in storage from Day 70. Day 74’s restrained plant-target trial uses inspected clear dry ground outside ordinary work/traffic, not a new permanent range or occupied line. The existing screen, one small earth bay, bed and rear food rack retain their layout. The new pelt foot layers appear after Day 73 fitting; no new trade or spare skin supply is added.
Current objects and processes through Day 79
Day 75 changes the low footwear’s heel-retention route without a new wardrobe silhouette. Day 76 modifies the existing dart A, while the thrower and bowed blank remain their previous objects. Day 78 adds one freshly released narrow deer-skin margin to the separate dirty-work support, promptly fleshed and still drying on Day 79. Its food share has already been eaten.
Day 79 adds a separate four-pronged wooden fishing spear. The old integral wooden-point spear, stone-pointed hand spear and modified dart remain distinct. The food rack, small earth bay, outside hearth and craft-side greenware board retain their arrangement; no firing, indoor combustion, stored meat or new home appears.
Firing ground and cooking support — through Day 84
Days 80–81 allocate the retained deer margin to one small tool guard at the dirty-work support. The craft-side greenware board remains separate. Day 81 clears and prepares the already identified outside northeast firing patch; Day 82 first uses it for the Day 72 pot and one witness half, with cooling in place through Day 83. This is not the ordinary hearth and not a newly discovered valley location.
The ordinary hearth remains southeast beyond the drip edge. Day 84 adds the low three-stone Open Cooking Hearth support here. The one new vessel completes its water and meal trials, then returns washed to protected drying at the craft side. The small witness is a non-food sample; earlier comparison remnants, storage rack, sleeping arrangement and map bearings stay unchanged. The older Day 64 inset remains explicitly dated rather than depicting all later additions.
Closing Moon 3 and the new-moon boundary — Days 85–89
One freshly selected green hazel half-stave receives a separate clean forked drying support beside the craft area, clear of traffic, dirty skins, food and hearth heat. Three new arrow-shaft blanks remain loose for inspection. A short trial cord stays with fibre work. The stave is coarsely shaped but never strung or loaded. No completed bow or arrows are added.
Day 88 repairs a local edge of the existing small daub bay under its retained bark protection. The ordinary hearth and its three low cooking supports retain their outside position. Day 89’s rain leaves the bed and craft-side wood within the dry strip; the new patch remains drying and the single pot gives another sound meal-use result. No additional skin, garment, preserved meat or map landmark is introduced.
Working state — completed Day 94
The same natural roof and modest screen remain. A portable pack frame belongs to the carrier equipment. A new stable fleshing beam and larger open hide support occupy the established southwest/downhill dirty-work side. Temporary separate food-rest surfaces do not turn the rear food rack or clean craft stone into raw-hide work space. The one full skin comes from the solo Day 93 deer; existing clothes remain unchanged. The limited new food is cooked/used by Day 94. No new room, indoor hearth, second pot, new water source or occupied neighbouring site appears.
Clothing and small mesh work — completed Day 99
The natural roof, external ordinary hearth, small screen and single cooking pot remain. The sole full skin leaves its larger dirty-side support for dry working and clean garment assembly; it no longer hangs there as an uncut material reserve. Completed removable sleeve/leg pieces air individually under cover. A small netting project uses the existing clean craft space; its finished hand net drains separately from dirty hide work and bedding. No indoor hearth, new room, new shared site or second pot appears.
Working state — completed Day 104
Small fishing tackle, the existing replacement spindle and one new notched shuttle use the established clean craft space. Fine wet line airs separately; modest repair mesh is kept with the hand net. The heavier full-length string candidate is stored recognisably beside its old short sample, away from the unstrung stave’s separate rests. The natural roof, modest screen, outside hearth, one pot, food area and dirty-material side remain. No room, new hearth, second pot or group occupation is added.
Working state — completed Day 109
The existing small dirty-side support handles the one new rabbit skin, then clears after its Day 108 garment allocation. The bow and recovered practice arrow use the clean rests; two original arrow blanks remain separate and unfinished. The provisional bow is stored unstrung after trials. The new pair of hand pockets airs with clothing. Natural roof, modest screen, ordinary outside hearth and single pot remain; no workshop room, extra pot, new pelt reserve or group provision appears.
Craft state — completed Day 114
The rock roof, modest screen, small daub bay and outside ordinary hearth remain. One new greenware cooking bowl and one comparable witness occupy the protected separate craft board, with direct heat avoided; both are unfired. One plain new wooden spoon serves the old working pot. The bow rests unstrung, its single arrow now with two modest vanes from a new feather lot; the other two blanks remain unfinished. Current complete clothing and both removable warming pockets persist. No building, second working pot, new food cache, spare pelt or group support is added.

06_structures-and-places/structures-and-.title: Structures and Places
06_structures-and-places/structures-and-.content:
Structures and Places
This section separates reusable construction knowledge from the atlas of this particular story. A named place may contain several structures and tools; the place itself is not a technology or a capability unlock. See Category Specification and Page Scope and Organisation.
Structures

Basic Lean-to — the shelter family, including the fallen-limb opening route.
Framed Debris Shelter — the staged second-moon sleeping enclosure.
Rock-Shelter Enclosure — a light weather screen and dry bed beneath a natural rock roof.
Raised Storage Rack — a food-only platform used with Dry Nut Storage.
Drying Rack — a camp framework supporting separate drying surfaces.
Kiln — a planned firing enclosure; no kiln has been acquired.

Valley atlas
Use Valley Map for bearings, terrain and route relationships. Its graphic is a Day 28 state; dated written additions govern later locations.

Traveller’s Camp — the original terrace camp, abandoned as the home on Day 61.
Western Overhang — the newly inspected and occupied home, with an inset through Day 64.
Projectile Practice Ground — the particular west-facing trial site, selected on Day 29 and prepared on Day 30.
Neanderthal Clearing — the neighbouring living/working area; Day 62 includes bounded accepted work at its outer edge.
Meeting Ground — the open approach where the first pitch is rebuffed.
Fallback Bench — a Day 33 candidate, still unsupplied.

A place entry records observations and dated changes. It neither duplicates general construction instructions nor silently adds inventory. More atlas entries are added when a location has enough recurring narrative or logistical importance to warrant one.
Construction update through Day 69
Rock-Shelter Enclosure now records the offset entrance and one small Earth-and-Fibre Infill trial. The Western Overhang inset remains dated Day 64; written later additions govern subsequent changes. The original camp remains abandoned, with no supplied retreat or new kiln.

06_structures-and-places/structures/fire.title: Open Cooking Hearth
06_structures-and-places/structures/fire.content:
Open Cooking Hearth
Structure and role
A small outside hearth combines stable pot supports, bare mineral ground, an air path and access for fuel. This design uses three low bedded stones around a modest fire gap. It is a constructed cooking arrangement, not the separate operation of Cooking in an Earthenware Pot and not a ceramic-firing kiln.
Setting and construction
Choose open ground clear of roots, overhanging cover and combustible stores. At Western Overhang the ordinary hearth stays southeast beyond the drip edge; the northeast firing patch is separate. Do not move combustion into the sleeping enclosure.
Select sound, dry support stone from dry ground, rejecting visible cracks, layering and damp material. A label such as river stone or granite is not a heat-safety guarantee. Stones can fracture on heating; the narrative choice is an authored field judgement, not a validated rock-identification procedure.
Bed three low supports firmly so the actual cold pot makes broad stable contacts and cannot tip under light rim pressure. Preserve an opening for small fuel and combustion air. Avoid squeezing the pot between supports or placing an edge across the fuel-feed opening. Test stability before lighting.
Operation and maintenance
Match the fire to the vessel and contents. Keep the load supported during heating and cooling; do not rearrange hot stones under a full pot. Use cold inspections to find loosened bedding, fractured support stone and rim instability. Remove accumulated ash without undermining the supports.
First instance
Day 84 adapts the existing outdoor hearth for the one small pot, then supports its water and meal trials. The daily image and general plate show one pot, three supports and low fuel. No chimney, indoor hearth, new camp location or claim of fuel efficiency is introduced.

06_structures-and-places/structures/firi.title: Kiln
06_structures-and-places/structures/firi.content:
Kiln
Status and scope
A planned controlled firing installation. This overview defines dependencies and design decisions; it is not a construction-ready kiln blueprint.
Requirements
A kiln needs a chamber suited to the intended temperature, fuel and air admission, an exhaust path, stable supports, safe access and a way to evaluate the firing. Pottery experience helps identify what the clay load needs. Pre-Kiln Firing is a useful development route rather than a universal physical necessity.
Design work
Choose the target material and firing range before choosing a geometry. Assess refractory quality, wall thickness, expansion, loading and airflow. Design a small trial that can fail without collapsing onto workers. Separate fuel supply, chamber maintenance and load cooling.
A named banked or updraft kiln is not enough: future instructions must specify dimensions, materials, draft, operating sequence and observable limits, backed by a relevant tested design.
Tests and scaling
Measure or otherwise calibrate temperature where possible; compare multiple firings and sacrificial samples. Inspect cracking and support movement. Plan repairs, fuel storage and ventilation.
Limits
An enclosure does not guarantee fuel economy or a hotter load. Do not infer wall temperature by touching hot walls. This note remains planned with no first-month construction or demonstration.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site enclosure. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.

06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.title: Basic Lean-to
06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.content:
Basic Lean-to
Purpose and base route
A low debris lean-to provides a sheltered resting space with wind protection, drainage and ground insulation. A debris shelter can be assembled from natural fallen branches without cordage; a lashed frame is an improvement.
Construction
Select stable ground above runoff and flood level, away from dead overhead limbs and active animal paths. Place a sound ridge support and lean smaller pieces into a stable frame. Cover to reduce wind and rain using appropriate layered material.
Build a substantial insulating bed separate from the outside hearth. Make the resting cavity small enough to reduce exposure without trapping smoke or eliminating ventilation.
Test
Inspect joints and covering before occupying. During rain, identify leaks and drainage. Replace compressed or damp bedding. In cold conditions assess whether you can remain warm at rest; a roof alone does not establish protection.
Limits and scaling
Collection takes time and may fail in wet conditions. A lashed lean-to using Simple Cordage and Basic Thatching can last longer but still needs repairs. No universal two-hour completion or guaranteed thermal performance is assigned.
The first month’s camp remains marginal during rain. Improved shelter reduces risk; it is not proof of winter readiness.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site enclosure. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.
Staged rebuilding from Day 41
Day 41 inspects the support, drainage and exit without dismantling the occupied roof. Days 44–45 add the first framed-debris return-side variant in the same footprint. The daily asset remains shelter-a. That upgrade has its own incomplete cover and test history; it does not rewrite the opening lean-to or create another camp.

06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.title: Framed Debris Shelter
06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.content:
Framed Debris Shelter
Structure, function and scope
A compact sleeping enclosure with a selected load-bearing frame, retained overlapping plant cover and a separately insulated resting layer. This family includes small fork-supported and ribbed variants; it is not a log house, animal-hide tent or certified winter dwelling. The base route uses suitable sound wood and stable bearing geometry. Cordage and more elaborate joints are optional routes with separate requirements.
Site and frame
Use Shelter Construction to select drained ground, inspect overhead support, keep an exit and stage the build. Arrange the resting space for the whole body, allowing movement and ventilation rather than treating a sealed cavity as inherently warmer or safer. A small span can reduce material and loading, but dimensions must fit the occupant and actual pieces.
For a fork-supported light rail, seat sound forked pieces on stable ground and verify resistance to rocking and rolling from outside the fall space. Fit ribs with secure upper bearing and non-creeping feet. The whole assembly must carry its intended covering in wet as well as dry conditions. Do not jack up a heavy retained fallen limb with improvised light props.
Natural bearing joints can reduce line demand. A selected lashing requires suitable cord, geometry and load checks; short ties used to retain a light cover do not establish structural rope capacity. No numerical universal load or span is assigned.
Cover, bed and operation
Sort Plant Covering Stock by retention and weather-facing role. Fit lower layers first where overlapping construction requires it, then direct upper runoff outside. Cover junctions and the entrance deliberately; a visually closed roof may still leak at its meeting line. Basic Thatching provides related layering judgement, but different plant materials need different treatment.
Keep Dry Plant Insulation as a separate clean sleeping layer. Check compression, cold ground contact and morning damp. Preserve ventilation and an accessible opening. Keep the present fire and hot stones outside this combustible enclosure; adding combustion inside requires a different proven exhaust and clearance design. R32 supports the exposure and combustion concerns, not the frame’s engineering.
Inspection and maintenance
Check supports, bearing contacts, rail rotation, rib feet, cover retention, runoff, entrance and bed. Inspect after weather and before occupation. Unload or withdraw if supports shift or cracks develop. Dry stock needs replenishment, and wet cover can both add load and lose insulation. Record the labour and materials required by repairs.
First local instance: Days 44–45
The existing northwest camp shelter, asset shelter-a, is rebuilt in stages in the same footprint. Its southeast entrance, craft spot, outside hearth and water routes remain fixed. Two light fork braces, a slender rail and seven return ribs are the ten newly selected members. The rail sits beside the retained limb; the limb’s original bearing is not dismantled or lifted.
Day 44 installs the braces, rail and three ribs, using 0.4 m short roll-restraint ties while preserving the old covered side. This is the first limited framework demonstration, not a weatherproof chamber. Day 45 installs four further ribs and allocates 6 kg mixed cover, with 0.8 m light retaining ties. The return slope is partly covered; the upper junction and southeast front remain unfinished. A breeze and short resting trial show limited improvement. Four kilograms of cover stock remain for further work. No rain or winter test has occurred.
The upgraded instance is one existing shelter, not a second building or supplied Fallback Bench. Its first-month Basic Lean-to state remains in the dated record and map. A successful completion still needs observed weather performance, maintained bedding, clothing, food and fuel; shelter alone cannot establish winter readiness.
First shower repair and entrance trial — Days 46–50
Day 46 allocates 3 kg existing coarse cover and 0.2 m light retaining line to connect the return cover at the upper junction without changing the heavy limb’s support. Day 47 showers reveal one inward path at a curled lap; it is unloaded locally, adjusted and extended with 0.5 kg protected cover. No further drip appears there during later watched showers, and no support movement is visible during inspection. This is a narrow weather result, not a wet-load or storm rating.
Day 49 collects 2.5 kg coarse cover and uses 2 kg as a movable offset brush wind baffle at one edge of the southeast mouth. Its support is the existing outer rib margin and ground; no new post, door, hinge or second structure appears. The clear passage and ventilation remain. One kilogram cover stays loose at Day 50. Separate clean bedding is renewed after the local wet edge and again on Day 50. The fire remains outdoors and the same northwest footprint is occupied. Clothing and supply still constrain winter readiness.

06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.title: Rock-Shelter Enclosure
06_structures-and-places/structures/shel.content:
Rock-Shelter Enclosure
Function and route
A light weather screen and insulated sleeping arrangement beneath an inspected natural rock roof. The rock carries itself; the constructed frame carries its own screen only. Site assessment, front enclosure and bedding are separate parts of the system.
Inputs and site
Use Shelter Construction to assess runoff, drips, overhead changes, usable dry floor, access, previous occupants and water. Reject doubtful overhead ground rather than treating a brief inspection as geological certification. Choose a shallow usable recess without assuming that deeper is drier or warmer.
Sound light Wood, Plant Covering Stock and separate Dry Plant Insulation support the base route. Natural bearings can reduce ties, but all screen supports need secure feet and resistance to rotation.
Construction and occupied checks
Clear the resting surface without creating a water-collecting pit. Separate bedding from damp soil and rock, and check how foundation and fill compress under the whole body.
Seat a low support and retain brush/bark against wind. Keep an accessible offset entrance and moisture escape; the screen is not an airtight seal. Direct runoff away from the occupied strip. Push and inspect the frame before adding covering, then reassess after use and weather.
A supported earth/plant-fibre infill is a later variant needing its own drying, loading and rain-protection checks. Day 61 uses brush/bark only. R40 informs moisture judgement, not a validated mix.
Fire, maintenance and alternatives
The current method keeps combustion outside the enclosed sleeping area. Rock overhead alone does not certify exhaust or clearances (R32). Inspect wet edges, changing rock/support conditions, screen retention and bedding compression. A temporary screen is useful while more closure proceeds.
A framed shelter elsewhere remains an alternative if the rock or water access is poor. No mud-coated wooden roof, indoor hearth, fitted door or permanent stone dwelling is implied.
Narrative instance
Day 61 establishes the first screen and bed at Western Overhang, followed by occupation. Day 64 adds a separate food rack. More front closure and a small supported infill trial belong to later days.
Days 65–69: return, entrance and trial infill
Day 65 adds a short supported return, retained overlapping brush/bark and a separate movable baffle beside the offset southeast entrance. High air access remains; the frame still carries only its own screen. A brief shower leaves the sleeping strip dry after compressed bedding is renewed. This is an observed limited use check, not winter certification.
Day 66 starts Earth-and-Fibre Infill in one low woven bay under roof cover. Its supporting lower rail stays off the ground and bark interrupts splash. By Day 69 a witness patch has a firm centre and the installed bay remains keyed under a light check, with fine edge shrinkage. Surrounding covering remains bark/brush; the whole front is not daubed. Routine hearth and future pottery firing stay outside the enclosure.
End-of-moon upkeep — Days 88–89
The single supported infill bay receives a local edge repair after its backing and wetting conditions are inspected. Bedding is settled and compressed fill renewed. The entrance and high ventilation gap remain open, and all combustion stays outside. After overnight rain, the bed and craft-side wood are still in the dry strip; the new repair is still drying. This is limited upkeep of the existing enclosure, not a newly completed winter house.

06_structures-and-places/structures/work.title: Drying Rack
06_structures-and-places/structures/work.content:
Drying Rack
Structure and scope
A supported rack holds material above ground for controlled drying trials. The frame and a validated meat-preservation process are separate capabilities.
Construction
Use sound poles and Tripod Lashing or another stable support. Secure crosspieces, test the load and keep the structure away from sparks and strong heat. Provide a clean surface appropriate to the material.
Keep raw hides, fibre and food on separate surfaces; a used hide-drying frame is not automatically clean cooking equipment.
Operation and limits
Observe airflow, damp folds and heat exposure. Smoke can add flavour and alter surfaces but does not prove that pathogens are destroyed or that food is shelf-stable. Pine bough smoke and creosote are not a universal food-preserving recipe.
R07 explains why low-temperature drying can leave pathogens alive. A future preservation method needs specific heat, drying, storage and verification controls.
First-month role
Day 6 installs a small drying frame for the pelt and tendon. Meat is cooked and eaten that day. No stored smoked-meat output is entered into the ledger.
Structure and operation
This page describes the constructed site framework. Its location, access and maintenance are distinct from the operation performed there. A named local place and movable objects used within it keep their own roles; classification creates no new construction or operating success.
Small support at the new home — Days 70–73
Day 70 makes a small removable support from sound light sticks and new ties at the separate dirty-material area of Western Overhang. The Day 70 and Day 71 rabbit pelts are promptly fleshed and receive protected airflow and condition-led working across the following days. This is a new small instance of the support family, not the old large frame moved from the abandoned camp, a food shelf or a meat-preservation result. Both skins leave loose stock for foot coverings on Day 73.
Separate material drying — Days 78–81
The existing small support at the overhang’s dirty-work area receives the one fresh deer margin. Its fold is opened for airflow, and a slight rain cover is adjusted without sealing the work into damp air. Day 80’s shaped guard blank dries around a wooden former here; Day 81 removes it as one finished cover. The frame is not converted to a food shelf, and no large skin or meat-preservation batch is added.
Separate clean wood support — Days 85–89
Two low forked rests with steadying ties form a separate clean support at the craft side for the one green bow stave. Day 86 adds three loosely stored shaft blanks. The structure keeps airflow around the pieces and leaves them individually inspectable; it neither forces a curve nor provides heated seasoning. The pelt support stays at the dirty-work area and the raised rack stays food-only. The dated secondary seasoning study below is a general design view rather than a literal map or certification of a knotted blank.
Clean wood-rest instance — Days 85–89

A general wood-seasoning material study. The visible knots are not approval of the selected blank: this plate illustrates airy storage, not the exact stock or a completed bow design.
Day 94 — larger skin support
One new light open support at the overhang’s dirty-work side holds the sole full deer skin with lightly spread margins after beam fleshing. It is separate from the little rabbit support, temporary food rest and clean bow-stock supports. It permits inspection and air access, not a claim of completed preservation or tanning. No old first-month dirty frame is silently moved from the abandoned camp.

06_structures-and-places/structures/work.title: Raised Storage Rack
06_structures-and-places/structures/work.content:
Raised Storage Rack
Structure and intended role
A low food-only platform separates containers and spreading surfaces from ordinary ground damp and allows inspection and airflow. It is not a sealed granary or an animal-proof cache. The first route uses two low fork-supported end assemblies with rails and crosspieces beneath existing overhead cover.
Materials and construction
Select sound Wood with useful bearing shapes. Trim with Oldowan Knife Flake and use tested Simple Cordage or appropriate flexible retaining line to hold parts against rolling. Keep the platform modest and accessible; the chosen pieces, joints and load govern its dimensions.
Seat the supports on stable ground. Fit the rails into restrained bearings and retain the slats so small containers do not tip through them. Use clean spreading surfaces appropriate to the food. Provide protected overhead cover and retain ventilation, rather than packing wet stock beneath a tight sheet.
Testing and operation
Press each end and the centre, inspect support settlement and rotation, and trial the actual intended container load. Reseat loose bearings before use. Recheck after load changes and damp weather. A successful modest trial does not rate a large platform or guarantee pest exclusion.
Keep this framework separate from raw-hide work and the Drying Rack. Materials exposed to dirty processing are not reused as clean food surfaces without appropriate preparation.
Narrative and next process
Day 64 installs the first rack in the dry rear-right strip of Western Overhang. Clean bark surfaces and the existing basket support Dry Nut Storage. Sound pieces and good arrangement remain necessary as the load grows. No fixed shelf life or winter reserve follows from building a shelf.
