07_technologies/adhesives/pine-pitch-man.title: Pine Pitch Manufacture
07_technologies/adhesives/pine-pitch-man.content:
Pine Pitch Manufacture
Goal
Compare small resin-adhesive batches for one defined non-food joint. Do not manufacture an untested large batch or claim a universal chemical recipe.
Method
Collect Pine Resin into a dedicated tray. Heat a small amount indirectly near, not in, flame. Provide a clear working area, ventilation and a means to withdraw from ignition.
Compare cooled unfilled resin with a small selected addition of clean finely crushed Charcoal. Add incrementally and keep an approximate record. Avoid smoke-generating overheating. Other fillers or plasticisers require separate tests and cannot be substituted blindly.
Apply a small sample to expendable wood and stone, allow it to cool, then inspect adhesion, brittleness and heat softening. Repeat a relevant wet trial if the joint may be exposed.
Output and limits
A successful small trial yields Pine Pitch Adhesive for a modest Simple Hafting test. Increasing filler can reduce performance. Binding and geometry remain important.
Do not use the formulation as a wound treatment or drinking-vessel seal without specific evidence. R03 documents ancient adhesives but does not validate this pine-resin mixture.

07_technologies/animal-processing/dry-pe.title: Dry Pelt Working
07_technologies/animal-processing/dry-pe.content:
Conceptual flexibility/support comparison. This is not another owned skin, a preservation guarantee or a complete preparation recipe.
Dry Pelt Working
Purpose and output
Turn a promptly cleaned hair-bearing skin into a flexible, untanned material through controlled drying, supported scraping and repeated flexing. This page describes a labour-intensive mechanical route. It does not use added fat, brain emulsion, salts, smoke or a vegetable tannin bath. Beam Fleshing removes adherent tissue first; softening has a different target and feedback.
Inputs and sequence
Start with sound, thoroughly fleshed skin. Keep hair clean, thin margins supported and the specimen off dirty ground. Spread it with air access and protection from rain. Work by the condition of each area; a drying margin and a still-cool thick centre will not be ready together. There is no accepted number of hours or days for this fictional specimen.
Support a manageable patch on smooth rounded wood. A sound blunt scraping edge should work the inner face without cutting into the skin or damaging hair roots. Alternate careful scraping with drawing, folding and flexing in several directions. Revisit stiff bands and thick patches rather than wearing through the easiest thin areas. Stop when the surface tears, the hair begins to loosen, or the skin condition suggests deterioration.
The Fleshing Beam is a useful existing support, not a mandatory form for every specimen. A smooth smaller rounded support or hand working suits other sizes. R66 describes controlled light re-dampening as a possible further stage; soaking, prolonged damp folding and heat drying are not silently adopted as shortcuts here.
Acceptance, labour and upkeep
Compare worked and unworked areas by ordinary bending and drape, without a hard fold or thin place taking all the force. Keep working through the material’s final moisture loss where needed. Reinspect after a dry rest before cutting or declaring a clothing panel suitable. Useful flexibility and sound hair attachment are necessary; neither certifies preservation or skin safety.
Large skins demand repeated attention and substantial hand work alongside ordinary subsistence. Avoid direct fire heat. Store with air access; dry damp clothing gently and rework stiff areas. Wet conditions, sweat and wear can defeat this method. Treat slipping hair, persistent dampness and tissue residues as failures needing reassessment, not as harmless stages.
Evidence and narrative scope
R65 describes drying and laborious scraping in Nunamiut caribou-clothing manufacture; R66 describes working untanned skins and their continuing care. These are culturally specific developed practices using different animals and tools. They support a possible mechanical route, not a red-deer recipe, a transplanted Arctic outfit, a local 40 ka attestation or a thermal rating.
Day 95 is the first explicit larger-skin drying/scraping/flexing sequence on this page. Earlier small-pelt flexing remains recorded under Fur-On Pelt Clothing and is not newly invented on Day 95. The authored skin response permits layout on Day 96, followed by Skin Limb Coverings; it does not supply durable waterproof leather.

07_technologies/animal-processing/large-.title: Large-Game Processing
07_technologies/animal-processing/large-.content:
The plate separates handling principles. Its generic carrier, skin study and parcels are not a measured layout, the traveller’s wardrobe, or a record of his actual hide and food holdings.
Large-Game Processing
Outcome and scope
Organise prompt handling, division, material care and transport of a large animal already confirmed dead. A hunting result is an input to this process, not proof of usable food, durable skin or successful long-term preservation. The first narrative route involves willing collaborators; Day 93 adds a smaller solo result with limited selected recovery. The method must account for the people actually present.
People, place and materials
Use the separation principles in Small Game Butchery, actual sound cutting edges such as Oldowan Knife Flake and sufficient clean handling surfaces. A larger carcass adds different loads, access problems and cooling needs; it is not simply a rabbit with a multiplied yield.
For collaborative work, Communication and Exchange establishes who is willing to do what and who may take the outputs. Where language is limited, demonstrate one immediate holding or carrying task and observe the response. Do not depend on untranslated commands for a coordinated strike, assume permission over the whole animal, or use another person’s silence as a contract.
Use Environmental Observation to choose stable working and return ground, with clean food and dirty hide/gut handling separated from drinking-water collection. The Day 78 instance draws on competent local experience; a solo variant must supply its own handling skill, support and carrying plan.
Handling and dividing the work
Confirm the animal is dead before approaching working positions. Prompt field dressing and appropriate division release heat from the large body and make loads manageable. Keep dirty implements, gut contents and trampled material from clean meat. Support the parts being worked so a helper does not enter another person’s cutting path. Stop and clarify when a holding cue changes.
Keep clean portions accessible to cooling air rather than immediately sealing a warm mass. Weather, load thickness and time matter; cold-looking surroundings do not certify a safe temperature. Protect from dirt and insects without obstructing cooling. Modern guidance uses controls absent here; this is not a validated prehistoric food-safety recipe.
Select actual transport loads, lifting arrangements and return trips before assuming the whole result can reach camp. Existing small carriers do not acquire a larger load rating. Separate skin care from food handling and flesh retained skin promptly; a fresh hide is not finished leather.
Outputs and allocation
Outputs may include clean meat, edible fat actually recovered, separate skin, bone and unwanted material, but none is automatically allocated to every participant. Record visible releases and retained shares. Cook/use promptly where verified cooling and storage cannot be maintained. A cooked meal, fresh material and preserved ration are different outputs.
The method does not establish shelf-stable meat. Food Reserve Management and any later preservation process retain their own requirements; a rack, smoke or a cold night is not an acceptance test.
Narrative instance and evidence
Day 78 records a local red-deer kill, with the traveller remaining behind during the strike and then helping under visible holding/carrying cues. He receives a modest meat-and-fat portion, eaten that day, and one trimmed narrow fresh hide margin, promptly fleshed and protected. He receives no whole hide or permanent supply agreement.
R41 supplies regional prey context. R45’s wildlife guidance addresses prompt dressing, heat loss, cleanliness and transport in a modern setting. R07 limits preservation claims. The particular hunt, consent, divisions and shares are authored events; neither the sources nor this draft certify that local method.
Solo recovery — Days 93–94
The traveller personally takes one smaller red deer with dart A and works without a helper. Two manageable frame trips bring one main skin, limited selected fresh food and equipment home; remaining carcass material is unrecovered, not a new cache. Prompt cleaning, separation and Meat Cooling and Holding accompany the actual cold interval. All retained food is cooked/used by the Day 94 cutoff. Communication and Exchange remains necessary for coordinating the collaborative variant, not for the solo base operation. The same full skin begins Beam Fleshing and open support; it is not yet clothing.

07_technologies/animal-processing/small-.title: Small-Game Trapping
07_technologies/animal-processing/small-.content:
A conceptual site-observation study, not an assembled trap, exact trail map or prediction of animal traffic.
Small-Game Trapping
Outcome and base route
Manage a limited circuit of existing small-game traps: read actual use, choose suitable ground, maintain the device, inspect frequently and handle the real result. The base narrative route uses Figure-4 Deadfall Trap sets. A functioning trigger and an encountered animal are separate requirements.
Site, device and effort
Follow several related signs in Tracking rather than treating one mark as a recurring appointment. Check runoff, firm supports, approach space and disturbance from the inspection route. Work on one important fault at a time. Brace a weight before reaching its mechanism; a remote non-animal release check belongs before reset.
Link the inspection circuit to other necessary travel without making checks optional. A failed or sprung set needs diagnosis: weather, a moving base, missing bait, an escape or another animal can have different implications. Catch, retrieval, dispatch and Small Game Butchery add labour after construction.
Other routes and evidence
Snare Trap adds line, attachment and trigger questions, informed by Cordage Testing. A retaining cage or mesh route would need its own device and quarry-specific trial. Neither is made by this page. Rabbit abundance is a local uncertainty: R56 cautions against transferring Mediterranean small-game patterns to the Cantabrian region.
Demonstrated scope
Day 90 reorganises one existing set around stable ground, drainage and an inspection approach, with a small drip cover and remote check. It starts managing a system more deliberately; no new catch probability, trap fleet, archaeological first date or dependable calorie supply is established.

07_technologies/ceramics/clay-vessel-mak.title: Clay Vessel Making
07_technologies/ceramics/clay-vessel-mak.content:
Clay Vessel Making
Goal
Form and dry experimental greenware. Making a shape is not yet making pottery or a usable cooking pot.
Method
Collect a small Clay batch and remove coarse debris. Compare test pieces at the intended moisture with and without a conservative selected temper addition. A coil that cracks does not tell you to add more sand by default.
Keep stored clay damp. Form a small pinch vessel with approximately even walls and a smooth transition between base and side. A modest 6–8 mm wall is the narrative trial target, not a universal optimum.
Dry slowly in shelter with airflow. Check the base and walls repeatedly. Time alone is not proof of dryness; thickness and weather matter. Repairing a dry crack with wet clay can introduce a new weak join.
Test and failure
Set aside a cracked test vessel rather than treating it as ready for cooking. Use small sacrificial samples to study drying and firing. The first narrative pot is formed on Day 11, fired on Day 15, then cooled overnight and rejected as a cooking vessel on Day 16.
Next process and limits
Pit Fire provides the first firing route. Pottery combines forming, firing and performance tests. A clay whorl is an optional separate object; it does not require a successful cooking vessel.
R10 supports later Palaeolithic ceramics elsewhere, not Neanderthal figurines or this exact early pot.
Comparison pair through Day 40
The two Day 34 samples from one body remain unfired. Thickness is the intended comparison variable; their external dryness does not establish dry centres. A cooler thicker sample on Day 39 supports waiting, not measuring internal moisture or declaring the thin sample accepted. Neither is broken or converted to a vessel by Day 40. A later sacrificial check or small firing must identify which pieces remain, record fuel and allow cooling before water-contact testing.
Readiness and sacrificial checks — Day 57
The two Day 34 same-body comparison pieces are re-examined, and one small corner from each is removed. Similar dry-appearing fresh sections without an obvious damp smear justify a cautious preheating trial, not a moisture measurement. Record the chipped edges before firing; retain the chips separately as unfired controls. Dry-looking surfaces, elapsed days and the absence of a cool contrast alone are insufficient acceptance. A dry missing corner is not patched with wet clay in this experiment. Day 58 fires the two larger remnants; it does not form a new vessel.
A new vessel for a defined job — Day 72 onward
A fresh modest local charge is screened/kneaded and pinch-formed into a small open pot with a deliberate wall-to-base transition, no handles or added foot ring. The fired comparison remnants remain intact; grass-rich wall earth is kept separate. One new vessel and a comparable witness dry at the protected craft side of Western Overhang, off the food rack and excluded wet corner.
By Day 74 the rim is firmer but the witness centre remains cooler/yielding. The pot remains unfired and is not filled, heated or demonstrated as a working Clay Vessel. Drying time is governed by body, section, air and weather rather than the date assigned to a later firing. The older cracked pot remains at the abandoned camp.
Drying continues while field work develops — through Day 79
The Day 72 pot stays on its protected separate craft-side board while footwear, projectile and food work proceed. A firmer surface and changing witness justify a deliberate readiness inspection before the planned firing; there is no automatic acceptance from seven days elapsed. Neither the shared hunt nor the new fishing catch supplies an already fired cooking vessel. The two earlier comparison remnants remain separate.
Readiness and the Day 72 charge — Days 81–83
Clay Drying and Inspection combines underside/rim/join observations with the fresh section of the comparable witness. On Day 81 the witness is broken into two halves, one kept raw and one selected for the next firing. The pot itself is not chipped, wetted or patched. Day 82 fires the selected half and whole vessel; Day 83 tests the cold fired and raw samples separately, then the actual pot. The earlier comparison remnants remain untouched. Local drying time and visual checks do not supply a universal moisture threshold.
Second useful job, second greenware specimen — Day 112
The single working pot’s food/water scheduling motivates a second plain open cooking bowl. A fresh modest charge from the established clay exposure is selected/kneaded and pinch-formed with a gradual base transition, without handles, spout or foot ring. One comparable same-body witness dries beside it on the separate protected craft board. No universal temper proportion or exact capacity is assigned. Both pieces remain unfired through Day 114; the old pot alone cooks.

07_technologies/ceramics/pottery.title: Pottery
07_technologies/ceramics/pottery.content:
Pottery
Capability
Pottery is the process of producing suitably fired ceramic objects. A first useful specimen demonstrates a working route; dependable repeated production and cooking-pot reliability require further results. A formed vessel or survival of the fire alone does not yet establish useful service.
Workflow

Select and characterise a Clay body.
Form and dry pieces through Clay Vessel Making.
Apply a tested firing route, initially Pit Fire.
Cool without thermal shock and inspect the load.
Test water stability, leakage, abrasion and the intended operating heat cycles.
Record failures and repeat with controlled changes.

The first-month vessel is rejected for cooking after a crack and leakage appear. Its fragments and intact portion can serve as non-food experimental samples.
Alternative roles
Small fired weights can be tested independently of cooking pots. A Spindle Whorl can also be wooden, so ceramics need not become the bottleneck for spinning.
Evidence and limits
R10 documents later Upper Palaeolithic ceramic objects elsewhere. It does not demonstrate cooking pots at the narrative’s date or substantiate the old Neanderthal figurine claim.
Water-tightness, thermal resistance and food-contact suitability need separate tests. No permanent unlock or first-month production mastery is recorded.
A material comparison before a new vessel — Day 59
The second-moon programme now has two fired comparison remnants with a limited cold wetting result. Neither is a newly accepted vessel. The process remains undemonstrated as repeatable useful pottery production; no change to demonstrated_day is warranted. A next small vessel must independently earn drying, firing, cold containment and intended-use results. Do not promote water stability of a flat piece to leak resistance or food suitability.
First useful vessel — Days 82–84
Day 82 fires the already dried Day 72 pot with one witness half. Day 83 recovers a coherent fired witness and an intact vessel that holds a small cold-water charge without steady leakage or breakdown. This is the first useful ceramic-vessel result and the first demonstration of this production route, not a claim of repeated manufacture. Day 84 adds a water-only use cycle and a fresh cooked meal on a separate second cycle, both gradually heated and cooled. Fired Earthenware, Open Cooking Hearth and Cooking in an Earthenware Pot separate material, support structure and operation.
The earlier failed vessel remains a failed historical trial, and the old comparison remnants remain non-food samples. Chemical food-contact suitability and durable repeated use are unresolved; one working pot is not an analytical result or production guarantee.

07_technologies/construction/earth-and-f.title: Earth-and-Fibre Infill
07_technologies/construction/earth-and-f.content:
Earth-and-Fibre Infill
Purpose and scope
This method is wattle and daub: the wattle is the woven rod/twig backing, and the daub is the workable earth mixture pressed through it. Earth-and-Fibre Infill is the descriptive title of this handbook page, not a different invention. The Day 66 specimen is a small trial of that method rather than a complete wall.
No new ingredient or tool is needed to make the existing trial qualify. Flexible rods, light supports, clay-rich earth, water and short gathered grass are already available in the story. Cut grass supplies fibre without requiring cultivated cereal straw. Extending the panel calls for more sound backing and suitable mix, followed by protected drying and checks for shrinkage, attachment and wetting. It does not require firing, dung or a later lime finish. R42 supplies the backing/daub terminology; this particular early use and mix remain authored choices.
Close fine air paths in a supported screen with a small unfired earth/fibre coating. The timber frame and woven backing carry the wet and dry infill. This is a wall treatment, not roof support, fired ceramic or a substitute for thick dry bedding.
Inputs and backing
Select clay-rich mineral earth from a stable exposure, excluding organic topsoil and coarse debris. Clay is the natural input; a building mixture is not automatically a suitable pottery body. Use short clean dry grass from Plant Covering Stock, a little water and a separate mixing surface. No dung, lime, cement or glue is required by this route.
Sound Wood forms secure bearings and a low woven backing made with Simple Coiling and Weaving. The backing must be stiff enough not to bow loose when pressed. Support feet and joints need checking before wet loading. Keep the patch above damp soil and within reliable overhead protection.
Mix and place a trial
Knead a modest charge with only enough water for working. Distribute short fibres through it. A handful that slumps or sheds loose aggregate is not ready merely because it is sticky. Local earth varies: compare small samples rather than copying a universal clay/sand ratio. Excessively sticky or badly shrinking material needs another mixture or a return to brush/bark.
Press through the backing and work against the far face to form connected keys around the rods. A surface smear which does not engage the backing is easily detached. Start with one small low bay, thin enough to inspect and supported at its lower edge. Keep other screen covering in service.
Drying and acceptance
Allow protected air access on both faces; keep bedding and food clear of mixing and fresh coating. Retain separate witness patches of comparable section. Drying takes weather-dependent intervals, not a fixed overnight cure. A dry face does not establish a dry centre. Avoid enlarging work into rain or likely freezing while the mixture remains wet.
Check the backing, support feet, sagging, loose flakes, crack development and the centre of a sacrificial patch. After the specimen firms, light pressure can check attachment without using it as a handhold. Serious separation, slumping or moving supports calls for removal/reworking, not another heavy coat. Fine shrinkage lines can be monitored; they do not establish durability.
Operation and maintenance
The intended output is an attached draught-closing panel under cover. Inspect after weather and repair local damage only when the source of wetting or movement is understood. Keep the entrance and deliberate ventilation open. Rock-Shelter Enclosure retains an outside hearth; this infill does not establish safe indoor combustion.
Narrative and evidence
Day 66 begins a small installed panel and witness patches at Western Overhang. By Day 69 one witness has a firm centre and the installed bay remains keyed under a light check, with fine edge shrinkage. No freeze/thaw or full winter validation has occurred.
Historic England’s timber-wall account describes daub on woven backing and vulnerability to damp (R42). Its material-properties guidance supplies moisture context (R40). The selected grass mix, small geometry and results are authored physical reasoning, not a reconstructed Palaeolithic specification. Experimental replication is still needed.
Edge repair at the same small bay — Day 88
A changed wind exposes an air path at a local shrinkage edge. The traveller checks sound backing, steady supports and the absence of a new drip before pressing a small fresh building-earth/grass repair into the join. Existing bark protects the wet patch while the inner face remains open to air. The high ventilation gap stays open. Day 89 leaves the repair drying rather than claiming a completed weather cycle or a full earth wall.

07_technologies/container-making/coiled-.title: Coiled Basket Making
07_technologies/container-making/coiled-.content:
Coiled Basket Making
Purpose
Produce and test a stitched coiled container from a flexible foundation and separate binding fibre. This page organises the manufacturing route; Simple Coiling and Weaving develops the coiling and tension-control skills used within it. This is an alternative to a willow stake basket.
Method
Select a foundation that bends to the initial radius without splitting. Start a small loop and secure it with a tested line. Add successive coils and stitch through suitable gaps or use Bone Awl to open a controlled path.
Raise the wall gradually, maintain consistent tension and stagger added material. Taper the final foundation and secure the finish so ends cannot pull free.
Test
Load lightly and inspect base, seams and rim. Avoid forcing a delicate eyed needle through thick wooden rods. A hand-sized trial can establish the motion without consuming enough fine cord for a whole basket.
Limits
Coiling, rod weaving and knotting a net are different operations. The narrative’s Day 19 coiled trial does not establish net production or a universal basket predecessor.
Preparation, fine binding line and stitch labour can make a coiled design expensive for the current camp. Compare Woven Foraging Basket before assuming the historical-looking route is optimal.

07_technologies/equipment-making/bow-mak.title: Bow Making
07_technologies/equipment-making/bow-mak.content:
A general wood-seasoning material study. The visible knots are not approval of the selected blank: this plate illustrates airy storage, not the exact stock or a completed bow design.
Bow Making
Process and stages
Begin with identified stave stock, preserve the chosen working fibres, prepare a rough body, manage drying, then judge and adjust limb bending through Tillering. Add compatible attachments, a suitable Bowstring and controlled system trials only when those stages permit it. This staged route is distinct from possession or mastery of a finished Self Bow.
Work and dependencies
Wood condition can make waiting part of production. Coarse preparation should retain room for drying movement and later adjustment. Stone edges can cut and scrape the material; the tool shape and control affect labour and the risk of cutting across useful fibres. A protected working place and clean separate supports keep timed material preparation compatible with other tasks.
String trials and shaft-stock preparation can proceed while the body seasons. They do not justify loading green wood or turning candidate blanks into accepted ammunition by changing their names. Prospective design images describe the subject, not additional objects or completed stages in the narrative.
First recorded work and limits
Day 85 starts selection and preparation of one hazel half-stave, and Day 87 coarsely shapes the same piece. The first date records actual work on the production route, not successful completion of every stage. Through Day 89 no bow is strung, tillered under load or shot. R51’s stone-tool reconstruction concerns a much later seasoned yew bow; it supports the relevance of cutting control, not this body’s timetable or performance.
A first practice system — Days 106–109
The same body moves from rough stock to limited low-deflection Tillering, fitted string and a low-braced Self Bow on Day 107. One of the existing shaft blanks becomes the first Arrow, with a rounded integral nose, self-nock and short new plant-thread reinforcement. Bow Shooting begins on Day 109 with a few short trials, then the body is unstrung. This early hazel specimen remains provisional; the sequence does not assert complete seasoning, a fixed drying time or hunting adequacy.

07_technologies/fire/camp-fire-managemen.title: Camp Fire Management
07_technologies/fire/camp-fire-managemen.content:
Camp Fire Management
Purpose
Maintain an outside fire for warmth, cooking and material work after ignition. The first route uses Bow Drill Fire; another validated ignition method can replace it.
Procedure
Clear a small site on stable ground away from debris bedding, roots, overhanging material and stored fuel. Prepare Tinder Bundle, kindling and a supply of Dry Fuel before ignition.
Transfer a successful flame into small dry pieces, then increase fuel gradually while preserving airflow. Match fire size to the task. A large fire wastes fuel and can still heat an exposed sleeper unevenly.
Keep a means to control spread. Protect an ember bed only where conditions permit, inspect it before leaving and treat restart as necessary if no live ember remains.
Test and maintenance
Record fuel collected and burned. At night, insulated bedding supplies the base protection; the narrative does not assume hourly feeding compatible with eight hours of uninterrupted sleep.
Limits
Smoke can discourage some animals or insects but does not guarantee safety. Carbon monoxide can accumulate even with little visible smoke. Do not enclose a fire in a debris shelter.
R14 supports evidence for ancient fire-making knowledge. The local group does not need the traveller to introduce fire.
Match the arrangement to the task — Days 81–84
The dry northeast firing patch is prepared and used separately from the ordinary outdoor hearth. The firing load cools untouched while ordinary meals continue by the established route. Day 84 gives the cooking hearth three low stable supports for the new pot, preserving airflow and a small fuel-feed opening. Open Cooking Hearth describes the structure; Cooking in an Earthenware Pot describes the wet-food operation. Neither fire moves beneath the sleeping enclosure.

07_technologies/fire/pit-firing.title: Pit Firing
07_technologies/fire/pit-firing.content:
Pit Firing
Purpose
A small open or shallow-pit firing trial for dry clay pieces. It is one route to ceramic manufacture, not a unique sequence through which all future firing must pass.
Preparation
Use dry sheltered ground, clear surroundings and Dry Fuel. Greenware from Clay Vessel Making must be dry through its section. Preheat gradually outside the main heat before increasing exposure.
Support the pieces so fuel collapse will not strike them. Arrange small dry fuel to admit air rather than burying everything under damp earth at ignition.
Firing and cooling
Raise heat gradually, then maintain sufficient heat for the tested body. The exact temperature-time schedule requires clay-specific replication. Fire colour and blackened surfaces are imperfect indicators, not a precise pyrometer.
Allow the fuel to burn down and the load to cool in place. Do not pour water over it or remove hot pieces. The narrative waits overnight.
Test and limits
Use sacrificial pieces for water stability, abrasion and fracture checks. A pot surviving the fire does not prove adequate firing, food suitability or thermal-shock resistance.
No fixed success percentage, guaranteed vitrification or automatic waterproofing is assigned. Fuel and supervision must be budgeted. Improvements are in Pre-Kiln Firing; a kiln is not a prerequisite.
Comparison load and limited result — Days 58–59
Two chipped main pieces from one clay body, with different section thicknesses, are gradually preheated at the established outside firing place, exposed to one modest dry-fuel firing and cooled untouched overnight. Their raw fracture controls remain at the craft spot. There is no measured temperature or new kiln. R38 documents unequal heat histories in instrumented open firings; this trial therefore records placement as a possible confound rather than treating one fire as identical exposure.
On Day 59 the cold thin piece remains coherent after a short comparative wetting check. The thick piece stays together but has a new hairline; raw chips soften and are discarded. The two fired remnants remain non-food specimens. This is not a water-tightness test, thermal-cycle acceptance, universal clay recipe or repeatable firing schedule. Experimental water is poured onto a separate test stone without placing samples in the clean vessels. The existing bark water-treatment route remains in service.
First vessel at the overhang — Day 82
The cleared northeast firing patch, already identified with the site’s arrangement, receives the single Day 72 pot and one witness half. Dry ground and light supported fuel allow gradual warming and an open firing without a new chamber. Heavy collapsing loads, hot handling and quenching are avoided. The load cools in place until cold on Day 83; the separate outside ordinary hearth continues cooking by the old route. No measured peak temperature, soak schedule or exact-clay guarantee is inferred from flame or surface colour. R46’s ethnographic fuel and time figures are not adopted.

07_technologies/fire/pre-kiln-firing.title: Pre-Kiln Firing
07_technologies/fire/pre-kiln-firing.content:
Pre-Kiln Firing
Purpose
Improve repeatability of an open firing site through support, wind control, airflow and controlled cooling. This page describes an improvement framework; it does not supply a validated firing schedule.
Method
Start from a documented Pit Fire trial. Record fuel, loading, weather and failures. Change one major variable at a time: a low wind screen, spacing between pieces, dry support material or fuel arrangement.
Keep an air path for combustion. An earth covering can retain heat but can also starve the fire or introduce moisture. Reduced oxygen is not automatically hotter or better.
Tests
Use comparable sacrificial pieces to check water stability and strength. Compare fuel cost and repeatability over more than one firing. Do not call a black ringing fragment fully vitrified solely from sound or colour.
Limits
Temperature and time both matter. Duration cannot compensate indefinitely for inadequate temperature. Enclosing the site also increases structural and ventilation requirements.
Kiln is a later controlled-chamber route. A surviving single piece establishes a result, not a dependable production process.

07_technologies/food-processing/acorn-le.title: Acorn Leaching
07_technologies/food-processing/acorn-le.content:
Acorn Leaching
Goal and preparation
Remove enough tannin from an identified acorn batch for the intended food use. Tannin concentration and processing behaviour vary by species, particle size and method.
Collect sound acorns, shell and reject damaged kernels. Record shelled edible mass. Crush to an appropriate size using clean stones.
First-month warm-water route
Use a tested Bark Container and Hot-Rock Boiling. Process a small batch so water can be changed without losing the meal. Cycle fresh hot water over the material, keep it separated from dirty handling equipment, and compare progress.
A reduction in bitterness is a useful process observation, not universal chemical validation. The number of cycles and completion criteria need species-specific evidence. Do not promise four cycles or ninety minutes for every batch.
Alternatives
Cold soaking or flowing-water leaching can avoid heating, with different time, containment and contamination requirements. A permeable basket or bag helps retain particles, but must itself be suitable for food.
Output and limits
Wet Acorn Meal is recorded separately and consumed promptly. Drying a thick cake near a fire is not sufficient proof of a durable travel ration.
The first narrative trial begins on Day 17 and yields a small wet batch on Day 18. The expedition uses dry nuts instead of an instantly manufactured large acorn brick.
Repeated small charges: Days 42–44
The Day 41 harvest is 0.8 kg sound shelled untreated input. A 0.6 L vessel cannot take that whole mass plus water and hot stones. Day 42 processes half in four roughly 0.1 kg charges; Days 43 and 44 each process 0.2 kg in two charges. Fresh-water/reheating estimates are 6 L and 2 kg extra fuel on Day 42, then 3 L and 1 kg each following day. Drinking water and ordinary fuel remain separately counted. Outputs of 0.65, 0.35 and 0.35 kg cooked wet meal include water and are entirely eaten on their production days. No wet food store or drying process is demonstrated.
R33 in Research Register provides an ethnobotanical comparison, not a validation of these local rates or the acceptance decision. Shelling, crushing, vessel capacity, fresh water, heat and repeated handling constrain throughput. The same remembered process does not guarantee the same completion time for another oak lot.
Repeat in small charges — Days 47–49
The 0.6 kg own shelled input collected on Day 46 is processed in three 0.2 kg portions, two charges per day. Each day models roughly 3 litres extra processing water and 1 kg extra heating fuel beyond ordinary cold-weather use. Reduced astringency and the already trialled local route remain limited authored acceptance observations, not a universal chemical test. The new output is about 0.35 kg wet meal each day, cooked and eaten with no retained wet food. R33 does not validate these yields.
Improve preparation without wetting the store — Day 71
Pounding and Grinding Stones provide a separate clean food pair. Coarse fragments are sorted on bark and reworked rather than allowing the whole charge to become fine powder. The useful result is less scattering and a more controllable small-charge input, not tannin removal by crushing. Existing bark-vessel water changes and cooking remain separate steps; meal is used that day. Dry untouched nuts remain storage input. A finer batch must still suit its containment and treatment; no new universal particle size, cycle count or time is established.
The new pot changes cooking, not leaching — Day 84
A fresh small meal charge still receives the established crushing and water changes in bark vessels. Only then is it cooked with water in the new pot. Ceramic walls transfer heat from an outside fire without stones in the food, making stirring easier. The whole meal is eaten that day. No fixed leaching schedule, new species identification or stored wet ration is inferred from this change of container.

07_technologies/food-processing/cooking-.title: Cooking in an Earthenware Pot
07_technologies/food-processing/cooking-.content:
Successive conceptual views of one vessel. The meal texture is schematic; the plate does not add a grain species, recipe quantity or extra pot.
Cooking in an Earthenware Pot
Purpose and inputs
Heat a water-containing meal through the walls of a ceramic vessel. Unlike Hot-Rock Boiling, the heat source stays outside the container. The route here uses one sound Clay Vessel, a stable Open Cooking Hearth, modest dry fuel, water, prepared food and a clean stirring tool.
Sequence
Inspect the cold vessel and support it securely. Begin with the pot and water at similar temperatures, then increase external heat gradually. Do not heat an empty unknown body fiercely or add cold water to a very hot vessel. Avoid inserting hot stones: impact and local heat would introduce different stresses.
A water-only trial is distinct from cooking. Watch for a new wet line, loss of contents, cracking or surface breakdown. Let the water and vessel cool together before emptying and close inspection. For the next meal, start again with an inspected cool vessel and a modest wet charge.
Keep food moving as it thickens so the base does not scorch or run dry. Reduce fuel when less heat is needed; leave room below the rim. Let heat decline before serving, keep hands off hot ceramic and avoid forcing the rounded pot out of its supports while loaded. Clean after cooling and dry with airflow before protected storage.
Food preparation and limits
Acorn Leaching remains necessary for an acorn charge; cooking in a different vessel does not remove tannins by itself. The narrative prepares a fresh small batch by its established route and consumes it the same day. No preserved food, catch surplus or new recipe yield is created.
Body, temper, porosity and heat history influence thermal performance. A cold containment check does not establish flame resistance, chemical food-contact suitability or repeatability. This is a draft account of an authored field trial; the local clay is not analytically certified for food contact. R47’s later experiments do not validate this fictional body.
Day 84
The pot completes a water-only heating/cooling cycle, is inspected cold, then cooks one leached meal on a second gradual cycle. It remains sound after cooling and washing. Useful observed service begins here, while durable production and later repeated use remain to be earned.
Continued first-vessel service — Day 89
The same pot cooks another freshly prepared small wet acorn charge over the ordinary outside hearth, warming with its contents and cooling before washing. The meal is consumed that day and the vessel remains visibly sound. This adds an observed use, not a second vessel, chemical certification or a long reliability record.
Handling and capacity dependencies — Days 111–114
Day 111 cooks one newly caught fish fresh in the sole useful pot; other water work must be scheduled or use the existing bark/hot-rock fallback. A second bowl is formed on Day 112 but remains greenware. Day 113 makes and trials one Wooden Spoon for moving food and lifting a cooling portion in the existing pot. The utensil does not lift hot pots, and a second vessel would still require suitable support and planned hearth turns. No extra hearth, storage life or measured fuel saving follows.

07_technologies/food-processing/dry-nut-.title: Dry Nut Storage
07_technologies/food-processing/dry-nut-.content:
Dry Nut Storage
Goal and inputs
Keep an identified seasonal nut harvest protected and inspectable before it is prepared for meals. This route uses the Raised Storage Rack, clean spreading surfaces and the Woven Foraging Basket beneath useful weather cover. Inputs, prepared food and wet cooked output are distinct states.
Preparation and arrangement
Select the established identified nuts. Separate visibly damaged, damp or spoiled material; shell and processing losses do not become edible reserve. Spread the candidate stock in modest layers for inspection and airflow, keeping recently wet inputs separate.
Use protection from direct rain and ground damp while permitting drying. Avoid burying damp stock in a deep packed basket. A loose basket cover can exclude some debris but does not seal out all pests.
Operation, outputs and checks
Inspect stored stock after wet weather and periodically while using it. Keep food clear of animal processing and waste. Remove a consequential damaged lot rather than hiding the loss in an unchanged reserve description.
Stored untreated acorns are processing inputs. Acorn Leaching and cooking supply meals as needed; wet meal is perishable. Dry hazelnut kernels and shell-bearing stock require their own condition assessment. Appearance is not universal food-safety certification.
Output is a protected inspectable batch, not a promised quantity of winter rations. Test drying and keeping performance through actual conditions, not a fixed calendar wait or universal shelf life.
Evidence, alternatives and narrative
R33 supplies a much later ethnographic storage/processing analogy; it does not validate local yield, species-specific keeping conditions or this rack. An appropriate natural dry shelf offers an alternative arrangement with separate contamination, access and retention checks.
Day 64 begins this process with own gathering, clean surfaces and a loose basket cover at Western Overhang. Stored acorns remain separate from meals eaten promptly. Food Reserve Management uses the result qualitatively without requiring an exact daily balance.

07_technologies/food-processing/meat-coo.title: Meat Cooling and Holding
07_technologies/food-processing/meat-coo.content:
A handling-principle study with generic food portions. It does not depict the deer’s fat/yield, add food stock, or establish temperature, safe keeping time or preservation.
Meat Cooling and Holding
Scope and purpose
Release retained body heat and organise prompt use of fresh meat. Cooling, short holding, freezing, drying and validated preservation are distinct processes. A shaded rack, cold-looking day or surface frost is not a measured food temperature.
Conditions and handling
Prompt dressing and manageable portions help heat escape. Protect clean food from dirty skin, soil and gut material while allowing appropriate air movement. A warm mass tightly wrapped in bark does not become cool because the wrapper feels cold. Consider portion thickness, time, ambient conditions and what can actually be cooked or transported.
Modern guidance uses time/temperature controls and refrigeration that the traveller cannot fully reproduce. R45 addresses field handling; R64 supplies a modern comparison. No exact safe holding period is assigned here. Lack of bad smell, colour change or visible spoilage cannot certify safety. If conditions cannot support holding, reduce what is retained and prioritise immediate use rather than naming a winter store.
Narrative trial
Day 93 is an authored cold, dry, frosty interval. Limited selected cuts go onto a separate airy bark-covered rest after prompt field handling. Fresh cooking begins that day; the remaining selected cuts are cooked and used across Day 94. The uncollected carcass stays outside retained food stock. This contingent event does not validate refrigeration or authorise carrying an old raw-meat balance into later days.
Further development
Food Reserve Management and a researched preservation route must address any longer keeping. R07 explains why smoke or low-temperature drying alone does not certify a safe dried ration. The cool-holding illustration is a handling principle, not proof of a temperature or shelf life.

07_technologies/material-processing/bark.title: Barkcloth Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/bark.content:
Barkcloth Processing
Scope
Prepare local bark fibres or panels for modest protective use. Beaten barkcloth and a stiff bark wrap are different products. The narrative initially has ties and overlapping rough panels, not a finished broad cloth.
Procedure
Select an identified locally available material. Test a small strip for separation, flexibility and skin irritation without assuming all inner bark behaves alike. Harvest modest amounts from suitable fallen or damaged material; dead bark may have degraded fibres.
Separate useful inner material with Oldowan Knife Flake. Try scraping, soaking or controlled beating on a supported surface as the material allows. Compare the result dry and damp before allocating the whole batch.
Test and limits
Check coverage, edge abrasion and durability during movement. A narrow strip that becomes flexible is not evidence of a full shoulder cape. Mark unsuccessful material and choose another route.
The older tropical options are removed. A universal one-to-three-hour barkcloth recipe is not validated for this Iberian setting.
Use
Basic Bark Clothing uses the successful limited panels. Bedding and shelter still supply much of the early thermal protection.

07_technologies/material-processing/nett.title: Nettle Fibre Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/nett.content:
Nettle Fibre Processing
Goal
Recover useful bast fibre, then prepare it for the intended line or yarn. Retting, extraction, cleaning, drying and spinning are distinct operations.
Water-retted route
Take a tested batch from Nettle Retting. Rinse downstream of clean-water collection, then drain. Break the woody core without crushing fibres, and peel off long bundles.
Scrape or rub gently to remove adhering debris. Compare a small clean sample before processing the remainder. Excessive abrasion shortens fibres. Dry protected with airflow, then split and align to the intended diameter.
Test
Flex and pull sample bundles. Reject weak or decomposed fibre. Record approximately how much usable dry output remains after cleaning. A heap of wet stems cannot be counted as the same mass of ready-to-spin fibre.
Alternative and limits
Direct mechanical extraction may avoid retting at greater labour or different quality. R11 supports multiple routes; exact local performance remains unmeasured.
The narrative begins extraction on Day 16 and keeps the remaining material states distinct. A Spindle Whorl does not remove this preparation bottleneck. A group must reproduce the complete chain before community capability is claimed.
Batch B: first accepted portion
Day 43 cleans and checks a selected dried portion, crediting 18 g usable dry fibre after rejection of weak/woody sections. Remaining coarse material is still in process. The stem bundle was unweighed, so no extraction efficiency is inferred. Day 45 allocates 10 g from the combined prepared stock to hand-made line; the output is not also credited as yarn.

07_technologies/material-processing/nett.title: Nettle Retting
07_technologies/material-processing/nett.content:
Nettle Retting
Purpose
Manage a batch through controlled biological breakdown to loosen bast fibre. This process includes placement, changing conditions, sample checks and the decision to stop; it is distinct from the hand skills used to strip and twist the output. Water retting is one option; dry or fresh mechanical extraction can provide other routes with different labour and quality.
Procedure
Identify and select mature suitable stems. Protect hands from stings, remove leaves and bind a modest labelled batch. Place it in a secured downstream processing pool, separate from drinking-water collection and food preparation.
Inspect samples regularly. Peel and flex a stem: fibres should separate while retaining useful strength. Smell alone does not define readiness. Remove a batch before fibres become weak or fragment.
Rinse and proceed to Nettle Fibre Processing. Do not promise readiness on a fixed day. Temperature, stem maturity, microbes and water conditions matter.
Alternative and limits
Dew retting uses field exposure and repeated turning but has different weather and contamination constraints. Mechanical stripping avoids waiting but can be labour-intensive and give rough output.
The narrative’s batch starts on Day 4 and passes its test on Day 16. Earlier status estimates are not a second chronology.
Evidence
R11 supports multiple extraction routes. It does not establish an exact wild-Iberian schedule, a universal strength increase or instant community adoption.
Second narrative batch
Day 31 starts a separately harvested small stem bundle B in the established downstream pool, secured with a short allocated bark tie and weighted retaining branch. It is not prepared fibre. Checks through Day 35 do not yet find useful separation, so the batch stays in process with no assigned output. The first batch’s twelve days do not determine this colder batch’s readiness or yield.
Checks through Day 40
Batch B stays secured in the established downstream pool. Day 39 begins to find some outer-bundle release; Day 40 still finds uneven separation across the bundle. Neither event creates prepared fibre. Continue sampling for useful separation and retained fibre integrity, rather than declaring readiness from elapsed days. Later removal, rinsing, extraction, protected drying and accepted usable yield must each be recorded.
Batch B: condition-led stop on Day 42
After distributed sample checks, the bundle begun on Day 31 is lifted and rinsed on Day 42. That ends its immersion, not the complete production chain. Selected strips dry under existing ventilated cover; the coarse remainder stays a separate unfinished portion. The old immersed tie is not returned as ready loose cord. R11 does not establish this elapsed time as a recipe.

07_technologies/material-processing/rawh.title: Rawhide Processing
07_technologies/material-processing/rawh.content:
Rawhide Processing
Goal
Dry a cleaned hide into untanned material for rigid cases and bindings. Fur may remain, but drying does not create durable soft leather.
Method
Flesh Animal Pelt promptly with a supported edge that does not tear it. Spread or support it under moderate even tension; do not pull a thin rabbit skin to extreme tension merely because a frame is strong.
Dry in protected moving air, away from scorching heat. Inspect frequently for damp folds, insects, tearing and deterioration. Adjust supports as the material changes.
Test
The dried skin should hold the intended shape without decomposition or weak holes. A rigid panel can be dampened locally for shaping, but repeated wetting changes dimensions and strength.
Limits
Dry rawhide is not a waterproof bottle. It softens and can deteriorate in damp conditions. Smoke is not a universal preservative and should not be used to certify cleanliness.
A Smoking Rack is optional equipment for a separated drying task. A clean supported frame can work without it.
Fur-On Pelt Clothing adds a temporary softening workflow; a tannery is a later process with different requirements.
Shaping a small retained margin — Days 80–81
The Day 78 deer strip is promptly fleshed, kept on the new home’s small dirty-work support and opened at its damp fold. Day 80 removes residual tissue and uses local dampening only where the stiff skin must turn around a smooth former. Light temporary ties hold the shape without closing off its air path. Day 81 removes the former and checks dry fit for one Stone-Edge Guard. This is stiff untanned skin put to a suitable small use, not clothing leather or a reconstruction of a known ancient sheath.

07_technologies/systems/food-reserve-man.title: Food Reserve Management
07_technologies/systems/food-reserve-man.content:
Food Reserve Management
Continuing service
Keep an explicit account of edible input, meals, losses and an accessible remaining reserve, then use it to limit optional work. The first route handles previously identified hazelnuts with the existing small basket and local comparison marks. It does not establish a preservation technology or certify food safety.
Day 29 introduces a repeatable rough portion comparison and scratch register. The traveller estimates the reserve in comparable portions. Kilograms in the author ledger are a separate model.
Routine and controls
Separate today’s intended food from the working reserve before becoming absorbed in an experiment. Inspect storage for dampness, pests and obvious damage. Keep food away from raw-animal work and waste. A basket provides containment, not a sealed pest-proof or rainproof store.
Record what actually enters as edible prepared food. Unopened shells and unprocessed acorns are not ready meals; wet acorn output is not counted as new energy because water made it heavier. Catch-specific fresh food remains separately accounted for.
After meals, update the portion account and note discarded food separately. Measurement and Records retains the comparison procedure so changing a handful does not quietly enlarge the reserve. Imperfect marks still reveal a persistent deficit.
Acceptance and ongoing supply
Useful operation means that a missing meal or loss changes the record, a depleted reserve changes tomorrow’s work, and no stock is counted twice. It is an accounting improvement, not proof of adequate nutrition, real kilogram accuracy or predictable gathering rates.
Compare ordinary days with days spent travelling or experimenting. When collection falls below consumption, optional work draws on a finite buffer. Increasing that buffer requires actual independent gathering or another established supply route.
Failures and fallback
Wet storage, a lost basket, contested patches and diminishing harvest can interrupt the system. Records do not rescue spoiled food or replace an absent food source. Smell and appearance cannot certify safety.
Day 35’s reserve is smaller than Day 28’s despite one small fish catch. The immediate fallback is to shorten optional practice and assign time to gathering, not assume a future deer kill, gift or trade. Drying fish, durable acorn storage and winter ration sufficiency remain unestablished processes.
Shelter work and the short reserve, Days 41–45
The new acorn route processes 0.8 kg shelled untreated input across Days 42–44, in vessel-sized charges. Wet output is cooked and consumed on each processing day; no reserve of dried meal is created. The kernel reserve declines from 1.31 kg at Day 40 to 0.93 kg at Day 45 despite these meals and one small fish. The next work must give food collection priority alongside the unfinished roof, rather than treating new structures as proof of seasonal surplus.
Short buffer after construction and scouting — Days 46–50
Longer independent gathering on Day 46 adds 0.75 kg edible kernels and 0.6 kg untreated acorn input. The acorns are processed as three 0.2 kg portions on Days 47–49, with two small charges each day. All wet meal is cooked/eaten; no dry travel cake or shelf-stable store appears. The Day 48 outing reduces gathering to 0.25 kg. Day 50’s small fish is consumed immediately. Kernels end at 0.94 kg, still around two recent daily portions, despite better clothing and shelter. The approved 7–10-day target remains unmet.
Qualitative seasonal provision — Day 64 onward
Dry Nut Storage gives an actual inspectable keeping arrangement at Western Overhang. Use the known seasonal patches, acknowledge declining access and organise processing inputs separately from ready food. Routine portions and daily balances are now background; describe a meaningful shortage, useful harvest, observed exchange or substantial loss when it affects work. Historical numerical estimates remain dated records, not an endlessly maintained current inventory.
A rack and some stored nuts begin seasonal provision. The continuing food plan also needs animal foods, useful access, water/fuel for processing and ordinary replenishment. Wet meal is used promptly; no smoked meat, fixed shelf life or winter sufficiency is granted by this change.
Shared result is not a standing ration — Day 78
Large-Game Processing gives access to an actual local result through accepted work. The traveller’s modest meat-and-fat share is cooked and eaten that day. It is not a whole carcass in reserve, a promise of future meals or a newly validated preservation method. Seasonal nuts, ordinary own trapping/fishing and future participation still have distinct roles.

07_technologies/systems/sanitation-and-c.title: Sanitation and Camp Hygiene
07_technologies/systems/sanitation-and-c.content:
Sanitation and Camp Hygiene
Goal
Reduce contamination using available separation, clean water and handling practices. The absence of germ theory among a fictional group cannot be inferred from a dirty-looking camp.
Camp arrangement
Keep drinking-water collection upstream and separate from waste, butchery and fibre retting. Choose a waste area away from water and routine foot traffic without assuming one fixed distance fits all ground.
Separate dirty raw-animal work from cooked food and delicate clean tools. Clean hands and implements after processing. Once Hot-Rock Boiling is available, reserve treated water and a clean vessel for appropriate uses.
Limits
This reduces some exposure without providing modern sterile facilities. A clear spring, clean-looking surface or absence of symptoms does not establish freedom from pathogens. Smoke is not sterilisation.
Teaching and scaling
Explain and demonstrate a specific separation, compare it with existing practice and check whether it remains workable. Larger camps need water supply, waste removal, food handling, drainage and responsibility for maintenance.
R06 and R07 establish important modern constraints; they do not validate every improvised camp practice.
Accessible remnants and animal investigation — Day 47
A large canid investigates the dirty flank while the traveller stays on the clean side. Its departure without damage does not establish deterrence. A trapped old scrap prompts removal of animal remnants, cleaning, protected pelt handling and inspection of the established separated waste route. Waste is not shifted into the watercourse or left as a bait pile just outside the shelter. Modern attractant management in R34 informs the reasoning, not a guaranteed prehistoric outcome. The animal replaces planned yarn work with watch and cleanup.
Moving the arrangement — Day 61
The move to Western Overhang retains separation rather than copying the old compass labels. Sleep and protected materials use the dry back-left strip; clean craft uses the front-right stone, with food storage later in the dry rear-right. Hearth and future firing ground stay outside; animal processing and waste lie farther southwest/downhill, away from the seep route. The old dirty frame stays behind. A new location creates no automatically clean borrowed surface or new water source.

07_technologies/systems/teaching-and-kno.title: Teaching and Knowledge Preservation
07_technologies/systems/teaching-and-kno.content:
Teaching and Knowledge Preservation
Goal
Build capabilities that survive the traveller’s absence. Knowing an instruction, copying a motion and independently producing a useful result are different milestones.
First teaching method
Use Communication and Exchange to establish the problem and the learner’s existing technique. Show a small operation with prepared inputs, then allow a willing learner to try without continual correction.
Compare output and failure signs. Repeat with a new input or changed condition to check transfer. When a process has several stages, demonstrate or explain each stage, including preparation and maintenance.
Verification and scaling
Record who has reproduced what, with which tools and materials. One spun short sample is evidence of that action; it does not establish fibre harvesting, retting, plying, net making or a community textile industry.
Later develop Measurement and Records, redundant teaching, shared tool specifications and arrangements for maintaining knowledge. Respect learners’ priorities and consent; novelty is not an entitlement to their labour.
The first month contains a failed approach, not a shared teaching trial. No willing learner has reproduced a method under the traveller’s instruction by Day 28. This system remains planned, with no demonstration date.

07_technologies/water/hot-rock-boiling.title: Hot-Rock Boiling
07_technologies/water/hot-rock-boiling.content:
Hot-Rock Boiling
Goal
Heat water to an observable rolling boil in a tested non-metal vessel. This is an alternative to a sound ceramic pot, not a method that requires pottery.
Method
Use a tested Bark Container, suitable Heating Stones and Water from the least visibly contaminated appropriate source. Prepare a stable vessel support and tested handling sticks.
Heat screened stones outside the shelter with faces clear of possible fragments. Transfer carefully, avoiding a sharp impact on the vessel. Stir or move the water safely so local hot spots do not masquerade as bulk boiling. Add enough heat for a sustained observable boil; steam alone is not the endpoint.
Follow the relevant time at boil: R06 gives one minute at ordinary elevation, and longer at high elevations. The fictional camp is low elevation. Count from the rolling boil, not from the first steam.
Test and limits
Watch seams and supports throughout. Stop on significant leakage, cracking stone or vessel damage. Keep cooling treated water apart from dirty collection implements. Boiling does not remove chemical toxins.
The Day 4 heat trial is stopped for leakage; Day 5 reaches the first observable boil. Wear interrupts treatment on Day 9, and Day 10 repairs restore it. The method is still a draft requiring practical validation of the exact bark-and-stone system.

08_eras/01_lower-paleolithic.title: Lower Paleolithic
08_eras/01_lower-paleolithic.content:
Lower Paleolithic
Orientation
A broad archaeological label for early stone-tool traditions, with boundaries that vary by region and research convention. It is not a skill level a society must finish before entering another era. Earlier toolmaking can coexist with later methods when it remains useful.
Connection to the handbook
Oldowan Toolkit describes a practical flake-and-core route; Acheulean Hand Axe describes a bifacial tool. Their labels identify historical traditions, not a universal progression or a guarantee that one tool outperforms another at every task.
A traveller at the chosen date can make a simple flake without recreating the entire history associated with it. What matters here is the raw material, striking skill, edge performance and work required.
Limit
The traveller’s first month is situated much later than this broad period. The era note provides historical orientation rather than the setting’s date or a hard prerequisite.

08_eras/02_middle-paleolithic.title: Middle Paleolithic
08_eras/02_middle-paleolithic.content:
Middle Paleolithic
Orientation
A regional archaeological framework associated with several prepared-core traditions and, in Europe, much Neanderthal material culture. It is not synonymous with one species, a fixed toolkit or limited cognitive ability.
Connection to the setting
At roughly 40,000 calibrated BP, the handbook is set near a complicated regional transition and overlap. World distinguishes the fictional valley from the regional evidence in Research Register.
The local people already work stone, hides, wood and fibres. The traveller’s first flakes are a response to his equipment shortage, not an improvement on their knapping. Cordage evidence (R01), manufactured adhesive research (R03) and inferred fire-making (R14) help constrain the portrayal.
Limit
Do not assign the group every technology found at every Neanderthal site. Describe what he observes and leave unseen practices open.

08_eras/03_upper-paleolithic.title: Upper Paleolithic
08_eras/03_upper-paleolithic.content:
Upper Paleolithic
Orientation
An archaeological framework used for later Pleistocene assemblages in parts of Eurasia. Tool traditions, ornaments and symbolic objects vary widely; the term does not mark a uniform biological or intellectual threshold.
Connection to the handbook
Bone Needle, Atlatl and ceramic experiments deserve their own local, chronological evidence when used as historical claims. The traveller can deliberately attempt a device outside its regional archaeological record, but the page must label that as a fictional intervention and state its manufacturing requirements.
R10 describes ceramic objects from a later Upper Palaeolithic context. That evidence cannot make the first-month Iberian pot or cooking ceramics historically routine.
Limit
A long list of later technologies is a set of research possibilities, not proof of inevitable adoption. Environmental opportunity, labour, materials and social transmission still determine whether a device is useful.

08_eras/04_mesolithic.title: Mesolithic
08_eras/04_mesolithic.content:
Mesolithic
Orientation
A regional term commonly used for some postglacial hunter-gatherer societies, with differing dates, definitions and material traditions. Other regions use different frameworks. It does not describe a universal intermediate stage between mobile foraging and farming.
Connection to the handbook
Broadening food sources, storage, transport and seasonal planning can make a community more resilient without requiring immediate agriculture. Small composite tools or fishing equipment are useful only where their resources and maintenance costs fit.
The Civilisation Roadmap treats such capabilities as possible parallel routes. A community can intensify selected resources while continuing to move seasonally.
Limit
Do not turn this label into a compulsory list of inventions, or assume that increasing sedentism, population and cultivation always occur together. Those relationships require local evidence and explicit narrative choices.

08_eras/05_neolithic.title: Neolithic
08_eras/05_neolithic.content:
Neolithic
Orientation
A regional archaeological term often associated with cultivation, domesticated animals and changing settlement patterns. These features develop on different schedules and do not form one package everywhere.
Connection to the handbook
Farming requires more than remembering how to sow seeds. The setting needs suitable wild populations, land access, seasonal knowledge, selection across generations, storage and a reason to accept labour and risk. Domestication is a sustained biological and social process.
Pottery, weaving, polished stone and permanent buildings should each have independent requirements. A sound pot can be useful to mobile people; a cultivated crop does not automatically create surplus or free specialists.
Limit
The mission roadmap must justify the transition with food budgets and labour, including failed harvests and competing options. Treat agriculture as a capability to evaluate rather than the predetermined end of every foraging society.
