09_reference/capability-dependency-map.title: Capability Dependency Map
09_reference/capability-dependency-map.content:
Capability Dependency Map
Default routes, alternatives and tests
The handbook follows capabilities rather than an archaeological technology ladder. Remembering an advanced design does not supply the material, precision, labour or test needed to rely on it. The categories follow Category Specification: materials are stocks, skills are practised abilities, equipment supplies object functions, structures arrange built sites, and processes organise inputs into an outcome. Local atlas places are outside this graph. Categories do not prescribe an invention order.
The graph below is an overview of the revised first month; Dependency Register is the complete generated table.
An arrow means an input or prerequisite in this selected route, not a claim about universal invention order. Wood, labour, water and other shared inputs are omitted from this small diagram for legibility; read the reference requirements.
flowchart TD
    stone[Selected knapping stone and hammer] --> flake[Usable flake tools]
    flake --> awl[Bone awl]
    bast[Prepared bast fibre] --> twisting[Practised twisting and joining]
    twisting --> cord[Finished bark cord]
    cord --> fire[Maintained friction-fire system]
    flake --> fire
    fire --> heat[Screened heating stones]
    flake --> vessel[Tested bark vessel]
    heat --> boiling[Observable water boiling]
    vessel --> boiling
    awl --> sewn[Sewn small hides]
    cord --> sewn
    flake --> fibre[Retting and nettle processing]
    fibre --> line[Nettle cord]
    awl --> whorl[Wooden whorl and spindle]
    flake --> whorl
    whorl --> trial[Trial yarn, then strength and throughput tests]
    fibre --> trial
    fire --> firing[Clay firing trial]
    firing --> pot[Leak and thermal tests]
    flake --> biface[Rough hard-hammer biface]
    flake --> thrower[Integral wooden-hook atlatl]
    thrower --> launch[Compatible dart and launch trials]

Where remembered knowledge can shorten a route



























































ObjectiveSelected routePossible shortcut or alternativeWhat still needs proofCuttingSharp unhafted flakeMake task-specific edges without first building a handaxeEdge durability and safe handlingBoiled waterBark vessel and hot stonesSuccessful pottery later changes heat handlingVessel seams, stone suitability and actual rolling boilSewingAwl makes holes; thread followsAn eyed needle improves selected fine workEye strength, thread wear and hide preparationBifaceHard-hammer removalsAntler billet can improve control in suitable stagesStone geometry and practised striking; antler is not mandatory for every bifaceSpinningDry wooden whorlCeramic whorl is another material routeBalance, fibre preparation, joins, plying and whole-process throughputThrowerIntegral hook in sound woodSeparate antler hook and hafting routeCompatible shaft, nock, grain strength and repeated launchesDurable containersWoven basket or sewn skin for suitable contentsCoiling, bark or sound ceramics for different tasksSize, load, leakage and drying needsAdhesive jointsBound handle with selected fitPine-resin mixture can supplement bindingHeat sensitivity, brittleness and joint-specific strength
R04 supports the distinction between rough hard-hammer bifaces and later refinement. A research-supported historical alternative is not automatically a tested manufacturing procedure here.
What the graph cannot show alone
A construction can be complete while operational performance is unknown. The Day 28 thrower is an example. A successful isolated test may still fail as a routine supply method; the single Day 22 fish is another.
The neighbouring people have their own demonstrated practices. Their skills are not unlocked by the traveller’s demonstration date. Communication, consent, teaching, repair capacity and food surplus govern whether a technique spreads. The graph must eventually include these capacities alongside physical inputs.
The Civilisation Roadmap extends this approach through measurement, agriculture, chemistry, machine tools, power, institutions and space systems. Later entries should expose critical paths and competing routes rather than mark an era as completed.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-2-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 2 Day 23
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-2-da.content:
Character Sheet - Moon 2 Day 23
This is the complete dry-use outfit at the end of Moon 2 Day 23, continuous Day 52. Use this sheet as the clothing reference for subsequent illustrations until a recorded change replaces a piece. The original approved Day 1 image remains the primary face, build and watercolour-style reference; see Illustration Continuity. This sheet records existing possessions and adds no clothing, materials or performance result to the story.
Identity
The same lean, sinewy man, apparently about thirty, with dark wavy ear-length hair, short dark beard/stubble, recognisable brow and nose, and natural skin tone. Keep ordinary anatomy and softly washed skin. Do not introduce scars, tattoos or etched patterns.
Complete outfit








































PieceAppearance and placementEstablished byRabbit-pelt crown padSmall shallow fur-out covering with folded margins and a loose forehead/back band. Face, human ears and much of the nape exposed. Plain worked fur: no animal head, eyes, muzzle, whiskers, ears or tail.Day 50Fox shoulder stripOne separate narrow rusty fur strip on his anatomical left shoulder. Front view: viewer’s right. Back view: viewer’s left. It does not spread into a cape or merge with the cap.Day 24Grass front panelSeparate flexible hanging grass screen, roughly 0.45 × 0.6 m, with a supported header below the collarbones, light paired retaining rows and loose accessible attachments.Day 49Grass back panelSeparate flexible screen, roughly 0.5 × 0.6 m, with its own supported top edge and retaining rows. The side view retains an open flank between front and back panels.Day 40Bark waist coverage and small pelvic padOverlapping rough bark panels on a simple waist fastening, with the existing small rabbit-fur pelvic pad. These remain beneath the torso screens; the detail study exposes the garment assembly without enlarging its coverage.Days 1 and 14Pair of bast solesTwo matching low, flat interlaced willow-bast footbeds, cord-bound margins, thin separate grass liners, forefoot and heel retention, open toes and exposed ankles.Day 52
The grass screens leave the upper chest, arms, sides and legs partly exposed. They are neither fine woven cloth nor the stiff willow bedding mat. The hat and shoulder strip are separate small pieces. There is no full fur coat, hood, leather footwear or trousers.
Construction and trial limits belong to Plant-Fibre Clothing, Fur-On Pelt Clothing, Basic Bark Clothing and Plant-Fibre Footwear. The footwear has only a brief level dry-walking result; sideways creep ended its incline trial. Wearing it on this reference sheet does not establish wet-ground, hunting or winter performance.
Applying the sheet to later scenes
Start each new scene brief with the full dated outfit above. State any removal and its reason before generation. Do not silently drop the grass panels, hat or footwear because a new task is the focus of the picture. Dry seated craft or ordinary dry camp use should retain suitable pieces unless the narrative specifies otherwise.
Close fire work, wet processing and projectile clearance can justify taking off the grass screens or other pieces; unstable ground can justify removing the experimental soles. Follow the actual scene and recorded limits rather than forcing the full outfit into every action. If removed garments lie within the scene’s field of view, show them protected nearby at their proper scale. If they are outside the crop, name their location in the saved scene brief so removal cannot become loss of ownership.
Day 52’s replacement illustration uses the short level dry-walking test after heel adjustment, so both soles are worn. Day 53’s replacement uses the packing stage after the extinguished ignition trial, with the dry-use outfit put back on. Day 55’s casting session remains barefoot, with both grass screens, the crown pad and the pair of soles shown protected nearby. Those specific moments do not supersede this inventory reference. Clothing made after Day 52 must first be earned in the narrative; do not send this outfit backward into earlier days.
Reference and review record
Generated with the built-in image-generation tool using the original Day 1 illustration for identity/style and the Plant-Fibre Clothing plate for grass construction only. The flawed Day 52 illustration was inspected to diagnose the animal-head error and was not supplied as a generation reference.
Exact prompt, reference roles and selected-output provenance: generation record. This is an editorial continuity aid, not an archaeological reconstruction or a tested clothing specification.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.content:
Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15
Dated appearance after the Day 73 dry fit
Moon 3 Day 15 - Close the Gap Above the Soles adds removable foot coverings from the separate Day 70 and Day 71 rabbit pelts. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 9 governs earlier scenes, including the Day 73 working moment before fitting. Use the original Day 1 identity/style with this new dated appearance for the fitted moment and subsequent dry-camp use.
The same lean adult has dark ear-length wavy hair, a short beard and smooth ordinary skin. The existing tan deer-sized body wrap remains hair-inward, overlapping in front, sleeveless and above the knees. Its repaired anatomical-left shoulder fold, loose shoulder ease, short chest tie below the throat and light waist fastening/hip keeper persist. The cap remains the plain grey-brown rabbit crown with the old fox panel forming tan-out hair-in side/ear/upper-nape coverage. No fox panel remains beneath the left shoulder. Waist layers and pelvic pad are concealed; both grass screens stay stored.
Both feet are now enclosed in low soft pale-tan skin coverings, fur inward, irregular folded/stitch-retained margins, toes and heels closed, top just above each ankle. They are not tall boots, fitted moccasin patterns or thick leather soles. Modest dry grass lining sits inside. Both original flat woven bast soles remain visibly beneath/outside, with the retained low ties and short new extensions passing round the combined layer. No bare toes project through the skin; lower legs above the low tops remain bare. Knots are not under the feet and top ties do not form tight ankle rings.
One whole new pelt supplies each foot; no spare glove, cap, legging or cloak material is implied. These are temporary limited dry-use layers, with moisture and wear still unresolved. For wet work or a deliberate removal, record that moment explicitly rather than silently losing established footwear. This sheet records appearance and material allocation, not an experimentally validated pattern.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 5
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.content:
Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 5
This dated reference records the garment made in Moon 3 Day 5 - A Wrap That Covers the Body. It replaces the previous clothing brief for scenes from the end of Day 63, without overwriting Character Sheet - Moon 2 Day 23. The original Day 1 image remains the primary identity/style reference.
Visible appearance
The same lean man, apparently about thirty, has dark wavy ear-length hair, short beard and ordinary smooth skin. The new garment is one worn worked deer-sized skin, wrapped over both shoulders with an overlapping front and an irregular hem above the knees. Hair faces inward; the outside is dull tan skin. A shallow upper-edge fold reveals a little brown inner hair. A small repaired fold at the anatomical left shoulder, an easily released upper-chest tie and a light existing waist fastening hold it. There are no sleeves, sewn trousers or newly fitted hood.
Both old grass screens are stored dry, not worn or destroyed. Bark waist layers and the small pelvic pad remain underneath. The separate narrow fox strip stays beneath the wrap at the anatomical left shoulder and is normally concealed; it is not decorative fur trim around the whole collar.
The old plain grey-brown rabbit crown pad remains visible, without an animal head, ears or muzzle. Both low flat woven bast soles, grass liners and low ties remain worn, with exposed toes and ankles. Lower legs and much of the arms remain uncovered during work; arms can be drawn inside the wrap at rest.
Applying the reference
Use this sheet for Day 63 after fitting and subsequent dry-use scenes until another recorded wardrobe change. Day 62’s transferred skin is not yet worn. During repair on Day 63 the wrap is a workpiece and the old screens are put back on temporarily; the chosen daily illustration uses the later fitted walking moment.
The sheet is appearance continuity, not a claim of waterproofing or complete winter protection. No second large blanket, boot supply, hood or spare cloak is acquired from the same skin.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 9
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-3-da.content:
Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 9
Dated appearance after fitting, Day 67
Moon 3 Day 9 - Warmth Without Losing Your Hands adjusts the existing body wrap and extends the existing cap by reallocating the fox shoulder panel from the traveller’s own earlier snare catch. Use the original Day 1 identity/style and this dated sheet for completed Day 67 and later scenes. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 5 remains correct through Day 66 and for the earlier Day 67 moments before the panel is moved from shoulder to cap.
The same lean adult man has dark ear-length wavy hair, a short beard and smooth ordinary skin. The body wrap is still the single worn deer-sized skin: dull tan outside, brown hair inward, overlapping front, both shoulders covered, no sleeves, hem above the knees. Its repaired fold remains at the anatomical left shoulder. A small amount of shoulder fullness and an overlap held at one hip under the existing light waist fastening improve movement. The short upper-chest tie remains below the throat.
The plain grey-brown rabbit crown now carries the old fox panel as a narrow dull tan-brown side-and-nape extension. The previously pieced skin is reused in full; it is not newly traded hide. Its brown hair faces inward and shows only a little at the turned edges. Side ends cover ears; the back reaches the upper nape. The human face and forehead remain open. It is a cap extension, not a separate hood, animal head, muzzle, ears or complete fur collar. The old loose forehead/back band retains it without a throat loop. The sides can fold up for close work, but are down in the chosen reference and daily scenes.
Both original flat woven bast soles, low ties and grass liners remain. Toes, ankles and lower legs are exposed. Old bark waist layers and pelvic pad remain concealed beneath the wrap. The narrow fox panel no longer lies beneath the anatomical left shoulder: it has all moved to the cap. There is no new offcut or duplicated shoulder layer. Both grass torso screens remain stored dry.
Limits and use
Show exactly the recorded clothing for each chosen moment. No hide boots, leggings, sleeves, new cloak or second large skin have appeared. This reference records appearance and allocation, not a cutting pattern, waterproofing claim or complete winter outfit. Movement trials improve fit without establishing severe-weather performance.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-4-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 20
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-4-da.content:
The complete earlier outfit remains. Only two removable thumb-less hand pockets are added, smooth skin out and hair in. Day 109 deliberately removes both for fine handling.
Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 20
Appearance after the Day 108 hand-cover fit
Moon 4 Day 20 - A Pocket of Warmth for Each Hand adds two removable small hand-warming pockets from the sole Day 105 adult-rabbit pelt. Original Day 1 remains the independent identity/style reference. Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 9 governs all earlier applicable scenes and supplies every retained layer; this sheet adds hand covers only.
Preserve the same lean man about thirty, dark ear-length wavy hair and short beard. The full grey-brown rabbit crown covers the TOP of the head, with tan fox ear/upper-nape sides. It is a plain material cap, without animal eyes, muzzle or ears. The old pale-tan overlapping above-knee body wrap stays over BOTH shoulders, hair inward, with its anatomical-left repair, chest tie and light waist fastening.
Both separate darker grey-brown sleeves still reach the wrists. Both overlapping matching leg panels cover knees/calves from under the wrap hem to the ankles. Their existing modest seams, attachment tabs and side keepers persist. BOTH feet retain low closed pale-tan rabbit-skin covers, with original woven bast soles visibly below/outside and low ties; no tall boots, new soles or bare toes.
When worn, the new hand covers are TWO compact pale-tan soft skin pockets with inward fur, rounded CLOSED ends and short wrist openings, loosely retained beneath the sleeve ends. Each encloses fingers AND thumb together. There is NO separate thumb lobe, articulated finger, long gauntlet cuff, wool, beadwork or modern glove. They are not sewn permanently to the sleeves.
They are removed for cutting, sewing, nock inspection and bow use. For the Day 109 practice session, BOTH rest together on clean dry bark beside the gear; both hands are deliberately bare, and the covers are put on for return. A light temporary sleeve keeper gives string clearance without replacing the garment. Show the appropriate moment rather than silently losing clothing or covering the release fingers.
The one new skin is wholly allocated to this pair and small seam-test scraps. No extra rabbit pelt, new hood/cloak, stronger footwear or blanket is provided. This sheet records fitted appearance, not waterproofing, a thermal rating or tested durable leather.

09_reference/character-sheet---moon-4-da.title: Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 9
09_reference/character-sheet---moon-4-da.content:
Character Sheet - Moon 4 Day 9
Dated appearance after the completed Day 97 fit
Moon 4 Day 9 - Warmth That Moves With You adds two removable sleeves and two overlapping leg coverings from the single personally acquired Day 93 red-deer skin. Use original Day 1 for identity/style and this sheet for clothing from the completed fit onward. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15 still governs Days 95–96 and all earlier applicable scenes. This sheet does not rewrite them.
The same lean adult of about thirty has dark ear-length wavy hair, a short beard and ordinary smooth skin. The full grey-brown rabbit-fur crown covers the TOP of the head; tan fox skin sides cover ears and upper nape, hair inward. The cap is plain material, never an animal head, mask or headband.
The old pale tan hair-in body wrap remains over BOTH shoulders, sleeveless in its own construction, overlapping in front and ending just above the knees. Retain the anatomical-left shoulder repair, short chest tie and light waist keeper. Its underside waist layers stay concealed. The earlier grass screens remain stored, and no fox strip remains under the shoulder.
The new sleeves are a slightly darker muted grey-brown skin outside, hair inward, loose around the elbows and extending from beneath the old wrap’s shoulder edges to the wrists. Each has a restrained longitudinal seam and a small folded upper attachment tab tied to sound wrap material clear of the old repair. They are separate fitted tubes, not a newly sleeved coat or a shoulder cape. Both bare hands remain visible.
Two matching skin leg panels begin beneath the old wrap’s hem, covering the knees and calves to the ankles. Side overlaps and a few loose retainers keep them closed; separate slim side keepers rise beneath the wrap to its existing waist fastening. They are not tight modern trousers, spiral bandages or rigid gaiters. Show natural movement and modest seams without decorative fringe, dozens of cord rings or invented ornaments.
BOTH feet retain the original pale-tan low closed rabbit-skin covers, hair/grass inward, with toes and heels enclosed. Original woven bast soles remain visibly outside and beneath, with low ties. Leg-panel ends overlap their low tops. Do not replace them with tall boots, bare feet, dark leather shoes or thick soles.
One full skin has become the four limb panels and small tabs/test scraps. No spare full hide, new mittens, hood, cloak, bedding skin or footwear is supplied. These dry-worked pieces need airing and renewed flexing; the sheet fixes appearance, not waterproofing or a thermal guarantee.

09_reference/civilisation-roadmap.title: Civilisation Roadmap
09_reference/civilisation-roadmap.content:
Civilisation Roadmap
The dependency problem
The endpoint is a society capable of building, operating and replacing space systems, then designing a defence mission appropriate to the threatening object. One remembered design is insufficient: industry needs reproducible materials, energy, measurement, supply chains, institutions and skilled people.
This is a research roadmap, not a claim that every listed historical step is necessary. Routes should be compared by time, labour, material access, failure cost and long-term maintenance.
Capability stages




























































StageRequired capabilitiesWhat must be demonstrated before advancingIndividual stabilityShelter, repeatable ignition, food access, water treatment, useful edges and containersSeveral days of maintenance without consuming the last reserve; fallback for failed fire or weatherCooperative productionShared communication, reciprocal exchange, local resource access, distributed skillsOthers reproduce useful processes and consent to continued workSustained surplusSeasonal food management, storage, sanitation, transport, durable shelterA group can feed specialists and tolerate bad harvests or interrupted routesMeasurement and recordsShared units, counting, geometry, durable marks, comparison standardsIndependent workers make compatible parts and diagnose failuresThermal and chemical industryControlled firing, fuel supply, refractory materials, extraction and separationRepeated batches meet known material and performance criteriaMechanical industryStructural metals, joining, bearings, seals, precision tools and power sourcesMachines can be built, serviced and reproduced by several workshopsElectrical and scientific industryConductors, insulation, magnets, generation, instruments, chemical purityStable power, calibrated measurements and reliable component manufactureTransport and communicationsRoads or waterways, vehicles, navigation, signalling and supply managementGoods, people and information move reliably beyond one settlementSpace systemsPropulsion, guidance, structures, testing, tracking, launch facilities and operationsUncrewed systems achieve defined flight goals with independently verified telemetryPlanetary defenceSurvey, orbit determination, target characterisation, mission design and coordinationThe actual threat and proposed intervention are analysed and tested at the necessary scale
Food production does not have to mean immediate agriculture. Productive fisheries, managed wild resources and storage may support some specialisation first. Domestication needs suitable organisms, generations and incentives; the protagonist cannot summon modern crops.
Shortcuts worth investigating
Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit reviews the current assemblage against archaeological parallels. The immediate bottleneck is seasonal resilience: an enclosed dry sleeping space, useful insulation, food reserves and protected fuel take precedence over adding experimental devices. Month Two Outline carries that priority into the next recorded work.

Measurement and experimental records before metallurgy: cheap concepts can prevent expensive trial-and-error.
Wooden spindles before ceramic whorls: an alternative material removes a firing dependency.
Water treatment before pottery: bark vessels and heated stones offer a tested alternative route.
Mechanical hafting before glue: geometry and binding can secure some tools; adhesive improves particular joints.
Community instruction before complex machines: parallel expertise may outperform one exceptional maker.
Starting with the most useful local metal route rather than compulsory bronze-first progression.
Delaying technologies that are physically possible but have poor returns at the current population or mobility.

For each proposed shortcut, write its actual requirements and a counterexample where it would fail. Avoid labelling an entire historical development a wrong turn without assessing the constraints faced by its inventors.
Later technical paths to expand
Each row is a research programme. Turn it into reference pages only after selecting a feasible route and defining a measurable acceptance test. These branches overlap; they are not compulsory historical eras.







































































ObjectiveBase inputs and supporting capabilitiesRoute decisionsAcceptance testReliable food storageIdentified foods, sound containers, pest control, seasonal records and clean handlingDry storage, tested drying, or another validated preservation process suited to the food and climateLoss and illness rates, edible reserve through a defined lean intervalRepeatable hot-work materialsClay and other candidate minerals, prepared fuel, controlled airflow and temperature assessmentFiring bodies, refractories and furnace lining must be tested separatelySeveral batches survive their intended heat, load and moisture conditionsUseful extracted metalSuitable ore, extraction chemistry, fuel or reductant, refractory vessel, separation and workability testsChoose by local ore and application; a copper-first or iron-first route has different costsReproducible material with measured properties sufficient for its actual jobReproducible mechanismsShared length standards, geometry, abrasives, cutting tools, suitable structural materials, joining and lubricationWooden machines can do selected jobs before a metal workshop; different loads require different bearings and wear surfacesIndependently made replacement parts fit and survive a specified dutyImproved precisionStable reference surfaces, alignment methods, cutting-edge materials, feed control and inspectionA workshop can improve its own tools incrementally; the first generation must be achievable with existing meansMeasured error and repeatability improve across independently built partsScaled mechanical powerA site-specific energy source, transmission, structure, maintenance and operatorsWater, wind, animal effort and other sources have different site and labour constraints; steam adds pressure-vessel and sealing demandsUseful output, uptime and maintenance cost under a recorded loadElectrical supply and instrumentsConductors, insulation, magnets, mechanical drive, calibrated comparisons and safe test methodsDemonstration current, reliable generation and an industrial distribution system are separate achievementsStable specified output, repeatable readings and repair by other workersControlled chemical supplyFeedstocks, separation and reaction methods, resistant vessels, mass records and contamination controlRequired purity depends on the next use; laboratory success is not bulk productionBatch consistency at the scale and purity needed by the consuming processSpaceflightProven structures, propulsion, guidance, power, tracking, computing, test facilities and trained operationsComponent tests, uncrewed flight trials and payload goals should expose separate dependenciesDefined flight outcome and independently checked telemetry, with failures analysedDefence missionSurvey instruments, long observation records, orbit models, target characterisation, space systems and coordinationChoose intervention against the specified object, timing and uncertainty; no single remembered device guarantees successQuantified mission effect and remaining uncertainty against the actual threat
The space branch cannot be made concrete until the asteroid specification is settled. R12 in Research Register supplies a real deflection demonstration, not the requirements for this fictional threat. First specify what departure humanity could already build and why that capacity was inadequate; otherwise the mission’s endpoint may contradict its opening.
How to assess an earlier innovation
Use a short comparison record: the problem, two routes, every input, required precision, available labour, time to a first useful result, maintenance, likely failure and who benefits. Then explain what remembered knowledge changes.
Knowledge can suggest a material substitution, remove an unnecessary intermediate step, guide an experiment or avoid a known failure. It cannot create a missing organism, local ore, energy source or cooperative workforce. Earlier feasibility and worthwhile adoption are different questions.
For example, the wooden spindle removes successful firing from one route. It may still be a poor investment if fibre preparation is the bottleneck or if a mobile group needs little fine yarn. A machine becomes a shortcut only when its entire process improves the relevant task.
A claimed historical wrong turn needs the same comparison under the resources, institutions and incentives of the people who chose it. The protagonist’s hindsight alone is not evidence that their choice was irrational.
Institutional dependencies
Communication and Exchange, Teaching and Knowledge Preservation, Measurement and Records and Sanitation and Camp Hygiene begin early. Larger production later needs resource agreements, dispute resolution, responsibility for shared equipment and succession.
The traveller’s mission succeeds only when capabilities survive his absence. Community production is verified separately from his own demonstrations.
Narrative scale
Days 1–28 cover immediate survival and first contact. The approved second-month outline follows independent seasonal preparation, practical testing and limited contact. Cooperation can develop later when repeated willing interaction and useful results justify it. Later parts should follow projects, migrations, generations and industrial programmes. Detail follows the dependency being tested, not a fixed calendar format.
Next chapter after revision
Month Two Outline covers Days 29–56 and was approved by the author on 3 October 2026. It keeps the traveller independent, prioritises cold-weather clothing and defence, and develops the atlatl through a disappointing early comparison followed by growing late interest. No trade, group provisioning or immediate recruitment supports his progress.
Day 29 begins from the actual Day 28 stock: inspect the green shaft candidates, prepare a compatible practice projectile only if suitable, and maintain food, water and fuel. A calendar date does not force a launch or large-game kill. Draft the daily work and introduce new capability pages from the approved outline, using Valley Map to maintain terrain, travel and camp continuity.
Opening week of Month 2 drafted
Days 29–35 now follow the approved outline in text. Use Survival Ledger for historical calculations and qualitative changes, the original Day 28 entry for that starting state, and Valley Map including its dated additions for locations. First launches remain erratic; the small bedding pad, comparison record and inspected retreat route do not solve winter clothing or food supply. Day 36 begins with the actual reduced reserve and unfinished batches rather than a fresh inventory.
Page scale and reflective rhythm
Page Scope and Organisation keeps equipment at the design-family level, with variants rather than one article per use. Structures and Places distinguishes construction knowledge from the local atlas. Measurement and Records is a skill; shared standards/calibration remain future systems.
Reflections appraises completed-day states at the approximate new/full moon milestones in Lunar Calendar. These reviews connect surviving capabilities, supply, danger and intention without advancing the event ledger.
Continuing from Day 40
Month Two Outline now records Days 36–40 (Moon 2 Days 7–11). The first observed atlatl comparison disappoints without closing off later interest. A repaired fish closure, one rabbit catch and a limited grass back panel are the new practical developments. Spear Throwing records local competence separately from the traveller’s atlatl practice; no community supply or shared production is gained.
The next work must confront the 1.31 kg kernel reserve, scarce loose binding and unfinished retting, pelt and clay trials. Food and fibre condition govern Days 41–42; scouting and lone-hunter failures belong to the following phase. A more consistent projectile, wider core coverage and a supplied refuge must still be earned before the Day 56 appraisal. The full-moon reflection remains scheduled for Day 44, not written from future outcomes.
Continuing from Day 45
Month Two Outline records Days 41–45. Shelter assessment has led to a limited return frame and partial covering, while acorn processing exposes the small vessel’s throughput cost. A selected 18 g fibre output is useful without completing the whole batch. The full-moon Reflection 04 - Full Moon - Moon 2 Day 15 uses only Day 44 state.
The next bottlenecks are food collection, the roof’s upper junction and weather performance, whole-body insulation, redundant fire/water and a supplied retreat. The current 0.93 kg kernel reserve cannot finance prolonged hunting or simultaneous workshops. Short practice can continue when those needs allow; no observer’s interest supplies shared production.
Continuing from Day 50
Month Two Outline now includes earned shower repair, an aborted deer approach, two-sided coarse core coverage and a limited crown pad. These improve particular tasks while leaving the food buffer short. Atlatl consistency, proper foot protection, spare ignition, a second water vessel and a supplied retreat remain dependent work. No alliance or reliable ceramic production is established. Subsequent industry still needs surplus and resilience, not a longer catalogue of prototypes.
Workshop foundations — Days 51–55
The next five entries put reproducible stock, ground contact, duplicate ignition, repeated vessel manufacture and an observable projectile trial ahead of extended routine narration. Wooden Mallet and Wooden Splitting Wedge begin a limited route to useful wooden blanks; Plant-Fibre Footwear has a narrow test rather than a solved winter outfit. Two independently made ignition kits and two tested bark vessels reduce particular interruptions while remaining at the same camp.
Day 55’s observer interest is an opening for future learning, with no cooperation yet demonstrated. The next scale change should follow a technical project and its adoption, keeping Teaching and Knowledge Preservation central. Remembered knowledge becomes a civilisation’s capability only when other people can choose, reproduce, maintain and extend useful work.
End of the second moon — completed Day 59
The closing sequence develops acceptance tests rather than a longer list of devices: retention on the existing soles, sacrificial drying inspection, a small comparison firing and a cold wetting check. Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1 separates these useful results from winter readiness, a food reserve, supplied retreat, ceramic vessel production and cooperation. Next work should organise one reproducible material/object route alongside a realistic surplus and retreat plan. Independent replication by another willing person remains a separate milestone.
Approved third-moon course correction — 14 October 2026
Moon Three Outline commits to abandoning the lean-to home for a newly inspected rocky overhang, with improved enclosure, dry bedding and selective earth/fibre wind sealing. Substantial hide clothing, seasonal gathered-food stores and ongoing animal-food access are the immediate projects. Pottery earns a practical container/cooking role, while a useful spear, renewed spear fishing and atlatl improvements support subsistence. Late bow/arrow preparation provides the next technical direction.
Keep workable relations and reciprocal practical contributions to the local group. Formal teaching and independent copying can develop when useful, rather than being a compulsory monthly finale. Retreat/cache provision is removed from the continuing programme.
From Day 60 the narrative uses brief qualitative continuity instead of exact daily food, fuel, cord, water and time accounting. Historical Days 1–59 and their reflections remain intact. Preserve significant acquisitions, object changes and sources in the story, without maintaining every resource level indefinitely. Warm, adequately supplied people and a useful working place remain foundations for the later industrial mission.
Winter foundations begun — completed Day 64
The first qualitative entries turn the approved course correction into a new working site, an earned larger skin, materially better core coverage and a food-storage process. Rock-Shelter Enclosure, Raised Storage Rack and Dry Nut Storage distinguish site framework from operation. Useful labour and observed exchange begin a practical relationship without a formal teaching finale. The next technical questions concern fuller enclosure, additional clothing coverage and food/hunting throughput.
A working home and compatible parts — completed Day 69
The next batch adds a weather-breaking entrance, a small Earth-and-Fibre Infill trial, useful wrap/cap fit, one renewed spear-fishing catch and a separate Stone Spear Point with selected shaft. These establish mechanisms and limited results rather than recurring survival routines. The new joint, vessel and enclosing foot/leg protection remain dependent work; the single caught fish is no preserved supply.
Useful assemblies and timed processes — completed Day 74
The joint, food preparation and clothing now serve identifiable work: a mechanically assembled Stone-Pointed Spear with a limited target result, Pounding and Grinding Stones supporting small acorn charges, and two self-caught pelts enclosing feet above the retained plant soles. The new pot is still greenware. Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16 appraises those limits and next dependencies. Reflection 05 is revised at the user’s request as a Day 59 precursor to the winter course correction, without future discoveries or changed historical balances.
Tool choice and productive participation — completed Day 79
The latest batch links a working outfit and modified dart to an actual field opportunity without making target success an automatic kill. Large-Game Processing identifies skilled handling and carrying as dependencies; the traveller’s accepted small role produces a real bounded share. The dedicated Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear is now made and trialled. Future clothing material has an actual source, while no preserved meat, whole hide, new pottery service or standing supply arrangement is invented.
A useful ceramic route — completed Day 84
The timed drying/firing sequence now reaches one useful pot: Clay Drying and Inspection, open firing, Fired Earthenware, cold containment, an Open Cooking Hearth and Cooking in an Earthenware Pot. First successful service is distinct from repeatable manufacture and long-term reliability. The small deer-margin Stone-Edge Guard makes one actual animal-material share useful without inventing a new clothing supply. Existing bark methods remain available; bow-stave work can follow without a kiln programme.
A workshop that can wait — completed Day 89
The closing new-moon review distinguishes useful daily service from unfinished material projects. The pot has a real cooking role, and the home can protect drying work through rain. Bow Staves, Arrow Shafts and Bow Making begin the next system without claiming a working bow; Tillering and Bowstring remain future requirements. Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1 gives food access and warmer, more durable coverage priority while the wood seasons. A useful ongoing relationship with local people remains a practical dependency for wider production, not a completed teaching institution.
Earlier fourth-moon proposal — 22 October 2026, superseded
Moon Four Outline sketches December as the development of a dependable winter base and useful shared work. It prioritises leg/foot coverage from actual skin material, more regular food participation, a second useful vessel and a bounded teaching result. Bow progress follows material condition. The proposal covers continuous Days 89–117, with the full-moon review at Day 103 and the closing new-moon review after the Day 118 boundary entry. Day 89 is already written. This earlier shared-work proposal is superseded by the solitary-winter direction recorded below. It is not a record of acquisitions.
Revised fourth-moon direction — 23 October 2026
The user keeps the broad winter plan but makes December solitary and postpones sustained cooperation until spring. Moon Four Outline now prioritises independently acquired skin for arms/legs, improved traps, seasonal food access and recovery/preservation, distinct use of spear/atlatl, and condition-dependent bow progress. A second pot needs an actual processing purpose rather than a teaching subplot. Flora and Fauna supplies the regional research and cautions. The mission still requires cooperation later; the solo winter establishes practical competence and exposes the limits of one person’s labour.
Independent winter work — completed Day 94
The first five new Moon 4 entries develop Small-Game Trapping, Cordage Testing, one Pack Frame and an actual solo hunting/recovery result. Meat Cooling and Holding handles a bounded fresh-food interval; it is not winter preservation. A Fleshing Beam and Beam Fleshing begin turning one full skin into future clothing material. The garment, durable dressing and longer food-keeping questions now have real inputs and consequences, while cooperation stays a spring direction.
Clothing enables fibre work — completed Day 99
Dry Pelt Working connects a real skin to Skin Limb Coverings instead of leaving cold-weather protection as a distant plan. Knotted Netting adds an open-mesh technique with uses beyond one trap, and Hand Net applies it to controlled retrieval. Further food-keeping work needs a fresh actual input; the earlier selected deer meat is gone. Bow stock and the separate snare candidate remain unfinished. The solitary-winter direction continues.
Fishing reach and fibre production — completed Day 104
A wooden gorge and attended hand line extend the existing fishing toolkit. The old spindle now supplies a deliberately plied lot; a notched shuttle improves small-mesh handling. One full-length bowstring candidate is manufactured separately while the actual bow body remains unstrung. The Day 103 full-moon review connects real warmth, food access, recovery, fibre supply and future cooperation without inventing a preserved surplus or group support.
Joining a first bow system — completed Day 109
Wood preparation, string manufacture, controlled limb work, nock fit and one projectile now meet in a limited working practice system. The practical result does not replace proven food routes. A separate real pelt gives exposed hands removable warming pockets, while older clothing and one useful pot continue. Further material supply, food keeping and more reliable weapon performance remain meaningful next work.
Improving interfaces rather than replacing systems — completed Day 114
Fletching modifies the existing arrow, while the established fishing fork remains useful in an actual winter opportunity. Pottery now has a second identified service job and one new drying specimen. Wooden Spoon connects stone-edge woodworking to food handling without waiting for a kiln or the second pot’s completion. Material condition still governs the next step; there is one working vessel and no preserved surplus or group provision.

09_reference/day-40-technology-and-winte.title: Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit
09_reference/day-40-technology-and-winte.content:
Day 40 Technology and Winter Audit
Finding
At Moon 2 Day 11 - A Covering That Can Be Worn, the traveller has a Palaeolithic subsistence toolkit with a few later or geographically distant experiments. A Middle Palaeolithic comparison best describes much of his everyday working equipment; the eyed needle and trial spear-thrower bring Upper Palaeolithic comparisons. No single archaeological era possessed precisely this assemblage. He is not at a Neolithic level: there is no farming, stockkeeping, reliable pottery production or settled food surplus.
His knowledge exceeds his production capacity. A leaking pot, an erratic dart and a dry-fit grass panel are genuine experiments, but they do not establish dependable cooking ceramics, hunting or cold-weather clothing. His seasonal resilience is well below what we should give an experienced local group in the narrative. This is an inference from his recorded limitations, not a measured ranking of cultures.
The greatest omission is a credible cold-season living system. Better shelter must become an immediate work programme, alongside insulation, food and protected fuel. Another attractive implement will not solve that gap.
Historical comparison
Dates below are examples of evidence, not invention dates or compulsory technological stages. Organic objects preserve unevenly; absence at a site cannot prove that its inhabitants lacked a technique. BP dates are approximate years before present, normally 1950. Global parallels do not establish presence in this fictional Iberian valley.


















































Capability actually recordedArchaeological comparisonConsequence for the handbookSimple flakes, scraper, chopper and rough bifaceThese belong to technological traditions much older than the setting. An object can resemble an Oldowan or Acheulean form without making its maker a member of that archaeological culture; see R04The existing page names should describe forms or teaching routes, not a sequence of eras he has personally completedWooden spear and elementary woodworkingPreserved Pleistocene weapons and worked wood substantially predate 40,000 BP. Schöningen has an unusually varied assemblage (R31); its dating has been revised and remains a research issueWoodworking is a major practical branch. A wooden point is credible, and local composite stone-pointed spears are also defensible (R21)Managed fire, hafting, adhesive and cordageNeanderthal fire-making evidence and manufactured adhesives already appear in the register. The Abri du Maras three-ply cord is associated with roughly 52,000–41,000-year-old deposits (Hardy et al., 2020)He cannot credibly astonish competent neighbours merely by displaying a cord or haft. His local material judgement can still be inferiorPlant bedding, coiling and twining trialsPlant bedding is documented at Sibudu around 77,000 BP and Border Cave at least 200,000 years ago (R24, R29). The latter is grass bedding, not proof of woven matsInsulation is an ancient foundation, not an optional modern comfort. A basket or fish cage does not by itself establish a Mesolithic package; the exact mechanisms remain authored trialsBone awl, usable eyed needle and limited sewingA 2024 synthesis places early eyed needles around 40,000 cal BP in Siberia and later in Europe; it also explains why awls can support fitted clothing without needle eyes (R28)The Day 12 needle is a plausible knowledgeable traveller’s experiment, not an established local Neanderthal possession. Its manufacturing success merits more scrutiny than its simple appearance suggestsAtlatl with one green, blunt, unfletched practice dartDirect European thrower evidence in R16 is later than the setting. A 2023 impact-fracture study argues for thrower use at Maisières-Canal around 31,000 BP (R27); this is indirect inference from stone armaturesPotential novelty remains plausible, earlier absence unproven. Current performance earns no hunting advantage; experienced hand throwing matters (R17)Clay vessels: one failed pot and two unfired samplesXianrendong pottery was made by foragers around 20,000–19,000 cal BP, long before agriculture (Wu et al., 2012)Pottery need not wait for farming. Here it remains an attempted anticipatory innovation; a useful water-holding vessel and a thermally reliable cooking pot are separate achievementsSmall traps, intermittent fishing and a predominantly gathered dietPerishable gear is particularly hard to date. Neither cordage nor a woven impression establishes this exact rear-cap fish cage, figure-4 mechanism or spring snareKeep those designs labelled as physical trials. Judge yield, maintenance and seasonal access rather than assigning a confident earliest date to every modern named mechanism
Neanderthal hide-working also deserves more weight. Specialized rib smoothers from French Neanderthal contexts were interpreted through comparison and experiments as hide-working tools (Soressi et al., 2013). This supports portraying skilled material workers, while leaving their precise garments and treatments uncertain. No borrowed tool, skin or instruction is credited to the traveller.
Winter: what the current camp does not supply
An open lean-to can be useful temporary cover. The label alone cannot determine whether a particular winter stay is possible. In this story, the combination of exposed sleeping space, modest bedding, bare front torso/head/feet and a very short food buffer makes it an inadequate planned winter home. Rain and wind are dangerous even before severe frost: wet exposure can cause hypothermia at cool temperatures (CDC). Local minimum temperatures, rain, wind and snow still require a narrower setting decision; there is no defensible universal wall thickness or survival temperature for the current shelter.
At Day 40 there are 1.31 kg of edible kernels, about 2.6 recent half-kilogram rations, and 24 kg usable dry wood. These are author-model stocks, not independently validated energetic margins. The grass garment covers only the back, the new rabbit pelt is unfinished, the second fibre batch is still processing and the fallback bench has no shelter or cache. See Survival Ledger.
The next structure should be a compact, substantially enclosed sleeping shelter with a stable frame, overlapping weather cover, wind protection, a controllable entrance and a whole-body bed that stays dry after compression. Choose between rebuilding at the present terrace and a separately inspected better site; a convenient cave must not appear by assumption. Survey drainage, overhead hazards, access and escape before committing scarce labour. Thick debris is labour and bulk, not a free substitute for sound framing or waterproofing.
A low framed/debris sleeping chamber is a better near-term candidate than a log house, masonry room or animal-hide tent. Sound fallen pieces, natural forks and supported joints may reduce the need for long structural lashings; they still need inspection and stability checks. The present fallen limb can be retained only if sound. Thin cross-cover, overlapping roof material and bulky bed fill are separate jobs and separate allocations. Do not make a short supply of fine nettle line carry an entire new building by assumption.
Keep combustion outside the proposed small combustible sleeping enclosure. Bringing the hearth inside is a different engineering problem involving exhaust, air supply, sparks and clearances; a smoke hole does not certify it. Wood combustion can accumulate carbon monoxide in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces (CDC). Rebuilding cannot silently move existing installations on Valley Map.
Missing foundations and priority order

Dry sleep and usable insulation. Collect sufficient cover and bedding in separate lots; assess compressed bedding, leaks, draughts and morning damp. Extend practical core protection and make modest head/foot trials. Dry rawhide is not supple, wet-resilient leather. Hide conditioning needs materials, work and tests, with a plant-based fallback if captures fail.
Seasonal calories and storage. The recurring productive hazel circuit is the largest unverified resource assumption. Research its plausibility at this place/date and model reduced access and diminishing returns. Expand only positively identified, locally available foods; refine the already introduced acorn processing and record its water/fuel costs. Protected nut storage needs drying, pest checks and loss records. Unvalidated smoked meat cannot become winter rations (R07).
Protected fuel, tinder and redundancy. Cover and inspect fuel; colder nights and wet weather change consumption. Protect an independently usable ignition provision and build a second tested water vessel. A prototype does not provide a spare. Shelter materials, cord, ordinary fuel and experimental firing compete for the same labour and stock.
Woodworking and repair capacity. Controlled splitting, wedges, wooden striking tools, abrasion and tested frame joints could give better returns than another weapon. Introduce only techniques and equipment actually needed for the chosen build, with wood selection and load checks. A handaxe is not automatically a convenient felling axe.
A supplied retreat and clean camp. The fallback site needs its own earned minimal cover, tinder and provisions before it offers much security. Keep processing waste and attractants away from sleep and reserve food. Escape and observation are feasible goals; a few brush obstacles cannot defend him against several determined people.

Not currently glaring omissions: metallurgy, agriculture, domestication, a bow, a large kiln or a loom. Each demands inputs and maintenance he lacks. A grinding/pounding setup, food carriers and cord production are worth improving when they relieve a measured bottleneck. Measurement is already a skill; his personal comparison staff can improve repeatability without pretending he has calibrated units.
Recommended adjustment to the remaining month
Read this alongside Month Two Outline. Preserve independent acquisition, cautious contact and the eventual narrowing atlatl gap, but make cold-season preparation the main work allocation.

Days 41–42: maintain food supply; appraise the existing shelter and possible construction site; check material availability and plan a staged build. Care for the pelt and inspect retting. Short projectile practice proceeds only within the actual budget.
Days 43–49: devote multiple recorded work sessions to framing, weather cover, bedding and clothing, then repairs under ordinary weather. Hunting attempts can be brief or aborted; they must not crowd out the build. Defer firing if it consumes the ordinary fuel reserve or dry-work space.
Days 50–56: improve observed failures, protected stores, spare fire/water provisions and the refuge. Let steadier casts attract interest during short practice. No deer kill or guaranteed food surplus is required.

The Day 44 reflection should assess shelter work, diminishing food access and labour choices against the actual completed ledger. By Day 56 the intended outcome is a materially better, inspected cold-weather camp, not a declared winter solution. If food, materials or weather prevent that result, the next strategic choice must explicitly include further relocation research rather than relying on narrative optimism.
Longer horizon
Remaining alone is a valid month-two constraint. Eventually, rebuilding civilisation needs distributed labour, shared standards, seasonal support and knowledge reproduced by other people. The bottleneck will move from remembering designs to supporting workshops and recovering from failure. Archaeological societies were not solitary inventors equipped with one specimen of each named object. Track the ability to maintain a working system alongside the growing topic index.

09_reference/flora-and-fauna---northern-.title: Flora and Fauna — Northern Iberia around 40,000 BP
09_reference/flora-and-fauna---northern-.content:
Flora and Fauna — Northern Iberia around 40,000 BP
Scope: a regional guide for a fictional valley
This reference guides future scenes in the low-elevation northern Iberian valley fixed by Setting Specification and World. Around 40,000 calibrated years BP lies within Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3), an interval with substantial climatic variation. A find somewhere in Iberia, a later glacial animal list or a modern distribution map does not establish an animal at this particular camp.
Use four distinctions: regional evidence, broader or later analogy, existing fictional local choice, and unresolved candidate. New regional possibilities enter the story only through an actual sighting, sign or discovery. They do not become food or material stock merely by appearing here.
The approximately 41,000-cal-BP Cova Eirós study is a particularly useful nearby-in-time comparison: it reconstructs a wooded landscape with open areas, rather than one uniform biome (R53). The eastern Cantabrian isotope study adds red deer and horse evidence across the transition (R55). These are different sites, not coordinates assigned to our fictional valley. Cova Eirós research; Cantabrian isotope study.
Landscape and vegetation
Retain sheltered woodland patches, river margins, rocky slopes and open grazing ground. Vary tree density with terrain. Do not paint modern continuous lush deciduous woodland everywhere, or replace every existing tree with treeless mammoth steppe. Cave pollen can be sparse or poorly preserved; pollen, charcoal and food remains answer different questions (R57–R58).


















































Plant or groupEvidence and use in this projectDecember consequencePine, PinusRegionally supported woody resource; avoid assigning a modern planted species (R58).Wood and fuel remain useful; pine presence is not proof of edible pine-nut supply.Birch, BetulaSupported in regional woodland mosaics (R57–R58).Wood and appropriate bark can remain resources, with local suitability checked.Oak, QuercusRegional evidence varies with site and phase; the known productive patch is a fictional local commitment (R57–R58).Existing stored acorns matter. Do not repeatedly refill the store with fresh winter harvests.Hazel, CorylusReported in the regional pollen record; abundance and earlier yields at our patch remain authored (R57).Wood can still be selected. The nut crop is seasonal, not a year-round ration.Willow and alderWillow is an existing river-margin choice; alder is a researched regional candidate, not a new observed patch (R57).Useful woody material may remain, but dormant growth is not a fresh leafy food source.NettleExisting fictional fibre patch, not newly demonstrated here by a dated local plant assemblage.Retained retted fibre and suitable old stems are plausible work inputs; no assumed crop of summer-quality shoots.Grasses and sedgesComponents of open and wet ground, with exact species left open (R57–R58).Selected dry material can serve bedding and lining. Damp vegetation does not provide the same insulation.Other fruits, nuts and edible underground partsEach needs identification, local discovery and an appropriate season.No convenient winter berries, chestnut grove, generic edible roots or cultivated cereals are added to balance a food shortage.
Modern British phenology places hazel ripening principally in late summer/autumn (R60). It is an analogy, not a reconstructed Iberian harvest date. For this December outline, the editorial rule is simple: nut storage and processing, rather than continuing productive nut collection. Sound overlooked fallen acorns may occur, but cannot support a recurring harvest plot. Phenology reference.
Ordinary animals and food candidates


















































Animal/groupEvidence levelNarrative use and limitsRed deer, Cervus elaphusStrong regional support, including near the target period (R53, R55); already observed.Best-established large-prey thread. A solo result needs approach, recovery and processing; a spear or dart does not guarantee one.Wild horse and large bovinesRegionally documented in the transition record (R55).Make open country feel inhabited; these are demanding animals, not easy individual winter provisioning.Roe deer and wild boarReported at Labeko Koba in smaller representation (R54).Possible woodland candidates; establish local presence before use. Neither is automatically the camp’s abundant prey.Ibex and chamoisRegional rocky-country candidates (R55).Use suitable terrain. Do not put convenient herds beside the bed or require hazardous cliff pursuits to solve clothing.Rabbit and hareSmall-game evidence exists, but northern patterns differ from Mediterranean Iberia (R56).Preserve the rabbits already caught as local fiction. Do not infer dense warrens, daily catches or plentiful hares as a replacement assumption.Fox, wolf and small woodland animalsExisting sightings/catches stand as authored local choices.Fox material is possible after an actual catch; predators are not a dependable fur shop. Small rodents and squirrel-sized catches provide limited food and skin area.Freshwater salmonidsNorthern Upper Palaeolithic fish evidence is mostly a broader/later comparison (R59).Trout-like fish are a plausible candidate, not a retrospectively identified catch. River access, clarity, flow and observed fish control each opportunity.BirdsLabeko Koba has a small published assemblage (R62).Birds can enrich the setting; identify a suitable local species before making it a major trapped food. Winter is not a standing egg harvest.
The rabbit correction concerns archaeological representation, not a proof that every northern habitat lacked rabbits. Leave earlier events intact while reducing future dependence on exceptional returns. Primary Coímbre study and author-deposited text.
For fish, modern trout biology allows late-autumn/winter spawning in some populations (R61). This can motivate observation of a shallow tributary, but is not evidence for a scheduled abundant run here. Brown water, floods or cold exposure can make fishing a poor choice. Do not introduce rainbow trout or presume a modern hatchery-like population. Modern trout ecology.
Extinct and unfamiliar animals
Labeko Koba records woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius), woolly rhinoceros (Coelodonta antiquitatis), giant deer (Megaloceros giganteus), aurochs (Bos primigenius), steppe bison (Bison priscus), cave bear (Ursus spelaeus) and cave hyena. Reindeer also occur, but are not extinct. The deposit combines different levels and accumulation agents; its animal list is not one simultaneous valley census (R54). Primary mammal report.
For the story, choose one occasional encounter that changes a decision: a distant mammoth on open ground, a rhinoceros occupying a route, or evidence of a large carnivore near a carcass. An individual, its sign and a possible interpretation are different levels of observation. A strange print alone should not become a confident species identification.
A cave lion or leopard is a broader regional Upper Pleistocene candidate, requiring a closer site/date check before an actual scene (R63). Avoid Smilodon, dinosaurs or importing an indiscriminate Ice Age menagerie. Megafauna should contribute scale and unfamiliarity; no December hunt for a mammoth, rhinoceros, bison or cave bear is planned. A predator’s leftovers are not an automatic safe cache of meat, fat and intact hide.
Consequences for the first winter
December combines remaining autumn stores with self-procured animal food, opportunistic fishing and a realistically earned larger hide. Lean small game alone is a poor foundation for sustained cold-weather work. Use fat or marrow only where the actual animal supplies it, and distinguish fresh eating from any researched preservation trial (R07, R45).
Trap design must follow observed quarry, material strength and habitat. A different knot cannot create missing animals. Small-pelt clothing requires sewing and real surface area; one deer hide is not implicitly a coat, trousers, boots, mittens and blanket. These constraints guide Moon Four Outline without restoring daily numerical resource ledgers.
Research trail
Research Register entries R53–R63 record publication identities, access level and limits. R53–R55 anchor regional fauna and environment; R56 checks small-game assumptions; R57–R58 cover vegetation; R59–R61 separate fish/seasonal analogies from direct evidence; R62–R63 bound optional birds and felids. The catch rates, local patch productivity, chosen weather and eventual encounters remain authored decisions.
A bounded winter bait observation — Day 101
A few earthworms are actually found in sheltered unfrozen leaf mould during a mild damp interval. They are bait, not an added human food supply. R71 describes year-round potential activity and cold-weather dormancy in modern settings; it neither identifies a prehistoric local species nor guarantees readily available bait in freezing ground. No productive winter nut harvest or new fish run accompanies this observation.

09_reference/illustration-continuity.title: Illustration Continuity
09_reference/illustration-continuity.content:
Illustration Continuity
Approved character and style
The user selected the watercolour-and-ink Day 1 image on 1 October 2026 and approved the protagonist’s appearance. Use _Artwork/survival/day-01.png as the primary visual reference in every later Survival scene. Do not redesign him from a text description alone.

Preserve his recognisable facial profile, nose and brow, dark wavy ear-length hair, short dark beard/stubble, skin tone and lean sinewy build. His apparent age in this reference is about thirty; the ageless premise does not mean an artificial young face. Retain ordinary human proportions. Use smooth transparent watercolour for skin and selective fine ink around contours; avoid dense hatching, repeated dots or etched grooves that can read as scars or patterned skin.
The approved style combines fine brown ink with luminous watercolour, warm paper texture, restrained earth colours and softly dissolved margins. Keep a wide approximately 16:9 composition and a readable action. Facial views, light and viewpoint can vary; identity remains stable. Avoid switching to photography, oil painting, engraving or fantasy effects.
Dated clothing reference — Day 52 onward
Use Character Sheet - Moon 2 Day 23 and _Artwork/character-sheets/moon-2-day-23/character-sheet.png as the additional clothing reference for scenes from the end of Day 52 onward. It fixes the complete dry-use outfit: plain shallow rabbit-fur crown pad, narrow anatomical-left fox strip, separate front and back hanging grass panels, bark waist coverage with small pelvic pad, and a pair of low bast soles. Keep the original Day 1 image as the primary identity/style reference. Supply both references with their roles stated; neither a recent daily rendering nor this sheet alone replaces the approved identity image. Do not apply later clothing to earlier dates.
Begin a scene brief with the complete dated outfit, then state any necessary removals, the reason and where each removed piece is kept. Dry craft does not automatically require a bare torso or bare feet. For wet, fire or projectile work, follow the narrative’s actual clearance and footwear limits. Depict protected removed pieces nearby when they fit the camera view; otherwise record their out-of-frame location. Until independently improved and tested, the soles remain experimental level dry-camp footwear.
The crown pad must read as shaped fur material, never an animal head or mask. Reject animal eyes, muzzle, whiskers, upright ears or tail. Review front, back and side coverage, both feet, and anatomical-left placement before selecting an image. A later wardrobe change needs a new dated sheet based on the narrative; it does not overwrite this historical cutoff.
Match a specific moment in the day
Read the entire day’s narrative and its frontmatter, then check the preceding day’s completed state. Survival Ledger holds historical calculations and later qualitative changes; use the appropriate period rather than treating old totals as current stock. Select one actual action. Do not illustrate every outcome as a montage or equip the morning traveller with objects he only makes that afternoon.
Define the moment, allowed objects, forbidden future objects, clothing, unfinished processes and weather before generation. A construction can be shown in progress without claiming a functioning capability. Scenes should distinguish a failed test from a successful one.
Use the original approved Day 1 image for character and style in new scenes, plus the applicable dated character sheet for clothing from Day 52 onward. A separate established equipment plate may additionally supply object geometry only when needed; record that limited role and do not import its layout, lettering or cutaway into the narrative. Describe the current camp and objects in the day-specific brief, using the ledger and narrative to establish their state. Do not pass the preceding day’s illustration forward as a reference. Keep object descriptions concrete about material, scale, unfinished work and permitted use.
