Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1 appraises the completed Day 59 cutoff. It adds no events. Both ignition kits and both bark vessels remain at main camp; the retreat, food buffer, second suitable shaft and voluntary independent learning remain projects. Future passages can follow these projects rather than extending supply-round narration by habit.

09_reference/moon-four-outline.title: Moon Four Outline
09_reference/moon-four-outline.content:
Moon Four Outline
Approved direction: the solitary first winter
The user approved the broad December direction and corrected the narrative arc on 23 October 2026: obtain food and clothing material independently; keep this first winter lonely; develop cooperation in spring. Earlier encounters, the worn wrap and the bounded Day 78 hunting/processing share remain written history. They do not become a continuing supply arrangement. The traveller chooses to establish a viable winter life of his own; the neighbours need not become hostile or disappear from the valley.
This revised sequence is a proposal for future pages. It replaces the 22 October shared-work/teaching plan. Flora and Fauna supplies the research frame. Continue natural connected prose, brief qualitative continuity and one principal technical question per foreground scene.
Calendar and starting position
December is the seasonal analogy: short days, cold rain, wind, frost and useful dry intervals, without imposing a precise modern weather record. Moon 4 has 29 days, continuous Days 89–117. Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain and Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1 are already written. Full-moon review: Moon 4 Day 15 / Day 103. Closing review: after the Moon 5 Day 1 / Day 118 boundary entry.
The Western Overhang remains home. Rock is its roof, the ordinary hearth stays outside, and the small daub bay’s edge repair is still drying at the opening. There is one useful pot. The existing tan sleeveless body wrap, full extended fur cap and two thin low rabbit-skin foot covers remain the starting clothes; both arms and lower legs need better coverage. All existing skin is allocated, including the entire deer margin already used as Stone-Edge Guard.
One green half-stave, three green arrow blanks and a short nettle trial line exist. The ordinary wooden spear, stone-pointed hand spear, modified dart A with its wooden point/two vanes, and four-pronged fishing spear remain distinct. Bowed dart B is unfinished. No new skin, fat, successful hunt or dependable winter ration is granted by the outline.
Clothing: make a real material result the early turning point
Independent acquisition is plausible, but rabbits alone should not promise a complete winter outfit. Combine improved small-game trapping with an early serious solo ungulate-hunting opportunity. Red deer is the best-established local candidate; a smaller individual is more manageable than a large stag, while still demanding skill. A roe deer is an alternative only if an actual local discovery establishes it. No newly discovered dense rabbit colony or convenient predator kill substitutes for the work.
Plan towards an earned solo larger-animal result in the opening third, preceded by equipment checks, field observation and an approach that fits the ground. Use an existing working system, with the spear or atlatl chosen for the actual opportunity. Do not postpone warmth until an unmade bow succeeds. The result supplies one identifiable hide plus a bounded food-processing task; recovery and carrying matter as much as the cast. This is the intended story event, not a promise that real solo hunting is dependable. If the scene cannot credibly deliver it, adjust the quarry, preparation and pacing rather than inventing a free hide.
Begin skin preparation promptly and continue it alongside other work. Uploaded knowledge offers possible routes, but the actual hair-retaining dressing/softening method needs research for the available materials and wet winter conditions. Drying alone is not tanning. Do not assume salt, alum, an unallocated dressing-fat supply or new lessons from a neighbour. Keep the existing wrap in service while new material is worked.
Prioritise arms as well as legs: a simple removable shoulder-and-arm layer or fitted sleeves that close exposed upper-body gaps, plus overlapping leg coverings with secure ties. Improve the feet where sound, tougher material is available. Lay out the actual hide before cutting and decide these allocations together. If it cannot supply all three jobs, use explicitly earned additional small pelts for patches/linings or obtain further material. Mittens and a sleeping cover remain later uses only if their material exists. Do not promise a full hooded coat, trousers, boots and blanket from one skin. Update the dated character sheet as soon as the new outfit is actually completed.
Food in December
Stop routine nut gathering. The hazel crop is over in this seasonal model. Continue to inspect, protect and process the remaining autumn stores; a sound overlooked acorn is incidental, not another productive harvest. No generic roots, winter fruit, eggs or unidentified fungi arrive to fill a hidden deficit.
Use several independent food routes: a maintained small-game trap circuit selected by observed signs; the early ungulate result and later opportunities; and fishing when water conditions offer safe, clear access. Existing rabbit catches remain true, but northern archaeological scarcity argues against making rabbits the whole system (R56). Hares, birds or other small mammals require actual local observation rather than an assumed replacement abundance.
An ungulate result gives the pot a new task beyond acorn meals: fresh wet cooking, marrow recovery and, if the animal supplies suitable fatty tissue, a small fat-processing trial. Fat is not inferred from carcass size. Account for the hide and food as separate materials without returning to daily stock tables.
The larger food result also creates a genuine preservation and storage problem. Investigate a small cooked/dried trial with a suitably controlled process and a protected, ventilated storage arrangement away from dirty skin work and the bed. R07 remains a material constraint: smoke, frost or a dry surface does not establish safe long-term keeping. Select the actual method and explain its limits before counting retained food. Do not have one person eat an entire deer fresh on the day, or declare that one kill guarantees food through winter.
Traps deserve a real technical development
Treat trapping as a system linking animal behaviour, placement, trigger, line/anchor or closure, weather protection and inspection effort. Select a modest circuit near useful routes. A larger number of poorly placed devices is not automatically progress.
First inspect and improve the existing Figure-4 Deadfall Trap route: stable support, consistent release and protection from interference. Revisit the failed Snare Trap through actual fibre condition, chafing, attachment and trigger behaviour, with non-animal loading trials before a new field set. The broken Day 23 snare is not still operating.
Then choose one distinct small live-capture cage/covered drop-door design if observed quarry and weaving stock make it worthwhile. This adds a retaining closure and can preserve useful skin area, but trapping, retention and humane dispatch still need a sourced method and actual trial. It is a proposed design family, not a claim of an attested 40,000-BP local trap. A small netting trial can instead serve the same winter cordage/weaving theme if a cage has no worthwhile application; neither is a compulsory extra device.
The Woven Fishing Trap remains an existing apparatus whose placement, funnel, closure and retrieval can be reassessed. Avoid converting it into a river-spanning weir or assuming floodwater increases catches. One observed near-bank fish opportunity can use the dedicated spear as a variation. Modern winter salmonid behaviour is an analogy, not a scheduled salmon bonanza (R59, R61).
How the weapons fit together






























SystemDecember jobWhat still needs to be learnedStone-pointed hand spearA close, carefully chosen opportunity in restricted ground; retain a useful handheld weapon.Actual approach, control, point/joint survival and recovery. Target trials are not a hunting record.Atlatl and dart AA deliberate field opportunity where casting room and a clear line exist.Repeatability, release in hunting conditions and the ability to recover the animal/projectile. Day 78 supplied no dart shot or personal kill.Dedicated fishing spearOccasional clear shallow-margin fishing.Reading fish position, refraction and feasible access in current conditions. It is not the hand spear or dart.Self bowParallel material work towards a practice specimen later in the month.Stave condition, compatible string, controlled limb behaviour and actual arrow preparation. It is not instantly a superior replacement for everything above.
Keep practice short and diagnostic, then let a real field choice give it meaning. Do not repeat whole spear-versus-atlatl comparisons. The bow offers a different possible handling/aiming arrangement, but its advantages must emerge through this person’s actual use. Wood condition can carry completion into the next moon; a calendar deadline is not a seasoning test (R50–R51). Never press bowed dart B into service merely to supply a spare.
A clear-eyed technology review


















































PriorityCandidateWhy it earns December workImmediateHair-retaining skin work, cutting layout, stronger seams and ties; suitable scraper/needle maintenanceConverts actual material into arm/leg warmth and more serviceable footwear. The processing support can improve control without becoming a new workshop building.ImmediateTrap placement, reliable triggers and better cordage/closuresExtends procurement beyond hours spent stalking, with real setting, checking and repair costs.Immediate after a catchCarcass recovery, limited carrying/dragging aid, clean separation of skin and foodA solo hunter cannot assume a whole carcass teleports home. Reuse existing carriers where suitable; a larger frame or drag mat needs its own real job.HighWet cooking, marrow/fat use and one researched preservation/storage routeMakes the actual food result useful for more than one meal and exposes the next production dependency.SecondarySmall net/mesh work or a modest cage trapChoose by a real local opportunity; tests fibre preparation, regular mesh or retaining doors without claiming passive abundance.SecondarySecond modest cooking vesselWorth making if concurrent processing, fat separation or a real capacity/breakage problem justifies it. No compulsory pottery duplicate or teaching subplot.ContinuingBowstring, arrow stock and condition-dependent bow workTimed work that can coexist with the urgent clothing/food projects.DeferLarge deer pits, a trapping fence, giant hunting nets, kiln, metallurgy, agriculture, oil lamp, formal teachingPoor immediate return or missing materials/labour. In particular, do not burn scarce edible fat merely to add an indoor-light invention.
These are connected choices, not a checklist requiring eight new inventions. Stronger cordage supports traps and later bow work; hide preparation creates warmth; food recovery and storage make longer craft projects possible. Keep shelter upkeep brief unless a real fault changes one of these decisions.
Proposed December sequence













































Moon daysForegroundIntended development1 / continuous 89 — writtenMeal after rain and the existing opening reviewRetain the completed state. His earlier intention to revisit the group can change without a retroactive rewrite.2–6 / 90–94Read winter animal signs, improve the trap circuit and choose an existing hunting system for a real solo opportunityAn early earned larger food/skin result if the approach supports it; immediate recovery and skin preparation.7–12 / 95–100Work the skin, make arm/leg coverage, strengthen critical seams; handle the food result and begin one distinct trap/closure improvementA convincing warmer outfit and a purposeful food-processing/preservation project.13–15 / 101–103Use the new clothes and procurement system through colder weather; full-moon reflectionJudge what actually supports a solitary winter, with the loneliness present in the experience.16–22 / 104–110Continue a promising trap/mesh route, exploit a suitable fishing or hunting opportunity, work on line/arrow stock and bow if readyBetter connected equipment, tested field roles and fewer fragile dependencies. A justified second pot can dry in parallel.23–29 / 111–117Apply the useful results; finish/test the second pot or practice bow only where ready; one restrained encounter with unfamiliar fauna can affect a choiceConsolidate a viable solitary base and choose the next technical bottleneck.Next moon day 1 / 118Boundary entry and new-moon reflectionClose on completed results; cooperation remains a prospective spring direction.
The timing can flex for material condition. Do not stretch every check, meal or unsuccessful set into a separate page, or impose a failure before each useful advance. Show warmth early enough to matter. The winter should feel lonely through work, silence and the absence of shared labour, rather than repeated speeches about isolation.
Fauna, future pages and the mission
Use Flora and Fauna for actual candidate choices. One distant megafaunal animal or credible sign can make this world feel unlike the modern countryside. Do not make exotic-animal kills the clothing plan, or march every researched species past camp. Keep the established valley map and terrain relationships.
Expand existing trap, clothing, hunting, cordage and food-processing pages as the new narrative demonstrates their limits and improvements. Add a separate skin-dressing route, garment variant, retention-trap design or preservation process only when each has distinct useful content. Keep future processes labelled as planned until actually performed. New substantive capability pages and the changed wardrobe need appropriate illustrations when the daily batches are commissioned; this planning revision creates no new equipment or artwork.
The mission is still present: a person must become warm, fed and able to reproduce useful processes before sustaining wider production. This winter can demonstrate independent competence and expose the costs of doing everything alone. Spring cooperation then becomes a consequential next stage. No new shared hunt, hide allocation, willing learner or group adoption is planned for December.
Written through Moon 4 Day 6 / continuous Day 94
Day 1 was already written; this first new five-day batch covers Days 2–6. Days 90–91 improve a real deadfall site and compare a new trap-line candidate without inventing catches. Day 92 adds one tested pack frame and further deer observation. Day 93 uses existing dart A for a first personal larger-animal result, then selects manageable food/skin recovery. Day 94 applies beam fleshing to the same whole skin and uses the remaining short-held food. The full skin is unfinished; arms/legs still need the next batch’s garment work. All group contact, new teaching and new wardrobe changes remain absent. Next reflection is Day 103.
Written through Moon 4 Day 11 / continuous Day 99
Days 95–97 turn the sole personally acquired deer skin into two removable sleeves and two overlapping leg panels, using a researched mechanical working route and actual body-based layout. No additional dressing fat or sinew is supplied. The new dated character sheet applies from the completed Day 97 fit. Existing low foot covers still need a stronger later solution. Days 98–99 choose the outline’s small-mesh alternative to a new cage: one knotted bag and a hand net assisting the existing woven trap’s retrieval cap. One small fish is cooked and used on Day 99. The earlier deer food was already used by Day 94, so no preservation trial is invented from leftover meat; a later real surplus must supply that project’s input. Dart A’s post-tip-reshaping trial, snare field acceptance, bow conditioning and a longer food-keeping method remain open. No extra garment share, teaching or group work appears. Next page is Day 100 / Moon 4 Day 12; full-moon reflection remains Day 103.
Written through Moon 4 Day 16 / continuous Day 104
Days 100–101 add one wooden fishing gorge and an attended hand-line route, with one actual small fish and fresh meal. Dart A has its short post-repair target check on Day 100. Days 102–103 reuse the existing spindle for deliberate plying and make a small notched shuttle/repair-sized mesh. Reflection 08 closes Day 103 before the next day’s work. Day 104 manufactures one full-length bowstring candidate with a worked-back eye and free adjustment end; the rough hazel body stays unstrung and no loaded tillering or shooting occurs. The original sample and snare candidate remain separate. Clothing, one pot and the solitary winter remain; no fresh surplus exists to justify pretending a preservation trial has occurred. Next page is Day 105 / Moon 4 Day 17; next reflection is Day 118.
Written through Moon 4 Day 21 / continuous Day 109
One occasional existing-deadfall rabbit on Day 105 supplies fresh food and a new skin. Staged preparation turns that sole pelt into two simple thumb-less warming pockets on Day 108; all older clothing persists. The bow’s single body starts low-deflection tillering on Day 106, receives its existing string and first plain arrow on Day 107, and makes a few short controlled releases on Day 109. It remains a provisional recently cut hazel practice system, stored unstrung, with no hunting claim. The new dated character sheet records hand covers and deliberate removal for work. Two original shaft blanks remain unfinished. No new group provision, preserved surplus or automatic second pot appears. Next page is Day 110 / Moon 4 Day 22. Next reflection remains Day 118 / Moon 5 Day 1.
Written through Moon 4 Day 26 / continuous Day 114
Day 110 fits two modest vanes to the existing arrow from a newly found feather lot, without altering dart A. Day 111 reuses the dedicated fishing fork for one fresh meal and exposes a real food/water scheduling bottleneck. Day 112 forms one second cooking bowl and a same-body witness; both remain unfired through Day 114. Day 113 carves a shallow wooden spoon that helps the old pot immediately. Day 114 gives the altered arrow limited short trials and keeps the bow unstrung in storage afterwards. Two old shaft blanks remain unfinished. The next three Moon 4 days can consolidate actual results and judge drying condition without forcing a firing deadline; the new-moon boundary/reflection remains Day 118. The solitary winter, qualitative continuity and full current wardrobe continue.

09_reference/moon-three-outline.title: Moon Three Outline
09_reference/moon-three-outline.content:
Moon Three Outline
Approved direction: establish a winter home
The user approved this course correction on 14 October 2026. Move from the old lean-to camp to a rocky overhang; make substantial warm clothing; secure seasonal food; develop useful cooking and hunting equipment. These foundations now lead the moon. Resource accounting becomes brief qualitative continuity, and the earlier retreat/cache programme is dropped.
Moon 1 and Moon 2 remain as written. Moon 3 Day 1, Moon 3 Day 1 - A Material Before a Vessel, remains intact. Its completed-day Reflection 05 - New Moon - Moon 3 Day 1 is revised at the user’s request to anticipate the winter priorities while retaining the Day 59 cutoff and historical snapshot. The correction begins with Moon 3 Day 2, continuous Day 60. The outline authorises the direction and intended progress; future pages still establish how discoveries, construction and exchanges occur.
The protagonist’s purpose remains technological. A dry sleeping chamber, a worked hide garment, seasonal storage, a sound spear joint and a cooking vessel are useful handbook subjects. Explain mechanisms and show consequential results. Ordinary gathering, fire care and water treatment can be glossed over when they do not change the project.
Calendar and seasonal pressure
Moon 3 is late autumn, roughly November in our planning analogy, about two months after the early-autumn arrival. No exact Gregorian arrival date or reconstructed local weather series is imposed. Shorter useful daylight, colder mornings, wet windy intervals and occasional frost make winter preparations urgent. Include dry intervals for building, skin work and firing rather than an uninterrupted succession of storms.
The Lunar Calendar model gives Moon 3 thirty days, continuous Days 59–88. The full-moon reflection is Moon 3 Day 16 / continuous Day 74. The next new-moon review is Moon 4 Day 1 / continuous Day 89, after that boundary day’s entry. Future reflections describe the completed state in prose, without daily resource-balance tables.
Starting point, without an inventory recital
He has working stone edges, simple woodworking tools, a wooden spear used previously for fishing, an experimental atlatl and dart, a fish trap, two ignition sets and two bark vessels. His shelter has improved but remains a poor winter commitment. The grass-panel outfit and little pelts provide limited coverage. He has two fired clay comparison pieces, but no accepted ceramic vessel.
Food access and material availability still constrain work. Explain a significant shortage, needed hide, new shaft or long drying process where it changes a decision. Do not record routine meals, fuel bundles, cord metres, water volumes and hourly balances every day. Preserve obvious continuity: an exchanged hide has a source, a consumed catch does not return, and a single skin cannot furnish an entire wardrobe without regard to its area.
Four project phases






























Moon daysMain developmentIntended progress1–8 / continuous 59–66Commit to the overhang, move essentials, establish dry sleep and a weather screen; obtain larger skin material and organise the autumn harvestA recognisable new winter home and the first substantial warm garment9–16 / 67–74Improve foot/head/limb coverage, food processing and storage; revisit spear fishing and work on a useful spear upgradeA coherent working outfit, more purposeful food provision and a practical weapon; full-moon appraisal17–23 / 75–81Improve the atlatl as a hunting system, develop opportunities with local people, continue clothing work and prepare the vessel for firingBetter access to animal foods and skins, useful field comparisons and a vessel ready for its actual role24–30 / 82–88Fire, cool and use the pot; consolidate the winter home and supplies; begin bow-and-arrow developmentA functioning winter arrangement with a useful cooking/container route and a credible next weapon project
Projects overlap naturally: the vessel dries while other work proceeds, and collecting useful food continues during the build. Each page has one main technical subject rather than several simultaneous workshops. Adjust the exact timing for weather and material condition without making failure compulsory before every success.
The rocky-overhang home
The move is a settled narrative direction, not another debate about remaining at the lean-to. Introduce a reachable overhang on the same side of the main river as the established routes, with usable water access and room for ordinary food/fuel work. Inspect rock stability, drips, runoff, wind, animal signs and evidence of other occupants. Its exact position is established in the discovery entry and then added to Valley Map and a new place note. The existing map does not already contain this site.
Choose a dry, useful overhang rather than a deep cave. Rock supplies much of the roof and rear protection. Build the missing weather-facing enclosure: a sound low frame and woven/brush screen, overlapping weather cover, a manageable entrance and thick clean dry bedding on an appropriately separated resting surface. Keep natural drainage outside the occupied space and allow moisture to escape.
Use clay-rich earth mixed with plant fibre selectively on supported front or lower wall panels to reduce draughts. First inspect a small panel as it dries. The earth is not a blanket coating on the old roof or a substitute for bedding. Wet earth adds loading and moisture; sheltering the panel from direct rain matters. R40 informs the moisture assessment, not a prehistoric construction specification.
Move usable tools, bedding and protected supplies to the new home once basic occupation is possible. Abandon the lean-to as the principal camp; record the move once. The old site can remain an abandoned location in the atlas, without being maintained as a second dwelling or defensive retreat. Do not turn the old fallback bench into this overhang or quietly build a cache there.
Re-establish clean craft, food, water, animal-processing, waste and firing relationships at the new site. Keep the ordinary hearth in the open outside the enclosed sleeping area. An overhang alone does not prove adequate exhaust; an indoor fire would require a separate design decision. The new sleeping screen, bedding and garments remain combustible.
A coherent winter outfit
Make larger animal-skin coverage an early practical objective. The first substantial garment should be an overlapping shoulder/body wrap, then a roughly fitted belted garment if the skin area and flexibility permit. Follow with head/neck coverage, leg wraps and enclosed foot coverings with renewable dry plant lining. Hand protection can follow from available pieces. A warm sleeping covering and the bed work together.
The earliest useful wrap should appear in the first phase rather than waiting until the latter half of the moon. Obtain one or more larger usable skins through accepted work/exchange or a realistically earned share of animal processing. Show who supplies the skin, its existing condition and what work or object is accepted in return. An already worked worn skin can give immediate coverage while fresh material is being prepared. Small catches alone do not instantly yield a large coat.
Local hide-working knowledge is a practical resource. The traveller contributes ordinary useful work and learns material judgements from competent people. Work new skins over several sessions; drying alone is not durable tanning. Research the chosen preservation/conditioning route when drafting that process. R28, R30 and R39 provide context, not a reconstructed local garment pattern.
The old grass panels and bark layers become temporary underlayers, spare material or items set aside as warmer coverage takes over. Describe that transition once. Clothing should look like functional coverage rather than an accumulation of ornaments. Allocate actual skin area between the main garment, hood/cap, foot pieces and other coverings. Update the character sheet after the new daily pages establish the wardrobe, so later images retain it.
Food for this month and the colder season
Use a combination of seasonal gathered food, ongoing animal food and protected stores, supported by local knowledge and accepted cooperation. The goal is credible access and useful preparation, not a guaranteed stock of a specified weight.

While sound nuts remain accessible, gather hazelnuts and acorns in worthwhile batches and create protected, ventilated storage off damp ground. Establish which patches he can use, declining returns and any useful local guidance.
Store suitable untreated acorns as processing stock and prepare meals as needed through the already established crushing/leaching/cooking route. Wet meal remains perishable. A sound basket, pounding surface, water access and workable batch size are important technologies.
Keep productive small-game traps in ordinary use, compressing uneventful checks. A catch becomes foreground when it changes food access, hide work or the next technical choice.
Alternate the fish trap with renewed spear fishing at appropriate clear, shallow accessible margins. His earlier spear-fishing trials used the ordinary wooden spear. The multi-pronged design has not yet been built; introduce it as a possible new fishing tool if the ordinary spear exposes a useful improvement.
Work towards an accepted role in local gathering, processing or hunting. Shared work can produce an explicitly observed share of food or skin without making the group responsible for feeding him. R41 supports the regional relevance of larger animal prey; it does not promise a catch or dictate this group’s arrangements.
Where surplus genuinely exists, make drying/preservation a deliberate food-technology project, researched for the method and conditions. Smoke, cold weather or a dry-looking surface does not alone establish durable meat stores (R07).

Animal food includes usable fat and marrow where actually available; greens, occasional fish and a few rabbits do not automatically fund months of cold-weather work. Known hazel and oak patches remain fictional local resource assumptions, not an inexhaustible winter harvest. If a source is poor, change the effort or cooperation rather than supplying an identical daily return.
Keep food away from dirty skin work, waste and damp. Inspect stores and acknowledge a consequential loss if it occurs, without logging every portion. Describe whether the supply is improving, strained or supporting a longer project. Quantities are useful only where they explain capacity, a significant processing batch or a material choice.
Spear, atlatl and the route towards a bow
Carry and maintain a useful spear, develop the atlatl for hunting, and keep relations with the nearby group workable. Defensive awareness belongs in ordinary behaviour. It does not require an escape-route chapter, a supplied fallback shelter or a sequence of warnings.
The existing Fire-Hardened Spear page covers the wooden spear. Shape and maintain a sound point; any fire-treatment comparison should remain a small material question. R05 found trade-offs under its tested treatment, so do not present charring as an automatic strength upgrade. A stone-pointed hafted spear is a useful next project: suitable shaft, shaped point, seating geometry and binding, followed by an appropriate joint/impact trial. Local competence can inform the work, with any borrowed or transferred component described clearly. The ordinary single-point wooden spear, also used for fishing, need not be dismantled to create every new weapon. It is distinct from the still-unmade Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear.
Continue the Atlatl through a suitable dart, retention/release, consistency and a hunting configuration. Improve real limiting parts instead of repeating broad target practice daily. Fletching and a point are useful when the shaft and joints justify them. Hunting adds approach, opportunity, recovery and processing; a good target result is not all of those skills.
Begin thinking and preparing for a bow during the latter part of the moon. Select actually available wood with useful grain and condition, prepare a stave, and explore a low-stretch string and suitable arrow stock. Tillering means controlling where the limbs bend; string fit, arrow straightness and fletching are separate requirements. His bow-drill bow is not an existing hunting bow.
A modest practice prototype is possible if material condition and the rest of the winter work permit. A finished hunting bow is not a required Day 30 outcome. If the stave needs further seasoning, the preparation still gives Moon 4 a clear project. Do not invent ideal yew, a ready bowstring or a finished arrow set to meet a deadline. The traveller’s remembered design is an authored anticipatory experiment, not a claim that the local group lacks bows.
Pottery with a useful winter purpose
Retain the successful comparison pieces as background information and shape one modest vessel with an approximately even section. Give it protected drying room at the new home while food, clothing and weapons progress. Fire on suitable separate ground when the body and weather allow, cool before handling, then establish water containment and an appropriate heating/cooking role.
The point is a container that makes meals or water treatment more manageable. Make the preparation, firing and first use clear without turning each minor inspection into a separate dramatic hurdle. Preserve the bark route while the ceramic route proves useful. Direct-fire cooking, food-contact suitability and repeated heating need attention appropriate to the chosen body and role; no universal safe firing recipe is implied.
A second matched vessel is worthwhile once the first route is useful. A large kiln, metallurgy programme or procession of ceremonial prototypes would distract from the month’s purpose.
Working daily subjects
These subjects organise the next writing batches. They are not final titles or a requirement that every project finish on its assigned date.

































































































































Moon day / continuous dayForeground subject1 / 59 — writtenCold clay comparison and the opening new-moon reflection2 / 60Find and inspect the overhang; decide to move rather than extend the lean-to3 / 61Establish dry sleep and basic weather protection, then move essentials4 / 62Reconnect with familiar people through useful work; pursue larger skin material5 / 63Fit the first substantial skin wrap, while preparing further clothing material6 / 64Build covered nut storage and organise a worthwhile seasonal gathering session7 / 65Improve the overhang’s front enclosure, entrance and dry bed8 / 66Try a supported earth/plant-fibre wall panel and manage draughts and runoff9 / 67Turn the wrap into better working coverage; improve head/neck protection10 / 68Return to spear fishing as a variation on the trap11 / 69Select a spear shaft and shape or obtain a suitable stone point12 / 70Seat and bind the hafted spear; inspect how the joint carries load13 / 71Improve acorn crushing and meal throughput; gather or process alongside willing locals14 / 72Form the small vessel and put it into protected drying15 / 73Improve foot/leg coverage and learn a useful hide-working method16 / 74Full-moon reflection: new home, warmth, food access, relations and useful tools17 / 75Check the working outfit through ordinary use; finish a consequential fit improvement18 / 76Develop a compatible second dart or improve the sound existing configuration19 / 77Compare controlled spear/atlatl performance and choose the next hunting configuration20 / 78Apply the equipment to an actual hunting opportunity or accepted shared outing21 / 79Return to fishing; build and trial the dedicated Multi-Pronged Fishing Spear if the material and near-margin opportunity still justify it22 / 80Process the actual food/skin result and improve protected storage or drying23 / 81Continue useful local work and inspect the vessel’s readiness for firing24 / 82Fire the vessel on separate outside ground, leaving it to cool25 / 83Inspect the cold vessel and test a limited water charge26 / 84Establish an appropriate heating/meal role and see what the pot makes easier27 / 85Select and begin preparing a bow stave from suitable available wood28 / 86Compare string materials and prepare suitable arrow stock29 / 87Begin controlled shaping/tillering or a modest practice trial if the material is ready30 / 88Consolidate the winter arrangement and select the next useful bow/container/food project
Useful results can occur without a mandatory failed attempt first. Weather and condition can move a firing or weapon trial. Ordinary supplies continue in the background. A large-game kill is possible but is not required to rescue the plot; realistic exchange and shared processing can establish a useful skin or food share.
The Moon 4 Day 1 boundary entry and new-moon reflection at Day 89 follow this moon. They must use their actual completed-day state.
Relations and the wider purpose
Keep on the right side of the group through respectful access, ordinary useful contributions, reciprocal learning and repeated familiar contact. Let relationships develop through the winter work. They need not culminate in a formal apprenticeship, leadership role or compulsory independent-copying test this moon.
Knowledge sharing remains important to Civilisation Roadmap, but warm working people and an adequately provisioned home are the immediate foundation. A willingly shared operation can appear when it is useful rather than becoming another scheduled performance. No exotic invention is an entitlement to skins, food or hospitality.
Lighter continuity from Day 60
Use the compact narrative template in Page Templates. Keep dates, capability links and only consequential changes: the camp move, a larger skin acquired, a new garment or weapon, a significant exchange, a serious shortage or an item actually lost. Routine food, fuel, water and sleep do not need numeric daily entries or inventory balances.
Reflections assess what now works, what still needs work and the next priorities in prose. Exact modelling through Day 59 stays as a historical record; it does not become a current inventory for the new period. Physical plausibility and major object/material continuity remain editorial responsibilities rather than a spreadsheet maintained throughout the story.
Intended end state
Aim for occupation of the rocky-overhang home, substantially warmer practical clothing, seasonal food stores plus ongoing food access, an improved spear and atlatl, renewed spear-fishing use and a ceramic vessel with an earned useful role. Bow-and-arrow preparation supplies the next technical direction.
The old lean-to is abandoned as the home, the fallback/cache programme is discontinued, and regular exact-resource reporting ends. None of these future achievements is entered into the actual daily history until its page is written. This revision creates no new daily prose, pictures, mapped discoveries or website publication.
Drafted opening batch — Moon 3 Days 2–6 / continuous Days 60–64
The move and first winter foundations are now written. Day 60 inspects Western Overhang, and Day 61 begins occupation with a basic rock-shelter screen and dry bed. Movable working equipment transfers once; the old camp is abandoned. Day 62’s accepted wood work earns one used worked skin; Day 63 fits a substantial wrap and sets both grass screens aside. Day 64 installs a food-only rack and begins inspectable seasonal nut storage.
The new place is distinct from the fallback bench. No mud panel, full front closure, new weapon, fishing catch, pot or meat-preservation result has yet occurred. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 5 fixes the dated clothing change. The next page begins from this actual state, with fuller enclosure and selective supported infill still to come.
Drafted second batch — Moon 3 Days 7–11 / continuous Days 65–69
Day 65 improves the entrance, screen and compressed bed; Day 66 begins one supported earth/grass bay, not a complete mud wall. Day 67 refits the wrap and moves the fox panel from its now-covered shoulder position to ear/nape coverage on the existing cap. This is material from the traveller’s own earlier trap catch, with no second exchange or new pelt. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 9 governs the fitted moment onward. Day 68 catches one small fish with the original wooden spear and uses it that day. Day 69 makes Stone Spear Point and selects a separate shaft; no completed composite spear or hunting trial has yet occurred. A firm-centred witness patch and retained small wall bay give a limited drying/attachment result.
Next is the actual supported spear joint and modest load test, then food-processing throughput, forming the vessel and further lower-leg/foot coverage. The full-moon reflection remains due after completed Day 74; this batch contains no lunar milestone. Ordinary supplies remain qualitative, and retreat planning does not return.
Drafted third batch — Moon 3 Days 12–16 / continuous Days 70–74
Day 70 seats/binds Stone-Pointed Spear and begins one self-caught rabbit pelt. Day 71 improves food preparation with Pounding and Grinding Stones and adds a second distinct rabbit pelt from another existing deadfall. Both catches are eaten on their catch days. Day 72 forms a modest open pot from a fresh charge, leaving the two fired remnants intact. Days 70–73 carry skin preparation across other work; Day 73 fits low enclosing pelt covers one per foot with the original bast soles and replaceable grass. Lower legs remain exposed; no durable tanning is claimed.
Day 74 gives the hunting joint a limited plant-target thrust trial and repeats short dry camp use of the footwear. The pot remains greenware with a yielding witness centre. Reflection 06 - Full Moon - Moon 3 Day 16 reviews only that completed state, qualitatively. Character Sheet - Moon 3 Day 15 governs after the fitted Day 73 moment. The next priorities remain durable coverage, better animal-food access and the atlatl’s limiting parts, with the multi-pronged fishing build still reserved for the later return. No second skin trade or retreat project is introduced.
Drafted fourth batch — Moon 3 Days 17–21 / continuous Days 75–79
Day 75 moves heel retention into the existing bast sole rather than thin skin stitch holes. Day 76 improves the existing dart A with two bound vanes and an integral wooden point; no second projectile or stone insert appears. Day 77 makes a limited equipment comparison and establishes immediate accompanying contact.
Day 78 follows a permitted local outing: the traveller makes no obstructed cast, local hunters take a red deer, and accepted holding/carrying work leads to a modest same-day meat/fat share and one narrow fresh hide margin. This is participation and recovery, not the traveller’s atlatl kill, whole hide or standing alliance. The margin is promptly fleshed and continues drying.
Day 79 makes and trials the dedicated four-pronged fishing spear from separate stock, with one small catch consumed that day. The original ordinary spear and composite hand spear remain intact. The greenware pot is still unfired. Next work can allocate/process actual material and consider appropriate preservation only if a genuine surplus exists; firing readiness and atlatl field development retain their separate requirements. No new reflection is due before Day 89.
Written through Moon 3 Day 26 / continuous Day 84
Days 80–81 turn the actual narrow deer margin into one Stone-Edge Guard without expanding the wardrobe. Clay Drying and Inspection supports readiness of the Day 72 pot. Day 82 fires it on the already identified separate patch; Day 83 establishes limited cold containment and the first useful ceramic-vessel result. Day 84 adds an Open Cooking Hearth at the ordinary outdoor hearth and one freshly leached meal via Cooking in an Earthenware Pot. Fired Earthenware distinguishes the changed material from raw clay and greenware. There is still only one new pot and no kiln. Bow-stave selection remains the next planned subject on Day 85; the next reflection remains Day 89.
Moon 3 completed, review at Day 89
Days 85–87 begin one green hazel stave, separate clean supports, three arrow blanks and short cord samples, then coarse shaping. Bow Making has begun; Self Bow, Bowstring and Tillering remain planned and undemonstrated. Day 88 repairs the existing small daub bay and reorders winter priorities. The month closes at continuous Day 88 / Moon 3 Day 30.
The already specified boundary entry, Moon 4 Day 1 - A Warm Meal After the Rain, reaches the new-moon milestone at Day 89 without starting a new major project. Reflection 07 - New Moon - Moon 4 Day 1 closes the Moon 3 appraisal at that completed cutoff. It records a better working home, improved but incomplete clothing, one useful pot, bounded participation in local food work and unfinished bow materials. Better skin material and food access take priority while wood seasons. This outline is now a completed planning record, not a promise that every winter task has finished.

09_reference/research-register.title: Research Register
09_reference/research-register.content:
Research Register
How to use this register
Sources support specific claims, not entire pages. Notes list identifiers in sources and explain their scope in the body. All links below were checked during the October 2026 editorial review. Abstract-level access is identified where full text was unavailable. The author summaries are paraphrases.
Historical evidence elsewhere does not establish presence in the fictional valley. Modern safety guidance identifies constraints; it does not certify an improvised prehistoric process. Uncited manufacturing specifications remain physical-reasoning drafts requiring experimental review.
R01 — Neanderthal cordage
Hardy et al. (2020), Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology and its cognitive and behavioral implications, Scientific Reports. Direct evidence includes a three-ply inner-bark cord fragment from Abri du Maras. This supports fibre-working ability, not a known spindle inventory for every group. Abstract/search access; publication identity also checked through PubMed.
R02 — Regional coexistence
Djakovic, Key and Soressi (2022), Optimal linear estimation models predict 1400–2900 years of overlap between Homo sapiens and Neandertals prior to their disappearance from France and northern Spain. Full article inspected. The overlap is modelled at regional scale; direct local interaction remains unresolved. Do not translate it into a dated occupation of this fictional valley.
R03 — Manufactured adhesives
Identifying Palaeolithic birch tar production techniques: challenges from an experimental biomolecular approach (2023), Scientific Reports. Supports ancient manufactured adhesives and the difficulty of distinguishing production methods. It does not establish the traveller’s pine-resin recipe or its strength.
R04 — Hard-hammer handaxes
Taphonomic and technological analyses of Lower Palaeolithic bone tools from Clacton-on-Sea, UK (2022). Includes discussion of rough handaxes manufactured with hard-hammer removals and later refined work with organic percussors. Supports making antler an improvement or method option, rather than an absolute gate for every biface.
R05 — Fire treatment and wood strength
“Fire hardening” spear wood does slightly harden it, but makes it much weaker and more brittle (2016). Abstract inspected. The experiment found increased hardness alongside reduced strength and fracture performance. Effects depend on treatment and wood; do not represent charring as a universal durability upgrade.
R06 — Drinking water treatment
CDC: About Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping, or Traveling. Full page inspected. Clear water can carry pathogens; observable boiling is a practical endpoint. Boiling does not remove chemical contamination. Temperature-time claims need an actual means of verification.
R07 — Meat drying and pathogen control
USDA FSIS: Jerky and Food Safety. Guidance inspected. Low-temperature drying can leave pathogens alive. Its modern validated procedures use controlled heat and measurements absent from the initial camp. The earlier narrative consumes game on the catch day and does not count unvalidated smoked meat as stored rations. Days 93–94 later introduce one explicitly bounded fresh-meat cooling/holding interval (R64), without certifying storage or preservation.
R08 — Plant identification
BfR: Odour test with pitfalls — what to look out for when collecting wild garlic. Supports the danger of confusing edible plants with poisonous lookalikes. Neither smell alone nor broad rules about colour, leaf count or bitterness are a reliable general identification procedure.
R09 — Giant hogweed
National Park Service: Species Spotlight — Giant Hogweed. Describes sap-associated phytophotodermatitis. This plant is removed from the setting’s friction-fire materials. Other plant candidates still need species-specific review.
R10 — Palaeolithic ceramics
Smithsonian Museum Conservation Institute record: Dolni Vestonice ceramics and Smithsonian Human Origins artifact scan. Supports Upper Palaeolithic ceramic objects at this later site. It does not support the old claim that Neanderthals made ceramic figurines, or demonstrate cooking pottery in Iberia at 40,000 BP.
R11 — Nettle extraction
Bacci et al. (2011), Effect of different extraction methods on fiber quality of nettle, Textile Research Journal. Abstract inspected. Compares several extraction routes. Cultivar, temperature and processing conditions limit transfer to wild prehistoric plants. The narrative’s twelve-day ret is an authored successful batch, not a universal duration.
R12 — Planetary defence
NASA: Planetary Defense — DART. Supports kinetic-impact deflection as one demonstrated modern technique. It does not imply that this fictional massive object can be diverted by a DART-sized mission or that the protagonist can skip space-industry dependencies.
R13 — Food composition reference
UK Government: Composition of foods integrated dataset (CoFID). Dataset landing page inspected; no specific cell was extracted for the first-month ledger. The ledger uses a declared approximate energy model rather than presenting a database-derived value. Wild plants, edible yield and activity requirements need separate research.
R14 — Neanderthal fire-making
